b: Certificates, privileges and limitations, currency, logging, medicals.

items.q: What three documents must you have on your person to act as pilot in command?
items.a: Your pilot certificate, a government-issued photo ID, and your medical certificate (or BasicMed course completion and physician checklist). This is required under 14 CFR 61.3 (Part 61, Subpart A — General; Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations), which says you may not act as PIC unless you carry these and present them on request to the Administrator, an NTSB representative, or any federal, state or local law enforcement officer.

items.q: What counts as acceptable photo identification for 61.3?
items.a: A valid government-issued photo ID: a US driver's license, a US or foreign passport, a military identification card, or an official federal, state or municipal government identification card. A student ID, a club card or a company badge does not satisfy 14 CFR 61.3 (Part 61, Subpart A — Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations).

items.q: What does 61.113 say a private pilot may and may not do?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.113 (Part 61, Subpart E — Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command), a private pilot may not act as PIC of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, and may not act as PIC for compensation or hire at all. You may fly for your own purposes and for pleasure, and you may be reimbursed only within the narrow exceptions the section itself lists.

items.q: What are the main exceptions in 61.113 that let a private pilot accept some payment?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.113 (Part 61, Subpart E — Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command) allows you to pay no less than your pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures and rental fees with your passengers; fly incidental to your business or employment; act as PIC of a charity, non-profit or community event flight meeting the section's conditions; conduct search and rescue under an authorized organization; demonstrate an aircraft as an aircraft salesman with 200 hours; and tow gliders or ultralights.

items.q: What is a high performance airplane, and what is required to act as PIC of one?
items.a: An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. Under 14 CFR 61.31(f) (Part 61, Subpart A — Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements), you must have received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a high performance airplane or an approved simulator or flight training device, and hold a one-time logbook endorsement saying you are proficient.

items.q: What is a high altitude airplane, and what training does the endorsement require?
items.a: A pressurized aircraft with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL. Under 14 CFR 61.31(g) (Part 61, Subpart A — Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements) you need ground training in high altitude aerodynamics and meteorology, respiration, hypoxia, time of useful consciousness, gas expansion and bubble formation, and decompression; plus flight training in normal cruise above 25,000 feet, simulated rapid decompression and emergency descent, then a one-time endorsement.

items.q: What must you do before acting as PIC of a tailwheel airplane?
items.a: Receive and log flight training from an authorized instructor covering normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings (unless the manufacturer recommends against them) and go-around procedures, then get a one-time logbook endorsement. This is 14 CFR 61.31(i) (Part 61, Subpart A — Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements). A pilot who logged tailwheel PIC time before 15 April 1991 is exempt.

items.q: What makes an airplane complex, and what is required to fly one as PIC?
items.a: A complex airplane has retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller — including one with a FADEC that controls engine and propeller together; for a seaplane it is flaps and a controllable pitch propeller. Under 14 CFR 61.31(e) (Part 61, Subpart A — Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements) you need logged ground and flight training in a complex airplane or approved simulator and a one-time endorsement.

items.q: Do the high performance, high altitude, tailwheel and complex endorsements ever expire?
items.a: No. Each is a one-time logbook endorsement under 14 CFR 61.31 (Part 61, Subpart A — Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements). Once given it is good for life and carries across aircraft in the category and class; nothing renews it. Currency and insurance requirements are separate matters and may still demand recent time in type.

items.q: What privileges does a commercial pilot certificate give you?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.133 (Part 61, Subpart F — Commercial pilot privileges and limitations), you may act as PIC of an aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and you may act as PIC for compensation or hire, provided you are qualified under Part 61 and under whatever other part of the chapter governs that operation — most often Part 91, 135 or 137.

items.q: Being paid does not by itself make an operation legal. What else must be satisfied?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.133 (Part 61, Subpart F — Commercial pilot privileges and limitations) makes the certificate a pilot qualification, not an operating authority. The operation itself must fit a part you or your employer are authorized under. If the flight amounts to common carriage, an air carrier or operating certificate under Part 119 with Part 135 or 121 operations specifications is required, and holding a commercial certificate does not supply it.

items.q: What exact limitation is placed on a commercial certificate issued without an instrument rating?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.133(b) (Part 61, Subpart F — Commercial pilot privileges and limitations) puts this wording on the certificate: "The carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited." It bites only on carrying passengers for hire; it does not stop you flying at night or beyond 50 nautical miles for other commercial purposes, or carrying property.

items.q: How is the no-instrument-rating limitation removed from a commercial certificate?
items.a: By satisfactorily completing the requirements of 14 CFR 61.65 (Part 61, Subpart B — Aircraft ratings and pilot authorizations; Instrument rating requirements) for an instrument rating in the same category and class shown on the commercial certificate. 14 CFR 61.133(b) then allows the limitation to be removed and a new certificate issued without it.

items.q: Which advisory circular explains common carriage versus private carriage?
items.a: AC 120-12A, "Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property." It is the FAA's guidance on when an operator needs an air carrier or commercial operator certificate. It sets out the four elements of common carriage, explains holding out, and gives the case history on how many contracts turn private carriage into common carriage.

items.q: What are the four elements of common carriage under AC 120-12A?
items.a: A carrier becomes a common carrier when there is (1) a holding out of a willingness to (2) transport persons or property (3) from place to place (4) for compensation. All four must be present. Remove any one — most usually the holding out — and the operation is not common carriage, so it falls outside the Part 119 certificate requirement.

items.q: What does "holding out" mean, and how can it happen?
items.a: Holding out is signaling a willingness to serve the public generally, whoever asks. AC 120-12A says signs and advertising are the most direct means but are not the only ones: holding out can be done through the actions of agents or salesmen who procure traffic from the general public, by physical presence at a location where the public seeks service, by word of mouth, or by any course of conduct from which the willingness may be inferred. No formal offer is needed.

items.q: What is private carriage, and what makes it private rather than common?
items.a: Carriage for hire that does not involve holding out. AC 120-12A describes it as carriage for one or several selected customers, generally on a long-term basis, usually under a written contract. It is often called contract carriage, though the AC notes that term is legally inaccurate under the Federal Aviation Act. The number of contracts must stay small; too many implies a willingness to contract with anybody.

items.q: How many contracts has the FAA treated as making an operator a common carrier?
items.a: AC 120-12A states that a carrier operating pursuant to 18 to 24 contracts has been held to be a common carrier, because that many contracts implies a willingness to serve the public generally. There is no bright line in the regulation — it is a judgment about whether the pattern of business shows holding out.

items.q: How few contracts has been accepted as genuine private carriage?
items.a: AC 120-12A notes that private carriage has been found in cases where three contracts were the sole basis of the operator's business. The point is that a small number of selected, long-term customers does not imply a willingness to carry anybody who asks, so no holding out occurs and no Part 119 certificate is required.

items.q: Why does the common carriage line matter so much to a new commercial pilot?
items.a: Because it decides whether the flight needs an air carrier or operating certificate. Under 14 CFR 119.1 (Part 119, Subpart A — Applicability; Certification: Air carriers and commercial operators), anyone conducting common carriage in airplanes must hold a certificate with Part 135 or 121 operations specifications. Flying common carriage on nothing but a commercial pilot certificate is illegal for you and for whoever hired you, and it typically voids the insurance.

items.q: Which operations may a commercial pilot be paid to fly without anyone holding a Part 119 certificate?
items.a: Banner towing, pipeline and powerline patrol, aerial surveying and photography, crop dusting and other agricultural work, parachute jump operations, ferry and training flights, and firefighting. 14 CFR 119.1(e) (Part 119, Subpart A — Applicability) expressly excludes these from Part 119, so a commercial pilot certificate plus the appropriate part — Part 91 for most, Part 137 for agricultural aircraft operations — is enough.

items.q: Why are banner towing, pipeline patrol and crop dusting exceptions to Part 119?
items.a: Because they are aerial work, not transportation. Nobody and nothing is being carried from place to place for compensation, so the second and third elements of common carriage are missing. The airplane is the tool doing the job rather than the means of moving a paying customer, so 14 CFR 119.1(e) (Part 119, Subpart A — Applicability) leaves them outside the air carrier certification scheme.

items.q: Why is a parachute jump operation not common carriage even though jumpers pay?
items.a: Because the jumpers are not being transported from place to place — they leave from over the same airport they departed. 14 CFR 119.1(e) (Part 119, Subpart A — Applicability) excludes nonstop flights conducted within a 25 statute mile radius of the departure airport for intentional parachute operations. Fly them somewhere and land them there and the analysis changes.

items.q: How does the FAA define currency, and how is it different from proficiency?
items.a: Currency is the legal question: have you met the recency of experience requirements to make this flight legally. It is a set of boxes in Part 61 with dates and numbers. Proficiency is the personal question of whether you can fly the airplane safely and to standard today. You can be perfectly current and badly out of practice; the regulations only measure the first.

items.q: What is the flight review requirement, and what does the review consist of?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.56 (Part 61, Subpart A — Flight review), you may not act as PIC unless within the preceding 24 calendar months you completed a flight review given by an authorized instructor and got a logbook endorsement. The review is a minimum of 1 hour of ground training on the current general operating and flight rules of Part 91, plus 1 hour of flight training on the maneuvers and procedures needed to exercise your privileges safely.

items.q: What can substitute for a flight review?
items.a: Passing a pilot proficiency check or practical test for a certificate, rating or operating privilege within the preceding 24 calendar months satisfies 14 CFR 61.56 (Part 61, Subpart A — Flight review). So your commercial checkride resets it. Completing one phase of the FAA WINGS pilot proficiency program in the preceding 24 calendar months also counts. A flight instructor who renews the instructor certificate under 61.197 is relieved only of the one hour of ground training, not of the flight portion of the review.

items.q: Which advisory circular gives guidance on conducting a flight review or IPC?
items.a: AC 61-98E, "Currency Requirements and Guidance for the Flight Review and Instrument Proficiency Check." It sets out how an instructor should plan and conduct a flight review or IPC, suggested syllabi and ground topics, guidance on personal minimums, and the recency of experience rules that surround them. It is guidance, not regulation — 14 CFR 61.56 and 61.57 are the rules.

items.q: What are the requirements to carry passengers by day in an airplane?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.57(a) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command), within the preceding 90 days you must have made three takeoffs and three landings as the sole manipulator of the controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and, if a type rating is required, the same type.

items.q: For the 90-day passenger rule, what do category, class and type each mean?
items.a: Category is the broad grouping — airplane, rotorcraft, glider, lighter-than-air, powered-lift. Class is the subdivision within it — single-engine land, single-engine sea, multi-engine land, multi-engine sea. Type is the specific make and model, and a type rating is required for airplanes with a maximum certificated takeoff weight over 12,500 pounds and for all turbojet-powered airplanes regardless of weight. These are the terms used in 14 CFR 61.57(a). Within the rotorcraft category the two classes are helicopter and gyroplane, just as the airplane category divides into single and multiengine, land and sea.

items.q: When must the three takeoffs and landings be to a full stop?
items.a: When they are made in a tailwheel airplane, under 14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command), and whenever they are being flown for night currency under 61.57(b). For day currency in a nosewheel airplane, touch-and-goes count.

items.q: What is required to carry passengers at night?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.57(b) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command), within the preceding 90 days you must have made three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop as sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category, class and type if required, during the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.

items.q: What are the three different definitions of night a commercial pilot must keep straight?
items.a: For night currency under 14 CFR 61.57(b), the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. For logging night flight time and for the definition in 14 CFR 1.1, the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight. For position lights, 14 CFR 91.209 (Part 91, Subpart B — Aircraft lights) requires them from sunset to sunrise.

items.q: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.57(c) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command), within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, and in the appropriate category of aircraft, you must have performed and logged in actual or simulated instrument conditions: six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.

items.q: Can instrument currency be regained in a simulator or training device?
items.a: Yes. 14 CFR 61.57(c) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command) allows the six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking to be performed in a full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device representing the category of aircraft, provided the device is approved for the tasks. An instructor is not required if the device qualifies, though many operators require one.

items.q: What happens if you let your instrument currency lapse?
items.a: You get a 6 calendar month grace period. Under 14 CFR 61.57(c) and (d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command), for the 6 calendar months after currency expires you may still regain it by flying the six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking. Once that grace period also passes — 12 calendar months in total since you were last current — you may only regain currency by passing an instrument proficiency check.

items.q: During the 6-month instrument grace period, what may you do and what may you not do?
items.a: You may not act as PIC under IFR or in IMC at any point during the grace period — the moment currency lapses, that privilege is gone. You may fly the six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking in VMC with a safety pilot, or in an approved simulator or training device, or with an instrument instructor acting as PIC. The safety pilot must hold at least a private certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft and a medical.

items.q: When is an instrument proficiency check required, and what does it involve?
items.a: When more than 12 calendar months have passed since you were last instrument current — that is, the 6-month currency window plus the 6-month grace period have both run out. 14 CFR 61.57(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command) requires an IPC consisting of the areas of operation and tasks listed for an IPC in the Instrument Rating Airman Certification Standards, in an aircraft of the appropriate category.

items.q: Who may administer an instrument proficiency check?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.57(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command): an authorized instructor holding an instrument instructor rating, a designated pilot examiner, an FAA inspector, a person approved by the Administrator to conduct instrument practical tests, or a company check pilot authorized under Part 121, 125 or 135. The standards used are the IPC table in the Instrument Rating ACS.

items.q: Under 61.51, what makes flight time loggable as instrument time?
items.a: You may log instrument time only for that flight time when you operate the aircraft solely by reference to instruments under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions. This is 14 CFR 61.51(g) (Part 61, Subpart A — Pilot logbooks). Being on an IFR flight plan is irrelevant; flying an airway in clear air in day VMC on an IFR clearance is not instrument time.

items.q: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.109(c) (Part 91, Subpart B — Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests), the safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft, must occupy the other control seat, and must have adequate vision forward and to each side or the aircraft must carry a competent observer. The aircraft must have fully functioning dual controls. The safety pilot is a required crewmember and so needs a medical or BasicMed.

items.q: What must your logbook show for each instrument approach and for simulated instrument time?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.51(g) (Part 61, Subpart A — Pilot logbooks) requires you to record the location and type of each instrument approach accomplished, and the name of the safety pilot for each simulated instrument flight. Recording the conditions of flight — actual or simulated — and the instrument time itself is what makes the entry usable for 61.57(c) currency.

items.q: What conditions must be met to log an instrument approach flown in actual conditions?
items.a: You must fly the initial, intermediate and final segments of the procedure — vectors to final satisfy the earlier segments — and be operating solely by reference to instruments in actual IMC from the final approach fix down to the MDA or DA/DH. If you become VMC before reaching minimums, the approach may still be logged provided you were in actual conditions past the final approach fix and continue to minimums. This is FAA InFO 15012 read with 14 CFR 61.57(c).

items.q: What conditions must be met to log an approach flown under simulated conditions?
items.a: You must be under a view-limiting device with a qualified safety pilot, fly the initial, intermediate and final segments, and keep the simulated conditions going all the way to the MDA or DA/DH. Lifting the hood at circling minimums or at the visual descent point loses the approach. FAA InFO 15012 is the FAA's guidance on this, and it supports 14 CFR 61.57(c) currency.

items.q: Do you have to fly the missed approach to log an approach?
items.a: No. Neither 14 CFR 61.57(c) (Part 61, Subpart A — Recent flight experience: Pilot in command) nor FAA InFO 15012 requires the missed approach segment; reaching the MDA or DA/DH under instrument conditions is the requirement. The FAA nevertheless recommends flying the missed approach for proficiency, and an examiner will expect you to be able to.

items.q: Can both pilots log pilot in command time during a simulated instrument flight?
items.a: Yes. The pilot under the hood logs PIC as the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which they are rated, under 14 CFR 61.51(e). The safety pilot may log PIC only for the time they are acting as pilot in command by prior agreement, since 91.109(c) makes the safety pilot a required crewmember; otherwise the safety pilot logs that time as second in command.

items.q: How do you decide whether you are proficient, as opposed to merely current?
items.a: By asking whether you can fly every task in the Airman Certification Standards to standard today, in the conditions you are about to fly in. If there is a maneuver, an approach or an emergency procedure you would not want to be tested on right now, you are not proficient in it. Currency is a legal minimum; proficiency is the honest self-assessment that the regulation cannot make for you.

items.q: What are personal minimums, and how do they relate to recency of experience?
items.a: Personal minimums are your own limits — ceiling, visibility, crosswind, night, fuel reserve, approach minimums — set above the legal minimums and written down before the flight, not decided at the airplane. They should tighten when recency is thin: less time in type, a long layoff, an unfamiliar airport or an airplane you have not flown at night all argue for wider margins. AC 61-98E discusses building them.

items.q: What class of medical certificate does a commercial pilot need?
items.a: At least a second class medical to exercise commercial pilot privileges, under 14 CFR 61.23(a)(2) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). A first class medical is required for airline transport pilot privileges. A third class, or BasicMed, only supports private, recreational, sport or flight instructor privileges.

items.q: Is BasicMed a medical certificate?
items.a: No. BasicMed is an alternative to holding an FAA medical certificate, created by Part 68 (Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate) and 14 CFR 61.113(i) (Part 61, Subpart E — Private pilot privileges and limitations). You hold no certificate under it; you carry a completed comprehensive medical examination checklist and proof of the online course, and you fly under a defined set of limits.

items.q: Can a commercial pilot fly for compensation or hire under BasicMed?
items.a: No. BasicMed operates through 14 CFR 61.113(i) (Part 61, Subpart E — Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command), which restricts you to the privileges of a private pilot and its conditions. Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and acting as PIC for compensation or hire, are outside it. To exercise commercial privileges you need a second class medical.

items.q: What must you do, and how often, to operate under BasicMed?
items.a: Complete a comprehensive medical examination with a state-licensed physician every 48 months using the FAA checklist, and complete the online medical education course every 24 months. Keep the completed checklist in your logbook and the course completion certificate, and comply with any treatment your physician directs. These are the requirements of Part 68 (Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate).

items.q: What are the eligibility requirements to use BasicMed in the first place?
items.a: You must hold a valid US driver's license, and you must have held an FAA medical certificate — regular or special issuance — at some point after 14 July 2006. Your most recent medical must not have been suspended or revoked, your most recent authorization for special issuance must not have been withdrawn, and your most recent application must not have been denied. Part 68 sets these conditions.

items.q: What are the current aircraft and operating limits for BasicMed?
items.a: The aircraft must be authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants and have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, excluding transport category rotorcraft, and you may carry no more than 6 passengers. The flight must be below 18,000 feet MSL, at no more than 250 knots indicated airspeed, and not for compensation or hire. These are the limits in 14 CFR 61.113(i), as expanded in November 2024.

items.q: Can you fly IFR or at night under BasicMed, and where may you fly?
items.a: Yes to both — BasicMed permits VFR or IFR, day or night, provided you hold the appropriate ratings and are current. Geographically, 14 CFR 61.113(i) (Part 61, Subpart E — Private pilot privileges and limitations) confines you to flights within the United States, unless the destination country has specifically authorized BasicMed operations, as the Bahamas and Mexico have.

items.q: How long is a first class medical valid for airline transport pilot privileges?
items.a: 12 calendar months if you were under age 40 on the date of the examination, and 6 calendar months if you were 40 or older. This is 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). Age is fixed at the date of the exam, and the certificate expires on the last day of the relevant month.

items.q: How long is a first class medical valid for commercial pilot privileges?
items.a: 12 calendar months regardless of age. Under 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration), a first class medical carries second class privileges for 12 calendar months whether you are 25 or 55; the under-40 and over-40 split applies only to the ATP privileges at the top and the private privileges at the bottom.

items.q: How long does a first class medical remain valid for private pilot or flight instructor privileges?
items.a: 60 calendar months if you were under age 40 on the date of the examination, and 24 calendar months if you were 40 or older. This is 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). A first class medical never stops being useful at once; it steps down through second class privileges and then third class privileges as the clock runs.

items.q: How long is a second class medical valid for commercial pilot privileges?
items.a: 12 calendar months regardless of age, under 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). The same 12 calendar months applies to an airline transport pilot acting as second in command in a Part 121 operation, or to flight engineer privileges.

items.q: How long does a second class medical remain valid for private pilot or flight instructor privileges?
items.a: 60 calendar months if you were under age 40 on the date of the examination, and 24 calendar months if you were 40 or older. This is 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). So after the 12 calendar months of commercial privileges expire, the same piece of paper still supports private flying for the balance of that longer period.

items.q: How long is a third class medical valid?
items.a: 60 calendar months if you were under age 40 on the date of the examination, and 24 calendar months if you were 40 or older, under 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration). It supports private, recreational, sport, student and flight instructor privileges only — never commercial or ATP privileges.

items.q: When exactly does a medical certificate expire, and which age is used?
items.a: It expires at the end of the last day of the month in which the period runs out — hence "calendar months". The age used is your age on the date of the examination, not your age when you fly, so an exam taken the day before your fortieth birthday gives you the longer under-40 durations. 14 CFR 61.23(d) (Part 61, Subpart A — Medical certificates: Requirement and duration) governs.

items.q: What is a SODA, and when is one issued?
items.a: A Statement of Demonstrated Ability. It is issued under 14 CFR 67.401 (Part 67, Subpart E — Certification Procedures; Special issuance of medical certificates) to a pilot with a disqualifying condition who demonstrates, usually through a medical flight test with an FAA inspector, that they can safely perform pilot duties despite it. Color vision deficiency and a missing or impaired limb are the classic examples.

items.q: What kind of condition qualifies for a SODA rather than a special issuance?
items.a: The condition must be static or non-progressive — it will not get worse. That is why a SODA does not expire and does not have to be re-demonstrated: it is issued once and stays valid as long as the condition is unchanged. 14 CFR 67.401 (Part 67, Subpart E — Special issuance of medical certificates) is the authority.

items.q: How does a special issuance authorization differ from a SODA?
items.a: A special issuance is a time-limited authorization for a condition that may change — a treated cardiac condition, diabetes, a psychiatric history — and it carries follow-up reporting and an expiry, after which it must be renewed. A SODA covers a static, non-progressive condition and does not expire. Both come from 14 CFR 67.401 (Part 67, Subpart E — Special issuance of medical certificates).

items.q: Even with a valid medical certificate, when may you not act as pilot in command?
items.a: When you know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make you unable to meet the requirements for your certificate, or you are taking medication or receiving treatment for a condition that makes you unable to meet them. That is 14 CFR 61.53 (Part 61, Subpart A — Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency), and it applies to BasicMed pilots too. A valid certificate in your pocket is no defense.

items.q: Can you exercise airline transport pilot privileges on a second class medical certificate?
items.a: Only as second in command. Pilot-in-command privileges of an airline transport pilot certificate need a first class medical; second-in-command ATP privileges, like commercial pilot privileges, may be exercised on at least a second class medical, good for those privileges for 12 calendar months at any age under 14 CFR 61.23 (Part 61, Subpart A - Medical certificates: Requirement and duration), the rule fixing which class you need and how long it lasts. It then drops to private pilot or flight instructor privileges.

items.q: What is a technically advanced airplane?
items.a: One with an integrated avionics suite made up of an electronic primary flight display, an electronic multifunction display with a GPS moving map showing airplane position, and a two axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system, with both displays continuously visible. The definition is in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), section 61.129 Aeronautical experience, at paragraph (j).

items.q: Why do complex, turbine powered and technically advanced airplanes get discussed together on the commercial course?
items.a: Because the aeronautical experience rule lets any one of the three satisfy the same requirement: 10 hours of training in a complex airplane, a turbine powered airplane, or a technically advanced airplane, for the single engine airplane commercial certificate. That is 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), section 61.129 Aeronautical experience, the rule listing the flight time a commercial applicant must log.

items.q: Which regulation sets the aeronautical experience for a commercial certificate, and what is its official title?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.129, Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), officially titled 'Aeronautical experience.' In plain English it lists the hours and the specific flights you must have logged before you may take the commercial practical test; paragraph (a) is the airplane single-engine land list. It works alongside 61.123 eligibility, 61.125 knowledge areas and 61.127 areas of operation. Part 141 students meet a reduced total instead.
items.concept: Section 61.129 is the aeronautical experience rule for the commercial certificate

items.q: How much total flight time does 61.129(a) require for a commercial airplane single-engine certificate?
items.a: 250 hours of total time as a pilot under 61.129(a), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' That total must contain at least 100 hours in powered aircraft, at least 100 hours of pilot-in-command time, the solo or duties-of-PIC flights, the 20 hours of commercial training, and the day and night cross-countries. An approved Part 141 course requires 190 hours instead, so know which rule you are training under.
items.concept: 250 hours of total flight time

items.q: Of the 250 hours, how many must be in powered aircraft?
items.a: At least 100 hours in powered aircraft under 61.129(a)(1), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Powered aircraft means anything other than a glider or balloon, so helicopter, powered-lift and airplane time all count toward this 100; the remaining 150 hours of the 250 may come from any pilot time, including glider or balloon time.
items.concept: At least 100 hours in powered aircraft

items.q: How much of the 100 hours in powered aircraft must be in airplanes?
items.a: At least 50 hours in airplanes, under 61.129(a)(1), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' So of the 100 powered hours, half must be airplane time; the balance may be in other powered categories. A Warrior II flight counts toward both the powered-aircraft 100 and the airplane 50.
items.concept: 50 of the 100 powered hours must be in airplanes

items.q: How many hours of pilot-in-command time does the commercial certificate require?
items.a: At least 100 hours of pilot-in-command time under 61.129(a)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' PIC here is logged under 61.51(e), which includes time as sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which you are rated, so dual received in your Warrior II as a rated private pilot is loggable PIC toward this 100.
items.concept: At least 100 hours pilot-in-command

items.q: Of the 100 hours pilot-in-command, how many must be in airplanes?
items.a: At least 50 hours of the pilot-in-command time must be in airplanes, per 61.129(a)(2)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The other 50 PIC hours may be in any other powered category or class you are rated for.
items.concept: At least 50 of the PIC hours in airplanes

items.q: How much cross-country pilot-in-command time is required for the commercial certificate?
items.a: At least 50 hours of cross-country flight time as pilot in command, per 61.129(a)(2)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' For this purpose cross-country under 61.1 means a landing at a point more than 50 nautical miles straight-line from the original point of departure, with the usual landing, navigation and planning elements.
items.concept: At least 50 hours PIC cross-country

items.q: How much of the 50 hours of cross-country PIC time must be in airplanes?
items.a: At least 10 of the 50 cross-country PIC hours must be in airplanes, per 61.129(a)(2)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The other 40 may be in any other powered category or class. In practice a private pilot building commercial time in a Warrior II will far exceed the 10.
items.concept: 10 of the 50 cross-country hours must be in airplanes

items.q: What are the two ways to satisfy the 10-hour solo requirement under 61.129(a)(4)?
items.a: Either 10 hours of solo flight time in a single-engine airplane, or 10 hours of flight time performing the duties of pilot in command in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor on board, under 61.129(a)(4), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' You must pick one path and complete all its required flights the same way; the two cannot be mixed within those flights.
items.concept: 10 hours solo in a single-engine airplane, or 10 hours performing the duties of PIC with an instructor on board

items.q: Describe the long cross-country required by 61.129(a)(4)(i).
items.a: One cross-country flight of not less than 300 nautical miles total distance, with landings at a minimum of three points, flown solo or performing the duties of pilot in command with an instructor aboard, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Total distance is the sum of the legs; three points means three landings, which with the departure airport is a four-airport route or a route returning home.
items.concept: One cross-country of not less than 300 NM total distance with landings at a minimum of 3 points

items.q: On the 300 NM commercial cross-country, what is the 250 NM requirement exactly?
items.a: One of the landing points must be a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The 250 is measured from the original point of departure to that landing point, not leg to leg, so plan the route to prove the straight-line distance on the chart or a flight planning log.
items.concept: One leg of the 300 NM cross-country a straight-line distance of at least 250 NM from the original departure point

items.q: How does the 300 NM commercial cross-country requirement change if it is flown in Hawaii?
items.a: If the flight is conducted in Hawaii, the longest segment need only have a straight-line distance of at least 150 nautical miles, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The rest of the requirement stands: not less than 300 nautical miles total distance with landings at a minimum of three points.
items.concept: Special circumstances with Hawaii on the long cross-country

items.q: What night flying is required by 61.129(a)(4)(ii) for the commercial certificate?
items.a: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings, flown solo or performing the duties of pilot in command with an instructor aboard, per 61.129(a)(4)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Night here is the 61.1 definition: the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight.
items.concept: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings

items.q: What two conditions attach to the 10 night takeoffs and landings for the commercial certificate?
items.a: Each landing must involve a flight in the traffic pattern, and they must be at an airport with an operating control tower, per 61.129(a)(4)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Touch and goes count so long as each is preceded by a circuit of the pattern; the tower must actually be operating at the time, so a tower that closes at 2200 local stops counting then.
items.concept: Each of the 10 night landings must involve a flight in the traffic pattern at an airport with an operating control tower

items.q: How many hours of training on the commercial areas of operation does 61.129(a)(3) require?
items.a: At least 20 hours of training from an authorized instructor on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1), per 61.129(a)(3), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Those 20 hours must themselves contain the 10 hours of instrument training, the 10 hours in a complex, turbine-powered or technically advanced airplane, the two 2-hour cross-countries, and the 3 hours of practical test preparation.
items.concept: At least 20 hours of training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1)

items.q: How much instrument training does the commercial certificate require, and how much of it must be in an airplane?
items.a: At least 10 hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device, of which at least 5 hours must be in a single-engine airplane, per 61.129(a)(3)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Up to 5 hours may be credited from an approved full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device under 61.129(i).
items.concept: At least 10 hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device

items.q: What four subjects must the 10 hours of commercial instrument training cover?
items.a: Attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills, recovery from unusual flight attitudes, and intercepting and tracking navigational systems, per 61.129(a)(3)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' In the Warrior II partial panel usually means losing the vacuum-driven attitude indicator and directional gyro and flying on the turn coordinator, magnetic compass, altimeter and airspeed indicator; confirm the panel fit against the POH.
items.concept: Content of the instrument training: attitude instrument flying, partial panel, unusual attitude recovery, intercepting and tracking navigational systems

items.q: Describe the day cross-country required within the 20 hours of commercial training.
items.a: One 2-hour cross-country flight in daytime conditions in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor, consisting of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure, per 61.129(a)(3)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' It is dual training time, not solo, and the 2 hours is flight time, not block time.
items.concept: One 2-hour day cross-country with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 NM

items.q: Describe the night cross-country required within the 20 hours of commercial training.
items.a: One 2-hour cross-country flight in nighttime conditions in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor, consisting of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure, per 61.129(a)(3)(iii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' It is separate from the day flight and from the 5 hours of night VFR solo or duties-of-PIC time.
items.concept: One 2-hour night cross-country with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 NM

items.q: What is the 3-hour practical test preparation requirement, and how recent must it be?
items.a: At least 3 hours in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor in preparation for the practical test, completed within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test, per 61.129(a)(3)(iv), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Calendar months means it expires at the end of the second month, so training in March is good for a test through the end of May.
items.concept: At least 3 hours with an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane in preparation for the practical test within the preceding 2 calendar months

items.q: Does holding an instrument rating satisfy the training required for a commercial certificate?
items.a: No. The instrument rating is a separate certificate action; 61.129(a)(3) still requires 20 hours of training on the 61.127(b)(1) commercial areas of operation, including the 10 hours of instrument training with a view-limiting device, the two 2-hour cross-countries, and the 3 hours of practical test preparation. Whether any earlier instrument training may be credited toward the 10 hours is an endorsement decision for your instructor; check 61.129(a)(3)(i) and current FAA legal interpretations.
items.concept: Note: an instrument rating alone does not satisfy the commercial training requirements

items.q: What is 61.127(b)(1), and why does it matter to your commercial training?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.127, Part 61, Subpart F, is titled 'Flight proficiency,' and paragraph (b)(1) lists the areas of operation for an airplane single-engine rating: preflight preparation; preflight procedures; airport and seaplane base operations; takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; performance maneuvers; ground reference maneuvers; navigation; slow flight and stalls; emergency operations; high-altitude operations; and postflight procedures. The 20 hours of commercial training and the practical test are both built on this list.
items.concept: Section 61.127(b)(1) areas of operation for the commercial single-engine airplane

items.q: Which regulation lists eligibility for a commercial pilot certificate, and what is its official title?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.123, Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), titled 'Eligibility requirements: General.' In plain English it is the checklist of who may be issued the certificate: age, English, the ground and flight training endorsements, the knowledge test, the aeronautical experience of 61.129, the practical test, and holding at least a private pilot certificate.
items.concept: Section 61.123 is the eligibility rule for the commercial pilot certificate

items.q: What is the minimum age for a commercial pilot certificate?
items.a: 18 years of age, per 61.123(a), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' You may take the knowledge test before turning 18, and you may hold a private certificate at 17, but the commercial certificate itself cannot be issued until your eighteenth birthday.
items.concept: At least 18 years of age

items.q: What is the English language requirement for a commercial certificate?
items.a: You must be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language, per 61.123(b), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' If a medical condition limits any of those abilities, the FAA may place an operating limitation on the certificate as needed for safety.
items.concept: Be able to read, speak, write, and understand English

items.q: What endorsement must you hold before taking the commercial knowledge test?
items.a: A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who either conducted the required ground training or reviewed your home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas of 61.125, per 61.123(c), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' Home study counts only if an instructor has reviewed it and signs for it.
items.concept: Logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the ground training or reviewed the home study on the 61.125 knowledge areas

items.q: What exactly must the instructor certify in the knowledge test endorsement?
items.a: That you are prepared for the required knowledge test, per 61.123(c)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The endorsement is a statement of readiness, not merely of attendance, and the testing center will not let you sit the test without it. Wording is in the current AC 61-65 endorsement guide.
items.concept: The instructor must certify that the person is prepared for the required knowledge test

items.q: What knowledge test must a commercial applicant pass, and what does it cover?
items.a: The commercial pilot knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas of 61.125, required by 61.123(d), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The passing score is 70 percent, and the test report is valid for 24 calendar months from the month it was taken, so the practical test must be completed within that window.
items.concept: Pass the required knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in 61.125

items.q: What is 61.125, and what sort of subjects does it list?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.125, Part 61, Subpart F, titled 'Aeronautical knowledge,' lists the ground subjects a commercial applicant must learn: the regulations relating to commercial privileges and limitations; accident reporting under NTSB 830; basic aerodynamics and principles of flight; meteorology and weather reports; safe and efficient operation; weight and balance; performance charts; night and high-altitude operations; and aeronautical decision making and judgment.
items.concept: Section 61.125 aeronautical knowledge areas

items.q: What endorsement must you hold before the commercial practical test?
items.a: A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127, per 61.123(e), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' That instructor must also have given or verified the 3 hours of test preparation within the preceding 2 calendar months required by 61.129(a)(3)(iv).
items.concept: Receive the required training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127

items.q: What must the practical test endorsement say about your readiness?
items.a: It must certify that you are prepared for the required practical test, per 61.123(e)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The examiner checks this endorsement, the knowledge test report, your logbook experience and your aircraft paperwork before the test begins. Endorsement wording comes from the current AC 61-65.
items.concept: The instructor must certify that the person is prepared for the required practical test

items.q: What is 61.127, and how is it used on the commercial checkride?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.127, Part 61, Subpart F, titled 'Flight proficiency,' lists the areas of operation you must be trained in and tested on. For an airplane single-engine rating under (b)(1) that is preflight preparation; preflight procedures; airport operations; takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; performance maneuvers; ground reference maneuvers; navigation; slow flight and stalls; emergency operations; high-altitude operations; and postflight procedures. The Airman Certification Standards expand each one into tasks.
items.concept: Section 61.127 areas of operation

items.q: Which experience must a commercial applicant meet, and does it depend on the aircraft?
items.a: You must meet the aeronautical experience requirements of 61.129 that apply to the category and class rating sought, per 61.123(f), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The hours differ by category and class: 61.129(a) is airplane single-engine land, (b) is multiengine, (c) and (d) are rotorcraft, and so on.
items.concept: Meet the aeronautical experience requirements of this subpart that apply to the aircraft category and class rating

items.q: What practical test must a commercial applicant pass?
items.a: The commercial pilot practical test on the areas of operation listed in 61.127 for the category and class sought, per 61.123(g), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' It is conducted to the Commercial Pilot Airman Certification Standards and includes both an oral and a flight portion; the airplane you bring must meet 61.45, which for the single-engine commercial means an airplane capable of performing all required tasks.
items.concept: Pass the required practical test on the areas of operation listed in 61.127

items.q: Must you already be a private pilot to be issued a commercial certificate?
items.a: Yes. You must hold at least a private pilot certificate issued under Part 61, or meet the requirements of 61.73, per 61.123(h), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' There is no route straight from student pilot to commercial pilot; the private certificate, or its military equivalent processed under 61.73, is the entry ticket.
items.concept: Hold at least a private pilot certificate issued under this part or meet the requirements of 61.73

items.q: What is 61.73, and who uses it on the way to a commercial certificate?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.73, Part 61, Subpart A (General), titled 'Military pilots or former military pilots: Special rules.' It lets a qualified United States military pilot obtain a civil pilot certificate and ratings on the basis of military qualification rather than by taking the normal private pilot course, and that certificate then satisfies the private pilot prerequisite in 61.123(h).
items.concept: Section 61.73 as the alternative to holding a Part 61 private certificate

items.q: What is the catch-all eligibility item at the end of 61.123?
items.a: You must comply with the sections of Part 61 that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought, per 61.123(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' That sweeps in items such as 61.31 endorsements for the airplane used, 61.39 prerequisites for the practical test, and 61.23 medical certificate requirements.
items.concept: Comply with the sections of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought

items.q: How many hours of training does the tailwheel endorsement require?
items.a: No minimum number of hours. 61.31(i), Part 61, Subpart A, specifies the maneuvers that must be trained, not a time; the instructor signs when you are proficient. In practice it runs five to ten hours, but the regulation sets no floor.
items.concept: Tailwheel endorsement does not require a minimum number of hours

items.q: Which specific maneuvers must the tailwheel training cover?
items.a: Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings, and go-around procedures, per 61.31(i)(1), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.' Wheel landings may be omitted only if the manufacturer has recommended against them for that airplane.
items.concept: Tailwheel maneuvers required: normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings, go-around procedures

items.q: Is there any exception to the tailwheel endorsement requirement?
items.a: Yes. A pilot who logged pilot-in-command time in a tailwheel airplane before April 15, 1991 is excepted, per 61.31(i)(2), Part 61, Subpart A. Nobody earning a certificate today can use that exception, and insurance will usually demand training and a checkout regardless of what the regulation allows.
items.concept: Tailwheel grandfather provision for pilots who logged PIC tailwheel time before April 15, 1991

items.q: Is there a minimum number of hours for the complex endorsement?
items.a: No minimum hours are specified in 61.31(e), Part 61, Subpart A. The instructor trains you to proficiency in that make and model and then endorses your logbook. Note that the commercial certificate separately requires 10 hours of training in a complex, turbine-powered or technically advanced airplane under 61.129(a)(3)(ii), which is a different requirement.
items.concept: Complex endorsement does not require a minimum number of hours

items.q: What form does complex training have to take before the endorsement is signed?
items.a: You must receive and log both ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane, or in an approved full flight simulator or flight training device representing one, and be found proficient in its operation, per 61.31(e)(1), Part 61, Subpart A. The instructor then makes the one-time logbook endorsement under 61.31(e)(2).
items.concept: Complex endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor

items.q: Does the high performance endorsement have an hour requirement?
items.a: No minimum hours are specified in 61.31(f), Part 61, Subpart A. What is required is logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and a finding of proficiency, followed by the one-time logbook endorsement. Exactly 200 horsepower is not high performance; the rule says more than 200.
items.concept: High performance endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor

items.q: What two kinds of training does the high altitude endorsement require?
items.a: Both ground training and flight training, received and logged from an authorized instructor in a pressurized airplane or in an approved simulator or flight training device, followed by a finding of proficiency and a one-time logbook endorsement, per 61.31(g)(1) and (g)(2), Part 61, Subpart A. There is no minimum hour requirement. A pilot who logged PIC time in such an airplane before April 15, 1991, or who passed an equivalent FAA or military proficiency check, is excepted.
items.concept: High altitude endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor

items.q: List the subjects the high altitude ground training must cover.
items.a: High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology; respiration; hypoxia and other high-altitude sicknesses; duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen; effects of prolonged use of supplemental oxygen; causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation, and how to prevent them; physical phenomena and incidents of decompression; and any other physiological aspects of high-altitude flight, per 61.31(g)(1)(i), Part 61, Subpart A.
items.concept: High altitude ground training subject list

items.q: What must the flight portion of high altitude training include?
items.a: Normal cruise flight operations above 25,000 feet MSL; proper emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression, without actually depressurizing the aircraft; and emergency descent procedures, per 61.31(g)(1)(ii), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.'
items.concept: High altitude flight training content

items.q: Which of the four 61.31 endorsements does your Warrior II require?
items.a: None of them. A 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II has fixed tricycle gear, a fixed-pitch propeller, a 160 horsepower carbureted Lycoming O-320, and no pressurization, so it is not complex under 61.31(e), not high performance under 61.31(f), not a high altitude airplane under 61.31(g), and not a tailwheel airplane under 61.31(i). Confirm the engine and propeller fitted to your serial number against the POH and the aircraft records.
items.concept: Which of the four endorsements apply to a 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II

items.q: When may an instructor log instrument time while teaching?
items.a: An authorized instructor may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument flight conditions, per 61.51(g)(2), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' The instructor cannot log instrument time for simulated instrument instruction given in visual conditions, although the student under the hood can.
items.concept: 61.51(g)(2) instructor logging instrument time in actual conditions

items.q: If simulator instrument time is used toward a certificate or rating, what extra entry is required?
items.a: The name and certificate number of the authorized instructor who provided the training must be entered, per 61.51(g)(4), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' Training credited toward a certificate or rating must be given by an authorized instructor present with you at the device, and the instructor signs the logbook.
items.concept: Simulator time used for a certificate or rating requires the instructor's name and certificate number

items.q: Do you need an instructor to use a training device purely for instrument currency?
items.a: For an instrument-rated pilot regaining or maintaining currency, no instructor is required in an approved aviation training device under 61.57(c), although an instructor or an authorized person may be needed to observe or sign depending on the device. Record the device, the date, the tasks, the approaches, holding and course intercepting and tracking. Confirm the current wording of 61.57(c) and any letter of authorization for the specific device.
items.concept: Simulator time used only for currency by an instrument rated pilot needs no instructor

items.q: What does 91.109 require of the airplane and the safety pilot for simulated instrument flight?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.109, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Flight instruction; simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests,' requires fully functioning dual controls and a safety pilot who holds at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft and has adequate vision forward and to each side. The safety pilot must also hold a medical certificate or BasicMed because that pilot is a required crewmember.
items.concept: Safety pilot qualification requirements under 91.109

items.q: When does 61.3 require you to hold an instrument rating?
items.a: To act as pilot in command of a civil aircraft under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR flight, per 61.3(e), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations.' You must hold the instrument rating on your certificate for the category of aircraft flown and be current under 61.57(c).
items.concept: Instrument rating required to act as PIC in IFR weather conditions

items.q: What does the regulation say about carrying your pilot certificate?
items.a: No person may act as pilot in command unless that person has a valid pilot certificate in that person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, per 61.3(a), Part 61, Subpart A. A plastic or paper FAA certificate does not expire, but it must be the current one for the privileges exercised, and a temporary certificate is valid only until the expiry date printed on it.
items.concept: Personal document: pilot certificate

items.q: When do you personally need a radio operator permit?
items.a: For flight outside the United States, where you need an FCC Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit, issued under 47 CFR Part 13 and valid for the holder's lifetime. It is not required for purely domestic flights within the United States. The aircraft separately needs an FCC radio station license for international operation.
items.concept: Personal document: radio operator permit for flight outside the United States

items.q: What is the IM SAFE checklist, and what does each letter stand for?
items.a: A personal fitness-for-flight self-assessment: I for Illness, M for Medication, S for Stress, A for Alcohol, F for Fatigue, E for Emotion and Eating. It is the practical expression of 91.17, Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs,' and 61.53, 'Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency,' and it is described in AIM 8-1-1, Fitness for Flight. If any item is a yes, you do not fly.
items.concept: IM SAFE preflight self-assessment, 91.17 and AIM 8-1-1

items.q: What does the I in IM SAFE ask you, and what rule backs it up?
items.a: Illness. Are you sick, and would the symptoms, even a head cold, affect your ability to fly safely? A cold blocks the eustachian tubes and can cause a painful or damaging ear or sinus block on descent. 61.53, Part 61, Subpart A, 'Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency,' forbids acting as a required crewmember while you know of any medical condition that would make you unable to meet the requirements for your medical certificate.
items.concept: IM SAFE I: Illness

items.q: What does the M in IM SAFE ask, and where do you check a drug?
items.a: Medication. Are you taking any prescription or over-the-counter drug, and is it or the underlying condition disqualifying? 91.17(a)(3) forbids acting as a crewmember while using any drug that affects your faculties in a way contrary to safety. Many antihistamines and sleep aids are grounding. Check the FAA's published list of Do Not Issue and Do Not Fly medications or ask an aviation medical examiner.
items.concept: IM SAFE M: Medication

items.q: What does the S in IM SAFE ask of you?
items.a: Stress. Are you under psychological pressure from work, money, family or health that will occupy your attention in the cockpit? Stress narrows attention and degrades decision making and short-term memory, which is exactly what you need on a commercial checkride or a single-pilot IFR approach. AIM 8-1-1 treats stress as a fitness item on a par with illness.
items.concept: IM SAFE S: Stress

items.q: What does the A in IM SAFE ask, and what is the legal limit?
items.a: Alcohol. Under 91.17, Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs,' no person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember within 8 hours after consuming any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, or with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater. Eight hours is the legal floor, not a physiological safe margin, and hangover effects persist well beyond it.
items.concept: IM SAFE A: Alcohol

items.q: State the exact numbers and penalties in 91.17.
items.a: 8 hours bottle to throttle and a blood alcohol concentration below 0.04 percent, and no acting as a crewmember while under the influence of alcohol or any drug affecting your faculties, per 91.17(a), Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs.' Refusing a test requested by a law enforcement officer, or refusing to furnish the results, is itself grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year or for suspension or revocation of your certificate under 91.17(c) and (d).
items.concept: 91.17 hard numbers: 8 hours, 0.04 percent, refusal to submit to a test

items.q: What does the F in IM SAFE ask, and why is fatigue so dangerous?
items.a: Fatigue. Are you tired, and have you had proper rest? Fatigue is insidious because it degrades judgment and attention before the pilot notices, and the fatigued pilot is the worst judge of his own state. It is a leading factor in night and long cross-country accidents, and AIM 8-1-1 treats it as a go or no-go item. Acute fatigue is cured by rest; chronic fatigue is not.
items.concept: IM SAFE F: Fatigue

items.q: What does the final E in IM SAFE cover?
items.a: Emotion and Eating. Emotion asks whether you are upset, angry or grieving, any of which captures attention and degrades judgment. Eating asks whether you are properly nourished and hydrated, because low blood sugar and dehydration cause headache, slow thinking and poor decisions, and they build up through a long day of commercial flying. Carry water and food on any flight of length.
items.concept: IM SAFE E: Emotion and Eating

items.q: What is the PAVE checklist, and what does each letter cover?
items.a: A preflight risk assessment covering the four risk areas of any flight: P for Pilot, A for Aircraft, V for enVironment, E for External pressures. You run it before the flight to identify hazards and set a personal go or no-go, and the FAA Risk Management Handbook and AC 60-22, Aeronautical Decision Making, describe how to score and mitigate each element.
items.concept: PAVE preflight risk checklist

items.q: What do you assess under the P of PAVE?
items.a: The Pilot. Your fitness and your qualifications: run IM SAFE for illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and emotion or eating, then check currency and proficiency, recent experience in type, night and instrument currency, and whether your personal minimums cover the conditions. Current is not the same as proficient.
items.concept: PAVE P: Pilot

items.q: What do you assess under the A of PAVE?
items.a: The Aircraft. Is it airworthy and legal: ARROW documents aboard, AV1ATES inspections current, no inoperative equipment outside 91.213, fuel and oil adequate, weight and balance within limits, and performance adequate for the runway, density altitude and terrain. For a Warrior II with 160 horsepower, the takeoff and climb charts in the POH are the deciding document on a hot day at a short strip.
items.concept: PAVE A: Aircraft

items.q: What do you assess under the V of PAVE?
items.a: The enVironment. Weather, terrain, airspace, airport conditions, runway surface and length, lighting, day or night, icing and thunderstorms, density altitude, and the condition of navigation aids and TFRs along the route. It is the widest of the four categories and the one that changes while you are airborne, so it needs reassessment in flight, not just before departure.
items.concept: PAVE V: enVironment

items.q: What do you assess under the E of PAVE, and why does it matter commercially?
items.a: External pressures. The forces pushing you to complete the flight: a paying passenger, a schedule, a checkride slot, getting home, the cost of a night in a hotel. As a commercial pilot these grow sharply, and they drive get-there-itis and continued VFR into instrument conditions. The defense is to set an alternate plan and a decision point before departure so the pressure meets a prior commitment.
items.concept: PAVE E: External pressures

items.q: What is the DECIDE model, and what does each letter stand for?
items.a: A six-step continuous decision loop: D for Detect a change has occurred, E for Estimate the need to counter the change, C for Choose a desirable outcome, I for Identify actions to control the change, D for Do take the necessary action, E for Evaluate the effect of the action. It is described in the FAA Risk Management Handbook and AC 60-22, Aeronautical Decision Making, and it repeats until the situation is resolved.
items.concept: DECIDE model for decision making and risk management

items.q: What is the first step of DECIDE, and why is it the one pilots miss?
items.a: Detect that a change has occurred. You cannot act on a problem you have not noticed, and most accident chains start with a cue that was present and unobserved, such as a slowly falling oil pressure, a ceiling coming down, or a fuel burn running ahead of plan. The defense is a deliberate scan and periodic cross-check of instruments, weather and fuel against the plan.
items.concept: DECIDE D: Detect a change has occurred

items.q: What is the second step of DECIDE?
items.a: Estimate the need to counter or react to the change. You judge how serious it is and whether it actually requires action, how much time you have, and what it threatens. Not every change needs a response, but assuming that it does not is how a minor deviation becomes an emergency.
items.concept: DECIDE E: Estimate the need to counter the change

items.q: What is the third step of DECIDE?
items.a: Choose a desirable outcome for the flight. Before you pick an action you decide what success now looks like, which may no longer be arriving at the planned destination. Setting the outcome first, for example 'a safe landing at a suitable airport within 30 minutes,' keeps the later options honest.
items.concept: DECIDE C: Choose what is the desired outcome

items.q: What is the fourth step of DECIDE?
items.a: Identify actions that could successfully control the change. You list the realistic options, for example continue, divert, hold, climb, descend, turn back, or declare an emergency, and weigh each against the outcome you chose. Generating more than one option is the point; a pilot who sees only one option has usually stopped thinking.
items.concept: DECIDE I: Identify the solutions

items.q: What is the fifth step of DECIDE?
items.a: Do take the necessary action. Commit and fly the chosen option, in the order aviate, navigate, communicate. Deciding and then not acting, or acting half way, is the common failure: a diversion begun late burns the margin that made it the safe choice.
items.concept: DECIDE D: Do the necessary actions

items.q: What is the sixth step of DECIDE, and what happens after it?
items.a: Evaluate the effect of the action. Did it fix the problem, and did it create a new one? The model is a loop, not a line, so evaluation feeds straight back into detecting the next change. This is also where you check that workload and fuel still support the new plan.
items.concept: DECIDE E: Evaluate the effects of the actions

items.q: How many holding patterns does 61.57(c) require you to fly?
items.a: The regulation does not say. It uses the plural, holding procedures and tasks, and gives no number, unlike the six approaches which are counted exactly. The conservative reading, and the one this guide takes, is more than one. Fly at least two entries from different directions inside the six month window and log them, and no examiner can argue with your record.
items.concept: The FAA does not specify how many holds are required, only more than one

items.q: What mnemonic covers the IFR recency requirements, and what does each letter stand for?
items.a: 6 HITS: 6 instrument approaches; H for holding procedures; I for intercepted a course; T for tracked a course; S for using navigational systems. The I, T and S run together as a single regulatory item, intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems, so the mnemonic expands three letters out of one requirement. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c).
items.concept: The 6 HITS mnemonic for the IFR recency requirements

items.q: May part of an instrument proficiency check be conducted in a training device?
items.a: Yes. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(d) allows certain tasks in an approved flight simulator, flight training device, or advanced aviation training device, within the limits of the rule and the device's letter of authorization. The check follows the instrument rating areas of operation and tasks in the airman certification standards, and the remaining tasks are flown in the aircraft.
items.concept: Some IPC tasks may be conducted in an Approved Aviation Training Device (AATD)

items.q: Who needs a third class medical certificate?
items.a: A third class medical is required for private pilot, student pilot and flight instructor privileges, and for recreational pilot privileges. A flight instructor needs one only when acting as pilot in command or as a required flight crewmember, and a sport pilot may use a valid U.S. driver's license instead. 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A (General), section 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration lists who must hold which class.
items.concept: Third class medical is required for Private Pilot, Flight Instructor or Student Pilot

items.q: You are being paid for the flight. What is the next question on the chart?
items.a: Who is providing the aircraft? The chart gives two answers. If the passenger provides the aircraft, I am selling only my piloting services and the flight stays a Part 91 operation. If I or a third party provide the aircraft, I am providing transportation as well as pilot skill, and I must work through the 119.1(e) list and the holding out question to see whether an operating certificate is required.
items.concept: Second decision box: Who is providing the aircraft?

items.q: Why does the passenger-provides-the-aircraft branch of the chart end at 'Part 91 Operation'?
items.a: Because I am furnishing only pilot services, not transportation, so Part 119 certification is never triggered and the flight is conducted under 14 CFR Part 91, 'General Operating and Flight Rules'. The chart groups the private pilot box, the instrument rating question and the piloting service requirements inside one shaded Part 91 block to show that all of them land in the same place.
items.concept: Passenger-supplied-aircraft branch ends at the Part 91 Operation block

items.q: Do published IFR takeoff minimums apply to you on a Part 91 flight?
items.a: No. Under 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, 91.175, 'Takeoff and landing under IFR', published takeoff minimums bind only operators who hold an operating certificate; a Part 91 pilot may legally depart in zero visibility. The chart puts 'IFR takeoff minimum does NOT apply' inside the Part 91 block and 'IFR takeoff minimum applies' under common carriage, so the contrast is the point. Legal is not the same as wise.
items.concept: Part 91 operations: IFR takeoff minimums do NOT apply

items.q: You are paid and you are supplying the airplane. Where does the chart send you next?
items.a: To the question 'Are you doing one of these things?', which points at the excepted operations list in 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, 119.1, 'Applicability', paragraph (e). Supplying both the aircraft and the pilot means I am furnishing transportation, so the chart now has to establish whether Part 119 certification is required or whether the job falls in one of the carve-outs.
items.concept: Branch: the aircraft comes from myself or a third party

items.q: Your flight is on the 119.1(e) list. What does the chart say happens next?
items.a: The chart says you potentially need a Letter of Approval, otherwise you are good to go. Most 119.1(e) operations need nothing more than a commercial certificate and a second class medical, but some, notably commercial air tours, require a letter of authorization from the FAA before the first flight. So being on the list clears you of Part 119 certification but not necessarily of all paperwork.
items.concept: 119.1(e) 'Yes' branch: potentially need a Letter of Approval

items.q: How far from the departure airport may a 119.1(e) commercial air tour go?
items.a: Within 25 statute miles of the departure airport. The chart lists the radius alongside the requirement that the flight begin and end in the same place. Note the chart uses statute miles here, not nautical miles. Go beyond that radius and the flight no longer fits the air tour exception in 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, 119.1, 'Applicability', paragraph (e).
items.concept: 119.1(e) item: commercial air tours within 25 statute miles

items.q: What paperwork does the chart show for a commercial air tour operation?
items.a: A letter of authorization from the FAA. Air tours are the chart's example of a 119.1(e) operation that is excepted from air carrier certification but still needs FAA approval before the first flight, which is why the chart's yes branch says 'potentially need a Letter of Approval.' The operator also falls under the national air tour safety standards.
items.concept: 119.1(e) item: commercial air tours need a letter of authorization

items.q: Your paid flight is not on the 119.1(e) list. What does the chart ask next?
items.a: Are you carrying people or property? This is the gate into the certificate-required side of the chart. If the answer is yes, I move on to the holding out question and then into Parts 121, 125, 129 or 135.
