Carrying persons or property for compensation is the second and third of the four elements of common carriage, so without it no air carrier rule can bite.
items.concept: 119.1(e) 'No' branch: Are you carrying people or property?

items.q: You carry people for hire but will not take just anyone. What does the chart ask then?
items.a: Whether the aircraft has 20 seats or greater, or a payload capacity of 6,000 pounds or greater. This question only appears on the no-holding-out branch, because it decides between Part 125 and Part 135 for private carriage. It is an either/or test: meeting either the seat threshold or the payload threshold is enough to push the operation into Part 125.
items.concept: Hold out = No leads to the 20 seat / 6,000 lb payload question

items.q: Private carriage in an airplane with fewer than 20 seats and under 6,000 lb payload falls under which part?
items.a: Part 135, and an operational certificate is required. The chart's no branch off the 20 seat / 6,000 pound question goes to 14 CFR Part 135, 'Operating Requirements: Commuter and On Demand Operations and Rules Governing Persons On Board Such Aircraft'. Most on demand charter in light twins and turboprops sits here, whether it is common or private carriage.
items.concept: Under 20 seats and under 6,000 lb payload, private carriage: Part 135

items.q: Which part governs a private carriage operation in a 20 seat airplane?
items.a: Part 125, and an operational certificate is required. The chart's yes branch off the 20 seat / 6,000 pound question points to 14 CFR Part 125, 'Certification and Operations: Airplanes Having a Seating Capacity of 20 or More Passengers or a Maximum Payload Capacity of 6,000 Pounds or More'. Part 125 exists precisely for large airplanes flown in noncommon carriage.
items.concept: 20 seats or more, or 6,000 lb payload or more, private carriage: Part 125

items.q: You are holding out to the public. What does the chart ask you next?
items.a: Scheduled? Once holding out is established the operation is common carriage, and the only remaining question is whether it runs to a published schedule. Yes sends me to Part 121, no sends me to Part 135. Either way an operational certificate is required and the published IFR takeoff minimums apply.
items.concept: Hold out = Yes leads to the Scheduled? question

items.q: Scheduled common carriage requires a certificate under which part?
items.a: Part 121. Scheduled operations holding out to the public fall under 14 CFR Part 121, 'Operating Requirements: Domestic, Flag, and Supplemental Operations', and an operational certificate is required. This is the airline branch of the chart: holding out, yes; scheduled, yes.
items.concept: Scheduled common carriage: Part 121 operational certificate required

items.q: Unscheduled common carriage requires a certificate under which part?
items.a: Part 135. Holding out to the public but flying on demand rather than to a schedule puts the operation under 14 CFR Part 135, 'Operating Requirements: Commuter and On Demand Operations and Rules Governing Persons On Board Such Aircraft'. This is the charter branch, and an operational certificate is required.
items.concept: Unscheduled common carriage: Part 135 operational certificate required

items.q: What operations fall under Part 129?
items.a: Foreign air carriers and foreign operators of U.S. registered airplanes engaged in common carriage. The rule is 14 CFR Part 129, 'Operations: Foreign Air Carriers and Foreign Operators of U.S.-Registered Aircraft Engaged in Common Carriage', and an operations specification is required. On the chart it hangs off the unscheduled side of the common carriage block alongside Part 135.
items.concept: Part 129 operational certificate: foreign air carriers and foreign operators of U.S. registered aircraft

items.q: When do published IFR takeoff minimums legally bind you?
items.a: When I am operating under an operating certificate - that is, in common carriage under Part 121, 125, 129 or 135. 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, 91.175, 'Takeoff and landing under IFR' imposes published takeoff minimums on certificate holders, while a Part 91 pilot is not bound by them. The chart contrasts the two blocks directly: Part 91 says does NOT apply, common carriage says applies.
items.concept: Common carriage: IFR takeoff minimums apply

items.q: On the chart, what happens if you are paid and supplying the airplane but carrying nothing and nobody?
items.a: The chart draws no exit at all for the no answer, because without persons or property there is nothing for Parts 121, 125, 129 or 135 to regulate. In practice the flight is a Part 91 operation: with no carriage of persons or property for compensation, two of the four elements of common carriage are missing and no operating certificate can be required.
items.concept: Flowchart detail the text does not show: the 'Are you carrying people or property?' box has no drawn No exit

items.q: How many certificate outcomes does the chart have, and what are they?
items.a: Four: Part 121 for scheduled common carriage; Part 135 for unscheduled common carriage and for private carriage below the size threshold; Part 125 for private carriage at or above 20 seats or 6,000 pounds payload; and Part 129 for foreign air carriers and foreign operators of U.S. registered airplanes. Note Part 135 is the only one the chart reaches by two different routes.
items.concept: Flowchart detail the text does not show: only four regulatory endpoints exist on the paid side

items.q: What is operational control?
items.a: The authority to initiate, conduct, or terminate a flight. Whoever holds operational control decides whether the flight goes, how it is conducted and when it stops, and therefore carries the regulatory responsibility for it. It is central to the carriage question because an illegal charter is usually one where the customer supplies the money but the pilot or operator quietly keeps operational control.
items.concept: Operational control defined

items.q: Which advisory circular explains what counts as compensation?
items.a: AC 61-142, 'Sharing Aircraft Operating Expenses in Accordance with 14 CFR 61.113(c)'. It sets out the FAA's very broad reading of compensation and explains how expense sharing by a private pilot differs from being compensated. It is the circular to cite when an examiner asks why accrued flight time or good will can amount to compensation.
items.concept: AC 61-142 is the reference for compensation

items.q: Does the FAA consider a profit motive to be compensation?
items.a: Yes. Profit or profit motive is one of the forms of compensation listed in AC 61-142. The intent to make money from the flight is itself enough; the FAA does not need to show that a profit was actually realized. This matters in cases where a pilot structures a flight hoping for business to follow even though no fee is charged for the flight itself.
items.concept: Compensation includes profit or profit motive

items.q: Does money have to change hands before the FAA calls something compensation?
items.a: No. AC 61-142 states plainly that the actual exchanging of funds is not required to be considered compensation. Free fuel, a free hotel room, a favor, future business or even flight time logged can all be compensation. The practical test the guide gives is whether the benefit is what would get you to do the flight when you otherwise would not.
items.concept: Actual exchange of funds is not required for compensation

items.q: What is 'good will' as a form of compensation?
items.a: Expected future economic benefit - flying someone for nothing now in the hope of business, a job, a referral or a favorable relationship later. AC 61-142, 'Sharing Aircraft Operating Expenses in Accordance with 14 CFR 61.113(c)' names good will as compensation, which is why a private pilot flying clients or potential customers for free can still be in violation of 61.113.
items.concept: Compensation includes good will in the form of expected future economic benefits

items.q: Can logging flight time itself be compensation?
items.a: Yes - in certain situations. AC 61-142 states that accruing flight time can be considered compensation, because the hours have real economic value to a pilot building toward a rating or a job. This is the reason a pilot cannot simply offer to fly somebody's airplane somewhere for free just to log the time, and why certain 'free' ferry flights are scrutinized.
items.concept: Accruing flight time can be compensation

items.q: What if the benefit from the flight goes to someone other than you?
items.a: It can still be compensation. AC 61-142 lists value for a third party recipient as a form of compensation, so a benefit flowing to an employer, a charity, a business partner or a family member counts just as if it had come to me directly. The FAA follows the value, not the name on the check.
items.concept: Compensation includes value for a third party recipient

items.q: Give the one-sentence rule of thumb for recognizing compensation.
items.a: Basically anything that would get you to do the flight when you otherwise would not can be considered compensation in the eyes of the FAA. That is the note the guide ends the compensation box with, and it is the safest working test for an oral exam. If a benefit is the reason the flight is happening, assume the FAA will call it compensation.
items.concept: The practical test: anything that would get you to do the flight when you otherwise would not

items.q: Where are the aircraft accident reporting rules actually written?
items.a: In 49 CFR Part 830, Notification and Reporting of Aircraft Accidents or Incidents and Overdue Aircraft, and Preservation of Aircraft Wreckage, Mail, Cargo, and Records. It is an NTSB rule in Title 49, not a Federal Aviation Regulation in Title 14. The AIM summarizes the same material under safety of flight, which is a fine place to look it up in the airplane, but the rule itself is 49 CFR Part 830.

items.q: Who writes Part 830 and who does it apply to?
items.a: The National Transportation Safety Board writes it, and it applies to the operator of any civil aircraft, and to certain public aircraft, within the United States and its territories. The duty to notify and to report falls on the operator, not on the FAA and not on the airport. On a rental or a flight you are conducting under Part 91, that is you as pilot in command and the owner between you; decide beforehand who makes the call.

items.q: Give me the Part 830 definition of an aircraft accident.
items.a: An occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft that takes place between the time any person boards the aircraft with the intention of flight and the time all such persons have disembarked, in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage. Three triggers only: death, serious injury, substantial damage. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions.

items.q: What is an incident, as Part 830 uses the word?
items.a: An occurrence other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operations. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. Every accident is also an occurrence affecting safety, but the word incident is reserved for the ones that fall short of death, serious injury or substantial damage. Only the listed incidents in 830.5 require immediate notification.

items.q: What is a fatal injury under Part 830, and why does the definition matter?
items.a: Any injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident, per 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. It matters because an occurrence that was classified as an incident on the day it happened becomes an accident if an injured person dies inside that 30-day window, and the reporting obligation follows the reclassification.

items.q: List the serious injuries in 49 CFR 830.2.
items.a: Any injury that requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours beginning within 7 days of the injury; a fracture of any bone except simple fractures of fingers, toes or the nose; severe hemorrhage or nerve, muscle or tendon damage; injury to any internal organ; or second or third degree burns, or any burn affecting more than 5 percent of the body surface. Any one of the five makes the occurrence an accident.

items.q: A passenger breaks a finger getting out of the airplane after a hard landing. Accident?
items.a: No. A simple fracture of a finger, toe or nose is expressly carved out of the serious injury definition in 49 CFR 830.2, so that injury alone does not make it an accident. Check the other two triggers before you relax: if the hard landing also caused substantial damage, it is an accident on that ground, and if the person is hospitalized more than 48 hours it is an accident on that ground.

items.q: Define substantial damage.
items.a: Damage or failure that adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft and would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. Note that it is a two-part test: the damage has to matter to the airplane's structure or how it flies, and it has to call for major repair or replacement.

items.q: What does Part 830 explicitly say is not substantial damage?
items.a: Engine failure or damage limited to an engine if only one engine is damaged; bent fairings or cowling; dented skin; small punctured holes in the skin or fabric; ground damage to rotor or propeller blades; and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. That exclusion list is what makes most light airplane mishaps incidents rather than accidents.

items.q: You clip a runway light on landing. Is that reportable? Work it out for me.
items.a: Start with the accident definition in 49 CFR 830.2. Was anyone killed or seriously injured? No. Did the airplane receive substantial damage? A scuffed wheel pant, a nicked tire or a bent gear leg is on the express exclusion list, so it is not substantial damage. On those facts it is an incident, not an accident, and nothing in 830.5 requires immediate notification, so there is no NTSB report unless the Board asks for one.

items.q: Same runway light, but the strike buckles the firewall and wrinkles the skin behind it. Now?
items.a: Now it is an accident. Buckled structure affects the structural strength of the airframe and normally requires major repair or replacement, which is squarely the substantial damage definition in 49 CFR 830.2. That makes it an accident, which means immediate notification of the nearest NTSB office under 830.5, preservation of the wreckage under 830.10, and a written report within 10 days under 830.15.

items.q: The runway light you hit turns out to cost the airport $40,000 to repair. Does that change anything?
items.a: Yes. 49 CFR 830.5, Immediate notification, lists damage to property other than the aircraft estimated to exceed $25,000 for repair, or fair market value in the event of total loss, whichever is less. Above that figure you must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately even though the occurrence is only an incident, and you file a written report only if the Board requests one.

items.q: What is the honest short answer on whether hitting a runway light is reportable?
items.a: That it depends, and here is the test. It is reportable as an accident only if someone was killed or seriously injured or the airplane took substantial damage, and gear, wheels, tires, flaps and wingtips are excluded from substantial damage by name. It is reportable as a listed incident if the damage to the light and its cabling exceeds $25,000. Otherwise you tell the airport and the operator, and nobody files with the NTSB.

items.q: Run the 49 CFR 830.5 immediate notification list for me.
items.a: Any accident, plus these incidents: flight control system malfunction or failure; inability of any required flight crewmember to perform duties because of injury or illness; turbine engine failure releasing debris other than out the exhaust; in-flight fire; in-flight collision; property damage other than the aircraft over $25,000; release of a propeller blade other than by ground contact; loss of more than half the cockpit displays; and an overdue aircraft believed to have been in an accident.

items.q: Who exactly do you notify after an accident, and how fast?
items.a: The operator must notify the nearest NTSB field office immediately and by the most expeditious means available, per 49 CFR 830.5. In practice that is a phone call; the NTSB publishes a 24-hour number and field office list, and a call to ATC or to the FSDO does not discharge the obligation even though both will certainly find out. Have the number in your flight bag, not on a website you cannot reach from a field.

items.q: What information does the NTSB want in that first notification?
items.a: 49 CFR 830.6 lists it: aircraft type, nationality and registration marks; names of the owner and operator; name of the pilot in command; date and time; last point of departure and intended point of landing; position with reference to an easily defined geographic point; number aboard, number killed and number seriously injured; nature of the accident, the weather and the extent of damage so far as known; and a description of any explosives, radioactive materials or other dangerous articles carried.

items.q: When is a written report due, and on what form?
items.a: Within 10 days after an accident the operator files NTSB Form 6120.1 with the Board, per 49 CFR 830.15, Reports. If an aircraft was overdue and is still missing, the report goes in after 7 days. For an incident, even one that required immediate notification, a written report is filed only when an authorized representative of the Board requests one.

items.q: Does reporting to the NTSB take care of your obligation to the FAA?
items.a: No, they are separate. Part 830 is the NTSB's rule. Separately, 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, says that a pilot who deviates from a rule in an emergency must send a written report to the Administrator on request. The FAA may also open its own inquiry into airman and airworthiness issues, and a NASA ASRS report, filed within 10 days, is a separate voluntary action again.

items.q: What is a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit?
items.a: An operator permit for the person using an aircraft radio station, issued by the Federal Communications Commission, not the FAA, under 47 CFR Part 87, Aviation Services. It is a lifetime permit, it is held by the pilot rather than by the airplane, and it has nothing to do with your pilot certificate or medical. It is form FCC 605 and it is granted without a test.

items.q: When do you actually need a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit?
items.a: For international operations. A pilot flying outside the United States, or operating an aircraft radio station on an international flight, needs the permit, and that is why it is on the list for a trip to the Bahamas, Canada or Mexico. It is not required for domestic flight within the United States, so it does not belong on the list of what you must have on your person to fly locally.

items.q: Who issues the permit, how long is it good for, and what does it cost you to keep?
items.a: The FCC issues it under 47 CFR Part 87, Aviation Services. It is valid for the lifetime of the holder and there is nothing to renew, no examination and no recurrent requirement. Because there is no expiry and no test, a pilot who does any international flying should simply get one and put it in the flight bag rather than try to time it against a trip.

items.q: What is the difference between the operator permit and the aircraft radio station license?
items.a: The permit belongs to the person operating the radio; the station license belongs to the aircraft and is also issued by the FCC. On an international flight you need both: the airplane must hold a current aircraft radio station license and the pilot must hold the restricted operator permit. Domestically, neither is required of a U.S.-registered aircraft operating within the United States.

items.q: How do you tell who has operational control in a real arrangement?
items.a: Look at the decisions and the money, not the labels. Who decides whether the flight launches and whether to divert or cancel? Who selects, hires and pays the crew? Who holds the aircraft's maintenance responsibility and the insurance? Who bears the financial risk and takes the profit? The party that initiates, conducts and terminates the flight has operational control, whatever the contract calls itself.

items.q: Why is operational control the hinge question in any lease or rental scenario?
items.a: Because it decides which operating rule applies. If the customer has operational control and you are merely a hired pilot, the flight is Part 91 and your commercial certificate is enough. If you have operational control and you are also furnishing the aircraft for compensation, you are holding yourself out as an air carrier and the flight needs a certificate under Part 119 and operations under Part 135.

items.q: A customer who is not a pilot hires you to fly his own airplane. Legal on a commercial certificate?
items.a: Yes. You are providing pilot services only; the customer provides the aircraft and keeps operational control, so it is a Part 91 flight and 14 CFR 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations, lets you be paid for it. Confirm the practical items: that you are named on his insurance, that you meet the policy's open pilot requirements, that you are current and qualified in type, and that the airplane is airworthy.

items.q: You arrive and the owner's airplane is leaking oil and is not airworthy. He offers to rent one instead. May you fly it?
items.a: Maybe, and the question to ask is who will have operational control of the rented airplane. If the customer rents it in his own name, satisfies the FBO's requirements and still decides the flight, you remain a hired pilot on a Part 91 flight. If you rent it and then carry him for compensation, you are supplying both the aircraft and the crew for hire, which is carriage for hire and needs a Part 119 certificate.

items.q: Why can't the customer simply rent the airplane and hand you the keys?
items.a: Because the rental agreement usually will not let him. Most FBOs will only rent to a pilot who has been checked out and is named on the policy, and your customer is not a pilot. If the FBO rents to him anyway, read the agreement: if it requires that the FBO approve the pilot, or if the FBO is really furnishing aircraft and crew together, the FBO may be the one holding operational control, and now it is their certificate problem.

items.q: What is a dry lease?
items.a: A lease of the aircraft alone, with no crew. The lessee takes possession of the airplane and holds operational control, provides or hires the pilots himself, and operates under Part 91 if the operation otherwise qualifies. A genuine dry lease is the normal, legal way for a non-pilot owner or a company to put an airplane and a hired pilot together without needing an air carrier certificate.

items.q: What is a wet lease?
items.a: 14 CFR 110.2, Definitions, defines a wet lease as any leasing arrangement whereby a person agrees to provide an entire aircraft and at least one crewmember. Providing aircraft and crew together for compensation is carriage for hire, so a wet lease by someone without a Part 119 certificate is an illegal charter no matter what the paperwork calls it. The common dodge is a dry lease on paper with the lessor quietly supplying the pilot.

items.q: What makes a 'dry lease' a sham in the FAA's eyes?
items.a: When the paperwork says dry but the lessor keeps control of who flies, when it flies and whether it goes. Warning signs: the lessor supplies or approves the pilot, the lessor schedules and dispatches, the lessee pays a per-hour price that looks like a charter rate, the lessee never sees the maintenance decisions, and the lessee could not operate the airplane without the lessor's organization. The FAA looks at substance, not titles.

items.q: Does a truth-in-leasing clause apply to a Warrior lease?
items.a: No. 14 CFR 91.23, Truth-in-leasing clause requirement in leases and conditional sales contracts, applies to large civil aircraft, meaning more than 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight. Your airplane is far below that. It is still worth knowing, because 91.23 is the rule that forces a lease to state who is responsible for operational control and for compliance, which is exactly the question you have to answer anyway.

items.q: The scenario keeps getting more complicated. What is the right professional answer?
items.a: To say out loud that the arrangement has become complex enough that I am not certain which rule applies, and then to decline the flight or get official guidance from the FSDO before flying it. An inspector will answer a question like this in writing. Guessing costs you a certificate; asking costs you a phone call, and a customer who will not wait for the answer is telling you something about the trip.

items.q: Why is 'I am only the pilot' not a defense if the operation turns out to be an illegal charter?
items.a: Because 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, makes you directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft, and enforcement actions in illegal charter cases routinely reach the pilot as well as the operator. You are the one who must determine which part you are operating under before you launch; nobody else on the ramp is going to do it for you.

items.q: What questions do you ask the customer before you accept a job like this?
items.a: Who owns or is renting the airplane and in whose name; who is paying for the airplane and who is paying me; who decides whether the flight goes and where; who is responsible for maintenance and for the airworthiness determination; am I named on the insurance and what are the open pilot requirements; and is there a written agreement I can read. If any answer is vague, the answer to the flight is not yet.

items.q: What does the regulation actually require you to brief your passengers on?
items.a: Less than you think. 14 CFR 91.107, Use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, and child restraint systems, requires the pilot in command to ensure each person aboard has been briefed on how to fasten and unfasten that person's safety belt and shoulder harness, and to notify them to fasten them before taxi, before takeoff and before landing. For a light Part 91 airplane that is the whole legal requirement.

items.q: If the rule only requires belts, why give a full briefing?
items.a: Because the rule is a floor and the passengers are your responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3. A passenger who does not know how to open the door, where the fire extinguisher is or that he should speak up about traffic is a liability in the one minute when it matters. A paying passenger is also judging your professionalism from the briefing, and on a checkride the examiner is the client and is grading exactly that.

items.q: Give me the SAFETY briefing.
items.a: S, seat belts, shoulder harnesses and seat adjustment, how to fasten and unfasten them. A, air vents, environmental controls and air sickness bags. F, fire extinguisher, where it is and how to use it. E, exits and emergency equipment, including the ELT and survival kit. T, traffic, talking and the sterile cockpit. Y, your questions. It is the standard content; 91.107 only compels the S.

items.q: What does the E of SAFETY cover in a Warrior specifically?
items.a: That there is one cabin door, on the right side, how the handle and the latch work, and that a passenger in the right seat may be the one who has to open it; where the emergency locator transmitter is and that it works automatically; where any survival gear and first aid kit are stowed; and that if we land off airport the plan is to get out, get clear of the airplane and stay together near it.

items.q: What else belongs in the briefing that SAFETY does not spell out?
items.a: The plan for the flight and what the passenger should expect: route, time, altitude, what the airplane will sound and feel like, and anything unusual such as stalls or steep turns. Smoking, loose articles, electronic devices, and not touching the controls. What to do if I become incapacitated: hold the wings level, press the push-to-talk and say mayday on the frequency. And that the passenger may always say he is uncomfortable.

items.q: How does the briefing change when the passenger is paying you?
items.a: It becomes part of the service rather than a ritual. Brief before boarding, calmly and without jargon; explain what you will be doing and why; set expectations about weather, timing and your authority to divert or cancel; and make clear the decisions are yours. A customer who hears the no-go criteria before the flight is far easier to turn around mid-trip. Then repeat the operational items, belts and exits, at the airplane.

items.q: Why does the currency and proficiency gap matter more once you fly for hire?
items.a: Because you will be asked to fly airplanes, routes, weather and schedules you did not choose, and the people paying you will assume that legal means competent. A commercial certificate raises the standard the public expects without changing the recency rules at all. The professional response is a personal currency standard tighter than the regulation, plus the willingness to say that you are legal but not proficient for a particular trip.

b: Documents, inspections, equipment, and what makes the airplane legal to fly.

items.q: What does ARROW stand for, and what requires those documents to be aboard?
items.a: Airworthiness certificate, Registration certificate, Radio station license (international flights only), Operating limitations, and Weight and balance data. 14 CFR 91.203 (Part 91, Subpart C — Civil aircraft: Certifications required) requires the airworthiness and registration certificates; 14 CFR 91.9 (Part 91, Subpart A — Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements) requires the operating limitations.

items.q: Does the airworthiness certificate expire, and what keeps it valid?
items.a: It has no expiry date. Under 14 CFR 21.181 (Part 21, Subpart H — Airworthiness Certificates; Duration), a standard airworthiness certificate stays effective as long as required maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations are performed in accordance with Parts 43 and 91, and the aircraft remains registered in the United States. Miss an inspection and the certificate is not valid, even though the paper looks the same.

items.q: Where must the airworthiness certificate be displayed?
items.a: At the cabin or cockpit entrance, so that it is legible to passengers or crew. 14 CFR 91.203(b) (Part 91, Subpart C — Civil aircraft: Certifications required) is explicit that it must be displayed, not merely carried — unlike the registration certificate, which need only be aboard.

items.q: What two things does an airworthiness certificate attest to?
items.a: That the aircraft conforms to its type certificate — including any supplemental type certificates and applicable airworthiness directives — and that it is in a condition for safe operation. Both must be true at the moment of flight. 14 CFR 91.7 (Part 91, Subpart A — Civil aircraft airworthiness) makes the pilot in command responsible for determining that the aircraft is in condition for safe flight.

items.q: What is a standard airworthiness certificate, and which aircraft get one?
items.a: FAA Form 8100-2, printed on white paper. It is issued to aircraft type certificated in the normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter or transport categories, and to manned free balloons and certain special classes. It is the certificate on essentially every production airplane a commercial pilot will fly, and it is issued under 14 CFR 21.183 (Part 21, Subpart H — Airworthiness Certificates). In the aircraft certification sense class is the broader term, meaning airplane, rotorcraft, glider or balloon, and category the narrower one, so the two words are used in the opposite sense from a pilot certificate.

items.q: What is a special airworthiness certificate, and which categories fall under it?
items.a: FAA Form 8130-7, printed on pink paper. It covers the primary, restricted, limited, light-sport and provisional categories, plus special flight permits and experimental certificates. These aircraft carry operating limitations a standard-category airplane does not — restricted category aircraft, for example, may not carry persons or property for hire.

items.q: What is an experimental airworthiness certificate?
items.a: A special airworthiness certificate issued to an aircraft that does not have a type certificate or does not conform to one — amateur-built aircraft assembled without the supervision of a production certificate holder, exhibition aircraft, racing aircraft, and aircraft used for research and development or crew training. It comes with operating limitations issued with it, and those limitations are part of the required documents aboard.

items.q: What is an airworthiness directive, and is compliance optional?
items.a: A legally enforceable rule issued by the FAA under Part 39 (Airworthiness Directives) to correct an unsafe condition in a product. Compliance is mandatory. 14 CFR 39.7 makes operating a product that does not meet an applicable AD a violation, and 14 CFR 91.403 (Part 91, Subpart E — Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations; General) makes the owner or operator responsible for ensuring compliance.

items.q: What is the difference between an emergency and a non-emergency airworthiness directive?
items.a: An emergency AD requires immediate compliance — often before further flight — and is issued without the usual notice and comment period because the unsafe condition is urgent. A non-emergency AD specifies a compliance time: a number of flight hours, a calendar period, or by the next scheduled inspection. Both are issued under Part 39 (Airworthiness Directives) and both are mandatory.

items.q: What is the difference between a recurring and a one-time airworthiness directive?
items.a: A one-time AD is complied with once — an inspection or a part replacement — and the aircraft is then permanently in compliance. A recurring AD must be repeated at a stated interval, such as every 100 hours or every 12 calendar months, and remains an open item in the maintenance records forever. Both are issued under Part 39 (Airworthiness Directives).

items.q: Who is responsible for making sure airworthiness directives have been complied with?
items.a: The owner or operator, under 14 CFR 91.403 (Part 91, Subpart E — Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations; General). The pilot in command carries a separate duty under 14 CFR 91.7 (Part 91, Subpart A — Civil aircraft airworthiness) to determine the aircraft is airworthy before flight, so as a renter or hired pilot you should check the AD compliance record along with the inspection entries.

items.q: What is a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin?
items.a: A non-regulatory FAA notice alerting owners, operators and mechanics to a safety concern that is not serious enough to justify an airworthiness directive. A SAIB may recommend an inspection or a modification, but there is no legal obligation to comply. If the FAA later concludes the condition is unsafe, the subject of a SAIB can become an AD.

items.q: How long is an aircraft registration certificate valid?
items.a: Seven years — it expires on the last day of the month, seven years after the month in which it was issued. The FAA extended the duration from three years to seven with a rule effective in January 2023, and existing registrations were extended accordingly. Registration is required by 14 CFR 91.203 (Part 91, Subpart C — Civil aircraft: Certifications required) and governed by Part 47 (Aircraft Registration).

items.q: Can you fly on a temporary registration, and for how long?
items.a: Yes. The pink temporary authorization copy of the registration application, AC Form 8050-1, authorizes operation for 90 days while the permanent certificate is processed, and it is valid only for flight within the United States. Part 47 (Aircraft Registration) governs; an international flight needs the permanent certificate.

items.q: What events terminate an aircraft registration before its normal expiry?
items.a: Sale or transfer of ownership; registration of the aircraft in a foreign country; a change of the aircraft's registration number; destruction or scrapping of the aircraft; cancellation at the owner's written request; and the holder losing United States citizenship without qualifying under one of the alternatives in Part 47 (Aircraft Registration). Any of these ends the registration, and without a valid registration the airworthiness certificate is not effective either.

items.q: When is an FCC radio station license required?
items.a: Only when the aircraft is operated outside the United States or communicates with foreign stations. The FCC dropped the requirement for purely domestic flights in 1996. For international operations the aircraft needs an FCC Aircraft Radio Station License and the pilot needs a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit. It is the R in ARROW that most often does not apply.

items.q: What counts as the operating limitations, and where do you find them?
items.a: The FAA-approved Airplane Flight Manual or the approved section of the Pilot's Operating Handbook for that specific airplane and serial number, together with placards, instrument markings and any supplements for installed equipment. 14 CFR 91.9 (Part 91, Subpart A — Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements) requires them aboard and forbids operating outside them.

items.q: What is the difference between an AFM, a POH and a PIM?
items.a: The AFM is the FAA-approved flight manual, and the approved sections are legally binding. The POH is the manufacturer's handbook for a specific airplane, containing the approved AFM material plus non-approved advisory material. The PIM, Pilot's Information Manual, is the generic model-wide publication sold as a reference — it is not serial-number specific and does not satisfy 14 CFR 91.9. Always read limitations from the airplane's own POH or AFM.

items.q: What weight and balance data must be in the airplane, and who produces it?
items.a: The current weight and balance record — empty weight, empty weight center of gravity, useful load and the equipment list — as revised after any change to the equipment fit. It is prepared and signed by a certificated mechanic or repair station whenever equipment is added or removed. Read the loading limits and arms from the POH or AFM for the aircraft being flown; they differ airplane to airplane even within a model.

items.q: Who is responsible for keeping an aircraft airworthy, and who decides it is airworthy today?
items.a: The owner or operator is responsible for maintaining the aircraft in airworthy condition, under 14 CFR 91.403 (Part 91, Subpart E — Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations; General). The pilot in command is responsible for determining before each flight that the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, under 14 CFR 91.7 (Part 91, Subpart A — Civil aircraft airworthiness), and must discontinue the flight if an unairworthy condition occurs.

items.q: How are inspections and maintenance tracked, and how long must the records be kept?
items.a: In the aircraft, engine and propeller maintenance records or logbooks, often kept in a tracking system such as ADLOG. Under 14 CFR 91.417 (Part 91, Subpart E — Maintenance records), records of maintenance and preventive maintenance are kept for 1 year or until the work is repeated or superseded, while total time in service, current AD status, current inspection status and major alteration records are kept permanently and transferred with the aircraft on sale.

items.q: What is the annual inspection requirement, and who may perform it?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.409(a) (Part 91, Subpart E — Inspections), no person may operate an aircraft unless within the preceding 12 calendar months it has had an annual inspection and been approved for return to service. It must be performed and approved by a certificated airframe and powerplant mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization, or by a certificated repair station or the manufacturer.

items.q: When is a 100-hour inspection required?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.409(b) (Part 91, Subpart E — Inspections), when the aircraft carries any person other than a crewmember for hire, or is given flight instruction for hire — and in the flight instruction case only if the operator provides the aircraft as well as the instruction. It applies to aircraft of 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight or less. It is required in addition to the annual, not instead of it.

items.q: By how much may a 100-hour inspection be overflown, and what does that do to the next one?
items.a: By not more than 10 hours, and only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done. 14 CFR 91.409(b) (Part 91, Subpart E — Inspections) then requires the excess time to be included in computing the next 100 hours — so if you fly 6 hours over, the next inspection is due at 94 hours, not 100. You may not overfly it simply for convenience or to finish a training day.

items.q: What is the difference between an annual and a 100-hour inspection?
items.a: The scope is identical; who signs it and when it is required differ. The annual is required every 12 calendar months for every aircraft under 14 CFR 91.409(a) and must be signed by a mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization. The 100-hour is required under 91.409(b) only when carrying persons for hire or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides, and any A&P may sign it. An annual counts as a 100-hour; a 100-hour never counts as an annual.

items.q: Can an annual inspection count as a 100-hour, or a 100-hour as an annual?
items.a: An annual satisfies a 100-hour and resets the 100-hour clock, because it is the same inspection done by a more highly qualified person. A 100-hour never counts as an annual, because the mechanic performing it need not hold an Inspection Authorization. 14 CFR 91.409 (Part 91, Subpart E — Inspections) is the authority.

items.q: What is a progressive inspection?
items.a: An FAA-approved program under 14 CFR 91.409(d) (Part 91, Subpart E — Inspections) that breaks the annual inspection into routine and detailed segments spread across the year, so the airplane is never down for long. The owner must submit a written request to the responsible Flight Standards office, provide a current inspection procedures manual, adequate housing and facilities and current technical data, and have it supervised by an IA holder, an appropriately rated repair station or the manufacturer. The complete aircraft must be inspected within each 12 calendar months.

items.q: What is the altimeter, static system and altitude reporting inspection requirement?
items.a: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system must have been tested and inspected in accordance with Part 43 Appendix E. 14 CFR 91.411 (Part 91, Subpart E — Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections) requires it before operating an airplane in controlled airspace under IFR. Pure VFR operation does not require it.

items.q: Who may perform the altimeter and static system tests?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.411(b) (Part 91, Subpart E — Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections): the manufacturer of the aircraft or of the tested instrument, a certificated repair station with the appropriate rating, or a certificated mechanic with an airframe rating — but the mechanic may perform the static system test only, not the altimeter or the encoder correspondence test.

items.q: What is the transponder inspection requirement, and does it apply to VFR flight?
items.a: Within the preceding 24 calendar months the transponder must have been tested and inspected in accordance with Part 43 Appendix F. 14 CFR 91.413 (Part 91, Subpart E — ATC transponder tests and inspections) applies whenever the transponder is used, VFR or IFR — so unlike the altimeter check, it is not an IFR-only requirement. 14 CFR 91.215 (Part 91, Subpart C — ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use) says where a transponder must be used.

items.q: Who may perform the transponder test and inspection?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.413(c) (Part 91, Subpart E — ATC transponder tests and inspections): a certificated repair station with the appropriate rating, a holder of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program under Part 121 or 135, or the manufacturer of the aircraft on which the transponder is installed if the transponder was installed by that manufacturer. A mechanic with an airframe rating may not sign off the transponder check.

items.q: How often must an emergency locator transmitter be inspected?
items.a: Within each 12 calendar months. Under 14 CFR 91.207(d) (Part 91, Subpart C — Emergency locator transmitters), the inspection covers proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and the crash sensor, and the presence of a sufficient signal radiated from its antenna. The inspection must be recorded in the aircraft maintenance record.

items.q: When must an ELT battery be replaced or recharged?
items.a: When the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life — or, for a rechargeable battery, 50 percent of its useful life of charge — has expired. 14 CFR 91.207(c) (Part 91, Subpart C — Emergency locator transmitters) also requires the new expiry date to be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the aircraft maintenance record.

items.q: When may an airplane be flown without an ELT installed?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.207(e) (Part 91, Subpart C — Emergency locator transmitters) allows up to 90 days with the ELT temporarily removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement, provided a placard is visible to the pilot and a record entry is made stating the date of removal, the reason and the aircraft's registration. 91.207(f) lists further exceptions, including training flights within 50 nautical miles of the departure airport and agricultural operations.

items.q: When must a VOR receiver have been checked, and for what kind of flying?
items.a: Within the preceding 30 days, and only if the VOR is to be used as a means of navigation under IFR. 14 CFR 91.171 (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations) is the rule. Purely VFR use of a VOR needs no check, and an airplane navigating IFR entirely by an approved GPS is not caught by it either.

items.q: What is the tolerance for a dual VOR check?
items.a: Plus or minus 4 degrees between the two indicated bearings to the same VOR. Under 14 CFR 91.171(c) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations), the two systems must be tuned to the same station and, with each using its own antenna where possible, the maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings is 4 degrees.

items.q: What is the tolerance for a VOT check, and how is it flown?
items.a: Plus or minus 4 degrees. Under 14 CFR 91.171(b)(1) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations) you tune the VOT frequency on the ground and the receiver should read 180 degrees TO or 360 degrees FROM, with the course deviation indicator centered. VOT locations and frequencies are published in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: What is the tolerance for a VOR ground checkpoint?
items.a: Plus or minus 4 degrees of the certified radial published for that checkpoint. 14 CFR 91.171(b)(3) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations) permits the use of a ground checkpoint designated by the Administrator and located on the airport surface; the checkpoints and their radials are listed in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: What is the tolerance for an airborne VOR checkpoint?
items.a: Plus or minus 6 degrees of the designated radial. 14 CFR 91.171(b)(4) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations) allows an airborne checkpoint designated by the Administrator. The wider tolerance reflects the difficulty of holding position accurately in flight compared with sitting on a painted spot on the ramp.

items.q: If no VOT or designated checkpoint is available, how may you check a VOR in the air?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.171(b)(5) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations), select a VOR radial that lies along the centerline of an established VOR airway, fly over a prominent ground point on that centerline more than 20 nautical miles from the VOR, at a reasonably low altitude, and note the bearing indicated. The permissible variation is plus or minus 6 degrees.

items.q: Can a repair station perform a VOR check, and to what tolerance?
items.a: Yes. Under 14 CFR 91.171(b)(2) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations), a certificated repair station may use a radiated test signal, and the maximum permissible bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees. The test signal must be radiated only by a repair station holding the appropriate rating and authorized by the FAA to do so.

items.q: What must be recorded after a VOR check, and where?
items.a: Four things: the date, the place, the bearing error, and the signature of the person making the check. 14 CFR 91.171(d) (Part 91, Subpart C — VOR equipment check for IFR operations) requires the entry in the aircraft log or other reliable record. The pilot may perform the check and sign the entry — no mechanic certificate is needed for any method except the repair station radiated signal.

items.q: Who may perform maintenance on an aircraft?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 43.3 (Part 43 — Persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations): the holder of a mechanic certificate, the holder of a repairman certificate, a certificated repair station, an air carrier with an approved maintenance program, the manufacturer in limited circumstances, a person working under the supervision of a certificated mechanic or repairman, and a pilot for preventive maintenance only.

items.q: Who may approve an aircraft for return to service after maintenance?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 43.7 (Part 43 — Persons authorized to approve aircraft for return to service): a certificated mechanic for maintenance and preventive maintenance; a mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization for an annual inspection or a major repair or major alteration; a certificated repair station within its ratings; the manufacturer for work it is authorized to do; and a pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate for the preventive maintenance that pilot performed under 43.3(g).

items.q: What must a maintenance record entry contain?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 43.9 (Part 43 — Content, form, and disposition of maintenance records): a description of the work performed or a reference to acceptable data; the date of completion; the name of the person who did the work if different from the person approving it; and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving the aircraft for return to service. The signature constitutes the approval.

items.q: What is a minimum equipment list, and what does operating with one require?
items.a: An FAA-approved, aircraft-specific document listing the instruments, equipment and procedures that allow the airplane to be dispatched with items inoperative under stated conditions and limitations. Under 14 CFR 91.213(a) (Part 91, Subpart C — Inoperative instruments and equipment) you need an approved MEL developed from the FAA master MEL for the type, plus a letter of authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office, and both must be carried in the aircraft.

items.q: What is the legal status of the MEL and the letter of authorization together?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.213(a) (Part 91, Subpart C — Inoperative instruments and equipment) states that the MEL and the letter of authorization constitute a supplemental type certificate for the aircraft. The letter of authorization becomes part of the aircraft flight manual, so operating outside the MEL's conditions is operating outside the approved configuration — not merely a paperwork lapse.

items.q: What else does the MEL itself have to contain to be usable?
items.a: It must be no less restrictive than the FAA master MEL for that aircraft type, and it must contain both the operational and the maintenance procedures — the O and M procedures — needed to fly with the item inoperative. Under 14 CFR 91.213(a) (Part 91, Subpart C — Inoperative instruments and equipment) the inoperative item must be placarded, recorded in the aircraft maintenance records, and repaired within the repair category interval assigned to it.

items.q: What are the MEL repair categories, and how long does each allow?
items.a: Category A: repaired within the interval specified in the remarks column of that MEL item. Category B: 3 consecutive calendar days. Category C: 10 consecutive calendar days. Category D: 120 consecutive calendar days. The clock starts at the end of the day the item was recorded, and running out of the interval grounds the aircraft until the item is fixed or a short-term extension is authorized.

items.q: Which aircraft typically have a MEL, and which use the alternative route?
items.a: MELs are generally developed for turbine-powered aircraft and aircraft over 12,500 pounds, and for commercial fleets under Part 121 and 135, because an FAA master MEL exists for the type and the operator wants dispatch flexibility. Small piston airplanes flown under Part 91 usually have no MEL and rely instead on 14 CFR 91.213(d) (Part 91, Subpart C — Inoperative instruments and equipment).

items.q: Without a MEL, how do you legally fly a small airplane with an inoperative item?
items.a: Follow the four tests in 14 CFR 91.213(d) (Part 91, Subpart C — Inoperative instruments and equipment). The inoperative item must not be part of the VFR-day type certification instrument and equipment list, not listed on the aircraft's own equipment list or kinds of operations equipment list, not required by 14 CFR 91.205 for the kind of flight, and not required by an airworthiness directive. It applies only to non-turbine-powered small airplanes, rotorcraft, gliders and lighter-than-air aircraft operated under Part 91.

items.q: Once the item passes the 91.213(d) tests, what must be done before you fly?
items.a: It must be removed and the cockpit control placarded and the removal recorded under 14 CFR 43.9, or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative". Then a pilot or an appropriately rated maintenance person must determine that the inoperative item does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft. Deactivation that involves maintenance must be done by a person authorized under Part 43. 14 CFR 91.213(d) is the authority.

items.q: What is the practical difference between operating under a MEL and operating under 91.213(d)?
items.a: A MEL is permissive: it lists what may be inoperative, with repair intervals, placarding and required procedures, and it is a supplemental type certificate you must comply with exactly. 91.213(d) is a test you apply item by item, with no approved list, no repair interval and a pilot judgment about hazard. If an airplane has an approved MEL, you must use it — you cannot fall back on 91.213(d) instead.

items.q: What is a special flight permit, and when is one used?
items.a: A ferry permit — a special airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR 21.197 (Part 21, Subpart H — Airworthiness Certificates; Special flight permits) issued for an aircraft that does not currently meet applicable airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight. You apply through the local Flight Standards District Office or an authorized designee under 14 CFR 21.199, and the permit carries operating limitations such as day VFR only, no passengers and a specified route.

items.q: For what purposes may a special flight permit be issued?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 21.197 (Part 21, Subpart H — Special flight permits): flying to a base where repairs, alterations or maintenance are to be performed, or to a point of storage; delivering or exporting the aircraft; production flight testing new production aircraft; evacuating aircraft from an area of impending danger; and conducting customer demonstration flights in new production aircraft that have completed production flight tests. An out-of-annual airplane needing a ferry to the shop is the common case.

items.q: What is preventive maintenance?
items.a: 14 CFR 1.1 defines it as simple or minor preservation operations and the replacement of small standard parts not involving complex assembly operations. The specific items a pilot may do are the list in Part 43, Appendix A, paragraph (c) — anything not on that list is maintenance and requires a certificated mechanic. Note that work on control surfaces is not preventive maintenance.

items.q: Who may perform preventive maintenance, and on which aircraft?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 43.3(g) (Part 43 — Persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations), the holder of a pilot certificate issued under Part 61 — other than a sport pilot certificate — may perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under Part 121, 129 or 135. A rented club airplane you neither own nor operate is outside it unless the club's arrangement makes you the operator.

items.q: What are some examples of preventive maintenance a pilot may perform?
items.a: From Part 43, Appendix A, paragraph (c): changing tires; servicing landing gear wheel bearings and shock struts; replenishing hydraulic fluid; replacing safety belts; replacing seats or seat parts with approved parts; replacing side windows; replacing bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights; replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap; cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers; replacing and servicing batteries; and simple fabric patches.

items.q: Must preventive maintenance be recorded, and who approves the aircraft for return to service?
items.a: Yes. A record entry meeting 14 CFR 43.9 (Part 43 — Content, form, and disposition of maintenance records) must be made, showing the description of the work, the date of completion, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving return to service. Under 14 CFR 43.7(f), a pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate may approve the aircraft for return to service for the preventive maintenance they performed.

items.q: May you fly VFR with an out-of-date altimeter and static system check?
items.a: Yes. The 24-calendar-month altimeter, static system and altitude reporting equipment check is required only to fly IFR in controlled airspace, not merely to fly in instrument conditions, so a VFR flight is legal with it lapsed under 14 CFR 91.411 (Part 91, Subpart E - Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections). The altimeter and encoder must still work for the required equipment lists, and the transponder test is a separate check.

items.q: Does an airplane used for flight instruction for hire always need a 100-hour inspection?
items.a: No. For instruction the 100-hour applies only when the person giving the instruction also provides the airplane, so a student's own airplane needs only the annual, under 14 CFR 91.409 (Part 91, Subpart E - Inspections), which sets both the 12-calendar-month annual and the 100-hour requirement. The 100-hour also applies to any airplane carrying persons other than crewmembers for hire.

items.q: What inspections must be current for the airplane to be legal to fly?
items.a: AAV1ATE: Annual inspection every 12 calendar months; Airworthiness directives complied with; VOR check every 30 days, for IFR only; 100-hour inspection when carrying persons for hire or giving flight instruction for hire in a provided aircraft; Altimeter and static system every 24 calendar months, for IFR only; Transponder every 24 calendar months; and ELT inspected every 12 calendar months.

items.q: What instruments and equipment are required for day VFR flight?
items.a: ATOMATOFLAMES: Airspeed indicator; Tachometer for each engine; Oil pressure gauge for each engine using a pressure system; Manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine; Altimeter; Temperature gauge for each liquid cooled engine; Oil temperature gauge for each air cooled engine; Fuel gauge for each tank; Landing gear position indicator if retractable; Anticollision lights; Magnetic direction indicator; ELT; Safety belts. See 14 CFR 91.205 (Part 91, Subpart C - Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements).

items.q: Why does the static system appear twice in AV1ATES, and what is its interval?
items.a: Because the static pressure system, the altimeter and the altitude reporting equipment are all covered by the same 24 calendar month test under 91.411, Part 91, Subpart E. The mnemonic lists the A and the S separately only as a memory aid. If the static system is opened and closed for maintenance, the system must be tested again before IFR flight.
items.concept: AV1ATES S: static system test every 24 calendar months, 91.411

items.q: What exactly goes on the placard, and does the removal have to be recorded?
items.a: The placard must read 'Inoperative' and be placed at the cockpit control of the affected item, per 91.213(d)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. If the item is removed rather than deactivated, the maintenance record entry required by 43.9, Part 43, 'Content, form, and disposition of maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration records,' must also be made. Placarding alone, with no record, is not enough when removal is the method used.
items.concept: Placard wording INOPERATIVE and the maintenance record entry

items.q: When is a test flight required after maintenance, and what does 91.407(b) say?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E, 'Operation after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration.' No person may carry any person other than crewmembers in an aircraft that has been maintained, rebuilt or altered in a manner that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate has flown it, made an operational check of the work, and logged the flight in the aircraft records.
items.concept: Required test flight after maintenance affecting flight characteristics, 91.407(b)

items.q: Who may fly the required post-maintenance check flight, and what must be logged?
items.a: An appropriately rated pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate, who flies the aircraft, makes an operational check of the maintenance performed or alteration made, and logs the flight in the aircraft records, per 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E. If the check flight shows the work was not satisfactory, 91.407(c) requires the aircraft to be re-inspected before it is flown again.
items.concept: Who may fly the 91.407(b) check flight, and what must they log

items.q: Your Warrior II has just had major work. Can you take a passenger on the first flight?
items.a: No. If the work may have appreciably changed the flight characteristics or substantially affected operation in flight, 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E, forbids carrying anyone other than crewmembers until the check flight is flown and logged. Required crewmembers may be aboard, so an instructor or safety pilot serving as a crewmember is permitted; a friend along for the ride is not.
items.concept: No persons other than crewmembers may be carried until the 91.407(b) check flight is complete

items.q: Up to what cabin pressure altitude is no supplemental oxygen required at all?
items.a: Up to and including 12,500 feet MSL cabin pressure altitude, no supplemental oxygen is required, for any length of time and for anybody on board. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' That band covers essentially all flying in a normally aspirated Warrior II, which cannot climb usefully much above it.
items.concept: Oxygen band: sea level up to and including 12,500 ft MSL, no supplemental oxygen required

items.q: What is the oxygen requirement between 12,501 and 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude?
items.a: The minimum required flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' A brief climb through the band needs nothing; a cruise segment longer than half an hour does. Nothing at all is required for passengers in this band.
items.concept: Oxygen band: 12,501 ft to 14,000 ft MSL, required crew uses it for that part of the flight over 30 minutes

items.q: What is the oxygen requirement above 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude?
items.a: The minimum required flight crew must use supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes. There is no 30 minute grace period once you are above 14,000 feet MSL. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Passengers still need not be provided with oxygen until the cabin pressure altitude goes above 15,000 feet.
items.concept: Oxygen band: above 14,000 ft MSL, flight crew must use oxygen at all times

items.q: At what cabin pressure altitude must supplemental oxygen be provided to the passengers?
items.a: Above 15,000 feet MSL, each occupant of the aircraft must be provided with supplemental oxygen. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Note the wording precisely: provided, not used. Passengers are not required to use it, while the required flight crew has been required to use it continuously since 14,000 feet.
items.concept: Oxygen band: above 15,000 ft MSL, oxygen must be provided to every occupant

items.q: What extra oxygen must a pressurized aircraft carry above 25,000 feet?
items.a: Above flight level 250, on top of everything else 91.211 already requires, the aircraft must carry at least a 10 minute supplemental supply for each occupant, to cover the descent after a decompression. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Above flight level 350 one pilot at the controls must wear and use an oxygen mask, with a narrow quick donning exception below flight level 410.
items.concept: Oxygen band: above 25,000 ft MSL, all lower requirements plus an additional 10 minutes of oxygen for each person on board

items.q: The oxygen altitudes in 91.211 are MSL altitudes of what, exactly?
items.a: Cabin pressure altitude, not the airplane's height above sea level. In an unpressurized airplane like the Warrior II the two are the same number, so the distinction never bites you. In a pressurized airplane cruising at flight level 250 with the cabin held at 8,000 feet, no oxygen is required, because cabin pressure altitude is what the rule measures.
items.concept: All the 91.211 MSL altitudes are cabin pressure altitudes, not aircraft altitudes

items.q: State the four cabin pressure altitude breakpoints in the supplemental oxygen rule.
items.a: 12,500, 14,000, 15,000 and 25,000 feet MSL. Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 the crew uses it after 30 minutes; above 14,000 the crew uses it throughout; above 15,000 every occupant must be provided with it; above 25,000 a pressurized aircraft adds a 10 minute supply per occupant. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Each new band begins one foot above the stated figure.
items.concept: The exact breakpoints of the oxygen ladder: 12,500, 14,000, 15,000 and 25,000 ft MSL

items.q: What does 91.21 prohibit, and on which flights does it actually apply?
items.a: It bars operating a portable electronic device aboard an aircraft, but only on two kinds of flight: an aircraft operated by the holder of an air carrier or operating certificate, and any other aircraft while it is being operated under IFR. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' A Part 91 VFR flight in your Warrior II falls outside the rule altogether.
items.concept: 91.21 general prohibition on portable electronic devices, and the two categories of flight it applies to

items.q: Name the first device 91.21 exempts from the portable electronic device prohibition.
items.a: Portable voice recorders. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' The exceptions exist because these devices either emit nothing capable of interfering with navigation and communication equipment, or are a necessity for the person using them. There are five exceptions in all: the first four are named outright and the fifth is a catch-all.
items.concept: Electronic device exception 1: portable voice recorders

items.q: Which hearing device is exempt from the 91.21 portable electronic device rule?
items.a: Hearing aids. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' Like the pacemaker exception, it is there because the device is a necessity for the person using it and because its emissions are negligible. No determination by the operator is needed for any of the four named items; only the fifth, catch-all category requires one.
items.concept: Electronic device exception 2: hearing aids

items.q: Which implanted medical device does 91.21 specifically exempt?
items.a: Heart pacemakers. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' It is third on the list of five exceptions, alongside portable voice recorders, hearing aids and electric shavers, with the fifth being anything else the operator has determined will not cause interference with navigation or communication systems.
items.concept: Electronic device exception 3: heart pacemakers

items.q: Which grooming device appears on the 91.21 exception list?
items.a: Electric shavers. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' It is the fourth of the five exceptions and the one applicants most often forget, which makes it a favorite oral exam question. In order the list reads portable voice recorders; hearing aids; heart pacemakers; electric shavers; and the operator determined catch-all.
items.concept: Electronic device exception 4: electric shavers

items.q: What is the fifth, catch-all exception to the portable electronic device rule?
items.a: Any other portable electronic device that the operator of the aircraft has determined will not cause interference with the navigation or communication system of the aircraft in which it is to be used. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' This is the hook that lets tablets, portable GPS units, headsets and the like be used on an IFR flight.
items.concept: Electronic device exception 5: any other device the operator has determined will not cause interference with navigation or communication systems

items.q: Who makes the determination that a portable electronic device will not cause interference?
items.a: The operator of the aircraft. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices,' provides that for an aircraft operated by an air carrier or commercial operator the determination is made by that certificate holder, and for any other aircraft it is made by the pilot in command or other operator of the aircraft. Flying your Warrior II under IFR, that is you.
items.concept: Who makes the no-interference determination under 91.21

items.q: What is a KOEL?
items.a: The Kinds of Operation Equipment List. It is a table in the Limitations section, Section 2, of a GAMA-format pilot's operating handbook and FAA approved airplane flight manual, and it lists, by kind of operation, the equipment that must be installed and operable for that operation. Typical columns are VFR day, VFR night, IFR day, IFR night and sometimes flight into known icing, with the number of each item required.

items.q: Where exactly do you look for the KOEL, and what else lives near it?
items.a: Section 2, Limitations, of the AFM or POH, usually right after the weight, CG and maneuver limitations. Do not confuse it with the equipment list in Section 6, which is an inventory of everything installed in that individual airplane with weights and arms, nor with the airworthiness limitations in Section 4 of the maintenance manual. The KOEL says what is required; the equipment list says what is fitted.

items.q: Does every airplane have a KOEL?
items.a: No, and that is the point of the question. The kinds of operation equipment list arrived with the GAMA standardized handbook format in the late 1970s, so many older certificated airplanes have an airplane flight manual with no Section 2 table at all, and some handbooks print only a short kinds of operation paragraph instead. Open the book before you assert that the airplane has one.

items.q: If the airplane has no KOEL, what governs required equipment?
items.a: You fall back to the regulation and the paperwork. 14 CFR 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, is the floor; then whatever the type certificate data sheet and the airplane's own equipment list require; then anything made mandatory by an airworthiness directive or required by the supplement to a supplemental type certificate; then any rule tied to the specific operation, such as 91.215 for a transponder.

items.q: Does any regulation actually mention the KOEL by name?
items.a: Yes. 14 CFR 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment, at paragraph (d)(2), requires that the inoperative item not be indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list or on the Kinds of Operations Equipment List for the kind of operation being conducted. That is why the KOEL is not optional trivia: it is one of the four tests you have to pass before you fly with something inoperative and no minimum equipment list.

items.q: An item is on the KOEL for VFR night but you are flying VFR day. Does it have to work?
items.a: Not on that account. The list is organized by kind of operation, so only the column for the operation you are conducting applies. If the item is required only for VFR night and you fly day VFR, the KOEL does not require it, and you then go on to check 91.205 for day VFR, the equipment list, any applicable airworthiness directive, and finally 91.213(d) to placard and deactivate it properly.

items.q: Is a flap position indicator required on this airplane?
items.a: No. Walk it through: there is no minimum equipment list, so start with 14 CFR 91.205(b) for day VFR and run the mnemonic; 91.205 requires a landing gear position indicator on a retractable, and says nothing at all about flaps. Then check the handbook's kinds of operation list, which does not list one, then the equipment list and any airworthiness directive. Nothing requires it, so the airplane is legal without it.

items.q: Walk the 91.205 day VFR list and show me where a flap indicator would appear if it were required.
items.a: Airspeed indicator, tachometer, oil pressure gauge, manifold pressure gauge for an altitude engine, altimeter, temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine, oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, fuel gauge for each tank, landing gear position indicator if the gear is retractable, anticollision lights, magnetic direction indicator, ELT, and safety belts and shoulder harnesses. Gear position is in there. Flap position is not.

items.q: Give me the general method for answering 'is this piece of equipment required?'
items.a: Five places, in order. 14 CFR 91.205 and any other operating rule that applies to the flight, such as 91.207 for the ELT or 91.215 for a transponder; then the kinds of operation equipment list in Section 2 of the handbook; then the airplane's own equipment list in Section 6; then any airworthiness directive or the flight manual supplement to an installed STC; and then, if it is inoperative, 91.213.

items.q: What is the title of 91.205 and what does it actually cover?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements. It applies to airplanes with a standard airworthiness certificate, which is why the rule does not govern an experimental or a limited category airplane in the same way. Paragraph (b) is VFR day, (c) adds VFR night, (d) adds IFR, and (e) covers flight at and above FL240.

items.q: Who may remove or deactivate the inoperative item, and who placards it?
items.a: Deactivation or removal is maintenance: it is done by a certificated mechanic or repair station unless it happens to be preventive maintenance a pilot may do under 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A. The placard reading INOPERATIVE goes on in either case, and the determination that the airplane is still safe for the flight is made by the pilot in command or by a mechanic. 14 CFR 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment.

items.q: Suppose the airplane did have a flap position indicator and it failed. May you fly?
items.a: Probably yes, but you have to run 91.213(d) rather than assume it. Check the VFR-day type certification requirements, the kinds of operation list, the equipment list and any AD. If it clears all four, deactivate or remove it, placard it INOPERATIVE and make the hazard determination, and then satisfy yourself operationally: without the indicator you confirm flap position by the handle detent, by the control feel, and by looking at the wing.

items.q: Why is 'the KOEL does not list it' not a complete answer on its own?
items.a: Because the KOEL is only one of the four tests in 91.213(d), and because some airplanes have no KOEL at all. An item can be absent from the KOEL and still be required by 91.205, by an airworthiness directive or by an STC supplement. The complete answer names the regulation first, then the handbook, then the equipment list, then the AD and STC paperwork, and says which one actually decided the question.

items.q: Which of the documents in ARROW is an FCC document?
items.a: None of them, and that is the trap. ARROW is the airworthiness certificate, registration certificate, radio station license if required, operating limitations and weight and balance data, and the R is the one that sometimes stands for the FCC station license, required only for international operations. The airworthiness and registration certificates are FAA documents; the operating limitations and weight and balance come from the manufacturer and the last weighing.

b: Atmosphere, stability, moisture, fronts, air masses, clouds, hazards.

items.q: Why does wind blow, and in which direction does air move between pressure areas?
items.a: Air always flows from areas of high pressure toward areas of low pressure, because it seeks the lower pressure. The difference in pressure over a given distance is the pressure gradient, and it is the driving force of all wind.
