A steeper gradient produces stronger wind; Coriolis force and surface friction then deflect the flow, but they do not start it.

items.q: How does air circulate around a surface high, and what weather comes with it?
items.a: In the Northern Hemisphere air circulates around a high clockwise and outward, and air from aloft descends to replace it. Descending air is compressed and warms, so its relative humidity falls and clouds become less likely, though not impossible. Highs generally mean clear skies, good visibility, stable air and fair weather.

items.q: How does air circulate around a surface low, and what weather comes with it?
items.a: In the Northern Hemisphere the flow is counterclockwise and inward, and the converging air has nowhere to go but up. Rising air expands, cools adiabatically, reaches its dew point and condenses, so lows bring clouds, precipitation, restricted visibility, and if the air is unstable enough, showers and thunderstorms.

items.q: What is an isobar, and what does the spacing between isobars tell you?
items.a: An isobar is a line joining points of equal atmospheric pressure reduced to sea level. Closely spaced isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong winds; widely spaced isobars mean a shallow gradient and light winds. On a surface analysis they are normally drawn every 4 millibars.

items.q: What is a ridge and what is a trough, and what weather does each bring?
items.a: A ridge is an elongated area of high pressure and a trough is an elongated area of low pressure. A ridge has sinking, drying air and usually fair weather; a trough has rising air, so expect cloud, precipitation and often a distinct wind shift as the trough line passes.

items.q: How do winds aloft differ from surface winds in relation to the isobars?
items.a: Above the friction layer, roughly 2,000 ft AGL, the wind blows essentially parallel to the isobars. Near the surface friction slows the air, which weakens Coriolis force, so the wind crosses the isobars at an angle of about 20 to 45 degrees toward the low, and blows perhaps 20 to 40 percent slower.

items.q: What causes convective currents, and what do they feel like in flight?
items.a: Uneven heating of the surface. Land heats and cools faster than water, and dry or paved surfaces faster than vegetation or lakes, so warm columns rise and cooler air sinks. The result is bumpy, turbulent air at low altitudes, worst on warm sunny afternoons below about 5,000 ft AGL, and it can make holding a stable approach path difficult.

items.q: What should you expect flying near buildings, trees or hangars in a strong wind?
items.a: Mechanical turbulence. Wind flowing over obstructions breaks into eddies that make the air rough and gusty downwind, and the effect increases with wind speed and obstruction size. On approach or departure over a line of buildings or trees expect sudden sink and drift, so carry a small margin of extra airspeed and be ready with power.

items.q: How does wind behave on the windward and leeward sides of a mountain ridge?
items.a: On the windward side the air is forced smoothly upward, so the ride is generally smooth with a steady updraft. On the leeward side the air spills down the slope and breaks up, giving strong downdrafts, rotors and severe turbulence. Cross ridges at roughly a 45 degree angle so you can turn away, and allow several thousand feet of terrain clearance.

items.q: What is atmospheric stability?
items.a: Stability is the atmosphere's resistance to vertical motion. In stable air a parcel that is displaced upward becomes colder and heavier than its surroundings and sinks back; in unstable air the displaced parcel stays warmer and lighter than its surroundings and keeps rising on its own.

items.q: What are adiabatic cooling and adiabatic heating?
items.a: Adiabatic means no heat is exchanged with the surrounding air. Rising air moves into lower pressure, expands and cools; descending air is compressed by higher pressure and warms. This is why lifted air eventually reaches its dew point and forms cloud, and why air sinking on the lee of a ridge arrives warm and dry.

items.q: What are the standard temperature and pressure lapse rates?
items.a: Temperature falls about 2 degrees C per 1,000 ft (about 3.5 degrees F), and pressure falls about 1 inHg per 1,000 ft in the lower atmosphere. Standard sea level conditions are 15 degrees C and 29.92 inHg. These are averages used for performance and altimetry, not what any particular day will actually do.

items.q: What are the dry adiabatic and saturated adiabatic lapse rates?
items.a: Unsaturated air cools at the dry adiabatic rate of about 3 degrees C per 1,000 ft as it rises. Once the air is saturated, condensation releases latent heat and slows the cooling to the saturated (moist) adiabatic rate, which varies from about 1.1 to 2.8 degrees C per 1,000 ft depending on temperature and moisture content.

items.q: How does comparing the actual lapse rate with the adiabatic rates tell you whether air is stable?
items.a: Measure the ambient lapse rate against the two adiabatic rates. Greater than the dry rate of about 3 degrees C per 1,000 ft means the air is absolutely unstable; less than the saturated rate of about 1.1 degrees C per 1,000 ft means absolutely stable; in between it is conditionally unstable, stable while dry but unstable once lifting saturates it.

items.q: What does stable air look and feel like to a pilot?
items.a: Stable air resists vertical motion, so any cloud spreads out into layers. Expect stratiform clouds, smooth air, steady continuous drizzle or light rain, poor visibility because haze, smoke and dust stay trapped near the surface, fog, and steady rather than gusty wind. Low ceilings that last, but a comfortable ride.

items.q: What does unstable air look and feel like to a pilot?
items.a: Unstable air lets a lifted parcel keep rising, so cloud builds vertically. Expect cumuliform clouds, turbulence, good visibility because the mixing carries the haze away, showery precipitation that starts and stops, and gusty surface winds. In its extreme it produces towering cumulus and thunderstorms.

items.q: What is the quick rule of thumb linking air temperature and moisture to stability?
items.a: Cool, dry air is generally stable and brings good flying weather; warm, moist air is generally unstable and brings poor weather. Warmth supplies the buoyancy and moisture supplies the latent heat that keeps a rising parcel warmer than its surroundings, which is exactly what an unstable atmosphere needs.

items.q: What effect does water vapor have on air density and on aircraft performance?
items.a: A water molecule is lighter than the nitrogen or oxygen molecule it displaces, so moist air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature, and it tends to rise. Moist air also takes longer to cool. For the pilot, high humidity raises density altitude, so expect longer takeoff runs and reduced climb performance.

items.q: What is a temperature inversion, where do you find one, and what are the hazards?
items.a: An inversion is a layer where temperature increases with altitude instead of decreasing, most often on a clear calm night when the ground radiates its heat away, and also just above a frontal surface. The layer is very stable and smooth, but if humidity is high it traps moisture and pollutants, giving fog, low cloud and poor visibility, with low-level wind shear at the top.

items.q: What is the difference between humidity and relative humidity?
items.a: Humidity is simply the amount of water vapor present in the air. Relative humidity is that amount expressed as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold at that particular temperature and pressure, so relative humidity rises as air cools even when no moisture is added.

items.q: What is the dew point?
items.a: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated, that is, the temperature at which it can hold no more moisture at the existing pressure. The spread between temperature and dew point is your measure of how close the air is to condensing.

items.q: What happens when the temperature and dew point become equal?
items.a: The air is completely saturated at 100 percent relative humidity, and moisture begins to condense out of it as fog, dew, frost, cloud, rain or snow. A small and shrinking temperature/dew point spread is the classic warning of fog or low stratus forming.

items.q: By what four processes do the temperature and dew point become equal?
items.a: Warm air moves over a colder surface and its temperature drops; warm and cold air masses mix; the air cools at night through contact with ground that has radiated its heat away; or the air is forced upward and cools adiabatically, by terrain, a front, or convection. All four cool the air to its existing dew point.

items.q: When does dew form and when does frost form instead?
items.a: If the collecting surface cools to below the dew point the water vapor condenses as dew. If that surface temperature is also below freezing, the vapor changes directly to ice and forms frost. Frost therefore needs both a below-freezing surface and a dew point below freezing.

items.q: Why must frost be removed before flight?
items.a: Frost does not change the wing's shape much, but its rough surface disrupts the smooth airflow over the wing, breaking up the boundary layer. That can cut lift by around 30 percent and increase drag by up to 40 percent, so the aircraft may not fly, or may lift off and settle back. Remove all of it; do not attempt to polish it smooth.

items.q: What general conditions are needed for fog to form?
items.a: Fog forms when the temperature and dew point are close, usually within about 2 degrees C, and the air is cooled to saturation or moisture is added to it, so the water vapor condenses and becomes visible as a cloud based at the surface. Light wind and a supply of condensation nuclei help it develop and deepen.

items.q: How does radiation fog form and when does it burn off?
items.a: On calm, clear nights the ground radiates its heat away rapidly, chilling the shallow layer of moist air in contact with it to the dew point. It needs clear skies, high humidity and little or no wind, forms over low ground and valleys, and normally burns off within a few hours of sunrise, though wind can also lift it into low stratus.

items.q: How does advection fog form, and why is it more persistent?
items.a: Warm, moist air moves horizontally over a colder surface and is cooled to its dew point. Unlike radiation fog it requires wind, typically up to about 15 kt, and it is common in coastal areas where a sea breeze carries moist marine air over cooler land. Because wind keeps supplying new moist air it can persist for days and can move in quickly.

items.q: How does upslope fog form?
items.a: Moist, stable air is forced upward along rising terrain and cools adiabatically until it reaches its dew point. It needs wind to push the air up the slope, and unlike radiation fog it can form under cloudy skies. It lasts as long as the upslope wind lasts, and it can cover very large areas of sloping plains.

items.q: How does steam fog form and what hazard comes with it?
items.a: Cold, dry air moves over much warmer water. Moisture evaporates into the cold air, immediately saturates it and condenses, so the fog appears to rise off the surface as steam. Because the air is being warmed from below it is unstable, so expect low-level turbulence and the possibility of icing in it.

items.q: What is ice fog and where does it occur?
items.a: Ice fog forms when the temperature is well below freezing, generally colder than about minus 25 degrees F, and water vapor turns directly into suspended ice crystals rather than droplets. It is common in arctic regions and in very cold, calm conditions in northern cities, and it can reduce visibility to near zero.

items.q: What are the four cloud families and their height bands?
items.a: High, middle, low, and clouds with extensive vertical development. High clouds have bases roughly 16,500 to 45,000 ft and are ice crystal; middle clouds run about 6,500 to 23,000 ft; low clouds from the surface to about 6,500 ft; and vertically developed clouds have low bases but tops that can exceed 60,000 ft.

items.q: What do the cloud prefixes and suffixes cirro-, alto-, nimbo-, -nimbus, castellanus and lenticularis mean?
items.a: Cirro- means high and ice crystal; alto- means middle level; nimbo- or -nimbus means precipitation, so nimbostratus is a rain-bearing layer and cumulonimbus a thunderstorm. Castellanus means turret-shaped tops, showing instability aloft. Lenticularis means lens-shaped and standing, the signature of a mountain wave. Fracto- means ragged or broken.

items.q: Which cloud types are the ones that mean trouble, and what does each warn of?
items.a: Cumulonimbus means a thunderstorm with all of its hazards, and towering cumulus means one is developing. Standing lenticular and rotor clouds mark mountain wave turbulence that can be severe even in clear air. Altocumulus castellanus warns of instability and turbulence at middle levels, and nimbostratus means continuous precipitation with icing potential in freezing conditions.

items.q: What is virga and why does it matter to a pilot?
items.a: Virga is precipitation that falls from a cloud but evaporates before reaching the ground, seen as trailing wisps beneath the cloud base. It matters because evaporation cools the air sharply, making it dense enough to plunge downward, so virga is a classic visual warning of a microburst or strong downdraft underneath.

items.q: What is freezing rain, and what does it tell you about the air above you?
items.a: Freezing rain is rain that falls as a liquid and freezes on impact with a surface whose temperature is below freezing. It tells you there is a layer of above-freezing air aloft over a below-freezing layer beneath, so if you meet it in a climb the usual escape is to climb into the warmer air, while descending may only make it worse.

items.q: How does hail form, and where can you encounter it?
items.a: Water droplets carried above the freezing level in a cumulonimbus freeze and are cycled up and down by the updrafts, accumulating layers of ice until they are too heavy for the updraft to support and fall out. Hail can be thrown out of the anvil into clear air well away from the storm, so clear air near a thunderstorm is no guarantee.

items.q: What is snow, and how do ice pellets differ from it?
items.a: Snow is precipitation in the form of ice crystals that fall from cloud where the air is below freezing throughout. Ice pellets are raindrops that froze before reaching the ground, which means there is a warm layer aloft with freezing rain in it, so ice pellets on the windscreen are a warning to change altitude or turn back.

items.q: What is an air mass, and what gives it its character?
items.a: An air mass is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and moisture throughout. It takes on those properties by sitting for days over a source region with uniform surface characteristics, typically under a slow-moving or stagnant high, so a polar continental region breeds cold dry air and a tropical ocean breeds warm moist air.

items.q: What are the air mass source region types and what does each bring?
items.a: Lower case gives moisture, capital gives temperature: cP, mP, cT, mT and A. Continental polar is cold and dry; maritime polar is cool and moist with low stratus, drizzle and fog; continental tropical is hot and dry; maritime tropical is warm and very moist, the source of most widespread cloud and thunderstorms; and arctic air is the coldest and driest of all.

items.q: How is an air mass modified by the surface it travels over?
items.a: If it moves over a warmer surface it is heated from below, becomes unstable, and gives cumulus cloud, turbulence, showers and good visibility. If it moves over a colder surface it is cooled from below, becomes stable, and gives stratus, fog, drizzle, smooth air and poor visibility. Passing over water adds moisture; passing over dry land removes it.

items.q: What is a front?
items.a: A front is the boundary layer between two air masses of different temperature and moisture. Because the two masses have different densities they do not mix readily, and the lifting that happens where they meet is what produces cloud and precipitation. Every frontal passage brings changes in temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and cloud.

items.q: What happens at a warm front, and what is its signature?
items.a: A warm air mass advances and overruns a retreating colder mass, sliding up over it on a shallow slope. It moves slowly, so weather extends hundreds of miles ahead: high cirrus first, then cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus and finally stratus, with steady light rain or drizzle, high humidity, poor to average visibility, and smooth stable air.

items.q: What happens at a cold front, and what is its signature?
items.a: A dense, cold air mass undercuts the warm air and forces it sharply upward along a steep frontal slope. It moves fast, so the weather is narrow but violent: cumulonimbus, heavy showers, thunderstorms, gusty shifting winds, hail and severe turbulence, followed quickly by clearing, cooler temperatures and much improved visibility.

items.q: What is a stationary front and what weather does it bring?
items.a: When the opposing forces of two air masses are roughly equal neither displaces the other and the boundary stalls in place. The weather is a mixture of warm front and cold front conditions, and because the front is not moving it can sit over an area for days with persistent low cloud, poor visibility and precipitation.

items.q: How does an occluded front form?
items.a: A fast-moving cold front overtakes a slower warm front, lifting the warm air completely off the surface so that it no longer touches the ground. Which of the two remaining cold air masses is colder then determines whether the result is a cold-type or a warm-type occlusion, and that decides the weather you get.

items.q: What is a cold-type occlusion and what weather comes with it?
items.a: In a cold front occlusion the air behind the fast cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front, so it stays on the surface and lifts both the warm air and the cooler air ahead of it. The result is a mixture of warm and cold frontal weather, with a band of cloud and precipitation and embedded cumuliform activity near the front.

items.q: What is a warm-type occlusion and why is it usually worse?
items.a: In a warm front occlusion the air ahead of the warm front is colder than the air behind the cold front, so the cold front rides up over that colder air rather than undercutting it. The lifting is deeper and the weather more severe: widespread rain and fog with embedded thunderstorms hidden in stratiform cloud, which is a serious hazard in IMC.

items.q: What happens to the wind as a front passes?
items.a: Because a front is the boundary between pressure patterns and lies in a trough of low pressure, the wind always shifts as it passes, veering clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. The shift is most abrupt and most violent with a cold front, where it can be accompanied by strong gusts, and it is the reason to expect a runway change or a tailwind on final.

items.q: What do temperature, dew point and pressure do before, during and after a frontal passage?
items.a: Ahead of the front pressure falls; it reaches its lowest point at the front and rises steadily behind it, which is the surest single indicator that the front has passed. Temperature and dew point drop sharply behind a cold front and rise behind a warm front, and the wind shifts clockwise in both cases.

items.q: What three ingredients does a thunderstorm require?
items.a: Sufficient water vapor, an unstable lapse rate, and a lifting action to start the parcel upward. The lifting can come from surface heating, terrain, frontal lift or convergence. Remove any one of the three and the storm cannot develop, which is why a stable or a dry air mass can be lifted vigorously and still produce nothing.

items.q: What are the three stages of a thunderstorm?
items.a: Cumulus, mature and dissipating. The cumulus stage is dominated by updrafts as the cell builds, the mature stage begins when precipitation reaches the surface and both updrafts and downdrafts exist together, and the dissipating stage is all downdraft as the cell rains itself out. A single cell typically runs through all three in under an hour.

items.q: What happens in the cumulus stage of a thunderstorm?
items.a: Continuous updrafts, reaching as much as 3,000 ft per minute, build the cloud rapidly upward as moisture condenses and releases latent heat. There is no precipitation falling out yet, because the updraft is still supporting the drops. The visual cue is a cumulus building fast into a towering cumulus with hard, sharply defined edges.

items.q: What happens in the mature stage of a thunderstorm, and why is it the most dangerous?
items.a: Precipitation begins falling from the base, dragging air with it, so updrafts and downdrafts exist side by side. That shear between them produces the most violent turbulence, along with heavy rain, hail, lightning, gust fronts at the surface, wind shear and the greatest icing potential. The anvil top appears as the cell reaches the tropopause.

items.q: What happens in the dissipating stage of a thunderstorm?
items.a: The downdraft spreads through the whole cell and cuts off the inflow of warm moist air that fed it, so the storm starves itself. Rainfall lessens, the cloud edges soften and the top spreads out into an anvil. Hazards are reducing but turbulence, lightning and downdrafts can persist, so the cell is not yet safe to fly through.

items.q: What is an air mass thunderstorm?
items.a: An isolated, randomly located storm produced by surface heating or convection within a single air mass rather than by a front. It typically lasts one to two hours, produces moderate rainfall and moderate turbulence, and is generally avoidable in visual conditions because you can see and circumnavigate it.

items.q: What is a squall line and why is it so dangerous?
items.a: A squall line is a narrow band of active thunderstorms that often forms 50 to 300 miles ahead of a fast-moving cold front, though it can develop in unstable air away from any front. It usually contains the most severe weather of all: continuous storms too tall to overfly and too long to circumnavigate easily, with severe turbulence, hail and shear.

items.q: How do tornadoes form in relation to thunderstorms?
items.a: A thunderstorm draws air into its base to feed the updraft; if that inflow has any rotating motion, the rotation is stretched and concentrated into a violent vortex. The funnel may be visible reaching the ground or may be embedded and hidden inside the storm cloud, so a tornado can exist where you cannot see it.

items.q: What causes the turbulence in and around a thunderstorm, and what marks it visually?
items.a: Adjacent updrafts and downdrafts shearing against each other, plus the gust front where the outflow spreads along the surface. The visual marker is a roll cloud, a turbulent horizontal rotor cloud at the leading edge of the storm's base, and it indicates the most violent low-level turbulence of the whole system.

items.q: What does an approaching thunderstorm do to your altimeter?
items.a: Pressure falls rapidly as the storm approaches, then rises abruptly as the cold outflow arrives, then falls again as it moves away. Because the altimeter reads pressure, a falling setting makes the instrument over-read your true altitude, so an old setting near a storm can leave you significantly lower than indicated.

items.q: What hazards does lightning present, and when is it present?
items.a: Lightning is always present in a thunderstorm; it is what makes it a thunderstorm. It can puncture the skin and damage structure, burn out or upset avionics and the compass, induce currents in wiring, and a single nearby flash at night can cause temporary blindness lasting long enough to lose control in IMC.

items.q: What is a microburst, and what is the performance sequence a pilot experiences flying into one?
items.a: A concentrated downdraft, typically under 1 mile across with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind-to-tailwind shear of up to 90 kt, lasting about 5 to 15 minutes. On approach you meet an increasing headwind with rising airspeed and a tendency to balloon; then a strong downdraft; then a sudden tailwind that collapses airspeed, lift and climb performance just when you are low and slow.

items.q: What two conditions must exist for structural icing to form?
items.a: Visible moisture, such as cloud, rain or drizzle, and an aircraft surface temperature at or below freezing. Both must be present at the same time. Note that it is the skin temperature that matters, not just the outside air temperature, so ice can form on an airframe cold-soaked from a descent even in air slightly above zero.

items.q: What is clear ice, how does it form, and why is it the worst kind?
items.a: Clear ice forms from large supercooled droplets that flow back along the surface before freezing, so it builds a hard, heavy, glossy sheet that spreads well beyond the protected leading edge. It is found in freezing rain and in cumuliform cloud, it is hard to see, hard to shed and adds a great deal of weight and drag.

items.q: What is rime ice and how does it form?
items.a: Rime forms from small supercooled droplets that freeze on impact, trapping air between them, so it is opaque, white, rough and brittle and stays near the leading edge. It is typical of stratiform cloud and colder temperatures. It is lighter than clear ice but its rough surface disrupts lift badly and it can block intakes and antennas.

items.q: What is mixed ice?
items.a: Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime, formed when droplets of varying size are present or conditions alternate, so part of the water freezes on impact and part runs back before freezing. It has the rough shape of rime with the hard adhesion of clear ice, and it is the most common form encountered in practice.

items.q: What is instrument icing and which instruments does it threaten?
items.a: Ice forming over the pitot tube, static ports and their drains, and over the fuel vents, stall warning vane and antennas. Blocked ports give false or frozen airspeed, altimeter and vertical speed indications. Use pitot heat before entering visible moisture in near-freezing air, and know the alternate static source procedure in the POH or AFM.

items.q: What is induction icing, and how is it usually protected against?
items.a: Ice forming in the engine's air induction path, restricting or blocking the air supply to the engine. In a fuel injected engine this is impact ice at the air filter, and the protection is an alternate air source, often a spring-loaded door that opens automatically or on selection. In a carburettor engine it is carburettor ice, protected by carburettor heat.

items.q: In what conditions does carburettor icing form, and what are the symptoms?
items.a: Most likely between about minus 7 and 21 degrees C with relative humidity above 80 percent, though it can occur up to about 38 degrees C in very humid air. Fuel vaporization and the venturi pressure drop can chill the air more than 20 degrees C. Symptoms are a gradual loss of RPM with a fixed-pitch propeller, or a loss of manifold pressure with a constant-speed propeller, then rough running.

items.q: How are the four icing intensities defined for reporting?
items.a: Trace is perceptible but accumulating no faster than it sublimates; light means the rate would be a problem only if you stayed in it over an hour; moderate means even a short encounter is potentially hazardous and de-icing or a diversion is necessary; severe means the equipment cannot control it and an immediate change of altitude or heading is required. As a rate guide these correspond to under a quarter inch, a quarter to one inch, one to three inches, and over three inches per hour.

items.q: How do you estimate the height of cumulus cloud bases from the surface temperature and dew point?
items.a: Divide the temperature/dew point spread in degrees Celsius by 2.5 and multiply by 1,000 for the approximate base in feet AGL. Unsaturated rising air cools about 3 degrees C per 1,000 feet while the dew point falls only about 0.5 degrees C per 1,000 feet, so the spread closes at 2.5 degrees C per 1,000 feet, or 4.4 degrees F per 1,000 feet. Example: 24 over 14 is a 10 degree spread, so bases near 4,000 feet AGL; a small spread means low bases, fog or low stratus.

items.q: On the leading edge of a wing, how do the shapes of rime, clear and mixed ice differ?
items.a: Rime forms a thin, conformal cap that hugs the leading edge and builds forward into the airstream. Clear ice spreads as a smooth thin layer that runs back along the upper and lower surfaces well behind the leading edge. Mixed ice makes the bulkiest and most irregular shape, thickened at the leading edge with rough runback behind, which is why it distorts the airfoil the most.

items.q: Walk me through the types of fog, one at a time.
items.a: Radiation fog, from ground cooling on a clear calm night; advection fog, from warm moist air moving over a colder surface; upslope fog, from moist stable air being lifted and cooled along rising terrain; steam fog, from cold air over much warmer water; precipitation-induced or frontal fog, from warm rain falling through cool air and saturating it; and ice fog in extreme cold. All of them are the same thing in the end: a cloud sitting on the ground.

items.q: What is the difference between mist and fog?
items.a: Visibility. Both are suspended water droplets at the surface; the reporting threshold is the line between them. It is coded FG for fog when the visibility is less than 5/8 statute mile, and BR for mist when the visibility is 5/8 mile through 6 miles. Haze, HZ, is dry particles rather than water. So a METAR reading 1/2SM FG and one reading 3SM BR describe the same physical process at different intensities.

items.q: What cloud type is a layer of low-lying fog?
items.a: Stratus. Fog is simply a stratus cloud whose base is at the surface, formed by the same cooling-to-saturation process, which is why radiation fog often lifts into a low stratus deck as the morning sun warms the ground rather than burning off cleanly. If the morning TAF shows fog clearing to a 300-foot overcast, that is what has happened, and the field is still well below VFR.

items.q: What is precipitation-induced fog and where do you meet it?
items.a: Warm rain falls through a layer of cooler air beneath it, evaporates into that air and saturates it, so fog forms in the rain. You meet it ahead of a warm front or around a slow-moving stationary front, often over a wide area and with a low ceiling above it. It is dangerous because it comes with precipitation and sometimes with icing, and because it forms where the pilot is already working.

b: Where the weather comes from and which briefing to ask for.

items.q: What is Flight Service, and how do you reach it for a weather briefing?
items.a: Flight Service is the FAA-contracted service that provides preflight briefings, flight plan handling and in-flight assistance. A briefing is available 24 hours a day by calling 1-800-WX-BRIEF, or online at 1800wxbrief.com; local and remote outlet numbers and frequencies are published in the Chart Supplement for the airport concerned.

items.q: What regulation requires you to obtain weather information before a flight, and what does it say?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B, "Preflight action") requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight before beginning it. For any flight away from the vicinity of the airport that expressly includes weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays, plus runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data.

items.q: What is a standard briefing and when should you request one?
items.a: The standard briefing is the complete preflight weather picture, and you ask for it when you have not obtained any prior information for that flight or you are planning six or more hours ahead. It is the default request for a cross-country and gives you everything in a fixed sequence so nothing is left out.

items.q: What items does a standard briefing contain, and in what order?
items.a: Adverse conditions first, then whether VFR flight is not recommended, the synopsis, current conditions, en route forecast, destination forecast, forecast winds and temperatures aloft, NOTAMs, ATC delays, and finally anything else on request such as MOA and military training route activity, ADIZ procedures or a search and rescue plan.

items.q: What does it mean when the briefer says "VFR flight not recommended"?
items.a: It is an advisory, given when the reported or forecast ceilings and visibilities along your route are at or below VFR minimums or are marginal in the briefer's judgment. It is not a prohibition or a clearance denial; the go or no-go decision remains entirely with the pilot in command, but it is a formal warning that should carry weight.

items.q: What is an abbreviated briefing and when do you ask for one?
items.a: A shortened briefing used to update information you already have, for example when your departure has been delayed, when you have already read the weather yourself online, or when you need only one or two specific items such as current conditions or NOTAMs. Tell the briefer the source and time of the information you already hold.

items.q: What is an outlook briefing and when is it appropriate?
items.a: An outlook briefing is requested when your proposed departure is six or more hours away. It gives forecast information only, intended for planning and initial go/no-go decisions, and it is not sufficient by itself for the flight; follow it with a standard or abbreviated briefing closer to departure.

items.q: What information should you give the briefer when requesting a briefing?
items.a: Whether the flight is VFR or IFR, the aircraft identification or your name, the aircraft type, departure point, proposed departure time, cruising altitude, route, destination and estimated time en route. Say which type of briefing you want so the briefer can format it correctly.

items.q: What was HIWAS, and does it still exist?
items.a: The Hazardous Inflight Weather Advisory Service was a continuous recorded broadcast of hazardous weather, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, convective SIGMETs, center weather advisories and urgent PIREPs over selected VOR frequencies. It has been discontinued; for in-flight hazard information contact Flight Service directly or use a datalink weather source.

items.q: What was TIBS, and is it still available?
items.a: The Telephone Information Briefing Service was a recorded telephone briefing of area and route weather, reached on numbers published in the Chart Supplement. Like HIWAS it has been discontinued as part of Flight Service modernization; check the current AIM Chapter 7 for the list of services actually in place before relying on any legacy product.

items.q: How do you get weather from Flight Service while airborne?
items.a: Call Flight Service by name on 122.2 or on the discrete remote communications outlet frequency shown on the sectional near the appropriate VOR or airport, giving your position. The old En Route Flight Advisory Service, Flight Watch on 122.0, was discontinued and its function folded into the normal Flight Service frequencies.

items.q: What are the current sources of aviation weather a commercial applicant should be able to name?
items.a: Flight Service by phone or at 1800wxbrief.com; the Aviation Weather Center at aviationweather.gov for METAR, TAF, GFA, advisories and charts; ADS-B FIS-B and commercial satellite datalink in the cockpit; ATIS, ASOS and AWOS broadcasts; and ATC or Flight Service by radio in flight.

b: Observations: METAR, SPECI, PIREP and how to read them.

items.q: What is a METAR and how often is one issued?
items.a: A METAR is a routine surface weather observation of conditions at an airport, issued once every hour, normally in the 55 to 59 minute window before the hour. It reports what is actually happening at the field at observation time; it is a report, not a forecast.

items.q: What is a SPECI and what triggers one?
items.a: A SPECI is a special unscheduled observation issued between routine METARs when there is a significant change in one or more of the reported elements, such as a wind shift, a visibility or ceiling change through an operational threshold, the beginning or ending of precipitation or a thunderstorm, or the onset of freezing precipitation.

items.q: What are the fields of a METAR, in order?
items.a: Report type; station identifier; date and time; modifier if any; wind; visibility; runway visual range; present weather; sky condition; temperature and dew point; altimeter setting; and remarks. Any element that is not occurring or cannot be observed is simply omitted, so a short METAR usually means benign weather.

items.q: How are the station identifier and the date/time group written in a METAR?
items.a: The station is the four-letter ICAO identifier, which in the contiguous United States is K plus the three-letter identifier. The date/time group is six digits followed by Z: two digits for the day of the month, four for the time, always in coordinated universal time, so 121853Z is the 12th day at 1853Z.

items.q: What do the modifiers AUTO and COR mean, and what are A01 and A02?
items.a: AUTO means the report came from an automated station with no human augmentation; COR means a corrected observation. In the remarks, A01 means the station has no precipitation discriminator and cannot tell rain from snow, while A02 means it has one. Automated stations also cannot report tornado activity, virga, or cloud above their sensor limit.

items.q: How is the wind group encoded in a METAR?
items.a: Five digits plus KT: three for direction in degrees true, rounded to the nearest ten, and two or three for speed, with G and the peak for gusts. 00000KT is calm, VRB means variable direction, and a direction varying 60 degrees or more with the wind above 6 kt is shown separately as, for example, 180V240.

items.q: How are visibility and runway visual range reported in a METAR?
items.a: Prevailing visibility in statute miles, with fractions, for example 1 1/2SM; automated stations report 10SM as their maximum. RVR follows as R, the runway number, a slash and the value in feet, so R22L/2400FT, with P for more than and M for less than the stated value, and V between two values for a variable RVR.

items.q: How is the present weather group built up in a METAR?
items.a: In a fixed order: intensity or proximity, then descriptor, then precipitation, then obscuration, then other phenomena. Intensity is a minus for light, nothing for moderate and a plus for heavy; VC means in the vicinity, 5 to 10 statute miles from the field. So -SHRA is light rain showers and +TSRA is a thunderstorm with heavy rain. In a United States METAR, VC means 5 to 10 statute miles from the point of observation; in a United States TAF it means 5 to 10 statute miles from the center of the runway complex; everywhere else it means within 8,000 meters.

items.q: What are the METAR descriptor and precipitation codes?
items.a: Descriptors are MI shallow, BC patches, PR partial, DR low drifting, BL blowing, SH showers, TS thunderstorm and FZ freezing. Precipitation is DZ drizzle, RA rain, SN snow, SG snow grains, IC ice crystals, PL ice pellets, GR hail, GS small hail or snow pellets, and UP unknown precipitation from an automated station.

items.q: What are the METAR obscuration and other phenomena codes?
items.a: Obscurations are BR mist (visibility 5/8 to under 7 SM), FG fog (under 5/8 SM), FU smoke, VA volcanic ash, DU widespread dust, SA sand, HZ haze and PY spray. Other phenomena are PO dust or sand whirls, SQ squalls, FC funnel cloud (+FC for a tornado or waterspout), SS sandstorm and DS duststorm. BR is mist, reported when visibility is 5/8 statute mile or more, and FG is fog, reported below 5/8 statute mile. A plus sign on funnel cloud, +FC, is a tornado or waterspout.

items.q: How is sky condition reported, and what makes a layer a ceiling?
items.a: By amount and height in hundreds of feet AGL: SKC or CLR for clear, FEW for one to two eighths, SCT three to four eighths, BKN five to seven eighths, OVC eight eighths, and VV for an indefinite ceiling with vertical visibility. The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration.

items.q: How are temperature, dew point and the altimeter setting encoded in a METAR?
items.a: Temperature and dew point are two digits each in degrees Celsius, separated by a slash, with M in front for a value below zero, so 04/M01 is 4 degrees C with a dew point of minus 1. The altimeter is A followed by four digits, the setting in inches of mercury with the decimal point omitted, so A2992 is 29.92 inHg.

items.q: What sort of information appears in the remarks section of a METAR?
items.a: Anything that clarifies or adds to the body: SLP sea level pressure in tenths of a millibar, PK WND peak wind, WSHFT wind shift, LTG lightning and its type and location, RAB and RAE for precipitation beginning and ending times, VIRGA, TWR VIS, P0015 for hourly precipitation in hundredths of an inch, and the T group for precise temperature and dew point in tenths.

items.q: Decode this: METAR KJAX 121853Z 24012G20KT 3SM -TSRA BR BKN012 OVC030 26/23 A2989 RMK TSB35.
items.a: Routine observation for Jacksonville on the 12th at 1853Z: wind 240 degrees true at 12 gusting 20 kt, visibility 3 statute miles in a thunderstorm with light rain and mist, broken at 1,200 ft and overcast at 3,000 ft AGL, temperature 26 degrees C, dew point 23, altimeter 29.89 inHg, thunderstorm began at 35 past the hour. SKC is reported only by a human observer and means no clouds at all, while an automated station with nothing below 12,000 feet reports CLR instead.

items.q: What are the four flight categories, and what ceiling and visibility defines each?
items.a: LIFR is a ceiling below 500 ft AGL or visibility below 1 SM; IFR is a ceiling of 500 to below 1,000 ft or visibility 1 to below 3 SM; MVFR is a ceiling of 1,000 to 3,000 ft or visibility 3 to 5 SM; and VFR is a ceiling above 3,000 ft AGL and visibility greater than 5 SM. The worse of the two values sets the category.

items.q: What is a PIREP and why does it matter?
items.a: A pilot report is a report of actual conditions encountered in flight, passed to Flight Service, ATC or a controlling facility and distributed to other pilots and forecasters. It is the only direct source of information on turbulence, icing, cloud tops, in-flight visibility and wind shear, none of which any ground observation can measure.

items.q: What are the thirteen elements of a PIREP form?
items.a: Location identifier of the nearest station; UA or UUA for routine or urgent; /OV location; /TM time in UTC; /FL altitude or flight level; /TP aircraft type; /SK sky cover; /WX flight visibility and weather; /TA outside air temperature in degrees C; /WV wind direction and speed; /TB turbulence; /IC icing; and /RM remarks.

items.q: Which PIREP elements are required, and which are optional?
items.a: The first five are always required: message type, location, time, altitude and aircraft type. After that at least one weather element must be reported, and the rest are included only if observed. If you cannot fill in a field, leave it out; a partial report is far more useful than no report.

items.q: What is the difference between UA and UUA, and what makes a PIREP urgent?
items.a: UA is a routine pilot report; UUA is urgent and gets immediate distribution. Urgent criteria are tornadoes, funnel clouds or waterspouts; severe or extreme turbulence including clear air turbulence; severe icing; hail; low-level wind shear within 2,000 ft of the surface; volcanic activity or ash; and any other condition hazardous to flight.

items.q: How are turbulence intensities and their frequency reported in a PIREP?
items.a: Intensity is light, moderate, severe or extreme, with light and moderate further split into turbulence and chop. Frequency is occasional for less than one third of the time, intermittent for one third to two thirds, and continuous for more than two thirds. Severe means momentary loss of control and large abrupt altitude changes; extreme means the aircraft is practically impossible to control. The turbulence entry carries the altitude band it was encountered in, not just the reporting airplane's level, so the next pilot knows what to climb or descend through.

items.q: Decode this: UA /OV KSAV180010 /TM 1615 /FL065 /TP PA28 /SK BKN040-TOP070 /TA 03 /TB LGT /IC LGT RIME.
items.a: A routine pilot report 10 nautical miles on the 180 radial from Savannah at 1615Z, at 6,500 ft, from a PA-28: a broken layer with a base near 4,000 ft and tops at 7,000 ft, outside air temperature 3 degrees C, light turbulence, and light rime icing. The /OV field can name a route between two stations rather than a single fix, and /SK can stack several layers with their bases and tops, ending in CLR ABV to say the air is clear above the highest layer reported.

items.q: In what order do the fields of a METAR appear?
items.a: Type, station identifier, date and time, modifier, wind, visibility, runway visual range, present weather, sky condition, temperature and dew point, altimeter, then remarks. Reading them in that fixed order is what lets you decode a report you have never seen; a field that is missing simply means there was nothing to report, as with sky clear and no weather at all.

items.q: How is icing reported in a PIREP?
items.a: In the /IC field, with intensity, type and the altitude band. Intensity runs trace, light, moderate and severe; type is rime, clear or mixed. So IC LGT-MOD RIME 072-089 is light to moderate rime ice between 7,200 and 8,900 feet. Pilot reports matter here because icing forecasts are coarse and cannot tell you where ice actually formed.

b: TAF, winds and temperatures aloft, and the graphical forecasts.

items.q: What is a TAF, how often is it issued, and how long is it valid?
items.a: A Terminal Aerodrome Forecast is issued four times a day, at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800Z, and is normally valid for 24 hours, with 30-hour TAFs at many larger airports. It is prepared about half an hour before the valid period begins and is amended as TAF AMD whenever conditions change materially.

items.q: What area does a TAF actually cover?
items.a: A TAF forecasts conditions expected within 5 statute miles of the center of the airport's runway complex, so it is a terminal forecast rather than an area forecast. Weather just outside that circle need not appear in it, which is why you pair it with the graphical forecast for the surrounding area.

items.q: What are the elements of a TAF, in order?
items.a: Report type; ICAO station identifier; issuance date and time in UTC; valid period as two day/hour pairs separated by a slash; then, for each period, forecast wind, visibility, weather, sky condition, and any non-convective low-level wind shear group. There is no temperature, dew point or altimeter setting in a TAF.

items.q: What does the FM change group in a TAF mean?
items.a: FM marks a rapid and permanent change, expected within an hour, to a new set of conditions. It is written FM followed by six digits for day, hour and minute, as in FM121600, and everything after it replaces the whole previous forecast line until the next change group.

items.q: What does BECMG mean in a TAF?
items.a: BECMG marks a gradual change expected to occur at some point within the stated window, written as two day/hour pairs, for example BECMG 1214/1216. Only the elements that are listed change; the rest of the previous forecast carries on unchanged, which is the key difference from an FM group.

items.q: What do TEMPO and PROB30 mean in a TAF?
items.a: TEMPO covers temporary fluctuations lasting under an hour each and in total less than half the stated period, for example TEMPO 1216/1220 with a time window in day/hour pairs. PROB30 indicates a 30 to less than 40 percent probability of the stated conditions, usually thunderstorms or precipitation, in the stated window. PROB40 is used as well as PROB30, and a PROB group is not used at all in the first nine hours of a TAF's valid period.

items.q: How is low-level wind shear shown in a TAF?
items.a: As a WS group: WS, three digits for the height of the shear in hundreds of feet AGL, a slash, then the wind at that height as three digits of direction and two or three of speed in knots. WS020/24045KT means non-convective wind shear at 2,000 ft AGL with a wind there of 240 degrees at 45 kt.

items.q: How are visibility and "no significant weather" written in a TAF?
items.a: Visibility is in statute miles without the SM decimal fractions being abbreviated, and anything greater than 6 statute miles is written P6SM. NSW means no significant weather and is used only in a TEMPO or BECMG group to show that previously forecast weather is ending. United States TAFs do not use CAVOK.

items.q: Decode this TAF line: TAF KTPA 121120Z 1212/1318 18008KT P6SM SCT035 TEMPO 1218/1222 3SM TSRA BKN025CB.
items.a: Tampa's forecast issued on the 12th at 1120Z, valid from the 12th at 1200Z to the 13th at 1800Z: wind 180 degrees true at 8 kt, visibility greater than 6 SM, scattered at 3,500 ft, with temporary periods between 1800Z and 2200Z on the 12th of 3 SM in a thunderstorm with rain and broken cumulonimbus at 2,500 ft. An equals sign at the very end of a TAF marks the end of the report, so anything after it belongs to a different forecast.

items.q: What is the Graphical Forecast for Aviation and what does it show?
items.a: The GFA is the interactive tool on aviationweather.gov that replaced the old textual area forecast. It displays observations and forecasts in map form in hourly snapshots out to about 18 hours ahead, covering clouds and ceiling, visibility and obstructions, surface wind, precipitation, thunderstorms, icing, turbulence and freezing levels for the contiguous United States and coastal waters.

items.q: How does the GFA help you with IFR planning and the alternate rule?
items.a: It gives forecast ceiling and visibility across the whole area rather than just at the reporting airports, so you can see whether a proposed destination or alternate sits inside a region of forecast IFR, and how that region is moving. Use it alongside the TAF, since it is the ceiling and visibility values that decide whether an alternate is required and whether one is legal.

items.q: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.169 (Part 91, Subpart B, "IFR flight plan: Information required") you must file an alternate unless the destination has a published instrument approach and, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after your estimated time of arrival, the ceiling is forecast to be at least 2,000 ft above the airport elevation and the visibility at least 3 statute miles.

items.q: What is the winds and temperatures aloft forecast and what conventions does it use?
items.a: A forecast of wind and temperature at standard levels, computed from the 0000Z and 1200Z upper air data and issued with valid times covering roughly 6, 12 and 24 hours ahead. Wind direction is always referenced to true north and speed is in knots; temperatures are in degrees Celsius.

items.q: What are the standard forecast levels for winds and temperatures aloft?
items.a: 3,000; 6,000; 9,000; 12,000; 18,000; 24,000; 30,000; 34,000 and 39,000 ft, with levels at or below 18,000 ft referenced to MSL and higher ones given as flight levels. Not every station carries every level, because levels close to the ground are omitted.

items.q: When are winds and temperatures aloft not forecast for a level?
items.a: No wind is forecast for a level within 1,500 ft of the station elevation, and no temperature is forecast for a level within 2,500 ft of the station elevation. That is why a station in high terrain shows blanks or dashes for its lowest levels, and why the 3,000 ft level never carries a temperature.

items.q: Decode the winds aloft group 731960.
items.a: The coded direction 73 exceeds 36, so subtract 50 from the direction and add 100 to the speed: the wind is 230 degrees true at 119 kt, and the temperature is minus 60 degrees C. Any coded direction from 51 to 86 uses this rule, which is how speeds of 100 kt and more are packed into two digits.

items.q: What do the codes 9900 and 7799 mean in a winds aloft forecast, and how are temperatures shown above 24,000 ft?
items.a: 9900 means light and variable, that is, less than 5 kt. 7799 is the code for a wind of 199 kt or greater, from 270 degrees. Above 24,000 ft all temperatures are below zero, so the minus sign is omitted and a bare number such as 55 means minus 55 degrees C.

items.q: How do you use the winds aloft forecast when choosing a cruising altitude?
items.a: Compare the forecast wind at two or three candidate levels for your route to find the best combination of groundspeed and fuel burn, taking into account the higher true airspeed but lower power available with altitude. Remember the directions are true, so convert to magnetic before comparing them with a heading or a runway, and account for the hemispheric altitude rule.

items.q: When the forecast makes an alternate necessary, what weather must the alternate itself be forecast to have?
items.a: At your ETA at the alternate the forecast must be at or above the alternate minimums: standard is 600 feet and 2 statute miles for a precision approach and 800 feet and 2 statute miles for a nonprecision approach, unless the approach chart lists nonstandard alternate minimums. If the alternate has no instrument approach, the forecast ceiling and visibility must allow descent from the MEA, approach and landing under basic VFR. Source: 14 CFR part 91, subpart B, section 91.169, IFR flight plan: information required.

items.q: Once you know an alternate is required, what is the next decision in the chart?
items.a: Whether your chosen alternate has non-standard alternate minimums and whether you can actually meet them. Some airports carry higher than standard alternate ceilings and visibilities, or are not authorized as an alternate at all, because of terrain, a missing weather reporting source, or an out of service monitoring facility. Check the alternate minimums section of the Terminal Procedures Publication before applying the standard 600-2 or 800-2 numbers.
items.concept: Second node: does the chosen alternate have non-standard alternate requirements that can be complied with

items.q: Your chosen alternate has non-standard minimums you cannot meet. What does the chart say?
items.a: Choose a different alternate. The flowchart loops you back: you may not file an airport whose published alternate minimums you cannot meet, and you may not file one annotated alternate NA at all. Pick another airport and run it through the same test, again checking its alternate minimums listing before applying the standard numbers.
items.concept: Branch: non-standard requirements cannot be complied with, so choose a different alternate

items.q: The alternate's forecast at your ETA is below 600-2. What does the flowchart say?
items.a: Go back and choose a different alternate. The loop in the chart returns you to the same place as a non-standard minimums failure. An airport you cannot legally file does not become filable by hoping the forecast improves; find another one, or delay or cancel the flight if nothing in range qualifies.
items.concept: Branch: alternate forecast minimums not met, so choose a different alternate

items.q: Without WAAS, how may you plan RNAV-only airports as destination and alternate?
items.a: You may plan on an airport served only by RNAV approaches at either the destination or the alternate, but not both. One of the two must have a non-RNAV approach you can fly. The restriction exists because a single GPS failure in a non-WAAS airplane would strip you of the approach at both ends of the flight. If your Warrior has a non-WAAS IFR GPS, this is the limitation that applies to you.
items.concept: Non-WAAS outcome: RNAV-only approaches at EITHER destination OR alternate, but not both

items.q: With a WAAS GPS, how may you plan RNAV-only airports as destination and alternate?
items.a: You may plan on airports served only by RNAV approaches at both the destination and the alternate. WAAS integrity monitoring removes the single failure concern that restricts non-WAAS aircraft. When you compute the alternate weather requirement, however, the AIM directs you to use the LNAV or circling minimums line, not the LPV line.
items.concept: WAAS outcome: RNAV-only approaches at BOTH destination AND alternate

items.q: What does a black triangle containing a white letter A on an approach chart tell you?
items.a: That the airport has non-standard alternate minimums, so the standard 600-2 and 800-2 do not apply and you must look the airport up in the alternate minimums section of the Terminal Procedures Publication. If the symbol carries NA beside it, the airport may not be used as an alternate at all. Its companion, a black triangle containing a white T, marks non-standard takeoff minimums or a departure procedure.
items.concept: The inverted triangle containing the letter A on an approach chart marks non-standard alternate minimums

b: AIRMET, SIGMET, convective SIGMET, center weather advisories.

items.q: What is an AIRMET and who is it aimed at?
items.a: An AIRMET is an advisory of weather that may be hazardous to light aircraft and to aircraft with limited capability, at intensities below SIGMET criteria. It covers conditions affecting an area of at least 3,000 square miles, and it is issued whether or not the conditions are actually being observed, so it is a forecast product.

items.q: In what form are AIRMETs issued today?
items.a: As the graphical G-AIRMET. The legacy textual AIRMET bulletin was discontinued over the contiguous United States in January 2025, so the product you look at is the graphical depiction on aviationweather.gov, which shows the hazard areas as shaded polygons at specific forecast times rather than as a written area description.

items.q: What is the G-AIRMET issue schedule and how far ahead does it forecast?
items.a: G-AIRMETs are issued four times a day, at 0300, 0900, 1500 and 2100Z, and are amended as conditions require. Each issuance gives forecast snapshots at 3-hour intervals out to 12 hours, so you see the hazard area at 00, 03, 06, 09 and 12 hours from the issue time rather than one smeared area covering the whole period.

items.q: What does AIRMET Sierra cover?
items.a: Sierra is the IFR and mountain obscuration advisory: ceilings less than 1,000 ft and/or visibility less than 3 statute miles affecting more than half the area at any one time, and extensive mountain obscuration by cloud, precipitation, smoke or other phenomena.

items.q: What does AIRMET Tango cover?
items.a: Tango is the turbulence and wind advisory: moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more, and non-convective low-level wind shear. In the graphical product these appear as separate turbulence, surface wind and low-level wind shear layers you can select individually.

items.q: What does AIRMET Zulu cover?
items.a: Zulu is the icing advisory: moderate airframe icing, and the forecast freezing level heights, including multiple freezing levels where a warm layer aloft creates more than one. Zulu is the product to check before any flight in visible moisture in cold conditions.

items.q: What is a SIGMET, how long is it valid, and what does it warn of?
items.a: A SIGMET is an unscheduled advisory of non-convective weather hazardous to all aircraft, valid for 4 hours, extended to 6 hours for hurricanes and tropical cyclones and for volcanic ash. It covers severe icing not associated with thunderstorms, severe or extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence not associated with thunderstorms, widespread dust or sandstorms lowering visibility below 3 miles, and volcanic ash.

items.q: What is the difference between an AIRMET and a SIGMET?
items.a: Severity and audience. An AIRMET describes moderate conditions that are significant to light aircraft, is scheduled four times a day, and is a routine advisory. A SIGMET describes severe or extreme conditions hazardous to all aircraft including airliners, is unscheduled and issued only when the weather warrants, and demands action rather than just awareness.

items.q: What is a convective SIGMET, when is it issued, and how long is it valid?
items.a: An advisory for thunderstorm-related hazards, issued hourly at 55 minutes past the hour and valid for 2 hours, with special issuances at any time as conditions require. Separate bulletins are produced for the eastern, central and western United States, and each includes an outlook for the following 2 to 6 hours.

items.q: What thunderstorm conditions trigger a convective SIGMET?
items.a: Any of: severe thunderstorms, defined as surface winds greater than 50 kt or hail at the surface greater than three quarters of an inch in diameter or tornadoes; embedded thunderstorms of any intensity; a line of thunderstorms at least 60 miles long affecting 40 percent of its length; or thunderstorms producing heavy or greater precipitation over 40 percent of an area of at least 3,000 square miles.

items.q: What hazards are implied by a convective SIGMET even when they are not written in it?
items.a: Severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear are always implied by the presence of a convective SIGMET and are therefore not spelled out separately in the text. Treat any convective SIGMET area as containing all three whether or not they are mentioned.

items.q: What is a Center Weather Advisory?
items.a: A CWA is an unscheduled nowcast issued by the meteorologist in the Center Weather Service Unit at an air route traffic control center, valid for up to 2 hours. It warns of conditions meeting or approaching SIGMET or convective SIGMET criteria, or of any weather already adversely affecting traffic flow in that center's airspace.

items.q: Are you legally required to avoid an area covered by an AIRMET or SIGMET?
items.a: There is no rule that prohibits flight into an advisory area, but under 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B, "Preflight action") you must be familiar with all available information for the flight, and under 14 CFR 91.13 you must not operate carelessly or recklessly. Flying a light aircraft into a SIGMET for severe icing or severe turbulence would be very hard to defend on either count.

items.q: AIRMET Tango includes low-level wind shear; what is LLWS and where would you expect to meet it?
items.a: LLWS is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance in the lowest levels, conventionally below 2,000 feet AGL, strong enough to cost an airplane airspeed and altitude on approach or departure. Expect it with thunderstorm gust fronts and microbursts, frontal passage, strong winds over rough terrain or obstructions, and temperature inversions with strong winds just above. Nonconvective LLWS below 2,000 feet AGL is the AIRMET Tango trigger; convective shear is carried in convective SIGMETs instead.

b: Prognostic, surface analysis, radar summary and how to read them.

items.q: What is the surface analysis chart, how often is it issued, and what does it show?
items.a: A computer-prepared analysis of observed surface conditions across the country, issued every 3 hours. It shows pressure systems with their centers, isobars, fronts and air mass boundaries, plus a station model at each reporting point giving wind, temperature and dew point, sky cover, pressure and precipitation.

items.q: How do you read the station model on a surface analysis chart?
items.a: The circle shows sky cover by how much of it is filled in, with a shaft pointing in the direction the wind is blowing from. Temperature sits at the upper left and dew point at the lower left in degrees Fahrenheit, sea level pressure at the upper right in the abbreviated three-digit form, and present weather symbols to the left of the circle.

items.q: How can you predict the surface wind from the pressure pattern on a chart?
items.a: Stand with your back to the wind and the low is on your left in the Northern Hemisphere. Working the other way, the surface wind blows roughly along the isobars but angled 20 to 45 degrees across them toward the low, and its speed follows the isobar spacing: tightly packed isobars, strong wind. As a rule of thumb the surface wind is about half the speed of the wind at 2,000 ft and backed about 30 degrees from it.

items.q: How are the four fronts drawn on a surface chart?
items.a: A cold front is blue with triangles, a warm front red with semicircles, a stationary front alternates blue triangles on one side with red semicircles on the other, and an occluded front is purple with alternating triangles and semicircles on the same side. The symbols always point in the direction the front is moving.

items.q: What happened to the weather depiction chart?
items.a: The weather depiction chart, formerly issued every 3 hours to show areas of VFR, MVFR and IFR, has been discontinued. The same information, and considerably more, now comes from the Graphical Forecast for Aviation on aviationweather.gov, where you can select ceiling and visibility and see both the current observations and the forecast.

items.q: What is the low-level significant weather prognostic chart and what does it cover?
items.a: A forecast chart covering the surface to FL240, issued four times daily with 12-hour and 24-hour panels. It depicts areas of IFR and MVFR, turbulence, and the freezing level, alongside the forecast positions of fronts and pressure centers. Much of its function is now served by the GFA, and the current prog charts on aviationweather.gov run out to 12, 24, 36 and 48 hours.

items.q: How do you read the area symbols on a low-level significant weather prog chart?
items.a: A smooth solid line encloses areas of IFR, a scalloped line encloses MVFR, and everything outside both is forecast VFR. Long dashed lines enclose areas of forecast turbulence with a symbol and a number showing intensity and the altitude band in hundreds of feet, and short dashed lines mark the freezing level with its height in hundreds of feet MSL.

items.q: How are the two panels of a prognostic chart read together?
items.a: The upper panels forecast significant weather, that is, cloud, flight category, turbulence and freezing levels, while the lower panels forecast surface conditions, that is, fronts, pressure centers and areas of precipitation. Read left to right for the progression in time, so you can see how a system is expected to move and develop across your route.

items.q: What does the mid-level significant weather chart cover?
items.a: The layer from 10,000 ft MSL to FL450, issued four times daily. It shows thunderstorms and cumulonimbus, the jet stream, tropopause heights, tropical cyclones, moderate and severe icing and turbulence, cloud cover and type, volcanic ash and any release of radioactive material into the atmosphere.

items.q: What does the high-level significant weather chart cover?
items.a: The layer used by turbine traffic, from about FL250 to FL630, issued four times daily. It depicts jet stream cores with their speeds and heights, areas of clear air turbulence, tropopause heights, cumulonimbus areas, tropical cyclones, volcanic ash and sandstorms. It is of limited use to a piston single but you should be able to recognize it.

items.q: What is the convective outlook, how often is it issued, and how are the areas classified?
items.a: A Storm Prediction Center forecast of severe thunderstorm potential, issued for Day 1 five times, Day 2 twice and Day 3 once each day. Risk areas are categorized as marginal, slight, enhanced, moderate and high, abbreviated MRGL, SLGT, ENH, MDT and HIGH, in increasing order of coverage and intensity of expected severe storms.

items.q: What is the radar summary chart, and what is used in its place today?
items.a: The old radar summary chart was a computer-generated depiction of precipitation echoes, showing echo type, intensity, coverage, tops in hundreds of feet, and the direction and speed of cell movement. It has been retired; the equivalent product today is the composite reflectivity radar mosaic on aviationweather.gov, available as a static image or a loop.

items.q: What do the radar intensity levels mean on a radar mosaic?
items.a: The color scale is reflectivity in dBZ: roughly under 30 dBZ is light precipitation, 30 to 40 moderate, 40 to 50 heavy, and above 50 extreme, with hail and severe turbulence likely. Green, yellow, red and magenta on a typical display correspond to those bands.

items.q: Why do echo tops and cell movement matter on a radar product?
items.a: Echo tops, given in hundreds of feet, tell you how deep the convection is and whether you could realistically climb over it, and a rapidly rising top means a growing cell. The movement arrow and speed tell you where the cell will be by the time you get there, which is what actually determines your deviation.

items.q: What are the limitations of any radar chart or mosaic?
items.a: It shows precipitation only, not cloud, ceiling, visibility, turbulence or icing, so an area with no echo can still be solid IMC. The mosaic is a composite assembled from many sites and can be older than its timestamp, ground clutter and beam blockage create false or missing echoes, and heavy rain can attenuate the beam so a stronger cell hides behind a nearer one.

items.q: Which weather products should you have printed and be ready to brief for a stage check or checkride?
items.a: A full weather brief from 1800wxbrief.com covering the route, the low-level significant weather prog chart, the surface analysis chart from aviationweather.gov, and the current radar mosaic showing precipitation echoes. Be ready to explain what each one shows, its issue schedule, and what in it affects your go or no-go decision for the flight.

items.q: On a radar mosaic, what is the difference between base and composite reflectivity?
items.a: Base reflectivity is a single low elevation sweep, so it is the cleaner picture of precipitation actually reaching the lower levels; composite reflectivity is the strongest return from every elevation angle in the column, so it shows the worst weather anywhere in the storm and pairs with the echo tops product. Composite always reads equal to or stronger than base, so a cell can look severe on composite while little is falling below. Neither shows cloud, turbulence or icing, only precipitation-size particles.

b: VOR, GPS, transponder, ADS-B, and the avionics that drive them.

items.q: What instruments and equipment must be installed and working for VFR day flight?
items.a: The mnemonic is ATOMATOFLAMES: Airspeed indicator, Tachometer for each engine, Oil pressure gauge, Manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine, Altimeter, Temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine, Oil temperature gauge, Fuel gauge for each tank, Landing gear position indicator if retractable, Anti-collision lights, Magnetic direction indicator, ELT, and Seat belts. This is 14 CFR 91.205(b) (Part 91, Subpart C - Instrument and equipment requirements: Visual flight rules, day).

items.q: Which items on the VFR day list only apply to some airplanes?
items.a: Four are conditional. A manifold pressure gauge is required only for an altitude engine, meaning a turbocharged or supercharged engine. A coolant temperature gauge is required only for a liquid-cooled engine, and an oil temperature gauge only for an air-cooled engine. A landing gear position indicator is required only if the gear retracts. Anti-collision lights are required on small civil airplanes certificated after 11 March 1996, and shoulder harnesses for front seats on airplanes manufactured after 18 July 1978.

items.q: What must be added to the VFR day equipment for flight at night?
items.a: The mnemonic is FLAPS: Fuses, meaning one spare set or three spare fuses of each kind required and accessible in flight; Landing light, but only if the flight is for hire; Anti-collision lights; Position lights, red on the left wing, green on the right and white at the tail; and Source of electrical energy adequate for all installed electrical and radio equipment. This is 14 CFR 91.205(c) (Part 91, Subpart C - Instrument and equipment requirements: Visual flight rules, night).

items.q: Is a landing light required at night in a privately operated airplane?
items.a: No. 14 CFR 91.205(c)(4) (Part 91, Subpart C - Instrument and equipment requirements: Visual flight rules, night) requires one electric landing light only if the aircraft is operated for hire. A private, non-commercial night flight is legal without one, though flying at night with no landing light is a poor practical decision and a night landing without one is a real skill loss.

items.q: When must position lights and anti-collision lights be on?
items.a: Position lights must be lighted from sunset to sunrise for any operation, and the aircraft may not be parked or moved in a dangerous area at night unless lighted or the area is well lit. Anti-collision lights must be on during all operations day and night, but the pilot in command may switch them off if it is in the interest of safety, for example in cloud where the strobes cause disorientation. This is 14 CFR 91.209 (Part 91, Subpart C - Aircraft lights).

items.q: What equipment must be added on top of the VFR lists to fly IFR?
items.a: The mnemonic is GRABCARD: Generator or alternator of adequate capacity; Radios, meaning two-way communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route; Attitude indicator, a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator; Ball, a slip-skid indicator; Clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds, installed in the aircraft; Adjustable altimeter, sensitive and settable for barometric pressure; Rate of turn indicator; and Directional gyro. This is 14 CFR 91.205(d) (Part 91, Subpart C - Instrument and equipment requirements: Instrument flight rules).

items.q: What extra navigation equipment is required at and above FL240?
items.a: If VOR navigation equipment is required for the route, the aircraft must also carry approved DME or a suitable RNAV system at and above FL240. If that equipment fails at or above FL240, you must notify ATC immediately and may continue to the next airport of intended landing where repairs can be made. This is 14 CFR 91.205(e) (Part 91, Subpart C - Instrument and equipment requirements: Flight at and above FL240).

items.q: Without a minimum equipment list, how may you legally fly with an inoperative item?
items.a: Work through 14 CFR 91.213(d) (Part 91, Subpart C - Inoperative instruments and equipment). The item must not be part of the VFR day type certificate equipment list, not required by 91.205 for the kind of flight, not required by an airworthiness directive, and not required by a supplemental type certificate or the aircraft equipment list. It must then be removed or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE, with removal or deactivation recorded by a pilot or mechanic as allowed, and the pilot in command must determine it is safe to fly.

items.q: Who decides that a flight with an inoperative item is safe to make?
items.a: The pilot in command. Even when 14 CFR 91.213(d) (Part 91, Subpart C - Inoperative instruments and equipment) is satisfied on paper, the final step is the pilot in command determining that the inoperative instrument or equipment does not constitute a hazard for the particular flight. A legal placard does not make a night IFR flight with a failed second radio a sensible one.

items.q: How does a magnetic compass work?
items.a: Two small bar magnets are attached to a float carrying the compass card, and the whole assembly swings freely inside a sealed case filled with acid-free white kerosene. The fluid damps the swing and lubricates the pivot. The magnets align themselves with the earth magnetic field, so the card turns and you read your heading against a fixed lubber line. It is self-contained, needing no electrical power, vacuum or air data, which is why it is the last heading reference standing.

items.q: What is magnetic dip and why does it matter?
items.a: Magnetic dip is the tendency of the compass magnets to point down toward the magnetic pole as well as toward it, because the earth field is not horizontal except near the equator. The closer you get to the pole the steeper the field and the more the card is dragged out of the horizontal, which is what produces the acceleration and turning errors and makes the compass progressively less usable at high latitude.

items.q: What acceleration and deceleration errors does the compass show, and on what headings?
items.a: On easterly or westerly headings only, acceleration makes the compass indicate a turn toward north and deceleration makes it indicate a turn toward south. The mnemonic is ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. The error is caused by magnetic dip acting on the weighted compass card, and it is zero on north or south headings.

items.q: What turning error does the compass show, and which way does it go?
items.a: The mnemonic is UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South. Rolling into a turn from a northerly heading, the compass lags and initially shows a turn in the opposite direction, so you must roll out early. Rolling into a turn from a southerly heading, the compass leads and initially shows a turn in the same direction but too fast, so you must roll out late. The error is greatest on north and south and zero on east and west.

items.q: What is the rule of thumb for rolling out on a northerly or southerly heading using the compass?
items.a: Take your latitude divided by two, plus 15 degrees. Turning to north, start the rollout that many degrees before the desired heading because the compass lags. Turning to south, continue that many degrees past the desired heading because the compass leads. At 30 degrees north latitude that is about 30 degrees of lead or lag. It is a rule of thumb for a standard rate turn, not a precise figure. Two details worth carrying: the error applies as stated in the Northern Hemisphere only, and UNOS is the mnemonic, undershoot north and overshoot south.

items.q: What is compass oscillation, and what causes it?
items.a: Oscillation is erratic swinging of the compass card, caused by turbulence, rough control inputs or any other irregular motion of the airplane. It is not an error in the magnetic system, it is the card physically slopping about in the fluid. Wait for smooth air and steady flight before reading the compass, and never set the heading indicator from a swinging card.

items.q: What is compass deviation, and how is it dealt with?
items.a: Deviation is compass error caused by magnetic and electrical fields inside the airplane itself: engine, radios, wiring, avionics and anything ferrous. It varies with heading and with what is switched on.
