It is minimized by a mechanic swinging the compass on a compass rose and adjusting the compensating magnets, and the residue is recorded on the deviation card mounted by the compass, which must be in place and legible.

items.q: What is magnetic variation, and where do you find it?
items.a: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north, which is the difference between the geographic pole and the wandering magnetic pole. You find it on charts as isogonic lines, lines joining points of equal variation, and the agonic line is where variation is zero. East variation is subtracted from true to get magnetic and west variation is added, remembered as east is least, west is best. The working mnemonic is east is least, west is best: subtract easterly variation from true heading and add westerly variation to get magnetic heading, reversing it the other way.

items.q: What is a VOR and what frequency band does it use?
items.a: VOR is VHF Omnidirectional Range, a ground station that lets an aircraft determine its magnetic bearing to or from the station along any of 360 radials. It transmits in the VHF band from 108.0 to 117.95 MHz, with the 108.0 to 111.95 range shared with localisers, which use the odd tenths and hundredths. Being VHF it is essentially free of the static that afflicts low frequency navaids.

items.q: How does a VOR determine which radial you are on?
items.a: The station transmits two signals: an omnidirectional reference phase and a rotating variable phase. The two are exactly in phase when you are magnetic north of the station, and the phase difference increases by one degree for every degree round the compass. The aircraft receiver measures that phase difference and displays it as your radial, so the reading is entirely independent of aircraft heading. Because the receiver measures bearing from the station, the indication is entirely independent of aircraft heading; several airplanes on the same radial pointing in different directions all show the same correct radial.

items.q: What are the main restrictions on VOR reception?
items.a: Four. VOR is line of sight, so terrain or being too low blocks it. Each station has a published service volume, and outside it accuracy is not guaranteed. Reverse sensing occurs if the course set does not match the direction of flight. And directly over the station there is a cone of confusion where the signal is unusable. Reception distance therefore increases with altitude.

items.q: What are the three standard VOR service volumes and their ranges?
items.a: Terminal gives 25 NM from 1,000 to 12,000 feet above the station. Low altitude gives 40 NM from 1,000 to 18,000 feet. High altitude gives 40 NM from 1,000 to 14,500 feet, 100 NM from 14,500 to 18,000 feet, 130 NM from 18,000 to 45,000 feet, and 100 NM from 45,000 to 60,000 feet. The class of each station is published in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: Do the standard service volumes still describe every VOR?
items.a: No. Alongside the original terminal, low and high volumes the FAA has added expanded VOR Low (VL) and VOR High (VH) service volumes, which extend usable range at higher altitudes to support the VOR Minimum Operational Network as ground stations are decommissioned. The VL and VH figures are larger than the legacy L and H at the same altitudes. Read the current tables and the class of the specific station in AIM 1-1-8 and the Chart Supplement. The expanded volumes are VOR Low and VOR High: they extend usable range at and above 5,000 feet AGL to 70 NM, and for VH above 14,500 feet to 130 NM. A facility with an expanded service volume is annotated in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: What is the cone of confusion?
items.a: A roughly cone-shaped volume of no usable signal directly above the station, because the VOR radiates outward rather than straight up. Passing through it the TO-FROM flag flickers and the course needle swings wildly, and the wider the cone the higher you are. Station passage is called at the first positive TO-FROM flip, not when the needle settles down again.

items.q: What is reverse sensing on a VOR, and when does it happen?
items.a: Reverse sensing is when the course deviation indicator tells you to fly the wrong way, so a needle to the left means the course is to your right. On a VOR it happens when you fly a TO course with a FROM indication or a FROM course with a TO indication, that is, when your aircraft heading is roughly opposite the course you have set. The cure is to set the course you are actually flying. It also happens on a back course localiser without an HSI.

items.q: What are the six ways of checking VOR accuracy, and what is the tolerance of each?
items.a: VOT, plus or minus 4 degrees. A repair station radiated test signal, plus or minus 4 degrees. A designated ground checkpoint, plus or minus 4 degrees. A designated airborne checkpoint, plus or minus 6 degrees. A dual VOR cross-check, no more than 4 degrees between the two receivers. And over a prominent ground landmark on a published radial, plus or minus 6 degrees. These are the methods in 14 CFR 91.171 (Part 91, Subpart B - VOR equipment check for IFR operations).

items.q: How often must a VOR be checked, and does that apply to VFR flying?
items.a: Within the preceding 30 days, and only for flight under IFR using that VOR. 14 CFR 91.171 (Part 91, Subpart B - VOR equipment check for IFR operations) prohibits operating an aircraft under IFR using VOR equipment unless it has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and found to be within the limits. VFR navigation by VOR carries no check requirement, though a wildly wrong receiver is still an airworthiness problem.

items.q: How do you use a VOT, and what should the indications be?
items.a: Tune the VOT frequency published in the Chart Supplement, usually 108.0, and center the needle. The correct indications are 0 degrees with a FROM flag or 180 degrees with a TO flag, remembered as "center one-eighty TO". Alternatively set 360 and read a FROM. The permitted error is plus or minus 4 degrees. A VOT radiates a test signal representing the 360 radial in every direction.

items.q: How do you conduct an airborne VOR check over a prominent landmark?
items.a: With no VOT, ground checkpoint or airborne checkpoint available, select a prominent ground landmark on or near a published radial at least 20 NM from the station, fly over it at a reasonably low altitude, and note the bearing indicated by the receiver. The permitted error is plus or minus 6 degrees, and the low altitude and distance keep you clear of the cone of confusion and reduce the angular error of any position uncertainty.

items.q: How do you carry out a dual VOR check?
items.a: With two independent VOR receivers sharing nothing but the antenna, tune both to the same station, center each needle with a FROM indication, and compare the two indicated bearings. The maximum permissible variation between the two is 4 degrees. It can be done in the air or on the ground and it proves the two receivers agree, though it would not catch both being wrong the same way.

items.q: What must be recorded after a VOR check?
items.a: Four things, remembered as date, error, place, signature: the date of the check, the bearing error found, the place at which it was made, and the signature of the person making it. 14 CFR 91.171 (Part 91, Subpart B - VOR equipment check for IFR operations) requires the entry in the aircraft log or other permanent record kept in the aircraft, and the person making the check may be the pilot.

items.q: What must you confirm before using a VOR for navigation?
items.a: Confirm the frequency is set and the station is positively identified by its Morse code identifier or recorded voice ident, that no OFF or NAV warning flag is showing, that you are inside the published service volume for that class of station, and that no NOTAM has taken it out of service. A VOR undergoing maintenance has its ident removed, so an unidentified but apparently steady needle must not be used.

items.q: What is DME and how does it work?
items.a: Distance Measuring Equipment. The airborne interrogator transmits pulse pairs on a UHF frequency, the ground transponder replies after a fixed delay, and the receiver measures the round trip time and converts it to distance, which it can differentiate to give groundspeed and time to station. It is paired with a VOR or localiser frequency, so tuning the VOR tunes the DME automatically.

items.q: What is slant range error and when is it greatest?
items.a: DME measures the straight line from aircraft to station, the hypotenuse, not the distance across the ground, so the indicated distance is always slightly greater than the horizontal distance. The error grows as you get closer and higher, and it is greatest directly overhead, where the DME reads your height above the station in nautical miles. As a rule the error is negligible if you are at least three times the station altitude away.

items.q: How accurate is DME, and to what range?
items.a: Better than half a nautical mile or 3 percent of the distance, whichever is greater, out to about 199 NM from the station, and it is line of sight like the VOR it is paired with. Most airborne units can track a limited number of stations at once. Indicated distance, groundspeed and time to station are only valid when tracking directly to or from the station.

items.q: Where is ADS-B Out required?
items.a: In Class A, Class B and Class C airspace; within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, the Mode C veil; above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL; in Class E at and above 10,000 feet MSL excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL; and in Class E over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 feet MSL within 12 NM of the coast. This is 14 CFR 91.225 (Part 91, Subpart C - Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast Out equipment and use). ADS-B Out is also required in Class E airspace over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 feet MSL within 12 nautical miles of the United States coastline.

items.q: How does ADS-B Out actually work?
items.a: Onboard avionics take a position from the Global Navigation Satellite System and broadcast it, roughly once per second, together with the aircraft identity, altitude, velocity and integrity data. Ground stations and other suitably equipped aircraft receive that broadcast directly. It is called dependent because it depends on the aircraft own navigation source, and automatic because it transmits with no interrogation and no pilot action.

items.q: What is the difference between ADS-B Out and ADS-B In?
items.a: Out is the transmit half: your aircraft broadcasts its position and state to ATC and to other aircraft, and it is what the regulation requires. In is the receive half: your aircraft picks up broadcasts from ground stations and other aircraft and displays them. In is entirely optional and gives you traffic and, on one of the two links, free weather. Having In without Out gives you an incomplete traffic picture.

items.q: What services does ADS-B In provide?
items.a: Two broadcast services. TIS-B, Traffic Information Service Broadcast, uplinks radar-derived traffic so you also see aircraft that are not ADS-B equipped, but only when your own ADS-B Out is triggering the service. FIS-B, Flight Information Service Broadcast, uplinks free weather and aeronautical information including METARs, TAFs, NEXRAD, PIREPs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, NOTAMs and TFRs. FIS-B is available on the 978 MHz link only.

items.q: What are the two ADS-B datalinks, and which may be used where?
items.a: 1090 MHz Extended Squitter, built into a Mode S transponder, and 978 MHz Universal Access Transceiver, a separate box. Either satisfies the rule below 18,000 feet in US airspace, but at and above FL180 and for international operations you must have 1090ES. FIS-B weather is broadcast only on 978. Read which link is fitted from the aircraft equipment list.

items.q: What do you do if your ADS-B Out fails, or if the airplane has none at all?
items.a: Both need an ATC authorized deviation under 14 CFR 91.225 (Part 91, Subpart C - ADS-B Out equipment and use). If the installed equipment fails, the request may be made at any time, including in flight, and ATC will normally accommodate you. If the aircraft was never equipped, the request must be made to the controlling ATC facility at least one hour before the proposed operation.

items.q: Where is a transponder with altitude reporting required?
items.a: In all Class A, Class B and Class C airspace; within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL; above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL; and in all airspace of the 48 contiguous states and DC at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL. This is 14 CFR 91.215 (Part 91, Subpart C - ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use).

items.q: What is the exception to the transponder requirement, and how do you get a deviation?
items.a: Aircraft not originally certificated with an engine-driven electrical system, such as balloons and most gliders, may operate without a transponder outside Class A, B and C and below the lower of 10,000 feet MSL or the ceiling of the Class B or C area. For everyone else, 14 CFR 91.215 lets ATC authorize a deviation: with an inoperative transponder the request may be made at any time, and for an aircraft never equipped it must be made at least one hour before the flight.

items.q: What are the transponder modes and what does each one report?
items.a: Mode A replies with the four digit squawk code only. Mode C adds automatic pressure altitude reporting, referenced to 29.92 so ATC applies the local correction. Mode S adds a unique 24-bit aircraft address, selective interrogation so the frequency is not saturated, and a datalink used for TCAS coordination and for 1090ES ADS-B Out. Where the rules say transponder they mean Mode C or better.

items.q: What are the emergency and standard transponder codes?
items.a: 1200 for VFR flight in the United States. 7500 for unlawful interference or hijack. 7600 for lost communications. 7700 for a general emergency. 7777 is reserved for military interceptor operations and is never squawked by civil aircraft. When changing codes avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700, which triggers alarms in the facility.

items.q: How often must the transponder be tested and inspected?
items.a: Within the preceding 24 calendar months for any use of the transponder, VFR or IFR. 14 CFR 91.413 (Part 91, Subpart E - ATC transponder tests and inspections) prohibits use of an ATC transponder unless it has been tested and inspected in accordance with Part 43 Appendix F within that period, and the work must be done by a certificated repair station, the manufacturer, or a holder of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program.

items.q: How does GPS determine your position?
items.a: Each satellite broadcasts its position and the precise time from an onboard atomic clock. The receiver measures the travel time of the signal and converts it to a distance called a pseudo-range, pseudo because the receiver own clock is imperfect. Ranges from three satellites give a two-dimensional fix, and a fourth resolves the clock error and gives altitude, so four satellites are needed for a three-dimensional position.

items.q: How is the GPS constellation arranged?
items.a: The baseline constellation is 24 satellites, currently flown with several spares, in six orbital planes inclined 55 degrees, at an altitude of roughly 10,900 NM, about 20,200 km, with an orbital period of about 12 hours. The arrangement guarantees that at least five satellites are in view from any point on earth at any time. GPS is one constellation within the wider Global Navigation Satellite System.

items.q: How is GPS course deviation displayed, and how is that different from a VOR?
items.a: GPS deviation is a linear distance in nautical miles, not an angular displacement. A VOR needle represents a fixed number of degrees per dot, so the same deflection is a few hundred feet close in and many miles far out. A GPS CDI keeps the same distance per dot regardless of range from the waypoint, and the scale changes only when the receiver changes mode.

items.q: How does GPS CDI scaling change through a flight?
items.a: En route the full scale deflection is typically 2 NM. Within 30 NM of the destination airport the receiver transitions to terminal mode and scales to 1 NM. On an approach, at about 2 NM before the final approach fix it transitions to approach mode and scales to 0.3 NM, with an angular splay inside that on a WAAS vertical approach. Confirm the mode annunciation before the final approach fix.

items.q: What is RAIM and what does it do?
items.a: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring. It is a function inside the GPS receiver that checks the integrity of the position solution by comparing redundant satellite ranges against each other. If one range is inconsistent with the others the receiver knows a satellite is faulty and warns you. Without it a GPS can produce a confidently displayed but badly wrong position, which is why integrity, not accuracy, is the limiting factor for IFR.

items.q: How many satellites does RAIM need?
items.a: Fault detection needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding. Fault detection and exclusion, which not only spots the bad satellite but removes it and keeps navigating, needs 6 satellites, or 5 plus baro-aiding. Four satellites alone give a position but no integrity check at all, so the receiver cannot tell you whether the position is trustworthy.

items.q: What is baro-aiding and how does it help RAIM?
items.a: Baro-aiding feeds pressure altitude from the aircraft static system into the GPS as a substitute for one satellite range, because a known altitude removes one unknown from the solution. That lets the receiver perform fault detection with four satellites instead of five, and exclusion with five instead of six. It requires a correct current altimeter setting to be entered or supplied by the air data computer.

items.q: What happens if you lose RAIM in flight, and what do you do?
items.a: You get a loss of integrity annunciation, typically an amber LOI or INTEG flag near the navigation source on the flight display. The GPS position is no longer verified, so it may not be used for IFR navigation or an approach. Tell ATC, revert to ground-based navigation or radar vectors, and if you are on a GPS approach, discontinue it and fly the missed approach.

items.q: What does WAAS add to GPS?
items.a: The Wide Area Augmentation System adds accuracy and integrity. A network of precisely surveyed reference stations measures the error in each satellite signal, sends it to master stations, and the corrections are uplinked through geostationary satellites to the WAAS receiver in the aircraft. The result is position accuracy of a few meters with integrity good enough for vertical guidance, which is what makes LPV and LNAV/VNAV approaches possible.

items.q: What are the GPS approach service levels, and how do they rank?
items.a: From best to worst: LPV, localiser performance with vertical guidance, the tightest lateral splay and a decision altitude; LNAV/VNAV, lateral navigation with vertical navigation, flown to a decision altitude with wider lateral limits; LP, localiser performance without vertical guidance, flown to a minimum descent altitude; and LNAV, lateral only, to a minimum descent altitude. LPV and LNAV/VNAV need WAAS; LNAV needs only a basic IFR GPS.

items.q: What does a service level downgrade mean when it happens on approach?
items.a: The receiver has decided it can no longer guarantee the integrity needed for the level you were flying, and it annunciates the downgrade, for example from LPV to LNAV. You must then fly the minima for the level actually annunciated, which means a higher minimum descent altitude and no vertical guidance, and you must have those minima briefed. If the downgrade occurs below the higher minima or the receiver flags loss of integrity entirely, go missed.

items.q: What happens if you lose the WAAS signal in flight?
items.a: You get an error or loss of WAAS message and vertical guidance is withdrawn, so an LPV or LNAV/VNAV approach downgrades to LNAV or is unavailable. If satellite navigation is lost entirely the navigator reverts to dead reckoning mode, annunciated DR, in which the displayed position is only computed from the last known position, heading and airspeed and is not usable for IFR navigation. Tell ATC and revert to another navigation source.

items.q: What is Required Navigation Performance, and what values apply where?
items.a: RNP is area navigation with onboard performance monitoring and alerting: the aircraft not only navigates to a required accuracy but knows and tells you when it cannot. Typical values are 2 NM en route, 1 NM terminal and departure, and 0.3 NM on approach, each to be met 95 percent of the flight time. RNAV without the monitoring and alerting is not RNP. This is described in AIM 1-2-2.

items.q: What is a line replaceable unit, and why are avionics built that way?
items.a: A line replaceable unit is a self-contained box that can be pulled and swapped on the flight line without dismantling the rest of the system. Modern flight decks are built from LRUs joined by a data bus: displays, air data computer, attitude and heading reference, magnetometer, engine and airframe interface, radios, transponder and servos. When one fails, that box is replaced and the system reconfigured, rather than the whole panel being rebuilt.

items.q: What are the main boxes in an integrated flight deck, and what does each do?
items.a: A primary flight display and a multifunction display; one or more integrated avionics units housing the comm, nav and GPS receivers and doing the system integration; an air data computer; an attitude and heading reference system; a magnetometer; an engine and airframe interface unit; an audio panel with marker beacon receiver; a transponder; optionally a datalink receiver; and autopilot servos. Each is a line replaceable unit on a shared data bus.

items.q: What does the air data computer do, and what does it feed?
items.a: The air data computer takes pitot pressure, static pressure and outside air temperature and computes indicated airspeed, true airspeed, pressure altitude, altitude, vertical speed and temperature, then puts them on the data bus as digital values. Everything that needs air data uses it: the display tapes, the autopilot, the transponder altitude report, TAS and wind computations, and baro-aiding for the GPS.

items.q: What is an AHRS and what is inside it?
items.a: An Attitude and Heading Reference System is a solid state replacement for the attitude indicator and directional gyro. Inside are three-axis accelerometers, rate sensors and tilt sensors, fused by a processor and corrected with magnetic heading from the magnetometer and, in most installations, groundspeed or GPS data. It outputs pitch, roll, heading, rate of turn and slip-skid to the displays and autopilot, with no spinning mass and no vacuum.

items.q: What does the magnetometer do, and why is it mounted away from the panel?
items.a: It senses the earth magnetic field, usually with three fluxgates on three axes, measuring both the horizontal and vertical components so the system can compensate for dip and deliver an accurate magnetic heading to the AHRS. It is mounted out in a wingtip or the tail, far from the engine, generators, wiring and avionics, because those produce exactly the local magnetic disturbance that would corrupt it.

items.q: What does the engine and airframe interface unit do?
items.a: It is the analogue-to-digital gateway for the airplane sensors. Fuel quantity and flow, oil pressure and temperature, cylinder head and exhaust gas temperatures, manifold pressure, RPM, bus volts and amps and the discrete annunciator inputs are all wired to it, and it converts them to digital data for the engine indication display and the annunciator window. It is why the engine gauges appear on a screen rather than as individual instruments.

items.q: What does the audio panel do in an integrated flight deck?
items.a: It is the switching center for all audio: it selects which comm radio you transmit on, which navigation, marker and identifier audio you hear, the intercom, passenger address and music inputs, and it usually contains the marker beacon receiver. Most have a fail-safe mode that connects the pilot headset directly to comm one if the panel loses power, and some autopilots are prohibited when the audio panel is inoperative.

items.q: In an integrated flight deck, where do the attitude and air data on the pilot display come from?
items.a: From remote-mounted line replaceable units, not from anything inside the display. A single air data computer and a single attitude and heading reference system, usually mounted behind the panel or in the tail, feed both the primary flight display and the multifunction display over the data bus. That means the screens are only monitors, and a failure of the remote sensor removes that data from every screen at once.

items.q: In a retrofit installation with two small electronic flight instruments, where do attitude and air data come from?
items.a: Typically from sensors built into each display unit itself, so each instrument is a self-contained attitude and air data source with its own pitot and static connection and, in most designs, its own internal backup battery. The two units are independent, which means a sensor failure normally affects only one screen. Some installations instead share a remote sensor, so read the airplane flight manual supplement for the actual architecture.

items.q: What does a single display failure cost you in each of the two architectures?
items.a: In an integrated deck, losing one screen loses you nothing but screen area: reversionary mode composites the flight, navigation and engine information onto the surviving display, because the sensors are remote and still alive. In a retrofit pair, losing one unit loses its own internal sensors too, so you lose that instrument function entirely and continue on the other unit plus the separate navigator and any mechanical standby instruments.

items.q: What is reversionary mode, and what is the equivalent in a two-display retrofit?
items.a: In an integrated deck, reversionary mode makes one display show everything: attitude, air data, navigation and engine indications together, either automatically on detecting a failed screen or by pressing the display backup button on the audio panel. In a retrofit pair the equivalent is that the second electronic instrument can be configured to show primary flight information, but the exact behavior and any composite mode is installation specific.

items.q: What standby instruments would you expect in each installation, and what do they need to keep working?
items.a: An integrated deck normally carries a separate standby attitude indicator, altimeter and airspeed indicator plus the magnetic compass, driven by an independent source such as vacuum, its own battery or the standby bus. A retrofit pair often relies on the second display and its internal battery, with a mechanical altimeter and airspeed indicator and the compass as the last resort. Confirm what is fitted, what powers it and how long its battery lasts from the flight manual supplement.

items.q: What single failure would take attitude away from both screens of an integrated deck, and how do you fly then?
items.a: Failure of the single attitude and heading reference system, or of the bus feeding it. Both displays show a red X across the attitude and heading, and reversionary mode will not bring it back because the sensor, not the screen, is gone. You fly on the standby attitude indicator, the standby altimeter and airspeed indicator, the magnetic compass and, if it is on a different source, the GPS track. A two-sensor retrofit installation is more tolerant of exactly this failure.

items.q: What are typical autopilot limitations you must know before using it?
items.a: They are airplane and system specific and must be read from the airplane flight manual supplement, but the common ones are: a preflight self-test must pass; the pilot must be in the correct seat with the seat belt fastened; it must not be used for takeoff or landing; there are minimum and maximum engagement speeds; there is a minimum engagement height and a minimum height on approach and after go-around; a maximum fuel imbalance; and it may be prohibited when the audio panel or trim is inoperative.

items.q: How does an autopilot actually move the controls?
items.a: Through electric servos, one per axis, connected to the control cables or surfaces through a gearbox with a slip clutch, plus a separate trim servo in most installations. The flight director computes the commands, the servos apply them, and the slip clutch means the pilot can always overpower the servo. The disconnect is on the yoke, and the electric trim interrupt switch stops a runaway trim.

items.q: Where are the antennas typically mounted, and why does it matter?
items.a: Comm and GPS antennas go on the top of the fuselage with a clear view of the sky for the satellites; the VOR, localiser and glideslope antenna is usually on the vertical stabiliser; the transponder and ADS-B antennas go on the belly so they see the ground radar; and a DME antenna, if fitted, is also on the underside. It matters on preflight, because a bent, cracked or missing antenna is a real airworthiness item.

items.q: What is a 406 MHz ELT and how is it different from the old 121.5 units?
items.a: A 406 MHz emergency locator transmitter broadcasts a digitally coded burst containing a unique registered identifier, and in most units a GPS position, to the search and rescue satellite system, then transmits a low-power homing tone on 121.5 MHz for the search aircraft. The satellites no longer monitor 121.5 alone, so a 406 unit gives a position within minutes and an identity, where a 121.5-only unit gives neither.

items.q: How and when may you test an ELT?
items.a: Only during the first five minutes after the hour, and for no more than three audio sweeps, with a listening watch on 121.5. Testing at any other time risks a real alert being missed or a search being launched. The switch has ON, OFF and ARM or standby positions, and the correct position for flight is ARM, which triggers the unit automatically on impact.

items.q: What are the ELT inspection and battery requirements?
items.a: The ELT must be inspected within the preceding 12 calendar months for proper installation, battery corrosion, controls and crash sensor operation, and sufficient signal radiated. The battery must be replaced or recharged when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired. This is 14 CFR 91.207 (Part 91, Subpart C - Emergency locator transmitters), and the new expiry date must be marked on the outside of the unit.

items.q: May you fly an airplane with the ELT removed?
items.a: Yes, for up to 90 days while the ELT is out for repair or replacement, provided the aircraft records show the removal and a placard is placed in view of the pilot reading inoperative ELT not installed, with the date of removal. 14 CFR 91.207 (Part 91, Subpart C - Emergency locator transmitters) also exempts certain operations, including ferry flights to have one installed and training flights within 50 NM of the airport.

items.q: What is a data link receiver on a flight deck, and what are its limitations?
items.a: It receives subscription satellite weather or free broadcast weather and traffic and puts it on the multifunction display: radar mosaic, METARs, TAFs, winds, lightning and, on some, traffic. The key limitation is that the radar picture is a composite that can be several minutes old even when the time stamp looks recent, so it is a strategic avoidance tool for staying well clear of convection, never a tactical tool for threading between cells.

items.q: What is the VOR Minimum Operational Network?
items.a: As the FAA decommissions VOR stations in favour of satellite navigation, it is keeping a reduced network of higher-power VORs so that an aircraft suffering a GPS outage anywhere in the contiguous states can navigate conventionally to a MON airport, defined as being within 100 NM and having an ILS or VOR approach that does not need GPS, DME or surveillance. It is the reason the expanded VOR service volumes were introduced.

items.q: Why do the flight display, the GPS and the compass sometimes show different headings or tracks?
items.a: They are different quantities from different sources. The magnetic compass gives raw magnetic heading with dip and deviation errors. The display heading comes from the AHRS corrected by the magnetometer using a stored magnetic variation model. The GPS track is where the airplane is actually going over the ground, which differs from heading by the drift angle. In a crosswind a difference between heading and track is normal, not a fault.

items.q: What is fault detection and exclusion, and how many satellites does it need?
items.a: It is the step beyond basic RAIM. Plain RAIM only detects that one satellite signal is bad and warns you; FDE identifies the faulty satellite, excludes it, and carries on navigating. FDE needs six satellites, or five plus baro-aiding from the static system, against five or four-plus-baro for detection alone. FDE availability is what allows GPS as a primary means over oceanic and remote areas; check the AFM supplement and the equipment guide for your installation to see what it supports.

items.q: What are the ELT switch positions, and where must the switch be set?
items.a: Set to ARM for every flight, so the unit fires automatically on the longitudinal g-load of a crash. ON transmits immediately and is for manual activation after a forced landing or ditching; OFF or standby is for maintenance and battery changes only. Many installations add a remote switch and a warning light on the panel. Confirm ARM on preflight, and after any hard landing listen on 121.5 and check the light. The rule requiring an armed, working unit is 14 CFR part 91, subpart C, section 91.207, Emergency locator transmitters.

items.q: What is a horizontal situation indicator and what does it give you?
items.a: It combines the directional gyro with a course deviation display from a VOR or GPS receiver, putting the course pointer and its deviation bar directly on the rotating compass card. That single picture shows the course, the airplane's heading and the deviation from that course in their true relationship, which removes the mental work of interpreting a separate needle. Electronic displays draw the same picture, usually with a moving map beneath it.

items.q: You are established on the 060 radial. What heading takes you to the station?
items.a: 240 degrees, the reciprocal of the radial, in zero wind. A radial is measured outbound from the station, so its reciprocal points inbound. Set 240 in the course selector to get a TO indication with correct sensing, then crab into any wind and hold the needle centered rather than chasing it back and forth across the center.

items.q: The CDI needle is right of center. Where are you, and what do you do about it?
items.a: You are left of the selected course, so fly toward the needle and turn right to intercept. That holds so long as the course selector is set to roughly the direction you are flying; set the reciprocal and the sensing reverses. Check that the TO or FROM flag agrees with your intent before making the correction.

items.q: How many degrees is each dot of CDI deflection, and what does the center circle stand for?
items.a: Full scale deflection is 10 degrees either side of the selected course, so on a standard five-dot indicator each dot is 2 degrees. The center circle, the donut, is one dot wide, so a needle just touching its edge is about 2 degrees off course. The display is angular, so the same deflection covers more ground the farther you are from the station.

items.q: Using the 1 in 60 rule, how far off course is 2 degrees of CDI deflection at 60 NM from the station?
items.a: About 2 NM. One degree subtends roughly one mile at 60 NM, so scale it with distance: those same 2 degrees are about 1 mile off at 30 NM and about 4 miles off at 120 NM. It is why VOR guidance tightens as you close on the station and why full scale far out can mean many miles of error.

items.q: What airspeed instrument is required for day VFR?
items.a: An airspeed indicator, per 91.205(b)(1), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements.' It is a differential pressure gauge comparing pitot ram air pressure against static pressure. Its color markings, the white and green arcs and the yellow arc and red line, are part of the operating limitations required by 91.9.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES A: airspeed indicator

items.q: What does 91.205 call the compass, and what must accompany it?
items.a: A magnetic direction indicator, per 91.205(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C, which in a Warrior II is the wet magnetic compass on the windshield post. It must be accompanied by a current deviation correction card showing the compass headings for at least every 30 degrees, and it must be legible and in place; the compass is also the only heading source that needs no electrical or vacuum power.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES M: magnetic compass

items.q: Is an ELT required for day VFR, and may you ever fly without one?
items.a: Yes, an emergency locator transmitter meeting 91.207 is required by 91.205(b)(13), Part 91, Subpart C. An aircraft may be operated without an ELT for up to 90 days while the unit is removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement, provided the aircraft records show the removal date and a placard reading 'ELT not installed' is placed in view of the pilot. Other exceptions in 91.207(f) cover ferry, training within 50 nautical miles and certain single-seat aircraft.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES E: emergency locator transmitter

items.q: What does 91.205 require for belts and harnesses, and when must they be worn?
items.a: An approved safety belt for each occupant 2 years of age or older, and a shoulder harness for each front seat on airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978, per 91.205(b)(12) and (b)(14), Part 91, Subpart C. Under 91.107 the pilot must brief occupants to fasten belts, and each occupant must have the belt fastened for taxi, takeoff and landing; a shoulder harness, if installed, must be worn for takeoff and landing unless the person cannot perform required duties with it on.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES S: safety belts and shoulder harnesses

items.q: What does the R of GRABCARD require?
items.a: Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route to be flown, per 91.205(d)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. Suitable means appropriate to the ground facilities or the satellite navigation to be used: for a Warrior II with a panel-mount VOR and an IFR-approved GPS, that means the equipment is installed, operational, and approved for the approaches and routes you have filed.
items.concept: GRABCARD R: radios, two-way communication and navigation

items.q: What are the exact requirements for the IFR clock?
items.a: A clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation, per 91.205(d)(6), Part 91, Subpart C. It must be installed in the aircraft; a wristwatch or a phone does not satisfy the rule. It is needed for timed approaches, holding, and estimates, which is why the seconds display is specified.
items.concept: GRABCARD C: clock showing hours, minutes and seconds

items.q: What does DV MONA stand for?
items.a: The magnetic compass errors: D for Deviation, V for Variation, M for Magnetic dip, O for Oscillation, N for North and South turning errors remembered as UNOS, A for Acceleration errors remembered as ANDS. All of these apply to the wet magnetic compass on the windshield post of a Warrior II, which is your only heading reference with no electrical or vacuum power.
items.concept: DV MONA mnemonic for magnetic compass errors

items.q: What does ANDS stand for, and when would it bite you in the Warrior II?
items.a: ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. Flying east or west, accelerating makes the compass show a turn toward north and decelerating a turn toward south. It bites on a partial panel instrument departure or when leveling off and adding cruise power on an easterly or westerly heading: the compass swings, and a pilot who chases it rolls into a turn he did not intend. Wait for steady speed before reading it.
items.concept: ANDS: accelerate north, decelerate south

items.q: An examiner points at a piece of avionics and asks whether it is required. How do you structure the answer?
items.a: Name the sources in order rather than guessing. For this flight: 91.205 for day VFR, 91.207 for the ELT, 91.215 for the transponder, 91.225 and 91.227 for ADS-B Out where it is required, then the handbook's kinds of operation list, the equipment list, and any AD or STC supplement. If it is on none of those, it is not required, and if it is inoperative I still owe 91.213(d) a placard.

items.q: Is a second navigation radio required for your VFR cross country?
items.a: No. 14 CFR 91.205(b) requires no navigation radio at all for day VFR, and 91.205(c) adds nothing of the kind for night. Radios become required by the airspace and the kind of operation rather than by the equipment rule: two-way radio for Class B, C and D, a transponder with altitude reporting where 91.215 says so, and ADS-B Out where 91.225 says so. For VFR pilotage, a second radio is good practice, not a requirement.

items.q: What is the difference between a TO and a FROM indication?
items.a: It tells you which half of the VOR's 360 radials the airplane is in, relative to the course set in the OBS. FROM means the selected course points away from the station and you are on the radial numbered the same as the course you have set; TO means the selected course points at the station and you are on the reciprocal radial. The ambiguity meter does not know your heading, only your position.

items.q: Which indication do you use to fix your position, and why?
items.a: FROM. A radial is a magnetic course outward from the station, so the FROM radial is the line you draw on the chart. Center the needle with a FROM flag, read the number under the index, find that radial on the VOR's compass rose and rule the line outward; you are somewhere on it. If you center the needle with a TO flag, the radial you are on is the reciprocal, and plotting the TO number puts you on the wrong side of the station.

items.q: Give me the full procedure for finding your position with one VOR.
items.a: Tune the frequency, identify the Morse code before you use it, rotate the OBS until the needle centers with a FROM indication, and read the radial. Draw that radial out from the station on the chart. You now have a line of position. Convert it to a point with a second radial from another VOR, with DME distance, or by seeing where the line crosses a ground feature you can identify beneath you.

items.q: How do you fix a position from two VORs?
items.a: Take a FROM radial from each and plot both; where they intersect is your position. Do them quickly and in succession so the airplane has not moved much between them. The accuracy depends on the crossing angle: near 90 degrees is excellent, and below about 30 degrees the fix is unreliable because a small bearing error smears the intersection a long way along both lines.

items.q: You are told you are over I-95 and asked where you are. How do you answer with one VOR?
items.a: Use the VOR for a line of position and the highway for the other. Center the needle FROM, read the radial, and plot it outward from the station; where that radial crosses the highway on the chart is your position. One radial plus one identifiable line feature gives a fix just as surely as two radials, and the crossing angle rule applies the same way: a radial that lies nearly along the highway gives a poor answer.

items.q: What are the accuracy limits of a VOR fix?
items.a: Line of sight, so reception depends on altitude and terrain, and the signal is unusable in the cone of confusion overhead. Bearing accuracy is limited by the permitted check tolerances: plus or minus 4 degrees on a ground checkpoint and 6 degrees in the air. Angular error becomes distance error with range, roughly one nautical mile per degree at 60 nautical miles, so a fix far from the station is a broad one.

items.q: How does DME turn one VOR into a fix?
items.a: The radial gives you a line and the DME gives you a distance arc from the station, and the two cross at one point. It is the quickest single-station fix there is. Remember that DME measures slant range, the straight line distance from the airplane to the station, not the distance over the ground, and the error is largest when you are high and close: directly overhead at 6,000 feet the readout is about one mile when the ground distance is zero.

items.q: Before you plot a radial, what must you confirm?
items.a: That the station is the one you think it is and is usable. Identify the Morse code or the recorded voice identifier, because an unmonitored or off-the-air VOR can still produce a stable, convincing and wrong needle; check for a NOTAM on the facility; confirm you are inside its service volume for your altitude; and confirm the receiver's last check is within 30 days if you intend to use it for IFR.

b: Powerplant, fuel, electrical, vacuum, flight controls, landing gear, ice protection.

items.q: What does the pitot-static system supply, and which instruments use which source?
items.a: It supplies ram air pressure from the pitot tube and ambient pressure from the static ports. The airspeed indicator is the only instrument using both. The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator use static only. In a glass installation the same two lines feed the air data computer, which computes the same quantities digitally and drives the tapes on the display.

items.q: How does an altimeter work?
items.a: A stack of sealed aneroid wafers, each holding a pressure of 29.92 inches of mercury, sits in a case vented to static pressure. As you climb, static pressure falls, the wafers expand, and the linkage drives the pointers or the digital readout. The Kollsman window lets you set the local altimeter setting, which mechanically shifts the scale so the instrument reads true altitude at field elevation in the current pressure. At and above 18,000 feet the altimeter is set to the standard 29.92 inches of mercury instead of a local setting.

items.q: How does an airspeed indicator work?
items.a: Ram air from the pitot tube is fed directly into a diaphragm, while static pressure is fed into the sealed case around it. The diaphragm expands as the difference between ram and static pressure grows, and that difference is dynamic pressure, which is a function of airspeed. So the instrument is really a differential pressure gauge with its dial marked in knots.

items.q: How does a vertical speed indicator work, and why is it slow?
items.a: A diaphragm is connected directly to the static line, while the case around it is connected to static through a calibrated leak. When you start a climb, pressure in the diaphragm falls immediately but the case lags, and that pressure difference deflects the pointer. Because the leak takes roughly 6 to 9 seconds to equalize, the instrument shows instantaneous trend at once but takes several seconds to settle on an accurate rate.

items.q: What happens if the pitot ram inlet blocks but the drain hole stays open?
items.a: The airspeed indicator drops to zero. With the ram inlet blocked, the trapped pressure bleeds away out of the drain hole until the diaphragm sees only static pressure inside and out, so there is no differential left and the needle falls to the bottom of the scale. Insects and covers left on are the usual causes, which is why the pitot tube is a preflight item.

items.q: What happens if both the pitot ram inlet and the drain hole are blocked?
items.a: The airspeed indicator becomes an altimeter. Pressure is trapped in the pitot line, so as you climb and static pressure falls the trapped pressure looks larger by comparison and indicated airspeed increases; in a descent it decreases. The classic trap is an iced-over pitot in a climb, where a chasing pilot pitches up to hold the rising indication and stalls.

items.q: What does a blocked static port do to each of the three instruments?
items.a: The altimeter freezes at the altitude where the blockage occurred. The vertical speed indicator freezes at zero. The airspeed indicator still works but reads wrong away from the blockage altitude: it reads correctly at that altitude, under-reads as you climb and over-reads as you descend. All three symptoms together are the signature of a static blockage rather than a pitot one.

items.q: What is the alternate static source and what does it do to your indications?
items.a: A valve that opens the static system to cabin pressure when the external ports block, usually with ice. Cabin pressure in an unpressurized airplane is normally slightly lower than ambient because of the venturi effect over the airframe, so with alternate static selected the altimeter typically reads higher than actual, the airspeed reads faster than actual and the vertical speed momentarily shows a climb. The correction table is in the POH; if no valve is fitted, break the glass of the vertical speed indicator.

items.q: What does pitot heat protect, and what does it not protect?
items.a: It heats the pitot tube and, in most installations, the stall warning vane, keeping the ram inlet and drain clear of ice. It usually does not heat the static ports, which are flush and less prone to blockage but not immune. Check it on preflight by feel with the master on and for the load it draws, and switch it on before entering visible moisture near freezing, not after the airspeed has already misbehaved.

items.q: What is rigidity in space?
items.a: The property of a spinning mass that makes its axis remain pointing in a fixed direction in space regardless of how the aircraft around it moves. It is what allows a gyroscopic attitude indicator or directional gyro to hold a stable reference while the airplane pitches, rolls and turns about it. Rigidity increases with the rotor mass, how far that mass is from the axis, and rotational speed.

items.q: What is gyroscopic precession?
items.a: The tilting or turning of a gyro in response to a deflecting force, in which the effect of the force is felt 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation from where it was applied. In instruments it is the mechanism used to erect the gyro and it is also the source of drift errors from bearing friction. In the airframe it is what makes a tailwheel airplane yaw when the tail comes up.

items.q: How does a vacuum-driven attitude indicator work?
items.a: The gyro is mounted with its axis vertical and spun by a jet of air drawn through it by the vacuum pump. Gimbals let the airframe move freely around it while the horizon bar stays level. Underneath, four pendulous vanes cover exhaust ports; when the gyro tips, the vanes swing and uncover a port so the escaping air pushes the gyro back upright. That is why the instrument self-erects and why it takes several minutes to settle after start. An added check: the vacuum attitude indicator should erect and settle within a few minutes of engine start, and it should be treated as unserviceable if it has not.

items.q: What are the errors and limits of a directional gyro?
items.a: It has no north-seeking ability of its own, so it must be set from the magnetic compass in straight and level unaccelerated flight and reset about every 15 minutes, because bearing friction and the earth rotation make it precess. Older units also have pitch and bank limits beyond which the gyro tumbles. A slaved heading indicator or an AHRS with a magnetometer removes the drift by continuously correcting to magnetic north.

items.q: Which instruments are usually vacuum driven and which electric, and why split them?
items.a: Traditionally the attitude indicator and directional gyro run on vacuum while the turn coordinator runs on electrical power, and it is deliberate. Splitting the power sources means one failure, a dead vacuum pump or a dead alternator and battery, cannot take away every gyro at once, leaving you an attitude or rate reference to fly partial panel. Confirm what drives what in the airplane you are flying.

items.q: How does a vacuum system work?
items.a: Cabin or engine-compartment air is drawn in through a filter, passed through the gyro instruments where it spins the rotors, and then sucked out by an engine-driven vacuum pump and dumped overboard. A vacuum regulator or relief valve bleeds in extra air to hold the suction at the value the instruments need, and a gauge or transducer displays the suction, typically around 4.5 to 5.5 inches of mercury, though you read the range from the POH.

items.q: What does a vacuum failure look like, and why is it insidious?
items.a: The suction gauge falls below the green arc or a low vacuum annunciator lights, and the attitude indicator and directional gyro slowly wind down. It is insidious because the gyros do not fail instantly; they decay over minutes, giving plausible but progressively wrong indications, and the attitude indicator typically shows a gentle bank and pitch that a pilot will follow into a spiral. Cover the failed instruments and fly on the turn coordinator, altimeter, airspeed and compass.

items.q: In a modern glass installation, what is the vacuum pump still there for?
items.a: Often nothing more than the standby attitude indicator. With attitude, heading and air data coming from solid state units, the only remaining air-driven instrument may be the mechanical standby gyro, so the pump, filter, regulator and a transducer that reports suction to the engine display are retained purely to keep that backup alive. Some installations delete vacuum altogether and use an electric standby with its own battery.

items.q: How are flaps typically actuated, and what tells you where they are?
items.a: Most light singles use an electric motor driving a jackscrew or torque tube, with the drive in one wing carried across to the other by a rod or cable so both flaps move together, and a position sensor driving a cockpit indicator. Others use a mechanical lever with detents or hydraulics. Because electric flaps move slowly and only while powered, a failure normally leaves them stuck rather than running away.

items.q: What do flaps do to lift, drag and stall speed?
items.a: Lowering flaps increases the wing camber, which increases the coefficient of lift and lowers the stall speed, and it increases drag. The first stages give proportionally more lift than drag, so they are useful for takeoff where permitted; the later stages give mostly drag, allowing a steeper approach without gaining speed. Flaps also lower the nose attitude for a given speed, improving the view on approach. Flaps work by increasing the wing's camber and its effective chord, which is the reason the same airspeed produces more lift. The practical payoff is a steeper descent angle and a higher descent rate flown without any increase in airspeed, which is what makes a short field or obstacle approach work.

items.q: What are the four common flap types?
items.a: The plain flap, a hinged section of the trailing edge. The split flap, which deflects only the lower surface and makes a lot of drag for the lift it adds. The slotted flap, which opens a gap so high-energy air from beneath re-energizes the boundary layer over the flap, giving the best lift increase for the drag and by far the most common on light airplanes. And the Fowler flap, which slides aft as it lowers, adding wing area as well as camber.

items.q: Describe the path induction air takes to the cylinders.
items.a: Outside air enters a ram air intake in the engine cowling, passes through the induction air filter, and flows into an airbox beneath the engine. From there it goes through the fuel and air control unit, where fuel is metered into it or the mixture is set, and is then ducted through the intake manifold tubes to each cylinder. Anything that restricts that path, filter ice or a bird nest, is a power loss.

items.q: What is alternate air, and what does it cost you?
items.a: A spring-loaded door in the airbox that opens automatically under engine suction if the induction filter or intake blocks, admitting unfiltered air from inside the cowling so the engine keeps running. Because that air is warmer and less dense, and unfiltered, you accept roughly a 10 percent loss of power at full throttle. Some installations also have a manual alternate air control. It is the fuel-injected equivalent of carburettor heat.

items.q: What is the difference between a carburettor and fuel injection?
items.a: A carburettor meters fuel into the airstream at one point, using a venturi to draw fuel from a float chamber, then distributes the fuel-air mixture through the manifold to all cylinders. Fuel injection meters fuel with an engine-driven pump and a control unit, then delivers it through individual lines to a nozzle at each cylinder intake port. Injection gives more even distribution, better fuel economy, better response and no venturi icing.

items.q: How does carburettor ice form, and in what conditions?
items.a: Fuel vaporizing and air accelerating through the venturi cool the mixture by as much as 60 to 70 degrees F, so ice can form in the throat and on the throttle plate even on a warm day. The risk is greatest with high humidity and outside air temperatures roughly between 20 and 70 degrees F, and it is worst at low power settings such as a descent, where the nearly closed throttle plate is easily blocked.

items.q: What are the symptoms of carburettor ice, and how do you cure it?
items.a: In a fixed-pitch airplane a gradual unexplained loss of RPM and rough running; with a constant-speed propeller a loss of manifold pressure at constant RPM. The cure is full carburettor heat, applied fully and left on. Expect an immediate further drop and rough running as the melted ice passes through the engine, which is confirmation that ice was present, followed by a recovery to normal or better than before.

items.q: What does carburettor heat do besides melting ice?
items.a: It supplies air that is hot and unfiltered, so it is also the alternate air source if the induction filter blocks. Because hot air is less dense, it enriches the mixture and reduces power, typically a small RPM loss, and it raises the risk of detonation at high power. That is why it is used at low power settings and for icing conditions, and why you lean if you must cruise with it on.

items.q: What are the drawbacks of fuel injection?
items.a: Three practical ones. It is more prone to vapor lock, where fuel boils in hot lines after shutdown on a hot day and the engine will not restart without the specific hot start procedure. Difficult hot starting generally. And a restart after an in-flight power loss can be more involved. Injected engines are also more sensitive to induction blockage, which is why the automatic alternate air door matters.

items.q: What are the four strokes of a piston engine, and what happens in each?
items.a: Intake: the piston travels down with the intake valve open, drawing in the fuel-air mixture. Compression: both valves close and the piston travels up, compressing the charge. Power: the spark plugs fire just before top dead center and the burning charge drives the piston down, which is the only stroke producing work. Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and the rising piston pushes the burnt gases out. Remembered as suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

items.q: What does it mean that an engine is horizontally opposed and air cooled?
items.a: Horizontally opposed means the cylinders lie flat in two banks on either side of a central crankshaft, which gives a compact, low-frontal-area, well-balanced engine that fits neatly in a cowling. Air cooled means cooling comes from ram air over finned cylinders rather than a liquid coolant loop, which saves the weight and complexity of radiators and plumbing but makes cylinder head temperature a number the pilot must manage.

items.q: How is air cooling actually organized, and what controls it?
items.a: Air enters through inlets in the cowling, is forced down across the finned cylinder heads and barrels by a pressure difference created by baffles and seals inside the cowling, and exits through the cowl outlet or cowl flaps. The pilot controls it with airspeed, power and mixture, and with cowl flaps where fitted: open for climb, closed in cruise and descent. Missing or hardened baffle seals are a real preflight item because they let the cooling air escape.

items.q: What does direct drive mean, and what is the alternative?
items.a: Direct drive means the propeller is bolted straight to the crankshaft, so propeller RPM equals engine RPM and there is no gearbox to add weight, cost or a failure point. The alternative is a geared engine, which lets the engine turn faster, where it makes more power, while the propeller turns slower, keeping the tips subsonic and the noise down, at the price of a reduction gearbox and its own inspection and handling requirements.

items.q: What does normally aspirated mean, and what limits such an engine with altitude?
items.a: Normally aspirated, or naturally aspirated, means the engine breathes ambient air with no supercharger or turbocharger. Because air density falls with altitude, the mass of air reaching the cylinders falls, and power falls with it at roughly 3 to 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet. Full throttle manifold pressure drops by about one inch per thousand feet, and eventually the engine cannot make enough power to climb, which is the absolute ceiling.

items.q: What does a turbocharger do, and how is it driven?
items.a: A turbocharger uses a turbine spun by the engine exhaust gases to drive a compressor that squeezes induction air before it reaches the cylinders, restoring sea level or higher manifold pressure at altitude. A supercharger does the same job but is driven mechanically from the crankshaft, so it consumes engine power directly. Turbocharging allows high true airspeeds and better climb performance high up, and it is what makes cabin pressurization practical on a piston airplane.

items.q: What is critical altitude, and what is the difference between turbocharged and turbonormalized?
items.a: Critical altitude is the highest altitude at which the engine can still maintain its rated manifold pressure at full throttle; above it, performance decays like a normally aspirated engine. Turbonormalized means the system only restores sea level manifold pressure, around 29 to 30 inches. Turbocharged or boosted means it can produce more than sea level pressure, so overboost becomes possible and must be limited by a wastegate or by the pilot.

items.q: What special handling does a turbocharged engine need?
items.a: Move the throttle slowly, because the system lags and a fast advance can overboost. Watch turbine inlet or exhaust gas temperature as a limit, not just cylinder head temperature. Lean strictly to the manual because the margin to detonation is smaller. And allow a cool-down at low power before shutdown, typically several minutes, so the bearings are not coked by hot oil sitting in a turbine that was glowing a moment earlier. Read the actual procedures from the POH.

items.q: What is detonation, what causes it and how do you cure it?
items.a: Detonation is the fuel-air charge in the cylinder exploding instead of burning progressively, producing a sudden pressure spike, high temperatures and hammering loads that can destroy pistons and valves. It is caused by too low a fuel grade, too lean a mixture at high power, high power with low airspeed, high induction air temperature, or an overheated engine. Cure it by enriching the mixture, reducing power, opening cowl flaps, lowering the nose to increase cooling airflow and turning off carburettor heat. Add high manifold pressure at low RPM to the list of causes, alongside low-grade fuel and an over-lean mixture.

items.q: What is pre-ignition, and how does it differ from detonation?
items.a: Pre-ignition is the mixture being ignited before the spark plug fires, by some incandescent hot spot in the cylinder such as a carbon deposit, a cracked electrode or a damaged valve. The difference is the trigger: detonation is a normal ignition followed by an abnormal, explosive burn, while pre-ignition is an abnormal, early ignition. Pre-ignition produces very high cylinder head temperatures, a rough engine and power loss, and it can destroy a cylinder in minutes. It also frequently causes detonation, and the two often occur together.

items.q: How do you recognize and respond to pre-ignition in flight?
items.a: Suspect it from a rapid rise in cylinder head temperature on one cylinder, a loss of power, roughness and possibly a high oil temperature, and note that a hot spot can keep the engine firing even with the ignition off. The response is the same first aid as detonation: enrich the mixture, reduce power, open the cowl flaps and increase airspeed to cool, then land as soon as practicable and have the cylinder inspected, because the damage is mechanical and will not fix itself.

items.q: Why must the mixture be leaned as you climb?
items.a: Because the carburettor or injection unit meters fuel by volume of air, not mass. As you climb the air thins but the fuel flow for a given throttle setting barely changes, so the mixture becomes progressively richer. An over-rich mixture costs power, fouls the plugs with lead and carbon, runs the engine rough and wastes fuel. Leaning restores the correct fuel to air ratio, giving the rated power, correct temperatures and the planned fuel burn. State the definition precisely: the mixture is a ratio of the mass of fuel to the mass of air, not of volumes.

items.q: What is the difference between best power and best economy leaning?
items.a: Best power is a mixture slightly rich of the peak exhaust gas temperature, typically around 75 to 100 degrees F rich of peak, giving the most power and cooler cylinders for climb and high cruise settings. Best economy is at or lean of peak exhaust gas temperature, giving the lowest fuel flow per mile at the cost of a little speed. Peak itself is the hottest place to run. Follow the specific method and limits in the POH, and never lean aggressively above about 75 percent power.

items.q: What happens if the mixture is far too rich or far too lean?
items.a: Too rich and the engine runs rough and cool, loses power, fouls the plugs, wastes fuel and may run black smoke; the excess fuel does at least cool the cylinders. Too lean and the engine runs hot, loses power, may run rough, and is exposed to detonation at high power settings, which is the damaging case. That asymmetry is why the standard immediate action for any suspected detonation or overheat is to push the mixture forward. The reason a rich mixture is used for takeoff and climb is that the surplus fuel cools the engine, and the specific penalty of running over-rich is spark plug fouling.

items.q: What is a magneto and how does it make a spark?
items.a: A magneto is a self-contained engine-driven generator of ignition current. A permanent magnet rotating inside a coil of wire induces a current in the primary winding; when the breaker points open, the collapsing field induces a very high voltage in the secondary winding, and the distributor sends that pulse to the correct spark plug. It is driven off the accessory gearing from the crankshaft, so its timing tracks the engine automatically.

items.q: Why does a piston airplane engine have two magnetos?
items.a: Two reasons. Redundancy: each magneto with its own set of plugs, harness and distributor is entirely independent of the other and of the aircraft electrical system, so a failure of one leaves the engine running. And performance: two plugs per cylinder firing simultaneously from opposite sides give two flame fronts, a faster and more complete burn, and therefore more power and better efficiency than a single plug could.

items.q: Why does a magneto keep the engine running with the master switch off?
items.a: Because a magneto generates its own electrical energy and needs no battery, alternator or bus. The ignition switch does not power the magneto; it grounds it through the P-lead to shut it off. That is why the engine will run with the master off, and why a broken or disconnected P-lead leaves a magneto live even with the switch at OFF, so a propeller can start the engine if someone turns it by hand.

items.q: How do you carry out a magneto check and what are the limits?
items.a: At the run-up RPM in the POH, with the mixture set, move the switch from BOTH to one magneto, note the drop, return to BOTH and let the engine stabilize, then check the other. The typical limits are a maximum drop of around 125 to 175 RPM on either magneto and a maximum difference between the two of around 50 RPM, but the exact figures are POH numbers for the engine you are flying. Some drop must occur on each.

items.q: What does an excessive magneto drop mean, and what does no drop at all mean?
items.a: An excessive drop, or a rough engine on one magneto, points to a fouled or failed spark plug, a bad lead, faulty timing or a failing magneto, and lead fouling can often be cleared by leaning aggressively at higher RPM and rechecking. No drop at all is not a good sign: it means the magneto is not being grounded, so the P-lead is broken or the switch is faulty and that magneto is hot. Do not fly, and treat the propeller as live.

items.q: What is an impulse coupling and why is it needed?
items.a: A spring-loaded coupling fitted between the engine and usually the left magneto that, at cranking speed, holds the magneto rotor back and then snaps it round, giving a fast rotation and a hot, retarded spark when the engine is turning far too slowly to make a usable one. The retard also prevents kickback. Flyweights sense when the engine is running fast enough by centrifugal force and disengage it. You hear it clicking during start.

items.q: Walk through what happens when you turn the key to start.
items.a: Priming puts fuel into the induction system or cylinders. Turning the key energizes the starter relay, the starter motor pinion engages the ring gear on the flywheel, and because the engine is direct drive the crankshaft and propeller turn with it. The turning crankshaft spins the magnetos, which with the impulse coupling produce a spark; the spark ignites the primed mixture; combustion begins and becomes self-sustaining, and you release the key so the starter disengages.

items.q: What is the aircraft engine oil doing, and what are its jobs?
items.a: Five. Lubricate the moving parts so metal does not run on metal. Cool, by carrying heat from the pistons, bearings and cylinder walls to the oil cooler, which is a significant fraction of total engine cooling. Clean, by picking up carbon and metal particles and carrying them to the sump and filter. Seal, by filling the gap between piston rings and cylinder walls. And preserve, by coating internal parts so they do not corrode.

items.q: What is a wet sump system, and how is it different from a dry sump?
items.a: In a wet sump the oil supply is carried in the bottom of the engine crankcase itself, and gravity returns it there after circulating. In a dry sump, scavenge pumps pull the oil out of the engine into a separate external tank, which allows aerobatic and inverted flight, better cooling and a larger capacity, at the price of more pumps and plumbing. Most light piston singles use a full-pressure wet sump.

items.q: Trace the path of oil through a wet sump engine.
items.a: Oil is drawn from the sump through a suction screen and pickup tube to the engine-driven oil pump. From the pump it passes the pressure relief valve, which caps system pressure, then the oil filter, then the thermostatically controlled oil cooler. From the cooler it goes into the oil galleries and out to the bearings, camshaft and valve train, and to the propeller governor on a constant-speed installation. It then drains back to the sump by gravity.

items.q: Why does the oil cooler have a bypass valve?
items.a: Because oil that is too cold is as bad as oil that is too hot: cold oil is thick, does not flow into bearing clearances properly, and holds water and acids that only boil off at operating temperature. A thermostatic bypass valve routes oil straight past the cooler until it reaches the correct temperature, then progressively sends it through the cooler. It is also why you do not take off before the oil temperature is in the green.

items.q: What oil is used in a piston airplane engine, and what does ashless dispersant mean?
items.a: Aviation grade oil of the weight and specification the engine manufacturer calls for, commonly a multigrade such as 15W-50 or 20W-50, or a straight grade seasonally. Ashless dispersant means the oil holds combustion by-products and particles in suspension so they are carried to the filter rather than deposited in the engine, and it leaves no metallic ash when burnt. Non-dispersant mineral oil is used only for breaking in a new or overhauled engine.

items.q: What does low oil pressure with rising oil temperature mean, and what do you do?
items.a: It usually means the engine is losing oil, through a leak, a failed seal or an over-serviced sump venting overboard, and with less oil there is less to carry heat away, so temperature climbs as pressure falls. Treat it as an impending engine failure: reduce power to the minimum needed, pick a landing site, and land as soon as possible. Low pressure with normal temperature may be a gauge or transducer fault, but is still a land-soon item.

items.q: What do high oil temperature with normal pressure, or high pressure, suggest?
items.a: High temperature with normal pressure suggests a cooling problem rather than a loss of oil: a blocked oil cooler, a stuck bypass valve, low oil quantity, a high power setting with low airspeed, or an over-lean mixture. Reduce power, enrich the mixture, lower the nose to increase airflow and open the cowl flaps. High pressure is usually cold thick oil at start, or a stuck relief valve, and should return to normal as the oil warms.

items.q: How much oil must be in the engine before flight?
items.a: At least the minimum for flight quantity published in the POH, which is normally well below the full mark, and never above maximum, because an over-serviced engine simply throws the excess out of the breather and coats the belly. Sump capacity and minima are airplane specific, so read them from the POH and add the filter capacity where the manual accounts for it separately. Also track consumption between flights, because a rising trend is a warning.

items.q: Where do the exhaust gases go after combustion?
items.a: The rising piston pushes the burnt gases out through the exhaust valve into a short stack from each cylinder, the stacks join into a collector and a muffler, and the muffler discharges through the exhaust pipe under the cowling. The muffler both silences the engine and is the source of cabin heat. On a turbocharged engine the same gas stream first drives the turbine.

items.q: How is cabin heat produced in a typical light airplane?
items.a: By a shroud wrapped around the exhaust muffler. Outside ram air is ducted into the gap between the shroud and the hot muffler, absorbs heat from the exhaust gases through the metal, and is then routed forward to a selector door controlled by the cabin heat knob. With the knob pushed in, the door is closed and the hot air is dumped overboard into the engine cowling; pulling the knob opens the door and directs the heated air into the cabin and defroster.

items.q: Why is a cracked exhaust muffler dangerous, and what are the symptoms?
items.a: Because cabin heat air passes over the muffler, a crack lets exhaust gas containing carbon monoxide into the heat duct and straight into the cabin. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odourless and binds to haemoglobin around 200 times more readily than oxygen. Symptoms are headache, drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, confusion and impaired judgment, easily mistaken for fatigue or hypoxia, and worse at altitude.

items.q: What do you do if you suspect carbon monoxide in the cabin?
items.a: Shut off the cabin heat, open fresh air vents or a window, use supplemental oxygen if it is available, avoid smoking, and land as soon as practicable to have the exhaust system inspected. Many airplanes carry a detector that annunciates at a low concentration, often around 50 parts per million, and a chemical spot card is a cheap backup. A cracked muffler found in flight is an unairworthy airplane, not something to fly home with the heat off.

items.q: What are the basic characteristics of a light airplane electrical system?
items.a: Almost all are direct current, single wire, negative ground, using the airframe as the return path. Systems are either 14 volt with a 12 volt battery or 28 volt with a 24 volt battery, the higher voltage allowing lighter wiring for the same load. Power comes from an engine-driven alternator with the battery as the starting source and the emergency reserve, feeding a set of buses through circuit breakers. Two figures to state plainly: the system is either 14 volts or 28 volts direct current, and the battery's role is as backup when the alternator or generator fails.

items.q: What is the difference between an alternator and a generator?
items.a: An alternator produces alternating current which is rectified to DC, is lighter for its output, and produces useful current at low RPM, so it charges the battery while taxiing. It does, however, need battery excitation to start producing. A generator produces DC directly, is heavier, and produces little output at low RPM, so a night taxi discharges the battery. Alternators also give more stable voltage across the RPM range.

items.q: What does the voltage regulator or alternator control unit do?
items.a: It holds the bus voltage steady, around 14 volts in a 12 volt system or 28 volts in a 24 volt system, by controlling the current fed to the alternator field winding. Charging voltage must be a little above battery voltage or the battery would never charge. A regulator failure high gives an overvoltage condition, which the overvoltage relay should trip; a failure low leaves the battery carrying the whole load.

items.q: What does a low voltage annunciation mean, and what should you do?
items.a: It means bus voltage has fallen below the threshold in the POH, commonly around 24.5 volts in a 28 volt system, so the alternator is no longer carrying the load and the battery is discharging. Try the reset: alternator side of the master off then on, and check the alternator field circuit breaker.
