If it does not restore, shed every non-essential load, keep one radio, the transponder and the essential flight instruments, and land at a suitable airport while the battery lasts.

items.q: What does a high voltage annunciation mean?
items.a: That the alternator is supplying too much voltage, commonly annunciated above about 32 volts in a 28 volt system, because the voltage regulator or alternator control unit has failed. Overvoltage cooks the battery and can damage avionics, so the protective circuit normally trips the alternator offline, which then shows as a low voltage condition. Treat it as the loss of the alternator: shed load and land where the airplane can be repaired.

items.q: How long will you have on the battery alone after an alternator failure?
items.a: Far less than most pilots expect, and the honest answer is read the POH figure for your airplane and assume less, because that figure assumes a new, fully charged battery. A typical light single with the load shed to the essentials might give 30 minutes to an hour. Plan on the shorter figure, tell ATC, and remember that electric flaps, gear and starter all need power you may not have later.

items.q: What is the purpose of splitting the electrical load across several buses?
items.a: So that failures and load shedding can be handled selectively. Non-essential heavy loads such as landing lights, pitot heat, flaps and cabin power sit on the main electrical buses; the radios and displays sit on avionics buses fed through the avionics master; and the flight-critical items sit on an essential bus that can be fed from an alternative source. A short in one circuit trips its breaker, and a bus can be isolated without losing everything.

items.q: What typically sits on the essential bus, and why?
items.a: The items you need to keep flying and get down: the primary flight display, the air data computer and the attitude and heading reference system, the number one navigation source, the number one communication radio, the engine and airframe interface with the voltmeter, and the standby indicator lights. It is the bus that the standby battery is connected to, so those items survive the loss of the main battery and alternator. Read the actual bus list from the POH.

items.q: What is a standby battery for, and what does the ARM position do?
items.a: It is a separate small battery, independent of the main battery, kept in reserve to power the essential bus if main ship power is lost. Set to ARM before flight, it is held on charge by the electrical system and stands ready to take over automatically; it is not powering anything while the alternator is working. It typically buys enough time to fly a descent and approach on the primary display, and its endurance is a POH figure.

items.q: What warnings appear in the annunciator window of a typical light single?
items.a: Commonly low oil pressure, low fuel quantity, low volts, high volts, standby battery status, low vacuum, starter engaged and, where fitted, high carbon monoxide. Red annunciations demand immediate action, amber ones demand attention and a decision. The exact list, colors and the values at which each triggers are airplane specific and are found in the POH and the flight manual supplements.

items.q: What is the split master switch, and why is it split?
items.a: It is two switches on one rocker: a battery half and an alternator or alternator field half. Splitting them lets you power the airplane from the battery alone, for example to check the flaps or lights before start, and lets you take the alternator offline without killing everything if the regulator fails. The battery half must be on for the alternator to be excited, so switching off the battery alone kills the alternator as well.

items.q: How do you handle a circuit breaker that has popped?
items.a: A popped breaker means the circuit drew more current than it should, which usually means a fault. You may reset a breaker once, after a short pause to let it cool, and only if the circuit is needed for safe flight. If it pops again, leave it out and treat that system as gone; a persistent short is a fire risk. Never hold a breaker in, and never pull one as a substitute for a switch except where a checklist tells you to.

items.q: What is the ammeter or loadmeter telling you?
items.a: A center-zero ammeter shows the current into or out of the battery: a positive reading means the battery is charging, a negative reading means it is discharging and the alternator is not keeping up. A loadmeter reads only positive and shows how much of the alternator output is being used, so a reading of zero means the alternator is producing nothing. Know which one is fitted, because the same needle position means opposite things.

items.q: What is the difference between a fixed pitch and a constant speed propeller?
items.a: A fixed pitch propeller has one blade angle built in, so it is efficient only at one combination of speed and power, and RPM varies with airspeed and throttle. A constant speed propeller has variable blade angle controlled by a governor, so the pilot selects an RPM and the governor changes pitch to hold it, letting the engine deliver its power efficiently across the whole speed range. Fixed pitch is simpler and lighter; constant speed gives better climb and cruise.

items.q: What is the difference between a climb propeller and a cruise propeller?
items.a: On a fixed pitch airplane, a climb propeller has a lower blade angle, or lower pitch, which reduces the load so the engine reaches higher RPM and full power at low airspeed: better takeoff and climb, lower cruise speed. A cruise propeller has a higher blade angle, giving better cruise speed and fuel economy at the cost of longer takeoff runs and a weaker climb. The choice is a fixed compromise made on the ground.

items.q: How does a constant speed propeller governor work?
items.a: The governor is engine driven and contains flyweights sensing engine RPM against the tension of a speeder spring set by the propeller control. If RPM rises above the selected value, the flyweights fly out, move a pilot valve, and direct engine oil under boosted pressure into the propeller hub to change the blade angle in the direction that increases load and brings RPM back down. If RPM falls, oil is released and the blades move the other way. It is a continuous, self-correcting loop.

items.q: What holds the blades and what happens on a single engine if oil pressure is lost?
items.a: On most single-engine installations, governor oil pressure drives the blades toward high pitch and low RPM, while a spring and the aerodynamic twisting moment or counterweights drive them back toward low pitch and high RPM. So a loss of oil pressure to the propeller lets it go to low pitch, high RPM, which is the fail-safe: full power is still available for landing, though RPM must be controlled with the throttle. Multi-engine propellers are the opposite and feather.

items.q: In what order do you move throttle and propeller controls?
items.a: Increasing power, propeller forward first, then throttle. Reducing power, throttle back first, then propeller back. The rule keeps you from combining high manifold pressure with low RPM, which loads the engine heavily. Beyond that, follow the manifold pressure and RPM combinations published in the POH cruise tables, which are the real authority on what is permitted for that engine. The throttle changes power and is indicated as manifold pressure, while the propeller lever selects the RPM the governor holds; the throttle knob is conventionally black and the propeller knob blue.

items.q: What are the four left-turning tendencies, and when is each strongest?
items.a: Torque: the engine turns the propeller right, so the airframe is rolled left, strongest at high power and low airspeed. Spiralling slipstream: the corkscrewing airflow strikes the left side of the vertical stabiliser and yaws the nose left, strongest at high power and low speed. Gyroscopic precession: raising the tail applies a force felt 90 degrees ahead, yawing the nose left, most noticeable in tailwheel airplanes. P-factor: at a high angle of attack the descending right blade takes a bigger bite than the ascending left one, yawing left.

items.q: What propeller damage must you look for on preflight, and why does it matter?
items.a: Run a hand along both blades looking for nicks, gouges, cracks, erosion and any sign of the tips having struck anything, and check the spinner and its attachment. A nick is a stress raiser in a component that is highly loaded in tension and vibrating constantly, and blade failures start at nicks. Nicks may only be dressed out by a mechanic within limits. Also treat every propeller as live, because a broken P-lead means the engine can start when it is turned.

items.q: What are the components of a typical light airplane fuel system, in order?
items.a: The mnemonic is TFRASS: Tanks, the Fuel selector, a Reservoir tank or collector, the Auxiliary or boost fuel pump, the Shutoff valve, and the Strainer or gascolator, after which fuel reaches the engine-driven pump and the fuel and air control unit, then the injector nozzles or carburettor. The exact layout, including which tanks feed what, is in the POH fuel system diagram.

items.q: What is the difference between a gravity feed and a pump feed fuel system?
items.a: Gravity feed relies on the tanks being above the engine, typically in a high wing, so fuel flows down to the engine with no pump needed, and the system is simpler. Pump feed is required where the tanks are below the engine, as in a low wing, and uses an engine-driven pump with an electric auxiliary pump for starting, takeoff, landing and as a backup. Fuel-injected engines use a pump even in high-wing airplanes.

items.q: When do you use the auxiliary or boost fuel pump?
items.a: Follow the POH, but the common uses are priming and starting, takeoff and landing where the manual calls for it, switching tanks, high altitude operations, and as a backup if the engine-driven pump fails or if you suspect vapor lock. The point is to have it running whenever a failure of the engine-driven pump would matter most, that is, when you are low, slow and have no time to troubleshoot.

items.q: What fuel selector limitations do typical light airplanes carry?
items.a: Usually a requirement to take off and land with the selector on BOTH where that position exists; a limit on how long you may slip or skid with one tank dry, often around 30 seconds; a restriction of single-tank operation to level flight; a prohibition on prolonged uncoordinated flight on a single tank at low quantity; and a statement that the fuel remaining once the gauge reads zero is not usable in flight. The actual limitations are airplane specific and come from the POH.

items.q: What is the difference between total, usable and unusable fuel?
items.a: Total is everything the tanks physically hold. Unusable is the quantity that cannot be reliably delivered to the engine in all approved flight attitudes, because it sits below the pickup or in a corner of the tank. Usable is the difference, and it is the only number you may plan with. Usable fuel is included in the empty weight only as unusable fuel, so check which figure the weight and balance uses. All three come from the POH.

items.q: What are the aviation fuel grades and their colors?
items.a: 100LL is blue and is the common grade today; 100, previously 100/130, is green; the old 80/87 was red; and jet fuel is clear or straw colored and smells of paraffin. Unleaded avgas approved by supplemental type certificate is also entering service. Color is a check, not a guarantee, because mixed grades turn clear. Use the grade or grades approved for your engine and placarded at the filler.

items.q: What happens if the wrong fuel grade is used?
items.a: A grade lower than approved lowers the detonation margin and can destroy the engine through detonation, especially at high power on a hot day. A grade higher than approved is generally tolerable but causes lead fouling of plugs and valves over time. Fueling a piston engine with jet fuel is catastrophic: it will not ignite properly, and the engine will fail shortly after takeoff. Watch the truck, check the placard, and sample and smell the fuel.

items.q: Why do you drain fuel samples, and what are you looking for?
items.a: To find water, sediment and the wrong grade of fuel. Drain every sump the POH lists, including the gascolator, especially after refueling, after rain, and after the airplane has sat. Look at the color to confirm the grade, look for suspended dirt or rust, and look for a clear separation line at the bottom of the sample. Continue draining until the sample is clean.

items.q: Where does water appear in a fuel sample, and why?
items.a: At the bottom, because water is denser than avgas and does not mix with it, so it settles and appears as a clear layer beneath the blue fuel with a visible curved boundary between the two. That is also why the drains are at the lowest point of each tank and why you must sample after refueling and after the airplane has stood long enough for the water to settle. Water in the lines can stop the engine.

items.q: How does water get into fuel tanks, and how do you prevent it?
items.a: Mainly by condensation on the inside of partly empty tanks as temperature falls overnight, and also from rain past a poor filler cap seal, from contaminated fuel at the pump, and from snow or ice on the wing at refueling. The best preventions are to fill the tanks after the last flight of the day when weight and balance allows, to keep the caps and seals in good order, and to sump thoroughly before every flight.

items.q: What happens if a fuel tank vent becomes blocked?
items.a: As fuel is drawn out, the tank cannot admit replacement air, so a partial vacuum forms that opposes fuel flow. The result is fuel starvation and eventually engine stoppage, sometimes preceded by fluctuating fuel flow or pressure, and in bad cases the tank can be deformed. Vents are on the preflight for exactly this reason, and many systems have a vented filler cap or a crossover vent as a backup.

items.q: What is vapor lock, and when is it most likely?
items.a: Vapor lock is fuel boiling into vapor in the fuel lines, so the pump moves gas rather than liquid and the engine is starved. It is most likely on a hot day with a hot engine, after a shutdown when the lines soak up engine heat, at high altitude where the boiling point is lower, and with fuel-injected engines. The remedy is the POH hot start procedure and use of the boost pump to push liquid fuel through and purge the vapor.

items.q: How is fuel flow measured, and why is a totaliser not a fuel gauge?
items.a: Flow is measured by a turbine type transducer in the line between the fuel control unit and the distribution unit, which counts the rotation of a small impeller and reports it as gallons per hour. A totaliser integrates that flow and subtracts it from a quantity you typed in, so it is only as good as your entry and it knows nothing about a leak downstream of the transducer. The tank gauges, however crude, measure what is actually there.

items.q: What does a low fuel annunciation mean, and how much time does it give you?
items.a: It means the indicated quantity in a tank has fallen below the trigger value, commonly around 5 gallons and usually requiring the condition to persist for a short period so a slip does not trigger it. It is a warning that you are into the last of the fuel, not a reserve indicator, and the time remaining depends entirely on power setting. Treat it as a reason to land, and read the actual trigger value and quantity from the POH.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of retractable landing gear?
items.a: Retracting the gear removes a large source of parasite drag, giving a higher cruise speed and better range for the same power, and it improves climb performance once clean. The costs are weight, complexity, cost, maintenance and a whole new set of failure modes, plus the possibility of a gear-up landing. Fixed gear is simpler, lighter and cheaper, and on slower airplanes the drag penalty is not worth the machinery to remove it.

items.q: How is retractable gear operated, and what tells you it is down?
items.a: By an electric motor driving a hydraulic power pack, by an engine-driven hydraulic pump, or in a few designs by an electric motor and jackscrews. Position is shown by three green lights or equivalent indications for down and locked, an in-transit light, and a gear-unsafe indication. There is also a warning horn that sounds if the throttle is retarded or the flaps are extended with the gear up, and most types have a mirror or visual check. Extension and retraction are the same cylinder worked in two directions: pressurizing one side of the piston displaces the fluid on the other side back into the reservoir. The position lights are required equipment, not a convenience: 91.205 requires a gear position indicator on airplanes with retractable gear, so verifying three green before landing is a legal check as well as a sensible one.

items.q: What is an emergency gear extension system, and what should you expect from it?
items.a: A means of getting the gear down without the normal power source: a hand pump, a free-fall release with gravity and airspeed doing the work, a hand crank, or a compressed gas blow-down bottle. Expect it to be one-way in most designs, meaning once used the gear cannot be retracted in flight, and expect it to need a specific airspeed and configuration. The exact procedure and the speeds are in the POH, and it should be practiced.

items.q: What are the common types of landing gear shock absorption?
items.a: Spring steel or composite struts, which flex to absorb the landing and are simple and maintenance free but return energy, so they can bounce. Oleo-pneumatic struts, which force oil through an orifice against a compressed air or nitrogen chamber, absorbing and damping energy, giving the smoothest ride but needing servicing for correct strut extension. And rubber bungee cords on some older designs. Check strut extension and tire condition on preflight.

items.q: How are the brakes and nosewheel steering arranged on a typical light single?
items.a: Brakes are usually independent hydraulic disc units on the main wheels, operated by the toe pedals through a master cylinder for each side, with no cross-connection, and a parking brake that holds pressure in the lines. Nosewheel steering is either direct through pushrods from the rudder pedals, giving positive steering, or a free castering nosewheel steered with differential braking. A shimmy damper stops nosewheel oscillation.

items.q: What does brake failure feel like, and what do you do?
items.a: A pedal that goes soft or straight to the floor, or the airplane pulling to one side, which points to a hydraulic leak or a failed master cylinder. Pump the pedals, use the remaining brake with rudder to keep straight, shut the engine down if a collision is imminent, and if it happens before takeoff, do not go. In flight, a discovered leak means planning a landing on the longest runway into wind and being ready to steer off into soft ground.

items.q: What is the difference between anti-icing and de-icing equipment?
items.a: Anti-icing prevents ice from forming at all and is switched on before entering the conditions: heated pitot tubes and stall vanes, heated windshield panels, heated propeller boots, hot air on leading edges, and fluid weeping systems. De-icing removes ice after it has formed and accumulated, principally pneumatic boots that inflate to crack the ice off. Using a de-ice system too early can leave a shell of ice bridged over the boot.

items.q: What ice protection systems might a light airplane carry?
items.a: Pitot heat and heated stall warning, standard on most. Heated static ports and fuel vents on some. Electrically heated propeller boots or a slinger ring spraying fluid onto the blade roots. A fluid weeping wing system, in which glycol is pushed through laser-drilled titanium panels on the leading edges, propeller and windshield. Pneumatic boots on twins and turboprops. And an alcohol or electrically heated windshield panel to preserve a view for landing.

items.q: What makes an airplane approved for flight into known icing?
items.a: A complete, certificated ice protection system covering the wing and tail leading edges, propeller, windshield, pitot and static sources, stall warning, fuel vents and often the antennas, plus an ice detection means, adequate fluid or electrical capacity, and an approved airplane flight manual supplement with its own limitations and procedures. Having pitot heat and a heated prop does not make an airplane known-ice capable, and flight into forecast or reported icing without that approval is a certification and a control problem.

items.q: What do you do if you pick up ice in an airplane not approved for it?
items.a: Treat it as an emergency and leave the icing conditions immediately: climb, descend or turn back to air that is warmer or free of visible moisture, and tell ATC what you need. Turn on all available protection, carry more power and more speed, and avoid using flaps, because tailplane ice plus flap can cause a sudden tailplane stall and pitch-over. Land at the nearest suitable airport, flying the approach faster and flatter than usual.

items.q: How is a cabin pressurized, and by what?
items.a: Air is bled from the compressor section of a turbine engine or supplied by a turbocharger or an engine-driven compressor on a piston airplane, cooled through an air cycle or vapor cycle system, and delivered into the sealed cabin. Pressure is maintained by controlling how fast the air leaves, not how fast it goes in. The result is a cabin altitude far below the aircraft altitude, allowing high-altitude cruise without oxygen masks.

items.q: What does the outflow valve do, and what is the safety or dump valve for?
items.a: The outflow valve regulates the rate at which air escapes the fuselage, and by throttling that escape it sets the cabin pressure while a constant inflow continues; the pressurization controller drives it to hold the selected cabin altitude and rate of change. The safety or dump valve is an independent backup that opens if differential pressure exceeds the structural limit, if the outflow valve fails, or when the crew selects dump, preventing the cabin from over-pressurizing.

items.q: What cabin altitude does a pressurized airplane typically hold?
items.a: Around 8,000 feet at the airplane maximum design cruising altitude, which is comfortable for most people and keeps blood oxygen saturation acceptable without supplemental oxygen. The limiting factor is the maximum differential pressure the fuselage structure is designed for, so above a certain altitude the cabin altitude must rise as the airplane climbs. Actual figures are airplane specific and are in the POH or AFM.

items.q: Define ambient pressure, cabin altitude and differential pressure.
items.a: Ambient pressure is the pressure of the air immediately surrounding the airplane, and ambient temperature is that air temperature. Cabin altitude is the cabin pressure expressed as the altitude at which that pressure would be found in the standard atmosphere. Differential pressure is the difference between cabin pressure and ambient pressure, that is, the load the fuselage structure is carrying, and it is the number the safety valve protects.

items.q: What are the three types of decompression?
items.a: Explosive decompression is faster than the lungs can vent, generally taken as less than 0.5 seconds, since unrestricted lungs need about 0.2 seconds, and it can cause lung damage. Rapid decompression is fast but slow enough that the lungs decompress faster than the cabin, so lung damage is unlikely. Gradual decompression is slow and is the most dangerous in one respect: it can go unnoticed until the crew is already hypoxic, which is why cabin altitude warnings exist.

items.q: What are the immediate actions after a decompression?
items.a: Oxygen mask on first, before anything else, because time of useful consciousness at high cabin altitude is measured in seconds. Then establish crew communication, begin an emergency descent to a safe altitude, declare the emergency, and check on the passengers and the airplane once you are lower. The order matters: a crew that troubleshoots before donning masks does not finish the descent.

items.q: What supplemental oxygen is required of the crew in an unpressurized airplane?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.211 (Part 91, Subpart C - Supplemental oxygen), at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 feet MSL, the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen for that part of the flight of more than 30 minutes duration. Above 14,000 feet MSL the required minimum flight crew must use it for the entire time at those altitudes. There is no altitude at which the crew may go without oxygen above 14,000.

items.q: What does the oxygen rule require for passengers?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.211 (Part 91, Subpart C - Supplemental oxygen), at cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet MSL each occupant of the aircraft must be provided with supplemental oxygen. Note the difference in wording: the crew must use it above 14,000, but passengers need only be provided with it above 15,000 and are not required to use it. Good practice is well below either figure, particularly at night.

items.q: What oxygen must be carried in a pressurized airplane at high altitude?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.211 (Part 91, Subpart C - Supplemental oxygen), above FL250 the airplane must carry at least a 10 minute supplemental oxygen supply for each occupant, over and above what is needed for the pressurization failure descent. Above FL350 one pilot at the controls must be wearing and using a secured, sealed oxygen mask, unless at or below FL410 there are two pilots at the controls and each has a quick-donning mask that can be put on with one hand within 5 seconds.

items.q: If one pilot leaves the controls above FL350, what must the other do?
items.a: The remaining pilot must put on and use an oxygen mask until the other pilot returns to the crewmember station. This is the condition attached to the quick-donning exception in 14 CFR 91.211 (Part 91, Subpart C - Supplemental oxygen): the relief from wearing a mask at or below FL410 depends on two pilots being at the controls, so the moment there is only one, that one wears the mask.

items.q: What is aviation grade oxygen, and why not use medical or industrial oxygen?
items.a: Aviation breathing oxygen is at least 99.5 percent pure with no more than a trace of water, and is supplied in green cylinders. Medical oxygen contains water vapor that would freeze in the regulator and lines at altitude and block the flow. Industrial oxygen may contain impurities and contaminants from the equipment used to handle it. Only aviation grade is approved, and cylinders and regulators must be kept clean and free of oil and grease, which can ignite in pure oxygen.

items.q: What is a cannula, and what is its altitude limit?
items.a: Plastic tubing that sits under the nose and delivers oxygen to the nostrils. It is far more comfortable than a mask, allows normal speech and eating, and is the usual choice for light airplane use. Because it does not seal, oxygen escapes and the user can dilute the flow by breathing through the mouth, so a cannula is generally approved only up to 18,000 feet cabin altitude. Above that a mask is required.

items.q: What is a continuous flow oxygen system, and how high can it be used?
items.a: The simplest type: oxygen flows constantly through a metering orifice into a mask with a rebreather bag, so the wearer inhales a mixture of oxygen and cabin air and the bag stores flow between breaths. It wastes oxygen during exhalation but is cheap and simple, which is why it is the passenger system and the drop-down mask you see in airliners. It is generally used up to about 25,000 feet.

items.q: How does a diluter-demand oxygen system work, and to what altitude?
items.a: It delivers oxygen only when the user inhales through a close-fitting mask, which saves a great deal of oxygen. An automix lever lets the regulator blend cabin air with oxygen according to altitude, or deliver 100 percent oxygen when selected. Because the mask seals against the face and prevents dilution with outside air, a diluter-demand system may be used up to about 40,000 feet.

items.q: What does a pressure-demand system add, and why is it needed above 40,000 feet?
items.a: It is a diluter-demand system that additionally supplies oxygen to the mask under positive pressure at cabin altitudes above about 34,000 feet, with airtight, oxygen-tight seals. Above roughly 40,000 feet the ambient pressure is so low that even 100 percent oxygen breathed normally cannot force enough into the bloodstream, so the gas must be pushed in under pressure, which pressurizes the lungs and makes exhalation the active part of breathing.

items.q: What keeps the gyro of an air-driven attitude indicator erect?
items.a: Pendulous vanes hanging under the gyro housing. Air that has spun the rotor escapes through four slots covered by these hinged vanes; if the gyro tilts, gravity swings the vanes, opening one slot and closing another, and the escaping air nudges the gyro back upright at a slow erection rate. That slow rate is why the instrument shows small errors after a prolonged acceleration or a sustained turn and then re-erects over a few minutes. Solid-state attitude sources use accelerometers and tilt sensors for the same job.

items.q: How are the intake and exhaust valves opened and closed on a piston airplane engine?
items.a: By a camshaft geared to the crankshaft and turning at half crankshaft speed. Cam lobes lift tappets, the tappets push hollow pushrods up to rocker arms on the cylinder head, and the rockers press the valves open; springs close them. Correct timing is what puts the four strokes in order, and the small overlap at the end of exhaust helps scavenge and cool the cylinder. Sticking valves, worn guides or a burned exhaust valve show as rough running and a low differential compression reading.

items.q: What does a traffic advisory system show you, and what are its limitations?
items.a: It shows nearby aircraft as symbols with relative altitude and a climb or descent trend, and calls them aloud. It is advisory only: it tells you where traffic is, never how to maneuver, so see-and-avoid and ATC instructions still govern. Limits: it only sees airplanes that are transponding or broadcasting, so no-electric airplanes, gliders and drones are invisible; uplinked traffic is complete only inside ground coverage; and displayed position can lag. Read the AFM supplement for what your installation is approved to do.

items.q: How much does avgas weigh, and where does that figure matter?
items.a: 6 pounds per US gallon for 100LL at standard temperature; turbine fuel is about 6.8 and engine oil 7.5 pounds per gallon. You use it every time a fuel load is converted into weight for the loading computation, and it is why full tanks with all seats filled often puts a light airplane over maximum gross weight or behind the aft limit. Fuel expands and contracts with temperature, so treat it as nominal, and take tank capacities and the weight per gallon used for your airplane from the POH weight and balance section.

items.q: Why does a fixed pitch propeller have maximum and minimum diameter limits?
items.a: Because the blade is one piece forged aluminum alloy and can only be dressed down so far. Nicks and gouges have to be filed out by a mechanic, and every repair removes material; once the propeller is below the minimum diameter listed on the type certificate data sheet it is unairworthy and must be replaced. The maximum diameter is the one certification tested for tip speed, vibration and ground clearance. Read the diameter limits and the ground clearance figure from the POH and the type certificate data sheet.

items.q: How does a panel carbon monoxide detector work, and what do you do when it alerts?
items.a: It samples cabin air with an electrochemical cell and annunciates once carbon monoxide reaches a low threshold, on the order of 50 parts per million, well before you would feel symptoms. On an alert: cabin heat off, fresh air vents or a window open, supplemental oxygen if carried, and land as soon as practical, then have the exhaust system and muffler shroud inspected before further flight. The detector is not a substitute for that inspection, and chemical spot cards fade with age and must be replaced on schedule.

items.q: What does a traditional attitude indicator do during acceleration and deceleration?
items.a: It shows a false pitch up during acceleration and a false pitch down during deceleration, because the erection mechanism and the pendulous vanes respond to the inertia of the acceleration as though it were gravity. It also shows a slight turn indication in prolonged turns on older units. An electronic attitude display fed by an attitude and heading reference system corrects these with air data and GPS inputs and does not show the error.

items.q: What does the turn coordinator show, and what powers it?
items.a: It shows rate of turn and rate of roll, the roll information coming from the gyro being canted rather than mounted flat. It is normally driven by direct current from the electrical system, deliberately split from the vacuum-driven attitude and heading instruments so that one power failure does not remove everything. The inclinometer ball beside it is not gyroscopic and shows slip or skid. Electronic displays draw the same rate-of-turn indication at the top of the attitude picture.

items.q: What is a standard rate turn, and how long does 90 degrees of it take?
items.a: A standard rate turn is 3 degrees per second, flown with the wing of the turn coordinator's miniature airplane on the left or right hash mark. A full 360-degree circle therefore takes 2 minutes, 180 degrees takes 1 minute, and 90 degrees takes 30 seconds. An electronic display shows the same rate as a pointer against the turn-rate marks at the top of the attitude indication.

items.q: What blade angle and RPM do you want for takeoff or a go-around, and what for cruise?
items.a: For takeoff and go-around you want a low blade angle and high RPM, a small bite of air taken many times a second, which gives the most thrust at low airspeed. For cruise you want a high blade angle and low RPM, a much larger bite taken less often, which is more efficient at speed as well as quieter and easier on the engine. The governor makes the change when you move the propeller control.

items.q: What happens to the center of gravity when the landing gear extends?
items.a: On a typical tricycle airplane it moves forward, because the nose gear swings toward the front of the airplane as it comes down while the main legs move comparatively little. The shift is small but real, and it adds to the nose down pitching moment and the drag increase you feel as the gear comes out on approach. Retracting the gear moves the center of gravity back again.

items.q: What happens to drag while the landing gear is retracting into the well?
items.a: Total drag momentarily increases. As the leg approaches the gear well, the airflow around the leg and the airflow over the wing or fuselage interfere with each other, so interference drag rises and briefly adds to total drag before the leg is stowed and the doors close. This is why climb performance improves only once the gear is fully up and locked, not at the moment you select it up.

items.q: What is the keel effect of extended landing gear?
items.a: The extended legs and wheels hang below the airplane's center of gravity and act like the keel of a boat, resisting yaw and roll away from straight flight. Extended gear therefore adds to directional stability, which is one reason an airplane can feel steadier on a gusty approach with the gear down. Retracting the gear takes that stabilizing surface away along with the drag.

items.q: What must an electronic primary flight display show?
items.a: At a minimum an airspeed indicator, turn coordinator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator, all presented electronically, and it must be continuously visible to the pilot rather than something paged up from a menu. That list is the definition used in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), section 61.129 Aeronautical experience, the rule setting out the flight time a commercial applicant must log.

items.q: What must an electronic multifunction display show?
items.a: At a minimum a moving map driven by GPS navigation with the airplane's own position shown on it. Like the primary flight display it has to be continuously visible, so a map that must be selected from a menu or that shares a screen which can be paged away does not count. The requirement is in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), section 61.129 Aeronautical experience.

items.q: What is a two axis autopilot, and what makes it more than a wing leveler?
items.a: A two axis autopilot controls both pitch and roll, so it can hold an altitude and a heading or track at the same time, and it must be integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system so it will fly a selected heading, follow a course, or couple to an approach. A single axis roll only autopilot or a plain wing leveler does neither of those things.

items.q: Walk me through a turbojet engine.
items.a: Air enters the intake, is squeezed by the compressor, then is mixed with fuel and burned in the combustion chamber. The hot expanding gas drives the turbine, which spins the shaft that turns the compressor, and what is left leaves through the exhaust at high velocity, and that jet of gas is the thrust. Intake, compressor, combustion chamber, turbine, exhaust is the order to memorize.

items.q: How does a turboprop differ from a turbojet?
items.a: A turboprop uses the same gas generator, but the turbine's job is to spin a shaft rather than to leave the energy in the exhaust. That shaft drives a reduction gearbox, which turns very high engine speed into a much lower propeller speed the blades can actually use, and the propeller then produces nearly all of the thrust. Only a small amount of residual thrust comes out of the exhaust.

items.q: How does a turbofan work?
items.a: A large fan at the front splits the incoming air into two streams. Most of it, the bypass air, goes around the core and is simply accelerated by the fan, while the remainder passes into the core and is compressed, burned and expanded through the turbine exactly as in a turbojet. Accelerating a large mass of air gently, rather than a small mass violently, gives better fuel efficiency and far less noise.

items.q: What does the day VFR list require about the tachometer?
items.a: A tachometer for each engine, per 91.205(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. In a fixed-pitch Warrior II the tachometer is your power instrument, because with no constant speed propeller RPM is the direct measure of power set; most also carry a recording hour meter used to track the 100-hour and oil change intervals. Confirm the green arc and redline for your airplane against the POH.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES T: tachometer for each engine

items.q: Which engines need an oil temperature gauge for day VFR?
items.a: An oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, per 91.205(b)(10), Part 91, Subpart C. A Warrior II's Lycoming O-320 is air-cooled, so the oil temperature gauge is required equipment, not an option. Oil carries away a large share of the engine's heat, so oil temperature is your early indicator of a cooling or lubrication problem.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES O: oil temperature indicator

items.q: When is a manifold pressure gauge required for day VFR?
items.a: Only for each altitude engine, that is a supercharged or turbocharged engine, per 91.205(b)(5), Part 91, Subpart C. A normally aspirated, carbureted Lycoming O-320 in a Warrior II is not an altitude engine, so no manifold pressure gauge is required; in practice airplanes with constant speed propellers carry one anyway to set power.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES M: manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine

items.q: What does the day VFR list require about oil pressure?
items.a: An oil pressure gauge for each engine using a pressure oil system, per 91.205(b)(4), Part 91, Subpart C. The Warrior II's wet sump Lycoming is a pressure system, so the gauge is required. Oil pressure should come up within about 30 seconds of start, or sooner in warm weather; if it does not, shut down. Confirm the green arc limits against the POH.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES O: oil pressure gauge for each engine

items.q: What does 91.205 require for fuel indication?
items.a: A fuel gauge indicating the quantity of usable fuel in each tank, per 91.205(b)(9), Part 91, Subpart C. Note it indicates usable fuel, and it is only required by certification standards to read accurately at empty. In a Warrior II that means you plan on time and known fuel flow, dip or visually check the two wing tanks before flight, and treat the gauges as a cross-check.
items.concept: A TOMATO FLAMES F: fuel quantity gauge for each tank

items.q: What kind of altimeter does IFR flight require?
items.a: A sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, per 91.205(d)(1), Part 91, Subpart C. Sensitive means it reads in 20-foot increments over a 1,000-foot per revolution scale, and the Kollsman window must be settable so you can apply the current altimeter setting. It must also have been tested with the static system within the preceding 24 calendar months under 91.411.
items.concept: GRABCARD A: sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure

items.q: What does the B of GRABCARD require, and what does the instrument tell you?
items.a: A slip-skid indicator, the inclinometer ball, per 91.205(d)(5), Part 91, Subpart C. It shows whether the airplane is in coordinated flight: ball to the inside of the turn means slipping, too little rate for the bank, and ball to the outside means skidding, too much rate for the bank. Step on the ball to correct. It needs no power, and in a Warrior II it is built into the turn coordinator.
items.concept: GRABCARD B: ball, the slip-skid indicator

items.q: What causes spark plug fouling?
items.a: Fouling occurs when low engine operating temperatures are coupled with running a rich mixture, leaving unburned fuel, carbon and lead deposits bridging the electrodes so the plug can no longer spark. Long low-power taxi, extended idling, and idle descents on a cool day are the classic setup, and the lead in 100LL makes it worse. In the Warrior the first sign is usually a rough or excessive drop on one magneto at runup.
items.concept: Spark plug fouling - low operating temperatures coupled with a rich mixture

items.q: Why do you lean the mixture for taxi?
items.a: Leaning before taxiing prevents the spark plugs from fouling, because at idle and taxi power the mixture is very rich and the engine runs cool, which is exactly the combination that leaves lead and carbon on the electrodes. Lean aggressively on the ground in the Warrior, to the point where the engine would quit if you opened the throttle. Remember to return the mixture to full rich before the runup and takeoff unless the POH allows otherwise.
items.concept: Leaning before taxiing prevents spark plug fouling

items.q: Why must you treat every propeller as live, even with the key off?
items.a: Because even with the ignition switch in the OFF position, if the ground wire between the magneto and the ignition switch becomes disconnected or broken, that magneto is still live, and the engine could accidentally start if the propeller is moved with residual fuel in the lines. Never stand in the propeller arc, never use the blade as a handhold, keep passengers clear, and if you must move a propeller, move it as though the engine will fire.
items.concept: Hot magneto hazard - broken or disconnected ground wire with the switch OFF

items.q: What engine is installed in this airplane?
items.a: A Lycoming O-320 rated 160 horsepower at 2700 RPM. POH 1.3 and 2.7 both approve either the O-320-D2A or the O-320-D3G, exactly as TCDS 2A13 does, and the FAA registry records this airplane's engine only as 0-320 SERIES. So the installed dash number has to be read off the engine data plate rather than asserted from the book.

items.q: Your instructor says the type certificate names the D3G. Is that right?
items.a: Only half right. The TCDS and the handbook both approve either engine; neither picks one. POH 1.3(c) and 2.7(c) print O-320-D2A or O-320-D3G side by side, and the registry entry for this airplane says only 0-320 SERIES. The correct answer in an oral is that both are approved for the model and mine is whichever is stamped on the data plate, which I would read before quoting it.

items.q: How much power does this engine make, and at what RPM?
items.a: 160 horsepower at 2700 RPM. The handbook says it three times: 1.3 rated horsepower 160, 2.7 maximum horsepower 160, and 7.5 rated at 160 HP at 2700 RPM. The tachometer red line is also 2700 RPM and is labeled maximum continuous power, so there is no separate higher takeoff rating to manage and no time limit to watch.

items.q: Describe the engine's basic configuration.
items.a: In the handbook's own words at 1.3, it is four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed, air cooled. Direct drive means there is no reduction gearbox, so propeller RPM equals crankshaft RPM. Section 7.5 repeats it as a four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed engine. It is carbureted rather than fuel injected, and normally aspirated.

items.q: What is the engine's displacement, and where does the name O-320 come from?
items.a: 319.8 cubic inches, POH 1.3. The Lycoming designation rounds that off: O for horizontally opposed, 320 for the approximate displacement in cubic inches. The absence of a prefix letter is the point worth making, because it says there is no gearing, no supercharging and no fuel injection, which is exactly the direct drive, carbureted, normally aspirated engine the handbook describes.

items.q: What is the compression ratio, and why does it matter on a Warrior?
items.a: 8.5:1, POH 1.3. It is the figure that separates the 160 hp D-series engine in this Warrior II from the 150 hp 7.00:1 engine in the earlier PA-28-151 Warrior, and the two airplanes look identical on the ramp. It also ties to the fuel: a higher compression ratio needs the higher octane, which is why the filler is placarded 100 or 100LL aviation grade and lower grades are not allowed.

items.q: How is this engine cooled?
items.a: By air. POH 7.5: engine air enters on either side of the propeller through openings in a nose cowling and is carried through the engine baffling around the engine and the oil cooler. The same baffled air cools the cylinders and the cooler, so there is no separate scoop for the oil. The preflight includes checking the engine baffle seals in the nose section.

items.q: Does this airplane have cowl flaps? If not, what controls engine temperature?
items.a: No cowl flaps at all. The cooling air is ducted by fixed baffling, so temperature is controlled by what the pilot does: lowering the nose for more airspeed and more cooling flow, keeping the mixture rich in the climb, and reducing the climb angle. On a hot day the tools are a shallower climb and a richer mixture, not a lever.

items.q: What are the engine mounts made of, and what is a dynafocal mount for?
items.a: POH 7.5: the engine mounts are constructed of steel tubing, and dynafocal mounts are provided to reduce vibration. Section 7.3 notes the steel tube engine mount is one of the few parts of the primary structure that is not aluminum alloy. A dynafocal arrangement aims the rubber isolators at the engine's center of gravity, so vibration is absorbed in the mounts instead of being fed into the airframe.

items.q: Trace the induction air path from outside the airplane to the cylinders.
items.a: POH 7.5: carburetor induction air enters a chin scoop on the lower right cowling and is passed through a wetted polyurethane filter to the carburetor air box, then through the carburetor and the intake manifold to the cylinders. It is an updraft, carbureted, normally aspirated installation, so there is no turbocharger and no automatic alternate air door; the only alternate path is carburetor heat.

items.q: Tell me about the induction air filter.
items.a: POH 8.11: a wet-type polyurethane foam filter, in the lower right front of the engine compartment behind four quarter-turn fasteners. It must be inspected at least once every 50 hours, and more frequently in dusty conditions. It is disposable, so if it is excessively dirty or shows any damage it is replaced rather than cleaned.

items.q: What do you know about the carburetor, and what does the handbook not tell you?
items.a: It is a float-type carburetor fed from a carburetor air box, with the throttle and mixture acting at it and a screen at its inlet cleaned every 50 hours; Figure 7-9 simply labels it CARBURETOR. What the handbook never gives is the make, model or float type, and the TCDS gives only carburetor settings, so I would not name a manufacturer in the oral. That is a case where the honest answer is better than a confident guess.

items.q: Where does carburetor heat air come from?
items.a: From a shroud around the muffler. POH 7.5: air for the muffler shroud is picked up from the nose cowling and carried through a duct to the shroud, and heated air enters the carburetor air box through a hose connected to the heater shroud. The same dual mufflers and heater shrouds supply cabin heat, the defroster and what Piper calls the carburetor deicing system.

items.q: Is the air you get with carburetor heat filtered?
items.a: No, and the handbook says so. POH 4.19: avoid prolonged ground operation with carburetor heat ON as the air is unfiltered. The heated air comes off the muffler shroud, downstream of the induction filter, so with heat selected the engine is breathing whatever dust is around. That is why the ground check of carb heat is brief and why heat comes off before takeoff.

items.q: Describe the carburetor heat control.
items.a: POH 7.11: a lever to the right of the control quadrant on the instrument panel, placarded with two positions, ON down and OFF up. It is an on-off control, not a modulating one. That is precisely why the handbook insists on full heat; there is no approved intermediate setting for the pilot to select.

items.q: Why does Piper say never to use partial carburetor heat?
items.a: POH 3.41 NOTE: partial carburetor heat may be worse than no heat at all, since it may melt part of the ice which will refreeze in the intake system. The handbook's rule is that when using carburetor heat always use full heat, and when the ice is removed return the control to the full cold position. Section 3.29 says the same thing: heat should be full on when carburetor ice is encountered.

items.q: What is the first indication of carburetor ice in this airplane?
items.a: A drop in RPM. POH 3.41: engine roughness is usually due to carburetor icing, which is indicated by a drop in RPM and may be accompanied by a slight loss of airspeed or altitude. The propeller is fixed pitch and there is no manifold pressure gauge on the panel, so the tachometer is the instrument that moves first.

items.q: Why is the carburetor ice indication different in a constant speed airplane?
items.a: Because a governor holds the RPM. With a fixed pitch propeller, a loss of power lets the propeller slow, so the tachometer falls and that is the cue. With a constant speed propeller the governor flattens the blades to hold the selected RPM, so the tachometer stays where it was and the loss appears as falling manifold pressure instead. This airplane has no manifold pressure gauge, so RPM is all there is.

items.q: You suspect carburetor ice and apply full heat. What should happen?
items.a: It gets worse before it gets better. POH 3.41: RPM will decrease slightly and roughness will increase; then wait for a decrease in roughness or an increase in RPM, indicating ice removal. If there is no change in approximately one minute, return the carburetor heat to OFF. Adjust the mixture for maximum smoothness meanwhile. If too much ice is allowed to accumulate, restoration of full power may not be possible.

items.q: Do you put carburetor heat on for every approach in this airplane?
items.a: Piper says no. POH 4.31: carburetor heat should not be applied unless there is an indication of carburetor icing, since the use of carburetor heat causes a reduction in power which may be critical in case of a go-around, and full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation. That is this handbook's position and it differs from the habit many pilots are taught.

items.q: What does the POH want you to do for a prolonged power-off descent?
items.a: POH 4.29: apply full carburetor heat before the power reduction if icing conditions are suspected, retard the throttle, lean the mixture as required, and verify power response approximately every 30 seconds by partially opening and then closing the throttle, which is clearing the engine. Leveling off, enrich the mixture, set power as required and select carb heat off unless icing is still suspected.

items.q: What is detonation, and what does this handbook say can cause it?
items.a: Detonation is uncontrolled, explosive burning of the charge after the spark instead of a smooth flame front, and it drives cylinder pressure and temperature up fast enough to damage pistons, rings and cylinders. This handbook names one cause directly, at 4.31: full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation. The other guards are the placarded minimum fuel grade and not running lean at high power.

items.q: How does preignition differ from detonation?
items.a: Preignition is ignition of the charge before the spark, by a hot spot such as a glowing deposit or a damaged plug, so the mixture burns against a piston that is still rising; detonation is a violent burn after normal ignition. Preignition can destroy a cylinder very quickly. This handbook does not discuss preignition at all, so I would offer that as general engine knowledge and take the detail from the Lycoming operator's manual.

items.q: How many magnetos does this engine have, and what else does the engine drive?
items.a: Two magnetos. POH 7.5 lists the engine as equipped with a starter, a 60 amp 14 volt alternator, a shielded ignition, two magnetos, vacuum pump drive, a fuel pump and a wetted polyurethane foam induction air filter. That list is the right answer to what the engine drives, and it is what tells you the vacuum gyros and the ignition survive a loss of the electrical system.

items.q: Why does the engine have two magnetos?
items.a: For redundancy and for power. Two independent ignition systems mean a failed magneto, lead or plug does not stop the engine, and firing the cylinder from two plugs gives two flame fronts, so the charge burns faster and more completely. The handbook never states a plug count, so the honest version is two per cylinder, one fired by each magneto, confirmed from the engine manual rather than claimed from the POH.

items.q: Why does the engine keep running with the master switch off?
items.a: Because a magneto is engine driven and self-exciting: it makes its own current from a rotating magnet and needs nothing from the airplane's electrical system. That is why the ignition does not appear in the POH 7.15 list of standard electrical accessories, and why an alternator failure, a flat battery or an electrical fire handled with master off still leaves you with a running engine.

items.q: How are the magnetos driven?
items.a: Off the engine. POH 7.5 lists the two magnetos among the engine-driven accessories alongside the vacuum pump drive, which points to accessory gear drive, but the handbook never states the drive arrangement in words. The safe answer is the principle, that they are engine driven and self-exciting and so need no electrical power, with the gearing detail taken from the engine manual.

items.q: Which spark plugs does each magneto fire?
items.a: The handbook does not say. POH 7.5 gives only a shielded ignition and two magnetos; there is no plug count and no harness assignment anywhere in the book. The right answer is two plugs per cylinder, one fired by each magneto, confirmed from the engine manual, rather than inventing a top-and-bottom split. That is a stronger answer than a confident wrong one.

items.q: What does a shielded ignition mean, and why is it fitted?
items.a: POH 7.5 describes the installation as having a shielded ignition. Shielding is metal braid over the leads and plug caps that contains the radio frequency noise a magneto system throws off, so it does not reach the radios and navigation receivers as a buzz that rises and falls with engine speed. The handbook gives no further detail on the harness than that phrase.

items.q: You pull the mixture to shut down and the engine keeps running. What does that mean?
items.a: A magneto is not being grounded, normally a broken or disconnected P-lead, so that magneto is live no matter where the key is. From then on the propeller is treated as hot: nobody touches it, the mixture stays at idle cut-off, fuel selector and master go off, and the airplane is written up before any blade is turned. It is the same defect that shows as a zero drop in the run-up.

items.q: At what RPM do you check the magnetos?
items.a: 2000 RPM. POH 4.19 says the magnetos should be checked at 2000 RPM, and the Section 4 GROUND CHECK list opens with throttle 2000 RPM. That is a published figure in this handbook rather than a school checklist number, and it is the same RPM at which the vacuum gauge should read 4.8 to 5.1 inches of mercury.

items.q: Is there a time limit on running on one magneto?
items.a: Yes. POH 4.19: operation on one magneto should not exceed 10 seconds. The handbook gives no reason, but the practical one is that extended single-magneto running at run-up power fouls the plugs that are not firing. It makes the check deliberately brisk: left, back to both, right, back to both, watching the drop and the split.

items.q: What does an excessive magneto drop tell you?
items.a: That one ignition system is not carrying its share: fouled or failed plugs, a bad lead or a magneto out of time. A drop beyond 175 RPM, or a split beyond 50 RPM, means the airplane does not go as it is. A rough-running magneto with a big drop usually points at a fouled plug, and the normal first attempt is to lean at higher RPM to burn the deposit off and recheck before calling maintenance.

items.q: What RPM drop should you see on the carburetor heat check?
items.a: This handbook does not publish one. The GROUND CHECK list says only carburetor heat check, and 4.19 gives the reasons without a number: to be sure the control is operating properly and to clear any ice formed during taxiing. So I look for a definite drop and a clean recovery, and I would say the POH specifies no figure rather than quote a school number as if it came from the book.

items.q: How is the starter operated?
items.a: From the ignition switch. POH 4.15: engage the starter by rotating the magneto switch clockwise, and when the engine fires release the magneto switch, so it is spring loaded off the key and not a separate button. Operating Tip 10.3(e) adds that radio, light and pitot heat switches should be checked off before engaging the starter so as not to create an overloaded condition.

items.q: Describe the exhaust system and what else it feeds.
items.a: POH 7.5: the exhaust system is constructed of stainless steel and incorporates dual mufflers with heater shrouds to supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster system and the carburetor deicing system. So the exhaust is not just plumbing; everything warm on this airplane comes off it, which is why a cracked muffler is at once a carbon monoxide problem and a carburetor heat problem.

items.q: Describe the throttle control.
items.a: POH 7.11: a lever on the control quadrant in the lower center of the instrument panel, accessible to both pilot and copilot, running on teflon-lined control cables, used to adjust engine RPM. On a fixed pitch airplane the throttle is the only power lever and the tachometer is the power instrument; there is no propeller control and no manifold pressure gauge to set.

items.q: What does the mixture control do, and how do you stop this engine?
items.a: POH 7.11: the mixture control lever adjusts the air to fuel ratio, and the engine is shut down by placing the mixture lever in the full lean position, that is idle cut-off. Shutting down on the mixture leaves no combustible charge in the cylinders, so the magnetos can then be switched off into a dead engine. The control lock has to be disengaged before the lever will come back.

items.q: What is the friction lock for?
items.a: POH 7.11: a friction adjustment lever on the right side of the control quadrant that increases or decreases the friction holding the throttle and mixture, or locks them in a selected position. It is set loose enough that the levers move deliberately and tight enough that they do not creep back on their own in the climb or in cruise.

items.q: Does this airplane have a primer, and why is it on the emergency checklists?
items.a: POH 7.13 calls it an optional engine priming system, with the pump immediately to the left of the throttle quadrant; in practice it is fitted, since primer locked appears on the placarded takeoff checklist, in Before Takeoff and in both engine failure checklists. An unlocked primer can feed raw fuel into the induction system and run the engine rough or rich, which is why it gets checked when power is lost.

items.q: How do you lean this engine in cruise?
items.a: POH 4.27: reduce to the desired cruise power setting and lean the mixture to peak RPM, then adjust the throttle if necessary for the final RPM setting; leaning to peak engine RPM gives best fuel economy. There is no EGT as standard equipment, so peak RPM is the handbook's leaning reference on this airplane, and 7.11 and 7.5 both send the pilot to the Lycoming operator's manual for more.

items.q: Do you ever take off with the mixture less than full rich?
items.a: POH 4.21 NOTE: the mixture should be set FULL RICH, but a minimum amount of leaning is permitted for smooth engine operation when taking off at high elevation. So full rich is the rule and leaning for takeoff is a density altitude exception, leaned only as far as smooth running. On approach 4.31 wants full rich as well, to ensure maximum acceleration if the throttle has to be opened again.

items.q: Tell me about the propeller.
items.a: A Sensenich two-blade fixed pitch propeller of aluminum alloy construction, model 74DM6-0-60 or 74DM6-0-58 per POH 2.7. Section 7.5 gives a 74-inch diameter with a 58 or 60-inch pitch, the pitch determined at 75 percent of the diameter. Fixed pitch is why RPM is the power indication, why an RPM drop is the first sign of carb ice, and why there is no propeller lever in the cockpit.

items.q: What static RPM should this engine make, and why does it matter?
items.a: POH 2.7 gives it by propeller model, at sea level in standard conditions at maximum permissible throttle: for the 74DM6-0-60, not above 2430 RPM and not below 2330 RPM; for the 74DM6-0-58, not above 2465 and not below 2365. It is the check that engine and propeller together are making rated power. The handbook refers to the maintenance manual for testing in non-standard conditions.

items.q: How do you warm this engine up?
items.a: POH 4.17: warm up at 800 to 1200 RPM for not more than two minutes, and the handbook warns that prolonged idling at low RPM may result in fouled spark plugs. On start, when the engine is firing evenly the throttle is advanced to 800 RPM. The warm-up is not run to a temperature; it is run until the engine passes the throttle test in the ground check.

items.q: How do you know the engine is warm enough for takeoff?
items.a: It is a functional test, not a temperature. POH 4.19 and the GROUND CHECK list: the engine is warm for takeoff when the throttle can be opened without the engine faltering. That is a better answer than guessing an oil temperature, because the handbook sets no takeoff minimum; it publishes only the oil temperature green arc of 75 to 245 degrees F and the 245 degrees F red line.

items.q: The engine runs rough in cruise. Walk me through the checklist.
items.a: POH 3.3: carburetor heat ON; if roughness continues after one minute, carburetor heat OFF; mixture adjust for maximum smoothness; electric fuel pump ON; fuel selector switch tanks; engine gauges check; magneto switch L then R then BOTH; if operation is satisfactory on either one, continue on that magneto at reduced power and full rich mixture to the first airport; and prepare for a power-off landing. It works induction, then fuel, then ignition.

items.q: Is there anything special about shutting down after using alternate fuel?
items.a: Yes, and it is in the NOTE to POH 4.33: when alternate fuels are used, the engine should be run up to 1200 RPM for one minute prior to shutdown to clean out any unburned fuel. Alternate fuel here means the commercial grade 100/130 that 8.21 allows when 100 or 100LL is not available. The rest of the shutdown is mixture to idle cut-off with the throttle full aft, then magnetos and master off.

items.q: What is the oil capacity of this engine?
items.a: 8 US quarts. POH 1.9 prints oil capacity 8 quarts and 8.19 opens with the oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts. TCDS 2A13 agrees independently: oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5 inches, 6 quarts usable. Note those are two different ideas, capacity and usable oil, and an examiner may well ask you to separate them.

items.q: The type certificate says 6 quarts usable. Is that your minimum for flight?
items.a: No. 6 quarts usable is a weight and balance figure from TCDS 2A13, which reads oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5, 6 quarts usable; it says how much of the oil is drainable and counted for loading, not how little you may dispatch with. The POH minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts, in Section 8.19. Mixing the two up is an easy way to get a follow-up question you do not want.

items.q: Why do some checklists say 6 to 8 quarts if the POH says 2?
items.a: Because that is an operator policy, not a handbook figure. One school's PA-28-161 checklist prints oil quantity 6 to 8 quarts as its preflight acceptance band, which is a sensible dispatch rule for an engine that uses oil on a long flight. The POH's own figure is the 2 quart minimum safe quantity in 8.19. The good answer names all three figures and says which is which.

items.q: Where is the oil cooler, and how is it cooled?
items.a: POH 7.5: the oil cooler is located on the left rear of the engine, mounted to the engine baffling, and the engine cooling air picked up in the nose section of the cowling and carried through the baffling is used on the left side for the oil cooler. There is no separate scoop for it; the same baffled air that cools the cylinders cools the oil.

items.q: What is the oil cooler winterization plate, and what is the rule for it?
items.a: POH 7.5: a winterization plate is provided to restrict air during winter operation. The placard in Section 2.25 gives the rule: oil cooler winterization plate to be removed when ambient temperature exceeds 50 degrees F. For a late November ride I would look for it on the preflight, know whether it is fitted, and know that I have to take it off once the temperature goes above that figure.

items.q: Is there a thermostatic bypass in the oil system, and how does it work?
items.a: There is one on the engine, but this handbook does not describe it. The words thermostat, bypass and vernatherm do not appear in the oil discussion; 7.5 covers the cooler and the winterization plate and 8.19 covers quantity, interval and grade. So the POH answer is the cooler and the plate, and I would say the thermostatic control of flow through the cooler is an engine-level detail I would confirm in the Lycoming manual rather than guess at the plumbing.

items.q: Is there an oil filter or a screen on this engine?
items.a: POH 8.19 names a full flow cartridge type oil filter and says it should be replaced each 50 hours of operation. The handbook does not describe a screen-only configuration, but it also does not state that every airframe has the filter, so which is actually fitted comes from the engine logbook and the accessory housing. It matters because it decides whether Lycoming's 50 hour or 25 hour interval applies.

items.q: How often is the oil changed on this airplane?
items.a: POH 8.19: the oil should be drained and renewed every 50 hours, and sooner under unfavorable operating conditions, with full flow cartridge type oil filters replaced each 50 hours as well. The full answer pairs that with the calendar limit on the same page: the interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four months, whichever comes first.

items.q: Is there a calendar limit on the oil change as well as an hours limit?
items.a: Yes. POH 8.19: the interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four months. So a training airplane hits the 50 hours first and a lightly flown private airplane hits the four months first. Quoting both is what makes the answer complete, because an airplane that has flown 20 hours in six months is still out of limits.

items.q: Lycoming talks about a 25 hour oil change. Where does that come from?
items.a: From Lycoming Service Bulletin 480, not from this handbook. It sets 25 hours with screen cleaning for an engine with a pressure screen system only, against 50 hours where there is a full flow filter, with four months either way. POH 8.19 publishes only the 50 hour and four month figures, so I would offer the 25 hour qualifier as Lycoming's and say it applies if the airplane turns out to have a screen rather than a filter.

items.q: What oil does this engine take?
items.a: The handbook deliberately does not freeze a brand. POH 1.9 and the NOTE at the end of 8.19 both refer the pilot to the latest issue of Lycoming Service Instruction 1014, Lubricating Oil Recommendations. What the POH does print is a viscosity table by average ambient temperature, with straight mineral grades under MIL-L-6082B in one column and ashless dispersant grades under MIL-L-22851 in the other.

items.q: It is a cold November morning. What oil grade should be in the engine?
items.a: The relevant row of the POH 8.19 table is 0 to 70 degrees F, which gives SAE 30 straight mineral, or 30, 40 or 20W-40 ashless dispersant. The all-temperature row allows 15W-50 or 20W-50 ashless dispersant, which is what most operators run year round. If the temperature ranges overlap, the table's own rule is to use the lighter grade oil.

items.q: What oil grade covers all temperatures?
items.a: The top row of the POH 8.19 table: 15W-50 or 20W-50 ashless dispersant under MIL-L-22851. The straight mineral column for that row is a dash, meaning no single grade mineral oil is recommended for all temperatures, which is the whole point of a multigrade. That row is why most Warriors on a flight line are on a 20W-50 all year.

items.q: What oil grade does the handbook call for in hot weather?
items.a: From the POH 8.19 table: above 80 degrees F, SAE 60 in either column; above 60 degrees F, SAE 50 straight mineral or 40 or 50 ashless dispersant; and 30 to 90 degrees F, SAE 40 in both columns. The rule printed with the table is that when operating temperatures overlap the indicated ranges, use the lighter grade oil.

items.q: What does the handbook call for below 10 degrees F?
items.a: The bottom row of the POH 8.19 table: SAE 20 straight mineral under MIL-L-6082B, or 30 or 20W-30 ashless dispersant under MIL-L-22851. In practice the all-temperature multigrade row, 15W-50 or 20W-50, covers that case too. A thinner oil in cold weather is about getting pressure and flow at start, before the engine has warmed.

items.q: The oil tables in Section 1 and Section 8 do not agree. Which one wins?
items.a: They really do differ, and spotting it is worth more than reciting either. Section 1.9 prints a shorter starting-viscosity table with no all-temperature row and gives 20W-30 below 10 degrees F, where 8.19 gives 30 or 20W-30. Section 8.19 is the servicing table and is the one I would quote, and I would say plainly that the handbook disagrees with itself and that Lycoming SI 1014 is the tie-breaker both sections point to.

items.q: What is break-in oil, and does this handbook require it?
items.a: This handbook says nothing about break-in oil. Section 8.19 refers the pilot to Lycoming Service Instruction 1014, and that document calls for non-dispersant mineral oil for the first 50 hours and after cylinder replacement until oil consumption stabilizes, for engines other than the O-320-H and O/LO-360-E series, so it does apply to this D-series engine. I would attribute the requirement to Lycoming, not to the POH.

items.q: What does the POH say about the dipstick?
items.a: Very little, and the honest answer says so. POH 4.13, nose section of the walk-around: check the oil level, and make sure that the dipstick has been properly seated. The handbook does not describe the filler neck, the access door or the dipstick markings, so I would not describe a calibrated scale from memory; I would read the stick in the airplane and compare it with the 8 quart capacity and the school minimum.

items.q: Describe the crankcase breather on this engine.
items.a: The handbook does not describe one. There is no mention of a crankcase breather or its routing anywhere in VB-1180. A breather does exist on the engine, venting blow-by and keeping crankcase pressure down, with the line routed so that it cannot freeze shut in cold weather, but that is engine manual material. I would say so rather than invent a routing, which is the same answer I would give for the thermostatic bypass.

items.q: What is the oil actually doing in the engine?
items.a: Lubrication first, and then cooling, sealing between the rings and the cylinder walls, cleaning by carrying combustion byproducts and metal to the filter, protecting against corrosion, and cushioning the bearings and gears. On this engine the cooling job is substantial because there are no cowl flaps and the oil cooler shares the baffled cylinder air, so high oil temperature in a climb is managed the same way as cylinder temperature.

items.q: What is the oil pressure green arc on this airplane?
items.a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 60 to 90 PSI. That is the band you want in cruise. The gauge also carries two yellow arcs and two red lines, which is unusual and is a favorite examiner question, so it is worth being able to give all six numbers rather than only the green arc.

items.q: How many yellow arcs are on the oil pressure gauge, and what are they?
items.a: Two, which catches people out. POH 2.9: a yellow caution arc at idle from 25 to 60 PSI, and a second yellow arc for ground warm-up from 90 to 100 PSI. So low pressure at idle and high pressure on a cold morning run-up are both expected, caution-range indications rather than failures, as long as they move into the 60 to 90 green band with warm oil at normal power.

items.q: What are the red lines on the oil pressure gauge?
items.a: POH 2.7 and 2.9 agree: minimum red line 25 PSI and maximum red line 100 PSI. Below 25 PSI the engine is outside its limit and the answer is the loss of oil pressure procedure; above 100 PSI it is also out of limits, which is usually cold, thick oil or a regulating fault. Between them sit the two yellow arcs and the 60 to 90 PSI green arc.

items.q: What are the oil temperature markings?
items.a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 75 to 245 degrees F, with the red line at 245 degrees F. The same 245 degrees F appears in 2.7 as the maximum oil temperature limitation, so the limit and the red line agree. There is no yellow arc on this gauge, so the answer is simply green to 245 and red at 245.

items.q: You get a low oil pressure light in flight. What does it actually tell you?
items.a: That a system may not be operating properly and that I should look at the gauge. POH 7.15 is explicit that the annunciator lights are provided only as a warning that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required. So the light sends me to the oil pressure and oil temperature gauges, and what those show decides whether this is a gauge problem or an engine problem.

items.q: How do you tell a failed oil pressure gauge from a real loss of oil?
items.a: By what the other indications do. POH 3.17 says a complete loss of indication may signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge, and that it may be advisable to make an off-airport landing while power is still available, particularly if other indications of actual oil pressure loss, such as sudden increases in temperatures, or oil smoke, are apparent, and an airport is not close. Rising oil temperature or smoke makes it real.

items.q: What is the procedure for high oil temperature?
items.a: POH 3.3, again only two lines: land at the nearest airport and investigate the problem, and prepare for a power-off landing. With no cowl flaps the only things that help on the way there are lowering the nose for more cooling airflow, reducing power, and enriching the mixture. If the pressure falls as the temperature rises, treat it as an impending engine failure and plan the landing accordingly.

items.q: Where are the oil gauges on the panel?
items.a: POH 7.19: in an engine cluster to the right of the pilot control wheel, which contains a fuel pressure gauge, a right and a left main fuel quantity gauge, an oil temperature gauge and an oil pressure gauge. Four of the gauges you are likely to be asked about are in that one cluster, with the tachometer, ammeter and annunciator panel elsewhere on the panel.

items.q: What is the oil arm, and when would you use it?
items.a: TCDS 2A13 gives oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5 inches aft of datum, with 6 quarts usable. It is a weight and balance number for an airplane weighed with the oil drained. The Section 6 loading form in the POH does not list oil separately, because it treats the oil as part of the basic empty weight, so in normal loading I do not enter it at all.

items.q: How much fuel does this airplane hold?
items.a: 50 US gallons total, 48 usable, in two 25 gallon wing tanks of which 24 gallons a side is usable. POH 7.13 puts it in one sentence: fuel is stored in two twenty-five gallon tanks giving the airplane a total capacity of fifty U.S. gallons, 48 gallons usable. Sections 1.7 and 2.21 and TCDS 2A13 all agree, and I plan with 48, never 50.

items.q: Why does the handbook define unusable fuel at the critical flight attitude?
items.a: Because fuel moves. POH 2.21: the unusable fuel has been determined as 1.0 gallon in each wing in critical flight attitude, not in level flight. The figure is set in the attitude where the outlet is most likely to be uncovered, so it is a conservative number.
