It is also why Operating Tip 10.3(i) warns about prolonged slips and skids uncovering the fuel outlet when the tank in use is not full.

items.q: What is the indicator tab in the filler neck, and how much fuel is it?
items.a: POH 7.13: each tank is equipped with a filler neck indicator tab to aid in determining fuel remaining when the tanks are not full, and the usable capacity to the bottom of the indicator tab is 17 gallons. So tabs is 17 a side, 34 gallons usable in total. On a weight-limited airplane that is how you fuel for a flight with four seats filled, instead of filling to the caps and leaving people behind.

items.q: What are the fuel selector positions?
items.a: Three: left tank, right tank and off. The selector face in Figure 7-7 is placarded L TANK 24 GAL, R TANK 24 GAL and FUEL OFF. The handle is on the left side panel forward of the pilot's seat. The point an examiner is usually driving at is the one that is not there, because this airplane has no BOTH position.

items.q: Does this airplane have a BOTH position on the fuel selector?
items.a: No. There are three positions only, left tank, right tank and off, confirmed on the Figure 7-7 selector face which is placarded L TANK 24 GAL, R TANK 24 GAL and FUEL OFF. So fuel management is an active job: run one tank, switch with the electric pump on, keep track of the time on each, and manage the lateral balance yourself.

items.q: Why is there no BOTH on a low-wing Piper?
items.a: The handbook gives no rationale, so I would separate the mechanism from my own reasoning. The sourced part is the arrangement: the tanks are in the wings below the engine, so there is no gravity feed and fuel is drawn up by an engine-driven pump with an electric pump as backup. Drawing both tanks through one suction line invites unporting and uneven feeding, so Piper selects one tank at a time and makes the pilot manage balance.

items.q: Where is the fuel selector and how do you get it to OFF?
items.a: POH 7.13: the selector is on the left side panel forward of the pilot's seat, and a button on the selector cover must be depressed and held while the handle is moved to the OFF position; the button releases automatically when the handle is moved back to ON. It is a guard against selecting OFF by accident in flight, and it is worth being able to find and work by feel.

items.q: What is the auxiliary electric fuel pump for?
items.a: POH 7.13: an auxiliary electric fuel pump is provided in case of the failure of the engine-driven pump. Note what that does not say. It is not the normal supply and it is not a primer; it is a backup that is switched on for the phases where an engine-driven pump failure would be least survivable. The switch is in the switch panel above the throttle quadrant.

items.q: Why do you turn the electric fuel pump off during the run-up?
items.a: POH 4.19 gives the reason outright: the electric fuel pump should be turned OFF after starting or during warm-up to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating. It is a functional check of the engine-driven pump, which is why the GROUND CHECK list has electric fuel pump OFF followed immediately by fuel pressure check. Prior to takeoff it goes on again to prevent loss of power during takeoff should the engine-driven pump fail.

items.q: When does the electric fuel pump come off after takeoff?
items.a: The Section 4 CLIMB checklist says OFF at desired altitude, not at a fixed height above the ground. The logic is the same as turning it on: it is there so an engine-driven pump failure in a critical phase does not become a power loss, so it stays on until the airplane is somewhere a power loss could be handled. It goes back on for the approach and landing.

items.q: Is there a fuel emergency where the electric pump goes off rather than on?
items.a: Yes, and it is the trap. Both engine fire checklists turn the electric fuel pump OFF, with the fuel selector OFF as well: engine fire during start is starter crank, mixture idle cut-off, throttle open, electric fuel pump OFF, fuel selector OFF; engine fire in flight is fuel selector OFF, throttle closed, mixture idle cut-off, electric fuel pump check OFF. Every other fuel emergency turns it on.

items.q: Where is the engine-driven fuel pump in the system?
items.a: POH 7.5 lists a fuel pump among the engine-driven accessories, and the Figure 7-9 schematic shows it labeled ENGINE FUEL PUMP in the line between the strainer and the carburetor, with the electric pump upstream of it. In normal operation it is the pump doing the work; the electric pump sits in parallel as the backup, which is why switching the electric one off in the run-up proves the engine-driven one is alive.

items.q: Trace the fuel from the tank to the cylinders.
items.a: From Figure 7-9: left or right main tank, then the fuel tank selector valve, then the fuel strainer, then the electric fuel pump, then the engine fuel pump, then the carburetor and on into the induction system. The primer taps off the line between the strainer and the carburetor, the fuel pressure gauge reads at the carburetor, and the quantity gauges read the tanks.

items.q: What does the handbook call the gascolator, and where is it?
items.a: It calls it the fuel strainer, and I would use the handbook's word. POH 7.13: a fuel strainer, located on the lower left front of the fire wall, has a drain which is accessible from outside the nose section. Section 8.21 puts the quick drain on the front lower corner of the fire wall, and the walk-around says to open the fuel strainer located on the left side of the fire wall.

items.q: How many fuel screens are there, and how often are they cleaned?
items.a: Three, and that detail scores. POH 8.21: at every 50-hour inspection, the fuel screens in the strainer, in the electric fuel pump, and at the carburetor inlet must be cleaned. Most candidates know only the strainer. The strainer itself is the one the pilot touches, through the quick drain on the front lower corner of the fire wall.

items.q: How many fuel drains does this airplane have, and where are they?
items.a: Three drain points. POH 8.21: each fuel tank is equipped with an individual quick drain located at the lower inboard rear corner of the tank, and the fuel strainer is equipped with a quick drain located on the front lower corner of the fire wall. So that is one per wing tank plus the strainer. I would still count them on the airplane, because the walk-around text uses the plural for the tank sumps.

items.q: What is the correct order for draining the fuel system?
items.a: POH 8.21: each of the fuel tank sumps should be drained first, then the fuel strainer should be drained twice, once with the fuel selector valve on each tank. Each time, enough fuel should be allowed to flow to ensure removal of contaminants, collected in a suitable container, examined for contaminants and proper fuel, then discarded. Most candidates drain the strainer once; doing it on each tank selection is the scoring detail.

items.q: When does the handbook require the fuel system to be drained?
items.a: POH 8.21: the fuel system sumps and strainer should be drained daily prior to the first flight and after refueling, to avoid the accumulation of contaminants such as water or sediment and to check for proper fuel. Section 7.13 says the same: the fuel drains should be opened daily prior to first flight, and the strainer should also be drained before the first flight of the day.

items.q: What cautions does the handbook attach to draining fuel?
items.a: Three, all in POH 8.21. When draining any amount of fuel, care should be taken to ensure that no fire hazard exists before starting the engine; after draining, each quick drain should be checked to make sure it has closed completely and is not leaking; and fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains. The leaking drain is the one that catches people out after a cold morning sample.

items.q: Is a fuel anti-icing additive approved on this airplane?
items.a: Yes, with limits. POH 8.21: the additive must meet specification MIL-I-27686 and be uniformly blended with the fuel while refueling, not exceeding .15 percent by volume and not less than .10 percent, which is about one and one half liquid ounces per ten gallons. The CAUTION on the same page is the part to remember: fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains.

items.q: Tell me about the fuel tank vents.
items.a: The walk-around checks one per wing: POH 4.13 says the fuel tank vent should be clear of obstructions on both the right and the left wing. Section 7 does not describe the vents at all, so I would not invent a type or a location beyond that. The purpose is standard reasoning: the vent keeps the space above the fuel at ambient pressure as fuel is drawn off, so no vacuum can build and starve the engine.

items.q: Where are the fuel quantity gauges, and what powers them?
items.a: POH 7.13: the fuel quantity and fuel pressure gauges are mounted in a gauge cluster on the left side of the instrument panel to the right of the control wheel, a right and a left main gauge. They are electrically powered, because 7.15 lists the fuel gauge among the standard electrical accessories. That matters directly to the alternator failure answer: as the battery runs down, the fuel gauges are among the things you lose.

items.q: Are the fuel gauges only accurate at empty?
items.a: That claim is not in this handbook. It comes from the certification rule, not from Piper, and the full text of VB-1180 makes no statement about gauge accuracy. What the POH does require is better: at 4.13 it has you open the fuel cap on each wing, visually check the fuel color, and confirm the quantity matches the indication on the gauge. So fuel is planned by known quantity and time, with the gauge as the cross-check.

items.q: What is the minimum fuel grade for this airplane?
items.a: POH 2.7: AVGAS ONLY, minimum grade 100 or 100LL aviation grade, and the filler placard reads FUEL 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE. Section 8.21 puts it more bluntly: the minimum aviation grade fuel for the PA-28-161 is 100, and since the use of lower grades can cause serious engine damage in a short period of time, the engine warranty is invalidated by the use of lower octanes.

items.q: You land somewhere with no 100LL. What can you put in it?
items.a: POH 8.21: whenever 100 or 100LL grade fuel is not available, commercial grade 100/130 should be used, and the handbook refers to Lycoming Service Instruction 1070. Lower grades are not an option; the same paragraph says their use can cause serious engine damage in a short period and invalidates the engine warranty. If I use the alternate fuel, 4.33 wants 1200 RPM for one minute before shutdown to clean out unburned fuel.

items.q: What would happen if this airplane were fueled with jet fuel?
items.a: It would not run on it. The airplane is placarded AVGAS ONLY, minimum grade 100, and jet fuel is kerosene, which is not an approved grade at all. In a spark-ignition engine with an 8.5:1 compression ratio it will not burn properly, giving severe detonation, roughness and power loss, usually shortly after takeoff. The defenses are the placard at the filler, watching the truck, and the handbook's own requirement to open the cap and check the fuel color at every preflight.

items.q: What is the difference between fuel starvation and fuel exhaustion?
items.a: Exhaustion is no fuel left on board; starvation is fuel on board that is not reaching the engine, typically the selector on a tank that is dry while the other is full. Starvation is the one with a cure in the air: the first line of the engine power loss checklist is fuel selector switch to a tank containing fuel. POH 3.9 warns that the engine will not restart instantly, because the empty lines have to fill, which may require up to ten seconds.

items.q: How long can this airplane fly on its fuel?
items.a: That has to come from the airplane's own performance section, but the structure of the answer is fixed: start from 48 gallons usable rather than the 50 gallon total, take off the regulatory reserve for the kind of flight, and divide what is left by the planned fuel flow at the chosen power setting. The cruise charts in the handbook I have are computed for a heavier airplane, so the fuel flow figures themselves must come from this airplane's own book.

items.q: Does slipping this airplane have any fuel implication?
items.a: Yes, and it is in the Warrior's own Operating Tips at 10.3(i): prolonged slips or skids which result in excess of 2000 ft of altitude loss, or other radical or extreme maneuvers which could cause uncovering of the fuel outlet, must be avoided, as fuel flow interruption may occur when the tank being used is not full. That matters directly to steep spirals and to slipping off height on a power-off landing.

items.q: What do the fuel pressure markings on the gauge mean?
items.a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 0.5 to 8 PSI, with the red line minimum at 0.5 PSI and the red line maximum at 8 PSI. Note that the minimum is half a PSI, not 5; the OCR of the handbook mangles it but the printed page reads .5. Those same two figures appear as power plant limitations in 2.7.

items.q: You lose fuel pressure in flight. What is the drill?
items.a: The checklist is two lines, POH 3.3: electric fuel pump ON, and fuel selector check on a full tank. That is the whole published procedure, and it makes sense because the two likely causes are an engine-driven pump failure, which the electric pump covers, and a selector on a tank that has run dry. If pressure and power do not come back, the next step is the engine power loss checklist and a power-off landing.

items.q: The engine coughs and the fuel pressure stays normal. What does that suggest?
items.a: Water. POH 3.11 makes the point directly: if power loss is due to water, fuel pressure indications will be normal, because the pump is delivering liquid, just not fuel. The handbook's advice is to allow the engine to windmill, and if the engine does not restart after a reasonable time, to try switching tanks. It is also the argument for draining the sumps and the strainer properly before the first flight of the day.

items.q: Which fuel filler placard belongs on this airplane?
items.a: The plain one: FUEL - 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE. The handbook prints a second, graphic AVGAS ONLY placard with GRADE 100LL and GRADE 100, but Section 2.25 restricts that version to serial numbers 28-8316037 and up. This airplane is 28-8116257, well below that, so it gets the first one. The handbook does the serial reasoning for you there, which is a cheap way to show you understand applicability.

items.q: Describe this airplane's electrical system in one sentence.
items.a: POH 7.15: the electrical system includes a 14-volt, 60-amp alternator, a 12-volt battery, a voltage regulator, an overvoltage relay and a master switch relay. The distinction an examiner may probe is in that sentence: it is a 14 volt charging system supplying a 12 volt battery, because the charging voltage has to sit above the battery's resting voltage for current to flow into it.

items.q: What is the alternator rated at, and how is it driven?
items.a: 60 amps at 14 volts, given in two places, POH 7.15 and 7.5. The handbook never states the drive in 7.5 or 7.15, but the walk-around at 4.13 says to check the alternator belt for proper tension in the nose section, so it is belt driven off the engine. The advantage over a generator worth stating is that an alternator gives useful output at low engine RPM, including on the ground at idle.

items.q: Where is the battery on this airplane?
items.a: On this serial it is aft of the main spar, not on the firewall. VB-880, the handbook that applies to serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300, says the battery is mounted in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar. The widely circulated VB-1180 handbook puts it on the forward right face of the fire wall, because Piper moved it between the serial blocks. I would open the airplane and look before answering in the oral.

items.q: Why does it matter where the battery is?
items.a: Because the consequences differ. Aft of the main spar it is a weight and balance item behind the center of gravity, under the rear seat area, and it is not reachable in flight; on the firewall it is in the engine compartment under the right cowl, where the servicing instructions in 8.25 about raising the upper right cowl would apply. The online handbook for this model gives the firewall answer, and for this serial that is the wrong one.

items.q: What is the battery's capacity in amp hours?
items.a: The handbook does not give one. VB-1180 prints the voltage only, 12 volts, and no amp-hour rating appears anywhere in it, so I would read the battery label or the equipment list rather than quote a figure. Warriors fly with both 25 and 35 amp hour batteries in service. The same gap means the handbook publishes no battery endurance after an alternator failure either.

items.q: What type of battery is it, and how is it serviced?
items.a: The handbook never names the chemistry, but 8.25 describes servicing that only fits a flooded lead-acid cell: the battery should be checked for proper fluid level, do not fill above the baffle plates, do not fill with acid, use only water, and a hydrometer check will determine the percent of charge. A sealed battery may have been fitted since, so that is something to confirm on the airplane.

items.q: How is the battery recharged, per the handbook?
items.a: POH 8.25: if the battery is not up to charge, recharge starting at a 4 amp rate and finishing with a 2 amp rate, and quick charges are not recommended. The same section says the battery box has a drain tube, normally closed off with a cap, which should be opened occasionally to drain off any accumulation of liquid, although that description belongs to the firewall installation.

items.q: Is the master switch a single switch?
items.a: No, it is split into BAT and ALT halves. The handbook does not describe the switch itself, but the Section 3 procedures operate the halves independently and in opposition, which only a split switch allows. Some airframes have the ALT half mechanically interlocked with the BAT half, so it is worth trying to move ALT alone on the ground to see which this one is.

items.q: Justify the split master switch from the handbook alone.
items.a: From the two Section 3 procedures. ELECTRICAL FAILURES turns the ALT switch OFF while the battery stays on, sheds load, checks and resets the ALT breaker and then puts ALT back on. ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD does the opposite, ALT switch ON and BATT switch OFF, to shed a runaway regulator while keeping the alternator feeding the airplane. You cannot fly either checklist with a single-pole master, so the book justifies the switch.

items.q: So the ammeter never shows a discharge?
items.a: Correct, it reads load, not charge or discharge. POH 7.15 says the ammeter as installed does not show battery discharge; it indicates the electrical load on the alternator in amperes. There is no negative side to the scale to swing into. That is exactly why alternator failure shows as a zero reading rather than a discharge, which is the indication the Section 3 checklist tells you to look for.

items.q: What should the ammeter read on a normal night flight?
items.a: POH 7.15 gives the example: the average continuous load for night flight with radios on is about 30 amperes, and this 30 ampere value plus approximately 2 amperes for a fully charged battery will appear continuously under these flight conditions. So a steady reading in the low thirties on a night flight is the system working, not a problem, and on a 60 amp alternator that is comfortable.

items.q: What does the ammeter read with everything off and the master on?
items.a: POH 7.15: with all the electrical equipment off and the master switch on, the ammeter will indicate the charging rate of the battery, and as each electrical unit is switched on it will indicate the total ampere draw of all the units including the battery. So the needle climbs as you add load, and with a fully charged battery and nothing on it sits at only a couple of amperes.

items.q: How do you confirm from the ammeter that the alternator is working?
items.a: By comparing the needle with what you have switched on. POH 7.15: the amount of current shown on the ammeter will tell immediately if the alternator system is operating normally, as the amount of current shown should equal the total amperage drawn by the electrical equipment which is operating. If I switch on the landing light and the pitot heat and the reading does not move, the alternator is not carrying the load.

items.q: What does a zero reading on the ammeter mean?
items.a: Alternator failure. POH 3.23 says it flatly: loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter, and the Section 3 checklist is written as if ammeter shows zero. That indication is itself proof the gauge is a loadmeter, because a center-zero charge and discharge ammeter would swing to discharge instead. Everything on the airplane is then running off the battery alone.

items.q: The handbook calls the same instrument three things. What are they?
items.a: Ammeter in Section 7.15 and in the Section 3 procedures, volt-ammeter in the 2.19 Day VFR required equipment list, and alternator gauge on the Figure 7-15 instrument panel layout. They are the same gauge. The one to keep in mind for a legality question is the required equipment list, because a volt-ammeter is one of the twelve items the handbook requires for day VFR in this airplane.

items.q: Where are the voltage regulator and overvoltage relay?
items.a: POH 7.15: the regulator and overvoltage relay are located on the forward left side of the fuselage behind the instrument panel. The regulator holds system voltage steady as engine speed and load change, and the overvoltage relay takes the alternator off line if the regulator runs away, which protects the radios and the battery from an overvoltage condition.

items.q: What is the overvoltage relay, and can you reset it in flight?
items.a: It takes the alternator off line if the regulator fails high, and yes, cycling the ALT switch is the reset. POH 3.23: if the alternator failure was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition, 16.5 volts and up, that procedure should return the system to normal. That is why the ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist turns the ALT switch off, sheds load, checks the breaker and then turns ALT back on before giving up on it.

items.q: What lights are on the annunciator panel?
items.a: POH 7.15: the annunciator panel includes alternator and low oil pressure indicator lights, and when the optional gyro system is installed it also includes a low vacuum indicator light. So three at most, and the third depends on whether this airplane has the vacuum system. Section 7.19 confirms the panel warns of a possible malfunction in the alternator, oil pressure or vacuum systems.

items.q: What does an annunciator light actually tell you?
items.a: Less than people think, and the handbook says so. POH 7.15: the annunciator panel lights are provided only as a warning to the pilot that a system may not be operating properly, and that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required. The light is a prompt to look at a gauge, not a diagnosis, and that is exactly how the Section 3 checklists are written.

items.q: The ALT light comes on in cruise with everything switched off. What now?
items.a: Add a little load and watch. POH 7.15, repeated as the first NOTE of the Section 3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist: when operating with light electrical load and a fully charged battery, the Alternator Inop. light may illuminate due to minimal alternator output, and if the alternator is functional a slight increase in electrical load should extinguish the Inop. indication. If it stays on, I check the ammeter for zero and run the checklist.

items.q: How do you check the annunciator panel?
items.a: With the press-to-test button. It is on the Section 4 GROUND CHECK list as annunciator panel press-to-test, and 4.19 repeats it: check the annunciator panel lights with the press-to-test button. The lights are also checked on the cockpit preflight with the master on, where the walk-around has you confirm the panel illuminates before turning the master off again.

items.q: What is on the standard electrical accessory list?
items.a: POH 7.15: starter, electric fuel pump, stall warning indicator, cigar lighter, fuel gauge, ammeter and annunciator panel. That list is the direct answer to what you lose when the electrical system fails, and the two items on it that catch people out are the stall warning horn and the fuel quantity gauges. Just as important is what is not on the list, because the ignition is not.

items.q: What is on the optional electrical accessory list?
items.a: POH 7.15: navigation lights, wing tip recognition lights, anti-collision light, landing light, instrument lighting and cabin dome light, with the note that the circuits will handle the addition of communications and navigational equipment. Lighting being optional in the certification sense does not make it optional for a night flight, where 2.19 requires position lights, instrument lights and anti-collision lights.

items.q: Does this airplane use fuses or circuit breakers, and where are they?
items.a: Circuit breakers, on the lower right instrument panel, per POH 7.15 and Figure 7-13; no fuses are described anywhere in the handbook. Section 7.19 adds that the radios and the circuit breakers are on the upper and lower right panel respectively. The handbook's own airmanship on them is Operating Tip 10.3(d): before attempting to reset any circuit breaker, allow a two to five minute cooling off period.

items.q: Is there an avionics bus on this airplane?
items.a: POH 7.19 describes one. An optional radio master switch near the top of the instrument panel between the radio stacks controls power to all radios through the aircraft master switch, and an emergency bus switch supplies auxiliary power to the avionics bus in the event of a radio master switch circuit failure. That switch is behind the lower right shin guard, left of the circuit breaker panel, and the radio master is optional, so I would confirm what is actually fitted.

items.q: Does this airplane have an external power receptacle?
items.a: Piper External Power is listed as optional in POH 7.33, through a receptacle on the right side of the fuselage forward of the wing, which lets an external battery crank the engine without getting at the airplane's own battery. The Section 4 procedure is master off and all electrical equipment off, connect the terminals, insert the plug, start normally, disconnect the plug, then master switch on and check the ammeter.

items.q: The ALT light is on and the ammeter reads zero. Give me the checklist in order.
items.a: POH 3.3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES: ammeter check to verify the alternator is inoperative; if the ammeter shows zero, ALT switch OFF; reduce electrical loads to minimum; ALT circuit breaker check and reset as required; ALT switch ON. If power is not restored, ALT switch OFF, reduce electrical loads and land as soon as practical, because the battery is the only remaining source of electrical power. Note that load shedding comes before the breaker reset.

items.q: What is the amplified reasoning behind the alternator failure checklist?
items.a: POH 3.23: loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter; if no increase in the ammeter reading is noted, alternator failure can be confirmed; check the alternator circuit breakers for a popped circuit; then attempt to reset the overvoltage relay, which cures a momentary overvoltage condition of 16.5 volts and up. If the ammeter continues to indicate zero, or the alternator will not remain reset, turn the alternator off, keep the load to a minimum and land as soon as practical.

items.q: After an alternator failure, what keeps working?
items.a: The engine, because the magnetos are self-exciting and need no electrical power; the vacuum gyros, because 7.17 makes the vacuum pump engine driven; the flaps, because 7.9 makes them manual, a cable and a handle; and the brakes, which are hydraulic through the toe pedals and the hand lever. None of those four depends on the battery, which is why this failure is a workload problem rather than an emergency.

items.q: After an alternator failure, what do you lose as the battery runs down?
items.a: Everything on the standard electrical list and the options: the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn, the fuel quantity gauges, the ammeter, the annunciator panel, the cigar lighter, all the lighting, the radios and transponder, and the turn indicator, which 7.19 says is the electrically operated one. The stall warning is the one candidates forget, and 4.37 states it: the stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF.

items.q: How long will the battery last after an alternator failure?
items.a: The handbook publishes no figure, and I would not invent minutes. No amp-hour rating appears anywhere in it either, so there is nothing to divide. The useful answer is the procedure: reduce electrical loads to a minimum, keep what I need for the approach, and land as soon as practical, treating whatever is left as a reserve of unknown size rather than planning a leg on it.

items.q: What is an electrical overload, and how would you recognize it?
items.a: POH 3.24 defines it in its own heading: alternator output more than 20 amps above the known electrical load. So it is recognized on the ammeter, by the needle reading far more current than the equipment switched on can account for, which points at a regulator failing high and driving current into the battery. It is the one case where you fly with the alternator on and the battery off.

items.q: Give me the electrical overload checklist.
items.a: POH 3.3: ALT switch ON, BATT switch OFF. If alternator loads are reduced, reduce the electrical load to minimum and land as soon as practical, with the NOTE that due to increased system voltage and radio frequency noise, operation with ALT on and BATT off should be made only when required by an electrical system failure. If loads are not reduced, ALT switch OFF, BATT as required, land as soon as possible and anticipate complete electrical failure.

items.q: Why are there two different urgencies in the overload procedure?
items.a: Because the two outcomes are different problems. If turning the battery off reduces the alternator loads, the airplane is stable on alternator power and the handbook says land as soon as practical. If the loads do not reduce, the fault is not the battery and the handbook says land as soon as possible and anticipate complete electrical failure. Being able to explain why the wording changes is better than reciting the steps.

items.q: You have an electrical fire in flight. What happens to the airplane when you do the drill?
items.a: The drill is POH 3.3: master switch OFF, vents open, cabin heat off, land as soon as practical. On this airplane that means losing the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn, the fuel gauges, the ammeter, the annunciator and the radios, while the engine keeps running on the magnetos and the vacuum gyros keep running off the engine-driven pump. Cabin heat goes off because its air comes off the muffler shroud.

items.q: What does the strobe light placard say, and why?
items.a: The placard in full view of the pilot reads: WARNING - TURN OFF STROBE LIGHTS WHEN IN CLOSE PROXIMITY TO GROUND OR DURING FLIGHT THROUGH CLOUD, FOG OR HAZE. The same warning appears in 7.15 and in Operating Tip 10.3(f). The reason is disorientation: the strobes reflect off cloud or fog and off the ground on the taxiway and can be blinding to the pilot and to others.

items.q: What switches should be off before you engage the starter, and why?
items.a: Operating Tip 10.3(e): check the radio, light and pitot heat switches off before engaging the starter, so as not to create an overloaded condition when the starter is engaged. The starter is the biggest single draw on the airplane, so everything else comes off first; it is also why the external power procedure has you start with the master and all electrical equipment off.

items.q: Describe this airplane in the handbook's own words.
items.a: POH 7.1: the Warrior II is a single-engine, fixed gear monoplane of all metal construction with low semi-tapered wings; it has four place seating and a baggage capacity of two hundred pounds. That one sentence answers a surprising number of questions, including why there is no gear emergency procedure anywhere in Section 3.

items.q: What airfoil does the wing use, and how is the wing attached?
items.a: POH 7.3: a NACA 652415 laminar flow, semi-tapered airfoil. The cantilever wings are attached to each side of the fuselage by inserting the butt ends of the main spars into a spar box carry-through located under the rear seat, which in effect gives a continuous main spar, plus an auxiliary front spar and a rear spar. The rear spar takes torque and drag loads and mounts the flaps and ailerons.

items.q: What is a stabilator, and what is the tab on its trailing edge?
items.a: A stabilator is a one-piece, all-moving horizontal tail: the whole surface pivots rather than a hinged elevator on a fixed stabilizer. POH 7.3 describes the tab in its own words: the stabilator incorporates an anti-servo tab which improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim; this tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, but with increased travel.

items.q: Why does a stabilator need an anti-servo tab?
items.a: Because an all-moving surface is aerodynamically over-sensitive: the whole tail generates the force, so very little stick force is needed and the pilot can easily overcontrol it. The anti-servo tab deflects the same way as the stabilator but with increased travel, which pushes back against the pilot and raises the control force as deflection increases. POH 7.3 says it improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim.

items.q: How does an anti-servo tab differ from a servo or balance tab?
items.a: By which way it moves. A servo or balance tab deflects opposite to the surface to help the pilot move it and lighten the controls; an anti-servo tab deflects the same way as the surface, so it opposes the movement and increases the force the pilot feels. POH 7.3 states the same-direction movement explicitly, with increased travel, which is the half of the answer most candidates miss.

items.q: How could you demonstrate the anti-servo tab on the walk-around?
items.a: By moving the stabilator by hand and watching the tab. Push the stabilator trailing edge down and the tab goes down with it, not up, which is the whole distinction from a balance tab. The same check confirms the surface is free and that the tab linkage is connected, and 7.9 adds the handbook's other point about it: the tab serves the dual function of providing trim control and pitch control forces.

items.q: How is pitch trim arranged on this airplane?
items.a: Through the same anti-servo tab. POH 7.9: a trim control wheel on the control console between the front seats, where forward rotation gives nose down trim and aft rotation gives nose up trim. There is no separate trim tab, so the one surface both trims the airplane and supplies the pitch control forces, which is the dual function the handbook describes.

items.q: What kind of flaps does this airplane have?
items.a: POH 7.9: manually controlled flaps, extended by a control cable from a handle between the two front seats, balanced and spring loaded to return to the retracted position. Section 7.3 calls them four-position wing flaps. Because they are mechanical rather than electric, they are one of the systems you keep after an electrical failure, and because they are spring loaded you feel the airplane want them back up.

items.q: What flap settings are available, and how do you select them?
items.a: POH 7.9: the handle is pulled up to the desired flap setting of 10, 25 or 40 degrees, with retracted making the fourth position. To retract, depress the button on the end of the handle and lower the control. Section 4 refers to 25 degrees as the second notch, which is the setting used for a short field takeoff over an obstacle and for both soft field takeoffs.

items.q: What happens to pitch when you move the flaps?
items.a: POH 7.9: when extending or retracting flaps there is a pitch change in the airplane, and this pitch change can be corrected either by stabilator trim or by increased control wheel force. The handbook does not say which way, so I would fly it and trim it rather than recite a direction. It is also why the takeoff and landing checklists both have flaps set before the critical phase, not during it.

items.q: Why does Piper warn you about standing on the flap?
items.a: Because only one of them is a step and only in one position. POH 7.9: when the flaps are retracted the right flap, provided with an over-center lock mechanism, acts as a step, and the NOTE adds that the right flap will support a load only in the fully retracted position. The warning is repeated five times in the handbook, in 7.9, 4.33, 4.35, the preflight caution and Operating Tip 10.3(c), which tells you how often it was ignored.

items.q: Describe the landing gear.
items.a: POH 7.7: fixed tricycle gear with three air-oil struts, Cleveland 5.00 by 5 nose wheel and 6.00 by 6 main wheels, with four-ply tires of the same sizes. Normal static load extension is 3.25 inches on the nose strut and 4.50 inches on each main, and the walk-around gives both a plus or minus .25 inch tolerance. A shimmy dampener is included in the nose gear.

items.q: What are the tire pressures?
items.a: POH 8.23: 30 psi for the nose gear and 24 psi for the main gear. Section 7.7 gives the same two figures but qualifies them at gross weight. Section 8.23 adds that the wheels and tires are balanced before original installation and the relationship of tire, tube and wheel should be kept on reinstallation, and that unbalanced wheels can cause extreme vibration in the landing gear.

items.q: How is this airplane steered on the ground?
items.a: Through the nose wheel and the brakes. POH 7.7: the nose gear is steerable through a 30 degree arc each side of center using the rudder pedals and brakes, with a bungee in the mechanism to reduce steering effort and damp bumps; later aircraft have the bungee removed and are steerable through a 20 degree arc each side. The handbook never defines later aircraft, so for a 1981 airplane I would give both and say I would confirm which this one is.

items.q: Describe the brake system.
items.a: POH 7.7: Cleveland single disc hydraulic brakes on the main gear only, with no brake on the nose wheel. They are actuated either by toe brake pedals attached to the rudder pedals or by a hand lever and master cylinder located below and behind the center of the instrument sub panel, with hydraulic cylinders above each pedal and next to the hand lever. The fluid reservoir is on the top left front face of the fire wall.

items.q: How does the parking brake work?
items.a: POH 7.7: it is incorporated in the master cylinder, and it is set by pulling back on the brake lever and depressing the knob attached to the left side of the handle. To release it, pull back on the brake lever to disengage the catch mechanism and let the handle swing forward. Because it works through the same master cylinder as the hand brake, a leak that loses the brakes loses the parking brake too.

items.q: How much warning does the stall warning give, and what powers it?
items.a: POH 7.29 and 4.37: the indicator activates at between five and ten knots above stall speed, and the NOTE at 4.37 says the stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF, because it is an electrical accessory. So in an electrical fire with the master off, or late in an alternator failure, the horn is gone and the only stall warning left is the airplane itself.

items.q: How do you check the stall warning on the preflight?
items.a: POH 4.13 and 4.37: turn the master switch ON, lift the detector and check that the horn sounds, then turn the master back off. That is the check the handbook gives. What it does not give is the mechanism, or which wing the detector is on; the lift detector on the left wing leading edge comes from the Piper maintenance manual rather than from this handbook, so I would attribute it rather than claim it as a POH fact.

items.q: Describe the pitot-static system on this airplane.
items.a: POH 7.21: pitot and static pressure are both picked up by a pitot head installed on the bottom of the left wing, and carried through pitot and static lines within the wing and fuselage to the gauges on the instrument panel. That is the detail people miss: there are no fuselage static ports at all. The system supplies the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the optional vertical speed indicator.

items.q: Where are the static ports on this airplane?
items.a: There are none on the fuselage. POH 7.21 is explicit that pitot and static pressure are picked up by a single pitot head on the bottom of the left wing, so the static source is part of that combined head. The walk-around says to remove the cover from the pitot/static head on the underside of the wing and make sure the holes are open and clear. The static wicks on the wings are nothing to do with it.

items.q: What are the static wicks for?
items.a: They are precipitation static dischargers, there to bleed off static charge the airframe picks up in cloud and rain so it does not interfere with the radios. The walk-around checks them on both wings for firm attachment and good condition. They have nothing to do with the static system, which is an easy trap on this airplane precisely because it has no fuselage static ports to point at.

items.q: Does this airplane have an alternate static source?
items.a: It is optional. POH 7.21: an alternate static source is available as optional equipment, with the control valve located below the left side of the instrument panel. So the honest answer is that I would look under the left side of the panel in this airplane and confirm. If there is none, the fallback for a blocked static source is to break the glass of the vertical speed indicator, accepting the reversed VSI.

items.q: If the alternate static source is fitted, how do you use it?
items.a: POH 7.21: with the valve in the alternate position the altimeter, vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator use cabin air for static pressure. The conditions are the scoring detail: the storm window and cabin vents must be closed and the cabin heater and defroster must be on during alternate static source operation, and the altimeter error is less than 50 feet unless otherwise placarded.

items.q: Does this airplane have pitot heat?
items.a: POH 7.21 lists a heated pitot head as optional equipment, which alleviates problems with icing and heavy rain, with the switch on the electrical switch panel to the left of the right control wheel. It is a substantial electrical load, so it is one of the first things to shed after an alternator failure, and Operating Tip 10.3(e) wants it off before engaging the starter.

items.q: Does this airplane have a vacuum system?
items.a: Section 7.17 is footnoted as optional equipment, and 7.19 lists the attitude gyro, directional gyro and suction gauge as panel options, so it has to be confirmed on this airplane. If it is there, 7.17 describes it: an engine driven vacuum pump, a vacuum regulator, a filter and the necessary plumbing. For IFR it is not optional at all, because POH 2.19 lists a vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator as day IFR equipment.

items.q: What does the vacuum system drive, and what is driven electrically?
items.a: POH 7.17 and 7.19: the attitude gyro and directional gyro are vacuum operated through a vacuum pump installed on the engine, while the turn and slip indicator is electrically operated. The split is deliberate: a single failure, vacuum or electrical, cannot take all the gyros, so there is always a surviving source of attitude or heading information to fly on.

items.q: What kind of vacuum pump is it, and what protects it?
items.a: POH 7.17: the vacuum pump is a dry-type pump, and a shear drive protects the pump from damage, so if the drive shears the gyros become inoperative. It is engine driven, which is the point for the oral: the gyros keep turning through an alternator failure or a master-off electrical fire, because the engine, not the battery, is driving them.

items.q: What should the suction gauge read, and when?
items.a: POH 7.17: the regulator is set so the normal vacuum reads 4.8 to 5.1 inches of mercury, which provides sufficient vacuum to operate all the gyros at their rated RPM. The ground check reads it at 2000 RPM and gives the same range. Note it is 5.1, not 5.2; three places in the handbook agree on 5.1, and the regulator that sets it is behind the instrument panel.

items.q: What does a gradual fall in vacuum mean, and what does zero mean?
items.a: POH 7.17 gives the complete diagnosis. A decrease in pressure in a system that has been constant may indicate a dirty filter, dirty screens, possibly a sticky vacuum regulator or a leak in the system; zero pressure would indicate a sheared pump drive, a defective pump, possibly a defective gauge or a collapsed line. In either case the handbook wants a mechanic to check the system before further damage or failure.

items.q: Your suction is low in slow flight on the checkride. Is that a failure?
items.a: Probably not. POH 7.17 says it outright: vacuum pressure, even though set correctly, can read lower at very high altitude above 12,000 feet and at low engine RPM, usually on approach or during training maneuvers, and this is normal and should not be considered a malfunction. So a low reading during slow flight or an approach is expected, and I would reassess it at cruise RPM before calling it a failure.

items.q: Where does cabin heat come from?
items.a: POH 7.23: heat for the cabin interior and the defroster system is provided by a shroud attached to the muffler, and 7.5 adds that the dual mufflers with heater shrouds supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster and the carburetor deicing system. So all the warm air on this airplane is air that has been passed over the exhaust, which is exactly why a cracked muffler is a carbon monoxide problem.

items.q: Why is a cracked exhaust muffler dangerous in this airplane?
items.a: Because cabin heat, defrost and carburetor heat all come off shrouds on the muffler, so a crack in the exhaust lets carbon monoxide into the air that is blown at the pilot. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless and shows as headache, drowsiness and poor judgment. The handbook's response to smoke or fumes in the cabin is in the Section 3 fire procedures: vents open, cabin heat off, and land.

items.q: Tell me about the seats and the restraints.
items.a: POH 7.25: the front seats are adjustable fore and aft and the right front seat tilts forward for access to the rear, with optional headrests and vertical adjustment. Shoulder harnesses with inertia reels are provided for each front seat occupant, and for the rear seats as standard or optional depending on the model year, which is a live question for a 1981 airplane. The Day VFR equipment list requires a safety restraint for each occupant.

items.q: How many cabin doors does this airplane have, and where?
items.a: One, on the right side. POH 7.3: on the right side of the airplane is a cabin door for entrance and exit, plus a baggage door aft of the rear seat. That single door is worth thinking about for emergency egress and briefing passengers, and it is why the open door procedure in Section 3 matters more here than on an airplane with a door each side.

items.q: A door pops open after takeoff. What do you do?
items.a: Treat it as a nuisance, not an emergency. POH 3.27: the cabin door is double latched, a partially open door will not affect normal flight characteristics, and a normal landing can be made with the door open. To close it in flight, slow to 89 KIAS, close the cabin vents and open the storm window; if the top latch is open, latch it; if the side latch is open, pull on the arm rest while moving the latch handle. If both are open, side latch first, then top.

items.q: Tell me about the baggage compartment.
items.a: POH 7.27: a 24 cubic foot baggage area behind the rear seat, with a maximum capacity of 200 pounds and an arm of 142.8 inches aft of datum, accessible from the cabin or through a large 20 by 22 inch outside baggage door. Tie-down straps are available and the handbook says they should be used at all times, with the NOTE that it is the pilot's responsibility to be sure the center of gravity falls within the allowable range.

items.q: There is a known typographical error in this handbook. Can you find it?
items.a: Yes. Section 1.15 BAGGAGE SPACE prints Maximum Ramp Weight (lbs) 22 and Maximum Landing Weight (lbs) 20, which are plainly wrong. Those two labels have been copied from 1.11 by mistake; 22 and 20 are the baggage door dimensions, as 7.27 confirms with a large 20 by 22 inch outside baggage door. Knowing that the handbook has an error in it is better evidence of reading it than reciting ten correct numbers.

items.q: What instruments are listed as options on this panel?
items.a: POH 7.19: a suction gauge, vertical speed indicator, attitude gyro, directional gyro, clock, tru-speed indicator and a turn and slip indicator or turn coordinator. Which of those are actually in this airplane has to come from the airplane and its equipment list, and it matters for a kinds-of-operation question, because the vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator are required for day IFR.

items.q: Does this airplane have an emergency locator transmitter?
items.a: POH 7.35 lists it as optional, in the aft portion of the fuselage just below the stabilator leading edge, reached through a plate on the right side held by slotted-head nylon screws. There is a three-position ON, OFF and ARM switch on the unit, normally at ARM, and a pilot remote switch on the left side panel. The handbook documents two different NARCO units, so which one is fitted here is something to confirm.

items.q: Is there a carburetor ice detection system on this airplane?
items.a: POH 7.39 describes one as optional: a control box on the instrument panel, a probe sensor mounted in the carburetor, and a red warning light to indicate the presence of ice. Its own WARNING is the part to quote: this instrument is approved as optional equipment only and flight operations should not be predicated on its use. If ice is present, the instruction is still to apply full carburetor heat.

items.q: Is there a gear-up landing procedure in this handbook?
items.a: No, and there cannot be one, because the gear is fixed: POH 7.1 calls it a single-engine, fixed gear monoplane and 7.7 refers to the fixed-gear PA-28-161. Section 3 contains no landing gear emergency of any kind. The forced landing procedure is POWER OFF LANDING, and I would say that confidently rather than improvising a gear emergency for an airplane that cannot have one.

items.q: Is there a ditching procedure?
items.a: No. Section 3 of this handbook contains engine fire during start, engine power loss during takeoff, engine power loss in flight, power off landing, fire in flight, loss of oil pressure, loss of fuel pressure, high oil temperature, electrical failures, electrical overload, spin recovery, open door, engine roughness and carburetor icing. There is no ditching procedure, so a water landing would be flown as a power off landing with the belts tight.

items.q: How do you know what the flaps are doing in this airplane without an indicator?
items.a: By the handle and by the airplane. The flaps are manually controlled by a handle between the front seats that locks into detents at 10, 25 and 40 degrees, so the number of notches you have pulled is the flap setting; the pitch change and the speed decay confirm it; and on a low wing you can see the flap itself from the cockpit. There is no electric motor and no position light to fail.

items.q: Does the manual flap system change your answer on required equipment?
items.a: It changes the practical answer, not the legal one. Legally you still work 91.205, the kinds of operation list, the equipment list and any AD. Practically, a cable-operated flap handle with mechanical detents is its own position indicator, which is why Piper never fitted one, and it is also why the flaps keep working after an alternator failure when the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn and the radios are gone.

items.q: The flaps will not extend. How do you handle it?
items.a: Fly the airplane first, then diagnose. The flaps here are mechanical, operated by a cable from a handle between the front seats, not electric, so a failure means a jammed handle, a broken or stretched cable or a flap obstruction, and there is no circuit breaker to reset and no motor to fail. Do not force the handle. Plan a no-flap approach to a long runway, brief it, and tell ATC so you get the length you need.

items.q: What if only one flap extends?
items.a: Treat it as an asymmetric flap condition and do not touch the handle again. The airplane will roll toward the retracted side and you will need aileron to hold wings level; retract both only if the handle will do it cleanly, otherwise leave the configuration alone and fly it as it is. Approach faster than normal, use a long runway, keep the bank shallow, and expect the roll tendency to change as the speed decays in the flare.

items.q: Does raising the flaps after landing matter in this airplane?
items.a: Yes, for braking. The handbook says braking is most effective when the flaps are raised and back pressure is applied to the control wheel, because raising the flaps dumps lift onto the wheels. Do it after the airplane is firmly on the ground and only with your eyes outside; this airplane's flap handle is between the seats and cannot be confused with a gear lever, but the habit of waiting until clear is still the safe one.

items.q: You have an engine fire in flight. Give me the memory items for this airplane.
items.a: Fuel selector OFF; throttle closed; mixture to idle cut-off; electric fuel pump checked OFF; heater OFF; defroster OFF; then proceed with the power-off landing procedure. The whole idea is to stop fuel reaching the fire. Note that the electric fuel pump goes off here, which is the opposite of every other fuel emergency, and the heater and defroster go off because their air comes from a shroud on the muffler.

items.q: Why do the heater and defroster go off in the engine fire checklist?
items.a: Because on this airplane the cabin heat and the defroster are fed from a shroud around the exhaust muffler, inside the engine compartment and right next to the fire. Leaving them open is an invitation for smoke and fire gases to come into the cabin. The same shroud is why a cracked muffler is a carbon monoxide hazard, and why the first action for suspected carbon monoxide is heat off and vents open.

items.q: Why would you descend at VNE with an engine fire?
items.a: Because time is the enemy. An in-flight fire can destroy the airframe in minutes, so you get the airplane down as fast as the structure allows: descend at up to but not exceeding VNE, which is 160 KIAS on this airplane, and the high airflow may also help starve or blow out the fire and keep the flames off the fuselage. Fly it in smooth air and with care, because at VNE there is no margin for a gust.

items.q: Is a slip useful in an engine fire?
items.a: It can be. A sideslip away from the side the flames are coming from can keep fire and smoke off the cabin and away from the fuel tank in that wing while you descend. It costs you some descent efficiency and it complicates the pattern to the field, so it is a tool rather than a step: use it if the flames are coming at the cabin, and prioritize getting the airplane on the ground either way.

b: Planning the flight, fuel, filing, and the rules that govern it.

items.q: How far apart should VFR checkpoints be spaced when planning a cross country?
items.a: No more than about 20 miles apart. Closer spacing than that wastes workload; much wider spacing means that if you miss one you have flown a long way before you get a chance to confirm position, and a small heading error has time to grow into a large lateral displacement. Put a checkpoint near every course change and near any airspace boundary you must respect.

items.q: What makes a good VFR visual checkpoint?
items.a: Something large, unique and unmistakable from above. Good ones are airports with paved runways, railroads, highways and major road intersections, large rivers, large lakes with a definable shape, towns with a prominent identifying feature, wind farms, open-pit mines, and VOR sites. The test is whether the feature could be confused with anything else within a few miles of it.

items.q: What makes a poor VFR checkpoint?
items.a: Anything small, common or seasonal: powerlines, private airports, grass runways, small streams, small lakes, dry rivers and lake beds, small towns, individual mountains, towers, ordinary road intersections, and areas of unique vegetation. These either vanish in haze, look like a dozen neighbors, or change with rainfall and season, so they cannot confirm position.

items.q: Why is a single tower or a small town a dangerous thing to navigate by?
items.a: Because they repeat. Towers are built in clusters and small towns look alike from 3,000 feet, so a mis-identified one confirms the wrong position and you fly on with confidence in an error. A checkpoint should be verified by at least two features together, for example a town where a railroad crosses a river, rather than one object on its own.

items.q: What does 14 CFR 91.119 require of you anywhere, regardless of the terrain below?
items.a: You must not operate below an altitude that would allow, if the engine failed, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface. This is the general rule of 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Minimum safe altitudes: General) and it applies on top of every other minimum in that section.

items.q: What is the minimum safe altitude over a congested area under 91.119?
items.a: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft. Congested areas are cities, towns, settlements and open-air assemblies of people. Under 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Minimum safe altitudes: General), the radius is measured from the aircraft, not from the edge of the town, so the buffer moves with you.

items.q: What is the minimum safe altitude over other than congested areas under 91.119?
items.a: 500 feet above the surface. Over open water or sparsely populated areas there is no 500-foot floor, but you may not operate within 500 feet of any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. This is 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Minimum safe altitudes: General).

items.q: When do the minimum safe altitudes of 91.119 not apply?
items.a: They do not apply when taking off or landing. 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Minimum safe altitudes: General) exempts the takeoff and landing phase, and separately allows helicopters, powered parachutes and weight-shift-control aircraft to go lower if the operation is conducted without hazard and, for helicopters, in accordance with routes and altitudes prescribed by the FAA.

items.q: What is the maximum elevation figure on a sectional and how much clearance does it give?
items.a: The large bold number in each quadrangle is the maximum elevation figure (MEF), the highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrangle rounded up, in hundreds of feet MSL. It is not an operating altitude. It includes only about a 100 to 200 foot rounding allowance above the obstacle and no vertical obstruction tolerance, so plan well above it rather than at it.

items.q: What are the VFR cruising altitudes and when do they apply?
items.a: Above 3,000 feet AGL in level cruise: on a magnetic course of 0 to 179 degrees fly odd thousands plus 500 feet, and on 180 to 359 degrees fly even thousands plus 500 feet. This is 14 CFR 91.159 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, VFR cruising altitude or flight level). Below 3,000 AGL any altitude is legal, and the rule is based on magnetic course, not heading. The rule keys off magnetic course, not magnetic heading, so apply variation before you choose the altitude.

items.q: What is the memory aid for VFR cruising altitudes?
items.a: Odd birds fly east: easterly magnetic courses, 0 through 179 degrees, get the odd thousands plus 500, so 3,500, 5,500, 7,500. Westerly courses, 180 through 359 degrees, get the even thousands plus 500, so 4,500, 6,500, 8,500. The extra 500 feet keeps VFR traffic vertically clear of IFR traffic flying the whole thousands.

items.q: Besides the hemispheric rule, what else should drive your choice of cruising altitude?
items.a: Terrain and obstacle clearance, the airspace you want to enter or avoid, winds aloft and the resulting groundspeed, cloud bases and the cloud clearances you must keep, oxygen requirements above 12,500 feet, glide range to a landing site, and engine performance, since a normally aspirated engine loses power with altitude. Pick the altitude that solves the most of these at once.

items.q: How much fuel must you carry to begin a VFR flight during the day?
items.a: Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes. That is 14 CFR 91.151 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions). It is a legal minimum computed at cruise, not a plan; most operators add far more.

items.q: How much fuel must you carry to begin a VFR flight at night?
items.a: Enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes, under 14 CFR 91.151 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions). The night reserve is larger because the alternatives if you must divert are fewer and harder to find.

items.q: At what speed is the 91.151 fuel reserve computed, and why does that matter?
items.a: At normal cruising speed, not at a slow endurance speed. That matters because your actual endurance at best-endurance power is longer than the reserve implies, but you may not plan on it. It also means the reserve shrinks in real terms whenever the actual fuel burn is higher than the book figure, which is the usual case with a worn engine or a leaned setting you did not achieve.

items.q: How much fuel is required for a flight in IFR conditions?
items.a: Enough to fly to the destination, then to the alternate if one is required, and then for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. That is 14 CFR 91.167 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions). No alternate fuel is needed if the rule permits filing without an alternate, but the 45 minutes always applies.

items.q: When is an alternate airport required on an IFR flight plan?
items.a: Use the 1-2-3 rule: if from one hour before to one hour after the estimated time of arrival the destination forecast is less than a 2,000 foot ceiling or less than 3 statute miles visibility, an alternate must be filed. This is 14 CFR 91.169 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, IFR flight plan: Information required). It also requires an alternate if the destination has no instrument approach procedure.

items.q: What weather must an alternate airport be forecast to have at your ETA there?
items.a: For a precision approach, a 600 foot ceiling and 2 statute miles; for a non-precision approach, an 800 foot ceiling and 2 statute miles; if no instrument approach is available at the alternate, the ceiling and visibility must allow descent from the minimum en route altitude, approach and landing under basic VFR. Standard alternate minimums are listed under 14 CFR 91.169, and individual airports may carry non-standard minimums.

items.q: What preflight action does 14 CFR 91.103 require before every flight?
items.a: You must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Preflight action) names in particular weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed as planned, and any known traffic delays advised by ATC.

items.q: What extra items does 91.103 require for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport?
items.a: For any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, plus any IFR flight, you must also know the runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, computed for the actual weight, altitude, temperature, wind and runway condition. Get those numbers from the POH or AFM for the aircraft you are flying, under 14 CFR 91.103 (Preflight action).

items.q: Give a working checklist for 91.103 preflight action.
items.a: The mnemonic is NWKRAFT: NOTAMs; weather reports and forecasts; known ATC traffic delays; runway lengths at airports of intended use; alternates available; fuel requirements; and takeoff and landing distance data. It covers every element that 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Preflight action) names, plus the NOTAM and airspace review that a briefing supplies.

items.q: What are the three types of weather briefing and when do you ask for each?
items.a: A standard briefing is the full picture and is what you request when you have had no prior information; an abbreviated briefing updates or fills a gap in a briefing you already have; an outlook briefing is for a departure six or more hours away and gives forecast information only. All three are available from Flight Service on 1-800-WX-BRIEF or through an approved online source.

items.q: What does filing a VFR flight plan actually get you?
items.a: It gets you search and rescue, nothing else. A VFR flight plan is not a clearance, does not reserve airspace, provides no separation, and does not give ATC any awareness of you. Its whole value is that if you do not close it, Flight Service begins looking for you along your filed route, which is why an accurate route and ETE matter.

items.q: Is a VFR flight plan required, and what does 91.153 ask for?
items.a: A VFR flight plan is not required by regulation, but if you file one the information required is set by 14 CFR 91.153 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, VFR flight plan: Information required): aircraft identification and type, full name and address of the pilot in command, departure and destination points, route, cruising altitude, true airspeed, departure and estimated elapsed time, fuel on board, alternate airports, number aboard and color of the aircraft.

items.q: How do you open a VFR flight plan, and what happens if you forget?
items.a: Filing does not open it. You must activate it after departure by contacting Flight Service by radio or phone, or by using an electronic service that activates on takeoff. If you never activate it, no one is expecting you, so nothing happens at your ETA and there is no search. An unactivated plan simply expires.

items.q: How do you close a VFR flight plan, and what happens if you do not?
items.a: Close it with Flight Service by radio or phone, or through the app you filed with. Closing is never automatic, and landing at a towered airport does not close it. If it is still open, Flight Service begins trying to reach you about 30 minutes after your ETA and then initiates search and rescue, which is expensive, embarrassing and diverts real resources.

items.q: What is the difference between a VFR flight plan and VFR flight following?
items.a: A flight plan is a search and rescue record held by Flight Service; flight following is a live radar service from ATC giving traffic advisories and, workload permitting, safety alerts. They are independent: you can have either, both or neither. Flight following gives no separation from VFR traffic and can be terminated by ATC at any time when workload requires.

items.q: What information do the sectional chart legend and symbology give you when planning?
items.a: The legend decodes airports, airspace, navaids, obstructions and topography: tower versus non-towered airport color, runway length and surface, field elevation and CTAF, airspace boundary lines and floors, obstruction heights in MSL and AGL, terrain contours and the maximum elevation figures. Read it before you plan a route, because a boundary or an obstruction you cannot identify is one you will fly into.

items.q: On a sectional, what do a blue airport symbol and a magenta airport symbol mean?
items.a: Blue means the airport has an operating control tower; magenta means it does not. The same color convention runs through the airspace: solid blue for Class B, dashed blue for Class D, solid magenta for Class C, dashed magenta for a Class E surface area. Airports with hard-surfaced runways of 1,500 to 8,069 feet are drawn with the runway pattern, longer ones show the actual runway layout.

items.q: What do the data lines printed beside an airport on a sectional tell you?
items.a: They give, in order, the airport name, then field elevation in feet MSL, a lighting code, the longest runway length in hundreds of feet, and the CTAF or UNICOM frequency. An L means lighting sunset to sunrise, an asterisk before the L means part-time or pilot-controlled lighting, and no L means no lighting. Confirm all of it in the Chart Supplement before you use it. A star beside the control tower frequency means the tower operates only part time, and a C in a solid box means that frequency becomes the CTAF once the tower closes. A star beside the lighting letter means lighting limitations exist.

items.q: What is the scale of a sectional chart and how often is it revised?
items.a: A sectional is drawn at 1:500,000, roughly 7 nautical miles to the inch, and most are revised every 56 days, with a few on a 168-day cycle. A terminal area chart is 1:250,000 and shows the Class B airspace in far more detail. Always check the effective date panel; an out-of-date chart is a legal and practical problem under 14 CFR 91.103.

items.q: What are isogonic lines and how do you use magnetic variation?
items.a: Isogonic lines are the dashed magenta lines joining points of equal magnetic variation, the angular difference between true north and magnetic north. Apply it to convert true course to magnetic course: east is least, so subtract easterly variation, and west is best, so add westerly variation. Variation is a property of the location, not the aircraft.

items.q: Walk through converting a true course into a compass heading.
items.a: Use TVMDC: True course, apply Variation to get magnetic course, apply Deviation to get compass course, and apply the wind correction angle to get the heading you actually fly. Wind correction is applied to true course first to give true heading in practice; the point is that variation comes from the chart, deviation from the aircraft compass correction card, and wind from the winds aloft forecast. Measure the course against a meridian, one of the vertical lines on the chart, since those point to true north and south.

items.q: What is the Chart Supplement and what does it give you that a sectional does not?
items.a: The Chart Supplement, formerly the Airport/Facility Directory, is the written directory of every public-use airport: runway dimensions and surface, lighting and its activation, traffic pattern altitudes and any non-standard patterns, fuel and services, communications and frequencies, noise procedures, remarks and hazards. It is a required part of familiarizing yourself with the airports of intended use under 14 CFR 91.103.

items.q: How do you plan the climb segment of a cross country leg?
items.a: Take the time, fuel and distance to climb from the performance charts for the aircraft you are flying, corrected for pressure altitude and temperature, then subtract the climb distance from the leg and compute the remainder at cruise groundspeed. Ignoring the climb understates both fuel and time, because climb burn is high and climb groundspeed is low, and the error compounds on every leg.

items.q: What is the standard procedure if you become lost on a cross country?
items.a: The five Cs: climb for better visibility, radio range and glide options; communicate, on the last frequency, 121.5, or the nearest facility; confess that you are unsure of position; comply with the instructions you are given; and conserve fuel by leaning and slowing to endurance power. Before all that, hold a heading, note the time, and try to match the largest feature you can see to the chart.

items.q: How do you plan and execute a diversion in flight?
items.a: Fly the aircraft first, then pick a suitable airport considering weather, terrain, fuel, runway length and services. Turn toward it immediately on an estimated heading, note the time, then refine the heading, distance, groundspeed, ETE and fuel with a rough measurement on the chart or the flight computer. Advise ATC or Flight Service, amend or close the flight plan, and continue to navigate while you calculate.

items.q: What is the point of establishing fuel checkpoints along the route?
items.a: To catch a burn rate that is worse than planned while you still have options. At each checkpoint compare fuel remaining against the planned figure and against the time still to run. A shortfall that appears halfway is a nuisance; the same shortfall discovered on the arrival is an emergency. Set a personal minimum landing fuel well above the 30 or 45 minutes of 14 CFR 91.151 and treat it as a hard limit.

items.q: When is an airport drawn as a plain circle on a sectional, and when do you see the actual runway layout?
items.a: It depends on the longest hard-surfaced runway. 1,500 to 8,069 feet of hard surface is drawn as the runway pattern inside a filled colored circle; longer than 8,069 feet is drawn to scale as the true runway layout with no circle around it. A field with no hard surface is a plain open circle. Confirm surface and length in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: How is a seaplane base depicted on a sectional?
items.a: As an anchor symbol, colored the same way as land airports, magenta for nontowered and blue for towered. There is no runway length to read, so the chart tells you very little. Go to the Chart Supplement for the water landing area, its dimensions and orientation, obstructions, available services and any seasonal ice limits.

items.q: What do the tick marks around an airport symbol on a sectional mean?
items.a: Fuel is available and the field is attended during normal business hours, which the legend takes as roughly Monday through Friday, 1000 to 1600 local. The tick marks do not tell you the grade, the price, whether self service exists, or whether anyone is there on a weekend. Check the Chart Supplement or telephone ahead.

items.q: What does a star beside a control tower frequency or a lighting code on a sectional mean?
items.a: Part time or limited operation. A star with the tower frequency means the tower is not open continuously, so the airport reverts to nontowered when it closes. A star with the lighting letter means limitations exist, such as pilot-controlled lighting, lighting for only part of the night, or only some runways lit. The Chart Supplement gives the hours.

items.q: What does a C in a solid box after a frequency on a sectional mean?
items.a: That frequency is the common traffic advisory frequency. At a nontowered field it is the UNICOM or MULTICOM you self announce on; at a part-time tower it is the tower frequency, which becomes the CTAF once the tower closes. Confirm it in the Chart Supplement before you use it, because frequencies change between chart cycles.

items.q: What does the lighting letter in a sectional airport data block tell you?
items.a: L means runway lighting is available from sunset to sunrise. A star before the L means limitations exist, such as pilot-controlled lighting, lighting for part of the night only, or only certain runways lit. No letter means no lighting is charted. The Chart Supplement lists the actual lighting, the activation frequency and the number of clicks.

items.q: How do you read the longest runway length from a sectional airport data block?
items.a: It is printed in hundreds of feet, so 42 means 4,200 feet, and it is the longest hard-surfaced runway unless the field has none. It is a planning number only. The Chart Supplement gives every runway with its true length, width, surface, weight bearing capacity, lighting and displaced thresholds, which is what you actually need to decide.

items.q: What does a number printed in brackets beside an airport on a sectional mean?
items.a: It is the ceiling of the Class D or Class E surface area in hundreds of feet MSL, so 29 in brackets means the airspace tops out at 2,900 MSL. A minus sign in front of the number means up to but not including that altitude. Above the bracketed value you normally find Class E, or the floor of an overlying Class B or Class C shelf.

items.q: What does a star drawn on top of an airport symbol on a sectional indicate?
items.a: A rotating airport beacon in operation from sunset to sunrise. A civil land airport beacon alternates white and green. Seeing one lit during daylight inside a Class B, C, D or E surface area is a hint that the field is below basic VFR, but it is only a hint and not a rule, so get the actual reported weather.

items.q: How do you read a VOR facility box on a sectional?
items.a: The box carries the facility name, frequency, three-letter identifier and Morse code, and the navaid is drawn as a compass rose oriented to magnetic north as of its last alignment. The symbol inside the rose tells you the type, plain VOR, VOR-DME or VORTAC. Identify the Morse code before navigating by it, and check NOTAMs for outages.

items.q: What does it mean when a VOR compass rose is drawn centered on an airport?
items.a: The VOR is on the airport itself, so you can use it to check the receiver on the ground and to fly published radials straight off the field. Where a ground checkpoint is designated, the airport listing in the Chart Supplement names it and gives the radial and distance, along with the tolerance you must be within.

items.q: How is an NDB shown on a sectional and what should you know about it?
items.a: As a magenta dotted circle around the station symbol, with a box giving the name, frequency and Morse identifier. It transmits in the low and medium frequency band and is tracked with an ADF, which suffers thunderstorm, shoreline, terrain and night effect errors. Most have been decommissioned, so check NOTAMs before planning around one.

items.q: How are obstructions charted on a sectional, and what do the two numbers mean?
items.a: The bold upper number is the top of the obstruction in feet MSL and the number in parentheses is its height in feet AGL.
