A taller symbol marks an obstruction 1,000 AGL or higher, radiating lines mark high intensity lighting, and paired symbols mark a group. Charted obstructions are not a complete list, so keep a margin.

items.q: How does a sectional tell you a runway has a right-hand traffic pattern?
items.a: By the letters RP followed by the runway numbers in the airport data, for example RP 9, 27. Without that note, expect left traffic, which 14 CFR part 91, subpart B, section 91.126, Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace, requires. A star with the RP means it is conditional; the Chart Supplement explains when.

items.q: How do you measure the length of a leg on a sectional chart?
items.a: Against the vertical scale only. One minute of latitude equals one nautical mile, so step the leg off along a line of longitude, or use the nautical mile scale printed in the chart margin. Never measure along the horizontal hashmarks: a minute of longitude shrinks as you move away from the equator, so a distance read that way is wrong.

items.q: True course 000, variation 4 west, 100 knots true airspeed, wind 330 at 15. What heading do you fly?
items.a: 359 degrees magnetic. True course 000 plus 4 degrees of westerly variation gives a magnetic course of 004. On the flight computer that wind gives a wind correction angle of 5 degrees left, so 004 minus 5 is a magnetic heading of 359. Make sure the wind and the course are both magnetic or both true before you combine them.

items.q: How do you turn ground speed and leg distance into an estimated time enroute?
items.a: Divide the distance by the ground speed, then convert the decimal hours to minutes and seconds by multiplying by 60. 30 nautical miles at 87 knots is 0.344 hours, which is 20 minutes 41 seconds. Use the ground speed the flight computer gives you for that leg, not true airspeed, and add the climb segment separately.

items.q: Work a short field takeoff distance for pressure altitude 977, 20 degrees Celsius, 2,400 pounds, 9 knots headwind.
items.a: About 1,674 feet to clear a 50 foot obstacle. Enter the short field takeoff table at maximum weight, take the 1,000 foot pressure altitude row against the 20 degree column and read 1,860 feet. The chart note allows a 10 percent decrease for each 9 knots of headwind, so subtract 186 feet. 14 CFR 91.103, Part 91 Subpart B, Flight Rules, titled Preflight action, requires you to have these figures.

items.q: Work a short field landing distance for a field at 411 feet, altimeter 29.48, 20 degrees Celsius, 9 knots headwind.
items.a: About 1,193 feet to clear a 50 foot obstacle. Pressure altitude is 29.92 minus 29.48, times 1,000, plus 411, which is 851 feet. The short field landing table at the 1,000 foot row and the 20 degree column gives 1,325 feet, and the 10 percent decrease for 9 knots of headwind takes off 132 feet. Round up rather than down.

items.q: What do red taxiway signs with white lettering tell you?
items.a: They are mandatory instruction signs, and you may not pass one without a clearance. A hold position sign such as 4-22 holds you short of that runway from the taxiway; 26-8 is a runway to runway hold; 8-APCH holds you clear of the approach to runway 8; and ILS holds you clear of the instrument landing system critical area. A red circle with a white bar is no entry.

items.q: What do black taxiway signs with yellow lettering mean?
items.a: They are location signs, telling you where you are right now. A black square with a yellow letter and a yellow border, such as B, is the taxiway you are on; the same sign carrying a runway number is the runway you are on. A black sign with a plain white number, such as 4, is runway distance remaining, given in thousands of feet from that point to the end.

items.q: What do yellow taxiway signs with black lettering mean?
items.a: They are direction and destination signs. A yellow sign with a black letter and an arrow, such as J with a right arrow, points to an intersecting taxiway; one with an angled arrow and a letter marks a runway exit; and a destination sign such as MIL or a runway number with an arrow points to the ramp, the military apron or the runway. Several may be grouped into a direction sign array.

items.q: What boundary and ending markers will you see while taxiing, and what do they mean?
items.a: A yellow sign with black dashes on a solid bar is the runway safety area or obstacle free zone boundary, and the ladder pattern is the instrument landing system critical area boundary; you are clear of the protected area once you have passed them. Yellow and black diagonal stripes are a taxiway ending marker, meaning the pavement does not continue.

items.q: Gusty wind splits two runways evenly. How do you choose the departure runway?
items.a: Compare them on headwind, crosswind and gust, then on what is off the departure end. Take the runway with a headwind component rather than any tailwind, and if the headwinds are equal, look at crosswind magnitude including gusts, runway length and surface, obstacles and terrain, the traffic flow in use, and where you would go if the engine quit. Then decide whether the result is inside your personal limits, not just the airplane's.

items.q: The wind is exactly between the two runways. What is left to decide it?
items.a: Everything that is not the wind. Runway length and width, slope and surface, the obstacle picture off each end, where the emergency landing options are, which runway the traffic is using, how long the taxi is with the wind on the tail, and which side the crosswind will be on. When the wind gives you no answer, the engine failure after takeoff should give you one.

items.q: On takeoff, does a crosswind from the left or from the right ask more of your right rudder?
items.a: From the left. The fin is behind the main gear and the center of gravity, so the airplane weathervanes into the wind: a left crosswind swings the nose left, and you hold the centerline with right rudder on top of the right rudder the left-turning tendencies already need. A right crosswind swings the nose right, which partly offsets P-factor, torque and slipstream. Say it that way and reason out loud; the examiner is watching the reasoning.

items.q: The prior candidate chose the runway with the wind from the left to save right rudder. Critique that.
items.a: The conclusion is defensible on other grounds but that reason is backwards. Weathervaning turns the nose into the wind, so a left crosswind increases the right rudder you need, it does not reduce it. What a left crosswind does give you is left aileron into the wind, whose down-going right aileron adds a little right-yawing drag, and that is a small effect. Choose the runway on components, length and emergency options, and get the rudder argument the right way round.

items.q: What do you do with the controls on a crosswind takeoff roll?
items.a: Full aileron into the wind as you start the roll, reducing it as the ailerons become effective, and rudder as needed to hold the centerline. Keep straight and keep the upwind wing down. Accelerate slightly past the normal rotation speed and lift off positively so the airplane does not settle back on one wheel, then establish a crab on the climbout. In this airplane the demonstrated crosswind is 17 knots.

items.q: Why does the emergency return matter when you pick the departure runway?
items.a: Because the wind that is a 15-knot crosswind on takeoff is the same 15-knot crosswind if you have to come back, and you will be coming back with a problem, probably low, possibly with partial power, on whichever runway you can reach. If the crosswind is marginal for a planned landing it is unacceptable for an unplanned one. Also look at what is straight ahead off each end: fields, water, trees, a city.

items.q: How does the climb segment fit into your navigation log?
items.a: As its own leg. The climb has a different true airspeed, a different wind and a different fuel flow from cruise, so compute time, fuel and distance to climb from the chart, plot where top of climb falls along the first leg, and start the cruise calculation from there. If the whole first leg is inside the climb you never reach the cruise numbers at all, which is a common planning error on a short first leg.

items.q: Do you work time, fuel and distance to climb at the destination too?
items.a: Yes, if you are planning a climb there, and the examiner is likely to ask for both ends. At the destination you work the same chart with that field's pressure altitude and temperature to find what a go-around, a missed approach or a departure on the return leg would cost, and you work the takeoff and landing distances against the runway you will actually use there, in the conditions forecast for your arrival.

items.q: Why is a line feature the right thing to look for when you are uncertain of position?
items.a: Because you cannot miss it and it converts a vague area into a line. A highway, a coast, a river, a railroad or a ridge runs for miles across your track, so flying a heading that must cross it eventually turns 'somewhere around here' into 'somewhere on this line'. Pair it with one VOR radial, a DME arc or a recognizable town along the feature and you have a point.

items.q: What is the deliberate offset technique, and when would you use it?
items.a: Aim deliberately to one side of a destination or a checkpoint that sits on a line feature, so that when you reach the feature you know which way to turn instead of guessing. Ten degrees of intentional error is better than zero degrees of uncertain error. It is an old pilotage technique and it is exactly the right tool when the checkpoint is a small airport on a long road or river.

items.q: You have fixed your position over the highway. What now?
items.a: Mark it on the chart with the time. Measure the new course and distance to the next checkpoint or to the destination, work the heading for the wind you now know you have, recompute the estimate and the fuel, and only then turn onto the new heading and start the clock. Tell ATC if you are talking to anyone. Resuming the flight plan properly is what the examiner is grading, not the fix itself.

items.q: How are power transmission lines shown on a sectional, and what good are they?
items.a: As a line with small tower symbols along it, and the individual towers are shown as obstructions with their heights when they are tall enough to matter. They make excellent long-range line features because they run straight for miles and cross open country where nothing else is visible. They are a hazard too: the wires themselves are invisible from the air and are not all charted, so never plan to fly along one at low altitude.

items.q: How are railroads shown, and what makes them good or bad checkpoints?
items.a: As a line with regular cross ticks, with single and multiple track variants shown differently. They are good because they are straight, long and unmistakable, and the place where a railroad crosses a highway or a river beside a town is a first-class checkpoint. They are bad on their own in country with several parallel lines, and abandoned lines that still show on the ground can mislead you.

items.q: What makes a line feature more useful than a point feature in pilotage?
items.a: You cannot fly past it without noticing. A tower or a small town can slide by unseen a mile off your track, but a highway, railroad, river, coast or ridge that lies across your course has to be crossed, which turns an uncertain position into a line and gives you a reliable timing point. Use point features to confirm position along the line; use the line to catch the error in the first place.

items.q: You chose I-95 as a reference on your cross country. Defend the choice.
items.a: It is a major interstate running broadly parallel to my route, visible from altitude in any light, unmistakable in width and traffic, and it is drawn on the chart with its number so I can tie my position to exits, interchanges and the towns along it. It gives me a continuous handrail rather than a single checkpoint, so if I lose the plot between waypoints I can always fly to it and refix.

items.q: What are the hazards of navigating low along a linear feature?
items.a: Everyone else is doing the same thing, so traffic concentrates along roads, rivers and valleys; the wires and towers along a power line or a road are at your altitude; and 14 CFR 91.119, Minimum safe altitudes: General, still requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius over a congested area, and 500 feet above the surface elsewhere. Fly to the right of the feature, not over it, and keep the altitude legal.

items.q: Walk me through your cross-country. Where are we going and how far is it?
items.a: Walterboro, Lowcountry Regional (KRBW) to Martin Campbell Field, Copperhill, Tennessee (1A3), 223 nautical miles on a true course of 305 degrees. KRBW is at 101 feet, 1A3 at 1,789 feet, so the destination field sits 1,688 feet higher than the departure field. At 105 knots true in no wind the leg runs about 2 hours 8 minutes. I refigure time and fuel on the navigation log against the actual winds aloft for whatever altitude I pick before I commit to it.

items.q: What regulation governs your preflight planning, and what exactly does it require?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.103, Preflight action. It requires me to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight. For a flight not in the vicinity of an airport that means weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed as planned, and any known traffic delays advised by ATC; and for any flight, runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data in the approved flight manual.

items.q: How much fuel does this leg take, and is the airplane's capacity a limiting factor?
items.a: About 17.9 gallons en route at 8.4 gallons per hour, or 22.1 gallons with a 30 minute day reserve, against 48 gallons usable. Planning a pessimistic 10.0 gallons per hour gives 21.3 gallons en route and 26.3 with the reserve, still a little over half the usable fuel. Capacity is not the limiting factor on this leg; the limiting factors are headwind, a diversion to an alternate, and whether the self-serve pump at 1A3 is actually working when I get there.

items.q: What is the legal fuel reserve for this trip, and where is it written?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.151, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions: enough to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night. At 8.4 gallons per hour the day reserve is 4.2 gallons, putting the total at 22.1 gallons; at night the 45 minute reserve is 6.3 gallons, so 24.1 gallons. Those are legal minimums. My personal minimum is one hour on board at landing.

items.q: Give me a 20-knot headwind the whole way. What does that do to your time and fuel?
items.a: Groundspeed falls to 85 knots, so 223 nautical miles takes about 2 hours 37 minutes instead of 2 hours 8, and fuel at 8.4 gallons per hour goes from about 17.9 to about 22.0 gallons en route. Add the 30 minute day reserve and I am near 26 gallons of the 48 usable. The fuel plan stays comfortable; the time plan does not, and in late November a 29 minute slip is the difference between arriving in daylight and arriving at an unlit mountain field.

items.q: How did you choose your waypoints on this route, and why those?
items.a: I chose them for unmistakable identification from the air, for spacing that gives me a usable groundspeed check, and so that each one also offers an out. I draw the 305 degree course line on the sectional first, then pick features that lie on or just beside it; I prefer a feature that is unique in that area, has vertical relief or contrast, and is backed up by a second feature nearby. Where the course passes near an airport I make that the checkpoint, so the checkpoint and the diversion field are the same place.

items.q: How far apart are your checkpoints, and why that spacing?
items.a: Roughly 10 to 20 nautical miles, which at 105 knots is about 6 to 11 minutes between fixes. Closer than that and I am head down more than I am outside; farther and an error grows too large before I catch it. Over the low country out of Walterboro I can stretch toward the long end because features are visible a long way; approaching the ridges I tighten them up, because a wrong valley identified late is very hard to unwind. I write the leg distance, the leg time and the running total on the log for each one.

items.q: What makes a good checkpoint out of Walterboro in the low country?
items.a: Something linear or large enough to be unmistakable from several miles off, and unique in that area. Rivers and major road and rail intersections, a town with a distinctive shape, a large body of water, a bridge, an airport, a power line crossing a river. The trap in the low country is sameness: one small town, one tree line and one farm pond look like the next, and a lone water tower is useless if there are six. I pick features that cross my course at an angle, and I pair each with a backup feature to confirm.

items.q: What makes a good checkpoint once you are in the mountains near Copperhill?
items.a: Terrain itself, read as shape: a lake, a dam, a river bend, a gap or a named peak, a highway through a pass, a town in a valley. Mountain checkpoints are chosen by relief and by hydrology, because roads disappear under trees and small towns are hidden in valleys. The trap is that one valley and one ridge look like the next from above, so I identify by the pattern of features rather than one feature, and I confirm with a GPS fix or a VOR radial before I commit to flying down a valley.

items.q: Where is your first checkpoint, and what do you do when you get there?
items.a: Far enough out that I am level and settled, typically 8 to 12 nautical miles from Walterboro, which at 105 knots is 5 to 7 minutes. Crossing it I note the time, compare it with the planned time to get my actual groundspeed, revise the estimates for the remaining legs and for fuel, confirm the heading is holding the course line, and check that the fuel burn matches the plan. That first time check is the one the examiner wants to see, because every later estimate on the log depends on it.

items.q: Your GPS quits halfway to Copperhill. Show me how you keep navigating.
items.a: I fall back to the heading, the clock and the chart, which is why I filled in the navigation log before departure. I note the time and the last known position, hold the planned magnetic heading for that leg, run the clock against the planned leg time, and look for the next planned checkpoint at the planned minute. I back it up with a VOR cross fix if one is receivable at my altitude, and I accept a diversion to a larger field with better terrain rather than groping along a valley on dead reckoning alone.

items.q: What is the difference between pilotage and dead reckoning, and which are you using?
items.a: Pilotage is navigating by reference to visible landmarks; dead reckoning is computing heading, groundspeed and time from a known position using true course, true airspeed, wind and variation. I am using both: dead reckoning gives me the heading to fly and the minute to expect the next feature, pilotage confirms it when the feature shows up. GPS is the third layer and the first to be taken away in the airplane, so the log has to stand on its own without it.

items.q: At a checkpoint you are four miles right of course after thirty miles. How do you fix it?
items.a: Use the sixty to one rule twice. Four miles off in thirty flown is an eight degree track error, so I turn eight degrees left to parallel the course. To rejoin by the next checkpoint thirty miles ahead I double it and turn sixteen degrees left, then take out the extra eight degrees once I am back on the line. The trap is correcting by feel and overshooting; the arithmetic is one division and takes five seconds, and it keeps the remaining leg times on the log honest.

items.q: Your true course is 305. How do you get the magnetic course you actually fly?
items.a: Apply the magnetic variation shown by the isogonic line nearest that part of the route: east is least, west is best, so westerly variation is added to the true course. The isogonic lines are the dashed magenta lines on the sectional, labeled with the value and the date. Variation changes along a 223 mile route, so I use the value for each part of the leg rather than one number for the whole trip, and then I apply the compass deviation card in the airplane to get the compass heading.

items.q: Where do you get the wind correction angle for this leg?
items.a: From the winds aloft forecast for the altitude I pick, worked on an E6B or a flight computer against the 305 degree true course and the true airspeed from the cruise chart. Winds aloft forecasts are given in true direction, which matches the true course, so I do the wind triangle in true and convert to magnetic afterward. The trap is mixing frames: surface winds in a METAR are true, winds from a tower or an AWOS voice broadcast are magnetic, and runway numbers are magnetic.

items.q: Where is your top of climb and top of descent on this leg?
items.a: Top of climb comes out of the time, fuel and distance to climb chart; top of descent I plan with the three to one rule. For descent, take the altitude to lose in thousands, multiply by three for nautical miles, and check the resulting rate against groundspeed. Coming from 8,500 feet down to a 2,789 foot pattern altitude at 1A3 is 5,711 feet, about 17 nautical miles and 11 minutes at 500 feet per minute. Starting the descent late over rising terrain is how people end up diving at a mountain field.

items.q: Do you need a fuel stop on this leg, and where would you put one if you wanted one?
items.a: No, 22.1 gallons planned against 48 usable does not require a stop, but I identify a fuel field near the halfway point anyway. The halfway point is about 111 nautical miles out. I look along the course on the sectional and in the Chart Supplement for a field with 100LL, an attendant or a reliable self-serve pump, and a runway long enough for the Warrior, and I write its frequency and field elevation on the log. That field doubles as my weather bail-out before the terrain starts rising.

items.q: What true airspeed are you planning, and where did the number come from?
items.a: I used 105 knots for the first cut, which gives 2 hours 8 minutes for the 223 nautical miles, but the planning number has to come from the cruise performance chart in my own handbook. That is Section 5 of Piper Report VB-880 for serial 28-8116257, entered with pressure altitude, temperature and the power setting I intend to use. The Section 5 charts in the VB-1180 book are computed for a 2,440 pound airplane and are not approved for this serial, so I do not plan from them.

items.q: Are you filing a flight plan, and what does the regulation say has to be in it?
items.a: Yes, a VFR flight plan, and 14 CFR 91.153, VFR flight plan: Information required, lists what goes in it. Aircraft identification and type, full name and address of the pilot in command, point and proposed time of departure, proposed route, cruising altitude and destination, estimated time en route, amount of fuel on board in time, number of persons aboard and any other information the pilot believes necessary. On a route like this the real value is the search and rescue trigger, since 1A3 has no tower to notice I never arrived.

items.q: Who opens and closes the flight plan, and what happens if you forget to close it?
items.a: I open and close it with Flight Service, on the radio, by phone to 1 800 WX BRIEF, or through the app I filed on; there is no tower at 1A3 to close it for me. If I do not close it, Flight Service begins communications search procedures at 30 minutes past my estimated time of arrival, and search and rescue follows. At a field with no tower and no UNICOM, closing on the ground by telephone or cell app is the realistic method, and I brief my passenger that I will do it before we leave the ramp.

items.q: What is VFR flight following, and who would be providing it on this route?
items.a: Radar advisories from ATC on a workload permitting basis, which on the Copperhill end means Atlanta Center. The Chart Supplement lists approach and departure service for 1A3 from Atlanta ARTCC on 133.1, with 342.425 as the paired military UHF frequency through the Mount Oglethorpe remote site. It is advisory service, not separation, and radar and radio coverage get thin at low altitude in the mountains, which is one more reason to cruise high rather than scud along the valleys.

items.q: What charts and publications do you want in the cockpit for this trip?
items.a: The current sectional charts covering the whole 223 mile course, the current Chart Supplement volume covering both airports, and the airplane's own flight manual. Check the VFR chart index and the edge panels of each sectional to see which charts the route crosses, because a 223 mile leg from South Carolina into Tennessee will not fit on one sheet. Confirm the effective dates on both the sectional and the Chart Supplement; an expired Chart Supplement is where stale fuel and lighting information comes from.

items.q: What is in the Chart Supplement for 1A3 that is not on the sectional?
items.a: The detail that decides whether the arrival works: displaced thresholds, runway end elevations, traffic pattern direction, PAPI angles, approach ratios, fuel hours and payment, lighting activation, the airport manager's telephone number and the narrative remarks. The sectional gives me field elevation, longest runway, CTAF and the lighting and fuel symbols only. For a 3,500 foot mountain runway with thresholds displaced 90 and 140 feet and a 4 degree PAPI, the sectional alone would leave me badly briefed.

items.q: What cruise altitude are you planning, and what rule drives the choice?
items.a: An even thousand plus 500 feet, so 4,500, 6,500, 8,500 or 10,500, because the magnetic course of roughly 305 degrees falls in the 180 to 359 degree half of 14 CFR 91.159, VFR cruising altitude or flight level. The rule bites only in level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface. Between terrain, radio coverage and glide options I would plan 8,500 and treat 6,500 as the fallback if cloud forces me down, not 4,500.

items.q: Does the hemispheric rule apply for the whole leg?
items.a: Only where I am in level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface. 14 CFR 91.159 begins with that condition, so low over the coastal plain in a climb or during a descent it does not control me. The subtlety on this route is that the ground rises toward Copperhill, so a given indicated altitude is more than 3,000 feet above the surface at Walterboro and may be less than that near the destination; the rule can switch off on me at the end of the flight rather than at the start.

items.q: Your course is 305. Is that eastbound or westbound for the cruising altitude rule?
items.a: Westbound, in the 180 through 359 degree bucket, so even thousands plus 500. The rule is written on magnetic course, not true course and not heading, so I convert the 305 degree true course with the local variation first; any plausible variation in the Carolinas, Georgia and Tennessee leaves it comfortably inside the same bucket. The classic error is using the magnetic heading after the wind correction angle, which on a strong crosswind day can cross the 359 to 360 boundary and give the wrong answer.

items.q: How does the 1,688-foot climb to the destination field change your altitude choice?
items.a: It compresses everything at the far end: less height above the ground for the same indicated altitude, a shorter descent, and fewer options under me. At 8,500 feet I am 8,399 feet above Walterboro but only 6,711 feet above the 1,789 foot field at Copperhill, and far less than that above the ridges before it. So I choose the altitude on height above terrain, not on height above sea level, and I plan the descent from the far side of the high ground rather than from overhead the field.

items.q: What is a maximum elevation figure, and how do you read one?
items.a: The large bold number in the middle of each quadrangle bounded by ticked lines of latitude and longitude on a sectional, given in thousands and hundreds of feet above mean sea level. A figure printed as a big 5 and a small 3 means 5,300 feet. It represents the highest known feature in that quadrangle, terrain or obstacle, with an allowance added for vertical error and for obstacles not portrayed. Read every MEF box the course line passes through, and the ones either side of it.

items.q: Is the MEF a minimum safe altitude? Why or why not?
items.a: No. It is the highest known thing in the box, not an altitude with any clearance built in for you to fly at. It carries a tolerance for charting and survey error and for unsurveyed obstacles, but it is not an obstacle clearance altitude and it is not an IFR minimum. To turn it into something I will fly I add my own margin, commonly 1,000 feet over flat terrain and 2,000 feet over mountainous terrain, and then round up to a legal VFR cruising altitude.

items.q: How do you set a safe minimum altitude for each leg of this route?
items.a: Take the largest MEF in the quadrangles that leg crosses, add a terrain margin, then round up to the next legal VFR cruising altitude and check it against cloud bases and oxygen. Over the low country I use 1,000 feet of margin; from the foothills to Copperhill I use 2,000 feet, because mountain downdrafts can exceed the climb rate of a 160 horsepower Warrior. I write the resulting minimum for each leg on the navigation log so I am not doing the arithmetic in turbulence.

items.q: What does 14 CFR 91.119 require, and does it help you over the ridges?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.119, Minimum safe altitudes: General, requires an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard anywhere; over congested areas 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000 foot horizontal radius; over other than congested areas 500 feet above the surface, and 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. It is a floor, not a plan. Over forested ridges the paragraph that actually governs me is the first one, because there is no undue hazard clause you can satisfy at 500 feet over trees.

items.q: Where along this course does the terrain start to rise, and how do you find out?
items.a: Read it off the sectional, not off a hunch: follow the course line and watch the MEF boxes, the contour tints and the spot elevations change. The chart changes color band by color band as the ground rises, and the MEF values step up quadrangle by quadrangle. I mark on the chart the point where the MEF first exceeds my planned cruise minus my margin, and I treat that point as the gate: by then I am at cruise, I have current destination weather, and I have decided to continue or turn around.

items.q: How much clearance do you want crossing a ridge, and why that much?
items.a: At least 1,000 feet, and 2,000 feet if the wind across the ridge is 20 knots or more. The reason is downdraft: air sinking on the lee side can descend faster than a 160 horsepower Warrior at gross weight can climb, so the only usable answer is height and an escape turn. Height also buys radio and radar coverage, glide distance, and time to recognize that the valley ahead is rising faster than I am.

items.q: How do you approach a ridge crossing, and at what angle?
items.a: Approach at roughly 45 degrees to the ridge line, with the altitude already made good well before you get there, so a single turn of about 45 degrees takes you back into the valley you came from. Crossing perpendicular commits you to a 180 in a confined space if the downdraft wins. I also cross where the terrain is lowest, climb on the upwind side where the air is rising, and never try to out-climb rising ground that is going up faster than I am.

items.q: Do you need supplemental oxygen on this trip?
items.a: Almost certainly not, because the practical cruise choices for this leg are 6,500 or 8,500 feet and the rule does not start until 12,500. That said, the answer depends on the altitude I actually file. If weather or terrain pushed me to 12,500 or above, 14 CFR 91.211, Supplemental oxygen, would start applying. In a normally aspirated Warrior at 2,277 pounds the service ceiling and the climb rate settle the question before the regulation does.

items.q: Give me the oxygen regulation, exactly.
items.a: 14 CFR 91.211, Supplemental oxygen. For unpressurized aircraft, the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight of more than 30 minutes duration at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL; must use it at all times above 14,000 feet MSL; and above 15,000 feet MSL each occupant of the aircraft must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

items.q: At what altitude would you use a pulse oximeter even though the rule does not require it?
items.a: From about 8,000 to 10,000 feet, especially at night, because the regulation is a floor and physiology is individual. Night vision degrades measurably from around 5,000 feet, and a smoker, a cold or dehydration lowers the altitude at which hypoxia bites. I carry a portable oximeter, check saturation at level off and every half hour, and treat anything that trends below the low 90s as a reason to descend, not as a number to argue with.

items.q: How do you find the highest obstacle near your course on the sectional?
items.a: Look for the obstacle symbols along and either side of the course line and read both numbers printed with each one. The upper figure in bold is the height above mean sea level and the figure in parentheses is the height above ground. A symbol with a group of ticks is a group of obstacles. Tall obstacles of 1,000 feet AGL and above get a different symbol, and lighted obstacles carry the light flash marks. Then cross check against the MEF box, which already includes them.

items.q: What is the difference between an MEF and a spot elevation with a dot?
items.a: A spot elevation with a dot is the surveyed height of that one point of terrain; the MEF is the highest known feature anywhere in the whole quadrangle, including obstacles, plus an error allowance. The highest spot elevation in a quadrangle is marked with a larger dot and bold type. Do not plan terrain clearance off a spot elevation, because the tower a mile away from it may be higher; plan off the MEF and then add your own margin.

items.q: Tell me about the runways at Walterboro.
items.a: Three runways, all asphalt and concrete: 5 and 23 at 6,002 by 100 feet, 17 and 35 at 5,705 by 100 feet, and 9 and 27 at 5,408 by 100 feet, at a field elevation of 101 feet. Three runways at 120 degree spacing means there is almost always a runway within 30 degrees of the wind, and all three are long enough that runway length is never the deciding factor for a Warrior. That makes the runway choice a question about wind, obstacles and the emergency return, not about length.

items.q: Give me your takeoff distance out of Walterboro.
items.a: It comes out of the takeoff performance charts in Section 5 of Piper Report VB-880, the handbook for serial 28-8116257, entered with pressure altitude, outside air temperature, takeoff weight, wind and flap setting. I read both the ground roll and the total distance over a 50 foot obstacle, then apply the chart's correction notes for any headwind or tailwind component and for a soft or wet surface. I do not use the Section 5 charts in the VB-1180 book; those are computed for a 2,440 pound airplane and are not approved for this serial.

items.q: Runway 5 is 6,002 feet. Is runway length a factor at Walterboro?
items.a: No, not for a Warrior at 2,277 pounds with a field elevation of 101 feet; the examiner is testing whether I can work the chart, not whether I will run off the end. What I do with the number is compare it against the accelerate and stop picture: how much runway remains at rotation, and whether 6,002 feet leaves me room to abort and stop on the pavement. Then I pick a point on the runway by which I must see a specified airspeed or I close the throttle.

items.q: What is the pressure altitude at Walterboro today, and how do you get it?
items.a: Set 29.92 in the altimeter and read it, or compute it as field elevation plus 1,000 times the quantity 29.92 minus the altimeter setting. With the altimeter setting at 29.92 the pressure altitude equals the 101 foot field elevation. At 30.12 it is 101 minus 200, about minus 99 feet; at 29.62 it is 101 plus 300, about 401 feet. The trap is reading the field elevation off the chart and calling it pressure altitude without touching the altimeter setting.

items.q: Compute the density altitude at Walterboro for me.
items.a: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature: approximately pressure altitude plus 120 feet for every degree Celsius the outside air temperature is above the standard temperature for that pressure altitude. Standard temperature is 15 degrees Celsius at sea level, falling about 2 degrees per thousand feet, so at the 101 foot field elevation it is about 14.8 degrees. At 25 degrees on the ramp, density altitude is roughly 101 plus 120 times 10, about 1,300 feet. An E6B or the chart in Section 5 gives the same answer.

items.q: Your POH prints Section 5 charts for a 2,440-pound airplane. Can you use them?
items.a: No. Serial 28-8116257 is covered by Piper Report VB-880, not VB-1180; the maximum gross weight is 2,325 pounds per FAA Type Certificate Data Sheet 2A13 item XVI-A, and every Section 5 chart in the VB-1180 revision is computed for the 2,440 pound airframe. Takeoff, climb, cruise, landing, glide and the stall speed chart all fall with it. The right answer is to plan from the VB-880 charts that belong in this airplane, and to say so rather than quote a number from the wrong book.

items.q: Work me through time, fuel and distance to climb out of Walterboro.
items.a: It is a two lookup subtraction on the time, fuel and distance to climb chart in Section 5 of VB-880. Enter the chart at the pressure altitude and temperature of the cruise altitude and read time, fuel and distance; enter it again at the pressure altitude and temperature of the departure field; subtract the second set from the first. Add the chart's fuel allowance for start, taxi and takeoff. The trap is reading the cruise value alone and forgetting that the chart is referenced from sea level.

items.q: Wind at Walterboro is 130 at 22 gusting 30. Which runway and why?
items.a: The wind splits runway 9 and runway 17 evenly at 40 degrees off each, so the components are identical and the tiebreaker is not arithmetic. Crosswind at the gust is 30 times the sine of 40 degrees, about 19 knots; headwind is 30 times the cosine of 40, about 23 knots. On the steady 22 it is about 14 knots of crosswind and 17 of headwind. I would break the tie on obstacles off each departure end, on which runway puts me closer to the course, and on which gives the better emergency return.

items.q: Give me the crosswind and tailwind components for that runway and show the method.
items.a: Crosswind equals wind speed times the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway; headwind or tailwind equals wind speed times the cosine of that angle. At 40 degrees off, the crosswind is about 64 percent of the wind and the headwind about 77 percent, giving 19 and 23 knots on the 30 knot gust. I always compute on the gust, not the steady wind. Runway numbers are magnetic and tower or AWOS winds are magnetic, but METAR and forecast winds are true, so convert before you take the angle.

items.q: Is the crosswind figure in the flight manual a limitation?
items.a: No. It is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component, the strongest crosswind in which the airplane was shown to be controllable during certification; it is not an operating limitation and nothing prohibits exceeding it. The VB-1180 revision prints 17 knots, and whether that is the figure in the VB-880 book for this serial has to be confirmed. What is limiting is my own demonstrated skill, and a 19 knot gusting crosswind on a checkride morning is a good reason to pick another runway or wait.

items.q: Would you be comfortable departing in 22 gusting 30 at 40 degrees off?
items.a: Not happily, and I would say so out loud. A 19 knot crosswind component at the gust is at or past the demonstrated figure for the airplane and past my personal minimum. The gust spread of 8 knots means an airspeed swing on rotation, and if I had to come straight back the same crosswind would be waiting on the landing. I would wait for the gusts to ease, use a runway with less angle if one existed, or not go. Declining a departure is a decision the examiner wants to hear me able to make.

items.q: Crosswind from the left on takeoff: which way does the airplane want to go?
items.a: Into the wind. The vertical fin and rudder are behind the main gear, so the airplane weathervanes toward the wind, and a left crosswind yaws the nose left, calling for right rudder. That right rudder adds to the right rudder already needed for the left turning tendencies of a climbing propeller airplane. A right crosswind yaws the nose right and is held with left rudder, which partly offsets those tendencies. Either way I hold aileron into the wind and rudder to keep the centerline.

items.q: Tell me about Martin Campbell Field.
items.a: 1A3, Copperhill, Tennessee, field elevation 1,789 feet, one runway 2 and 20 at 3,500 by 75 feet of asphalt in good condition, no tower, no UNICOM, CTAF 122.9. Thresholds are displaced 90 feet on runway 2 and 140 feet on runway 20, the pattern is left for 2 and right for 20, and there is a two light PAPI on the left of each end, 3.00 degrees for runway 2 and 4.00 degrees for runway 20. There is 100LL by 24 hour credit card self service and no weather reporting on the field.

items.q: How long is the runway at 1A3, and how much of it can you actually land on?
items.a: The runway is 3,500 feet, but landing distance available is 3,410 feet on runway 2 and 3,360 feet on runway 20, because the thresholds are displaced 90 and 140 feet. I may not touch down before the threshold, so the usable landing length is the published length minus the displacement. That is the number I compare my POH landing distance against, and on a 75 foot wide mountain runway it is the only honest comparison.

items.q: Why isn't the landing distance available 3,500 feet on either end?
items.a: Because both thresholds are displaced: 90 feet on runway 2 and 140 feet on runway 20, which is pavement I may roll on but may not land on. A displaced threshold exists because something on the approach, an obstacle or a road, forces the touchdown point farther down the runway. The arithmetic is simple, 3,500 minus 90 is 3,410 and 3,500 minus 140 is 3,360, and the trap is planning against 3,500 and then discovering 140 feet of it is painted with arrows.

items.q: Can you use the pavement before a displaced threshold for takeoff?
items.a: Yes. Pavement behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoff in that direction and for rollout after landing in the opposite direction; it is only the landing touchdown that is prohibited. It is marked with white arrows leading to an arrowhead and a solid bar at the threshold. A blast pad or a stopway, marked with yellow chevrons, is different and is not usable for anything. If the Chart Supplement publishes declared distances for 1A3, I use those rather than inferring from the displacement.

items.q: What is the slope of the runway at 1A3, and which way?
items.a: It rises toward the runway 20 end: the runway 2 end is 1,771.7 feet and the runway 20 end is 1,788.7 feet, a rise of 17 feet over 3,500 feet, about one half of one percent. So a takeoff on runway 2 is uphill and a takeoff on runway 20 is downhill; a landing on runway 2 rolls out uphill and a landing on runway 20 rolls out downhill. Half a percent is slight on its own, but combine a downhill landing on 20 with a tailwind and the margin on 3,360 feet disappears quickly.

items.q: Which runway are you planning to land on at 1A3, and might you not have a choice?
items.a: Wind decides in principle, but at a one runway mountain field the terrain often decides for me, and a right hand pattern on runway 20 is the clue that something is in the way on the left. Runway 20 gives the downhill rollout and the 4.00 degree PAPI; runway 2 gives the uphill rollout and a 3.00 degree PAPI. I brief both, note that runway 20 has only 3,360 feet of landing distance available, and check the Chart Supplement remarks and any NOTAMs before I decide.

items.q: What is the traffic pattern at 1A3?
items.a: Left traffic for runway 2 and right traffic for runway 20. A nonstandard right hand pattern on one end of a single runway almost always means terrain, an obstacle or a noise sensitive area on the left side, and here the Chart Supplement also notes a mountain ridge along the east side of the runway. I would fly the published direction, announce it on CTAF 122.9, and overfly well above pattern altitude first to get the lie of the valley before descending into it.

items.q: Why would runway 20 have a right-hand pattern?
items.a: Because something on the left side of runway 20 makes a left pattern unsafe or impractical, and in this terrain that usually means high ground. The Chart Supplement remark about a mountain ridge along the east side of the runway and the mountain ridges on the approach point the same way. The practical consequence is that the pattern is flown away from the rising ground, the downwind may be closer in than I am used to, and a go around from runway 20 has a built in turn direction I must plan before I need it.

items.q: Describe the visual glideslope guidance at 1A3.
items.a: A two light PAPI on the left side of each runway end: 3.00 degrees for runway 2 and 4.00 degrees for runway 20. A two box PAPI gives one red and one white on path, two white high and two red low, so it is coarser than the four box version. Note also that each PAPI is sighted to its own threshold, which on runway 20 is 140 feet down the pavement, so flying the PAPI to touchdown already puts me past the displaced threshold rather than at the runway end.

items.q: Why would the runway 20 PAPI be set at 4 degrees instead of the usual 3?
items.a: Because something on the approach requires a steeper path to clear it; a 4 degree PAPI is the visual evidence of an obstacle or terrain problem off that end. The airport record also publishes a 19 to 1 approach ratio to the displaced threshold on runway 20. A 19 to 1 slope is about 3.0 degrees, so the 4 degree PAPI is deliberately steeper than the minimum clearance slope. I treat the steeper PAPI as the airport telling me where the obstacles are.

items.q: What does flying a 4-degree path do to your rate of descent on final?
items.a: It raises it by about a third over a 3 degree path. Rate of descent in feet per minute is roughly groundspeed in knots times 101.3 times the tangent of the path angle. At 70 knots groundspeed a 3 degree path is about 370 feet per minute and a 4 degree path about 495 feet per minute. That extra 125 feet per minute arrives with the throttle further back, so I watch for carburetor ice, and I resist the instinct to let the airspeed build to make the descent feel normal.

items.q: What does a steeper-than-normal visual path do to your landing?
items.a: Less air distance from 50 feet to touchdown, so I touch down nearer the threshold, but a higher sink rate to arrest in the flare and less margin for carrying extra speed. If I fly the 4 degree PAPI at the right speed I land short and stop short, which is what I want on 3,360 feet. If I fly it fast I either float past the arrows and eat the margin, or I check the sink late and arrive hard. The answer is speed discipline on short final, not technique in the flare.

items.q: The airport record gives 19 to 1 on runway 20 and 17 to 1 on runway 2. What are those?
items.a: Approach slope ratios: the horizontal distance per foot of height needed to clear the controlling obstacle on that approach, measured to the threshold. A 19 to 1 ratio is a slope of about 3.0 degrees and 17 to 1 is about 3.4 degrees. The steeper the ratio, the closer or taller the controlling obstacle. Note that the 19 to 1 on runway 20 is measured to the displaced threshold, which is itself 140 feet down the pavement, so the displacement is part of how the clearance was achieved.

items.q: Runway 2 has a 3-degree PAPI but a 17 to 1 approach ratio. Does that combination bother you?
items.a: Yes, and it is worth resolving on the ground rather than on short final. A 17 to 1 ratio is about 3.4 degrees, which is steeper than the 3.00 degree PAPI, so on the published figures the PAPI path is shallower than the slope that clears the controlling obstacle. I would read the full Chart Supplement entry for 1A3, look for an obstruction note or a remark on the runway 2 approach, check NOTAMs for the PAPI and the obstacle, and telephone the airport manager if it is still unclear.

items.q: Compute the density altitude at 1A3 on a warm afternoon.
items.a: Standard temperature at the 1,789 foot field elevation is about 11.4 degrees Celsius, so every degree above that adds roughly 120 feet. At 25 degrees Celsius the deviation is 13.6 degrees, so density altitude is about 1,789 plus 1,630, roughly 3,400 feet. At 30 degrees it is near 4,000 feet. Pressure altitude first, from the actual altimeter setting, then the temperature correction; an E6B or the Section 5 density altitude chart gives the same number.

items.q: What is the standard temperature at 1,789 feet, and why do you care?
items.a: About 11.4 degrees Celsius, from 15 degrees at sea level less 2 degrees per thousand feet. I care because every performance correction on this field starts from the deviation between the actual temperature and that figure. The trap at a mountain field is reading the OAT as cold because the air feels cold, when on a sunny afternoon the field can be well above standard for its elevation, and the airplane behaves as if it were at 3,000 or 4,000 feet rather than 1,789.

items.q: What does a 25-degree day do to your takeoff roll out of 1A3?
items.a: It lengthens it substantially, because the airplane is operating at roughly 3,400 feet of density altitude rather than 1,789, with less thrust from the propeller, less power from the engine and more true airspeed needed for the same indicated rotation speed. The number comes from the takeoff distance chart in Section 5 of VB-880 at that pressure altitude and temperature. The trap is entering the chart at field elevation instead of density altitude conditions and getting a comfortable answer that the airplane will not deliver.

items.q: Give me your takeoff distance out of 1A3 and tell me if 3,500 feet is enough.
items.a: Read ground roll and total distance over a 50 foot obstacle from the takeoff chart in Section 5 of VB-880, entered at the 1A3 pressure altitude, the actual temperature and the actual takeoff weight, then correct for wind and runway slope. Compare against 3,500 feet of takeoff run, remembering that the pavement behind the displaced threshold is usable for the takeoff roll. The real question is not whether I get airborne but whether I clear what is beyond the end, which is why the 50 foot distance matters more than the ground roll.

items.q: Time, fuel and distance to climb out of 1A3 on the way home?
items.a: Same two lookup subtraction, but starting 1,688 feet higher than at Walterboro, so the climb segment takes longer and burns more for the same cruise altitude. Enter the climb chart in Section 5 of VB-880 at cruise pressure altitude and temperature, enter it again at the 1A3 pressure altitude and temperature, and subtract. The trap at a mountain field is that the terrain ahead does not wait for the chart, so I also check that the resulting rate of climb will clear the rising ground on departure.

items.q: Give me your landing distance at 1A3 and compare it with what you have.
items.a: Read ground roll and total distance over a 50 foot obstacle from the landing chart in Section 5 of VB-880 at the 1A3 pressure altitude, temperature and landing weight, then compare against 3,410 feet available on runway 2 or 3,360 feet on runway 20. Correct for any tailwind component, which on this short a runway dominates everything else. Then add a personal factor, because the chart figure assumes a new airplane, a dry runway, maximum braking and a touchdown right at the threshold.

items.q: What safety factor do you apply to the book landing distance, and why?
items.a: I add at least 50 percent, so I want the available landing distance to be at least one and a half times the book figure, and I use more on a short mountain runway. The chart numbers come from a factory test pilot in a new airframe, flying the exact speed, touching down on the numbers and braking hard, on a dry level surface. None of those describe me arriving at 1A3 after two hours in turbulence. The published figure is a best case, not a planning number.

items.q: The remark reads 8400 FT MTN RIDGES IN APCH; 5000 FT MTN RIDGE ALONG E SIDE OF RWY. What does that mean?
items.a: Read the Chart Supplement entry for 1A3 yourself and work out whether those figures are elevations above mean sea level or distances from the runway, because the entry as published is ambiguous. 8,400 feet would be higher than anything in Tennessee, which argues for distance, but do not take my word for it; compare the figures against the terrain contours, spot elevations and MEF boxes around Copperhill on the sectional, and if they still do not reconcile, telephone the airport manager and ask.

items.q: Does it matter which reading of that remark is correct?
items.a: Yes, and it matters either way, which is why you resolve it before you go. Read as elevations, those figures would set the minimum altitude at which I may approach the valley at all and would make the arrival an exercise in terrain clearance. Read as distances, they tell me how close the ridges sit to the final approach and to the east side of the runway, which sets my pattern size, my go around turn direction and whether a right hand pattern on runway 20 is merely published or physically mandatory.

items.q: What traffic pattern altitude will you fly at 1A3?
items.a: Check the Chart Supplement entry for a published traffic pattern altitude, because mountain fields often publish something other than 1,000 feet above the field. If none is published, the standard for a light single is 1,000 feet above airport elevation, which at a 1,789 foot field is 2,789 feet mean sea level. Write the mean sea level figure on the log, not the above ground figure, because at 1,789 feet of field elevation the two numbers are far enough apart to cause a real error in the pattern.

items.q: What does WILDLIFE INVOF RWY mean for your arrival?
items.a: Wildlife in the vicinity of the runway, which at a mountain field in late November means deer at dusk and dawn more than birds. I plan to arrive in good light, overfly the field above pattern altitude and look at the runway and the grass either side before descending, use the landing light, keep the approach speed honest so I have braking margin, and be ready to go around. On a 3,360 foot runway with a ridge on the east side, a late go around for a deer is not a comfortable maneuver.

items.q: What is your go-around decision point landing at 1A3?
items.a: I set two gates and brief them out loud: stable on speed and on the PAPI by 300 feet above the field, and touched down within the first third of the available landing distance. On 3,360 feet the first third is about 1,120 feet past the displaced threshold. If either gate is missed, I go around. At a one runway field in a valley the go around also needs a direction decided in advance, which on runway 20 means following the published right hand pattern away from the ridge.

items.q: What is the maximum gross weight of this airplane?
items.a: 2,325 pounds in the normal category and 2,020 pounds in utility, from FAA Type Certificate Data Sheet 2A13 item XVI-A, which covers serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300. Serial 28-8116257 falls in that block. Maximum baggage is 200 pounds in the normal category and zero in utility. I use 2,325 pounds, not the 2,440 pounds printed in later revisions of the Warrior II handbook, because that number belongs to a different serial range.

items.q: Why isn't the gross weight 2,440 pounds? The handbook says 2,440.
items.a: Because the handbook in front of me is the wrong revision for this serial number. Piper Report VB-1180 covers serials 28-8316001 and up and prints 2,440 pounds; the airplane is serial 28-8116257, which belongs to Report VB-880 and to Type Certificate Data Sheet 2A13 item XVI-A, where the normal category maximum takeoff weight is 2,325 pounds. The airframe is the same Warrior II, but the weights, anything that scales with weight, and the whole of Section 5 do not carry across.

items.q: Run the weight and balance for you, me, 25 pounds of bags and full fuel.
items.a: At 220 pounds for me, 280 for you in the front seats, 25 pounds of baggage and 48 gallons of fuel, the airplane comes out at 2,277 pounds with the center of gravity at 87.45 inches aft of datum. That is 48 pounds under the 2,325 pound maximum and inside the envelope. Front seats are at 80.5 inches, rear seats at 118.1, fuel at 95.0 and baggage at 142.8; full fuel is 48 gallons at 6 pounds per gallon, which is 288 pounds at a moment of 27,360 inch pounds.

items.q: What is your forward CG limit at 2,277 pounds, and how did you get it?
items.a: About 86.5 inches, by straight line interpolation between 83.0 inches at 1,950 pounds and below and 87.0 inches at the 2,325 pound maximum. The slope is 4.0 inches over 375 pounds, which is 0.01067 inches per pound; 2,277 less 1,950 is 327 pounds, times 0.01067 is 3.49 inches, added to 83.0 gives 86.49. The aft limit is 93.0 inches and does not vary with weight. Those limits must be confirmed against the envelope in Report VB-880 for this serial.

items.q: How much margin do you have at the forward limit, and is that comfortable?
items.a: 0.96 inches, since the loaded center of gravity is 87.45 inches and the forward limit at 2,277 pounds is about 86.49 inches. Legal, but less than an inch, and that is exactly the situation the previous candidate on this ride was asked about. The margin is small because two heavy adults sit at 80.5 inches, well forward, and nothing of consequence is loaded aft. It is a loading problem with a loading answer, not a reason to leave fuel behind.

items.q: What happens to the center of gravity as you burn fuel on the way to Copperhill?
items.a: It moves forward, because the fuel arm of 95.0 inches is aft of the loaded center of gravity at 87.45 inches, so removing weight from behind the CG pulls the CG forward. Burning the planned 22.1 gallons, about 133 pounds, takes the airplane from 2,277 pounds at 87.45 inches to roughly 2,144 pounds at about 86.98 inches. So the center of gravity itself travels about half an inch forward over the leg, and it keeps going if I fly longer.

items.q: So does burning fuel take you closer to the forward limit on this flight?
items.a: No, it actually takes you further from it, and this catches people out. The center of gravity moves forward about 0.47 inches, from 87.45 to about 86.98 inches, but because the forward limit slopes it moves forward faster: at 2,144 pounds it is about 85.07 inches rather than 86.49. So the margin grows from 0.96 inches at takeoff to about 1.9 inches at landing. The correct answer is that both the CG and the limit move, and you must plot takeoff and landing conditions, not just one.

items.q: What if you leave the 25 pounds of bags behind to save weight?
items.a: It makes the forward CG problem worse, not better. Taking the 25 pounds out of the 142.8 inch baggage compartment removes 3,570 inch pounds of aft moment, leaving 2,252 pounds at about 86.83 inches against a forward limit of about 86.22 inches, so the margin shrinks from 0.96 inches to roughly 0.61. On this loading the baggage is ballast that is helping. The reflex to throw weight off an airplane that is not over gross is the wrong reflex.

items.q: How much baggage could you add before you hit gross, and where does that put the CG?
items.a: 48 pounds takes the airplane to the 2,325 pound maximum, and it puts the center of gravity at about 88.6 inches. Each pound at the 142.8 inch baggage arm adds 142.8 inch pounds; 48 pounds adds 6,854 inch pounds to the 199,123 inch pound total, giving 205,977 inch pounds over 2,325 pounds. The forward limit at gross is 87.0 inches, so the margin goes from 0.96 inches to about 1.6, and the aft limit of 93.0 inches is still well away. Baggage limit is 200 pounds, so volume is not the issue; gross weight is.

items.q: What does a forward center of gravity do to the airplane?
items.a: It makes it more longitudinally stable and less maneuverable, and it costs performance. The longer arm from the CG to the horizontal tail means a stronger nose down restoring moment, heavier elevator forces, more download on the tail to trim, and therefore more effective weight on the wing: higher stall speed, higher cruise drag, slightly reduced cruise speed and a longer takeoff run. It also makes the flare heavier, which on 3,360 feet of mountain runway matters.

items.q: What does forward CG do to your stall speed and your landing at 1A3?
items.a: It raises the stall speed, because the tail download has to be carried by the wing as if it were extra weight, and it makes the flare heavier. Arriving at 1A3 on the 4 degree PAPI with a forward CG, I will need more back pressure and more trim to check the sink rate, and if I am a little fast the airplane will want to land flat or on the nose wheel. The fix is speed discipline and trim, and recognizing before departure that the loading is nose heavy.

items.q: Give me the loading arms for this airplane.
items.a: Front seats 80.5 inches, rear seats 118.1 inches, fuel 95.0 inches, baggage 142.8 inches, all aft of datum, with a maximum of 200 pounds in the baggage compartment. The handbook also uses a start, taxi and run up allowance of minus 7 pounds at the 95.0 inch fuel arm, which is minus 665 inch pounds. Those arms are geometry, seat and tank positions, so they are the same across the Warrior II serial range even though the weights and the envelope are not.

items.q: What is the aft limit, and are you anywhere near it?
items.a: 93.0 inches, constant at all weights, and at 87.45 inches I am 5.55 inches forward of it. With two adults in the front seats, nobody in the rear and only 25 pounds of baggage, this loading cannot get near the aft limit. The aft limit would come into play with rear seat passengers and a loaded baggage compartment, and that is the loading that reduces stability, lightens the elevator and makes stall recovery harder. On this trip the forward end is the one to watch.

items.q: Is the center of gravity envelope in the handbook you are carrying the right one?
items.a: Not if it is the VB-1180 book: its Section 6 envelope is captioned for a 2,440 pound maximum gross weight and that is not this airplane. The forward limit at the 2,325 pound maximum has to come from the envelope in Piper Report VB-880 for serial 28-8116257. The 83.0 inch forward limit at 1,950 pounds and below and the 93.0 inch aft limit are probably identical, but probably is not a word I want to use on a checkride; I confirm them in the right book.

items.q: Where is the maximum baggage weight placarded, and what is it?
items.a: 200 pounds in the normal category, placarded on the baggage door, which reads BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS. In the utility category it is zero, and the same placard says UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION, NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. The 200 pound figure is a structural and volume limit rather than one derived from gross weight, so unlike the weights it is the same across the Warrior II serial range. On this flight the limit that bites first is gross weight, not the 200 pounds.

items.q: There is no weather reporting at 1A3. How do you get destination weather?
items.a: I build it from the nearest reporting stations and the area forecasts, and I accept that I will never have an observation of the field itself. The Chart Supplement gives the nearest automated station as the AWOS-3PT at Blairsville, Georgia, KDZJ, 20 nautical miles southeast on 119.325. I pair that with the nearest terminal aerodrome forecasts, the Graphical Forecast for Aviation, PIREPs, satellite and radar, and a telephone call to the airport manager or a local operator.

items.q: What is an AWOS-3PT, and what does it report?
items.a: An automated weather observing system, type 3, with precipitation type and thunderstorm or lightning sensing added. A basic AWOS-3 gives wind, visibility, sky condition and ceiling, temperature, dew point, altimeter setting and density altitude; the P adds precipitation type and the T adds thunderstorm or lightning reporting. Blairsville broadcasts on 119.325. It is unattended and sensor based, so it reports what is over the sensor and nothing about what is over the ridge.

items.q: Blairsville is 20 nautical miles away. Is that good enough for Copperhill?
items.a: No, it is an input, not a substitute. Twenty nautical miles in mountainous terrain can be a different airmass: different valley, different elevation, different exposure to the wind, and ridges in between that generate their own cloud, turbulence and fog. A clear Blairsville observation does not guarantee Copperhill is open, and a poor one does not guarantee it is closed. I use it for altimeter setting and trend and treat the arrival as one I may have to abandon.

items.q: What altimeter setting do you use arriving at 1A3, and what does the rule say?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.121, Altimeter settings: below 18,000 feet MSL, set to the current reported setting of a station along the route within 100 nautical miles; if none is available, use the setting at the departure airport; and if neither is available, set the elevation of the departure airport. With no reporting at 1A3 the practical source is Blairsville on 119.325, 20 nautical miles away and well inside the 100 nautical mile radius, or an altimeter setting from Atlanta Center.

items.q: Where does your destination forecast come from if 1A3 has no TAF?
items.a: From the nearest terminal aerodrome forecast sites around the destination plus the Graphical Forecast for Aviation, read as a picture rather than a point. Identify the reporting and forecast airports on the sectional and in the Chart Supplement within 30 to 40 nautical miles, note their elevations, and adjust mentally for the fact that 1A3 sits higher in a valley. The trap is treating the nearest TAF as if it applied over the ridge; in mountain terrain it is an indication of the airmass, nothing more.

items.q: What is the Graphical Forecast for Aviation, and how do you use it on this leg?
items.a: A set of web based graphics that replaced the textual area forecast, showing observations and forecasts of clouds, visibility, precipitation, winds and icing at three hour steps out to eighteen hours. On a 223 mile leg it is how I see the whole route at once and spot where the ceiling slopes down into the terrain. I use it to pick the altitude and the go, no go gate, then confirm the detail with METARs, TAFs, PIREPs and the winds aloft forecast before departure.

items.q: Define AIRMET and SIGMET, and tell me the types.
items.a: An AIRMET is an in flight advisory of weather hazardous to light aircraft; a SIGMET is an advisory of weather significant to the safety of all aircraft. AIRMETs come as Sierra for mountain obscuration and instrument flight rules conditions, Tango for moderate turbulence and sustained surface winds of 30 knots or more and low level wind shear, and Zulu for moderate icing and freezing levels. SIGMETs cover severe turbulence, severe icing and widespread dust or sandstorms; convective SIGMETs cover thunderstorms.

items.q: Which AIRMET would you be watching most closely on this route?
items.a: Sierra, for mountain obscuration, because it is the one that closes Copperhill without closing anything else. Tango matters because wind across ridges makes the last fifty miles unpleasant and makes the arrival into a one runway valley field marginal, and Zulu matters in late November because the freezing level can sit at or below my cruise altitude. Mountain obscuration is the one that turns a legal VFR flight into a flight with nowhere to go.

items.q: What is mountain wave, and what conditions produce it?
items.a: A standing wave pattern set up downwind of a ridge when stable air is forced over it. The ingredients are wind of about 25 knots or more roughly perpendicular to the ridge line, wind speed increasing with height, and a stable layer at or just above the ridge tops. The result is smooth strong lift on the upwind side, strong sink on the lee side, and violent rotor turbulence beneath the wave crests, with the sink and the rotor both capable of exceeding what a 160 horsepower Warrior can climb through.

items.q: What would tell you mountain wave is likely before you take off?
items.a: The winds aloft forecast and the cloud forms. Look for 25 knots or more at ridge top level, roughly perpendicular to the ridges, strengthening with altitude; an AIRMET Tango; PIREPs of moderate or greater turbulence in the lee of the mountains; and lenticular, cap and rotor clouds reported or visible. In dry air the wave can be present with no cloud at all, which is the dangerous case, so the winds aloft forecast is the primary clue rather than the satellite picture.

items.q: You hit a strong downdraft crossing a ridge in this Warrior. What do you do?
items.a: Turn toward lower terrain immediately, usually a turn of about 45 degrees back toward the valley I came from, and accept the altitude loss while I fly out of the sinking air. I do not try to out climb it; a 160 horsepower airplane at 2,277 pounds cannot. I hold best angle or best rate speed, apply full power, and if I am in a wave I may find the descent continues until I leave the sinking air laterally. The prevention is crossing at 45 degrees with height already in hand.

items.q: Where is the turbulence worst relative to a ridge, and where is the air rising?
items.a: Air rises on the windward side and sinks on the lee side; the worst turbulence is in the rotor beneath and downwind of the ridge, at and below ridge top height. So I climb on the upwind side where the air helps me, cross with height, and expect sink and rough air once I am past the crest. The practical rule for this route is that the last hour into Copperhill is the rough hour, and the time to decide about it is on the ground at Walterboro.

items.q: What is a rotor cloud, and what does it tell you?
items.a: A ragged, churning, roll shaped cloud that forms beneath the crest of a mountain wave, downwind of the ridge, in the layer of reversed and violently turbulent flow. It marks the most severe turbulence associated with a wave and should be avoided entirely; encounters have caused structural damage and loss of control. If I can see rotor cloud, lenticular cloud or a cap cloud over the ridges ahead, the correct answer on this trip is to stay out of the mountains, not to pick my way through.

items.q: What is valley fog, and when would you expect it at a place like Copperhill?
items.a: Radiation fog that forms and pools in valleys on clear, calm nights when the ground cools, the air in contact with it cools to the dew point, and the cold dense air drains downhill into the low ground. Expect it around dawn, after a clear calm night, with a small temperature and dew point spread, and expect the airport in the valley to be in it while the ridges above are clear. Late November gives long nights and strong radiational cooling, so it is a real planning item on an early departure home.

items.q: It is late November. What is your icing concern in a Warrior on this route?
items.a: Serious, because the airplane has no ice protection of any kind and is not approved for flight into known icing. I check the freezing level in the winds aloft forecast and in AIRMET Zulu, and I plan a cruise altitude with the freezing level well above me or well below me and visible moisture avoided either way. Carburetor ice is the other half of the answer; the Lycoming O-320 is carbureted and will make ice in cruise and especially on a low power descent.

items.q: Talk me through carburetor ice on the descent into 1A3.
items.a: Descending at low power into a humid mountain valley is the classic setup, and in a fixed pitch airplane the first symptom is a slow unexplained drop in RPM followed by roughness. I apply full carburetor heat before reducing power, leave it on through the descent, and expect a further RPM drop and possible roughness as the ice melts. Partial heat can be worse than none because it can raise induction air into the icing range. Heat air is unfiltered, so I take it off before taxiing in dust.

items.q: What is afternoon convection going to do to this trip?
items.a: Mountain terrain heats faster than the surrounding air and triggers buildups over the ridges in the afternoon, so the same route that is smooth and clear at nine in the morning can be blocked by cells by three. The practical answer on this leg is to go early. If the forecast is for afternoon convection I move the departure, not the arrival; and once airborne, a cell between me and a one runway valley field with no weather reporting is an automatic diversion, not a deviation.

items.q: Thunderstorms along this route. What are the hazards and how far do you stay away?
items.a: Severe or extreme turbulence, hail that can be thrown clear of the cloud, lightning, icing, microburst wind shear, heavy rain and a sudden loss of visibility. I stay at least 20 nautical miles from any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo, I do not fly under an overhanging anvil, and I do not try to pass between two cells. In mountain terrain the cell and the ridge together remove the option of going underneath, which is how a light single ends up boxed in.

items.q: How do you get pilot reports for this route, and how do you file one?
items.a: From Flight Service on 1 800 WX BRIEF or on frequency, from the aviation weather website, from the preflight briefing, and in the air by asking Atlanta Center or Flight Service what they have. I file one by giving Flight Service the location, time, altitude, aircraft type, sky condition, visibility, temperature, wind and the remark. On this route a PIREP of turbulence or mountain obscuration near the ridges is worth more than any forecast, because there are no observing sites up there.

items.q: What would make this a no-go for you?
items.a: Mountain obscuration or a ceiling that puts the ridges in cloud; forecast or reported moderate or greater turbulence near the destination; a freezing level at or below cruise with visible moisture; convection along the last fifty miles; or an arrival that lands after dark at an unlit, unattended field with no weather reporting. Any one of those on its own is a no go for this airplane and this leg, and I would rather say so at Walterboro than discover it over the ridges.

items.q: What are the external pressures on this trip?
items.a: A paying customer, a destination that only works if the airplane gets there, a limited weather window, the daylight deadline, and the quiet pressure of not wanting to look indecisive on a checkride. External pressure is the E in PAVE and it is the one that makes pilots accept weather they already decided was unacceptable. The countermeasure is to set the limits before the flight, write them down, and give the customer the alternatives early rather than at the last minute.

items.q: The customer has to be in Copperhill tonight and the weather is marginal. What are your options?
items.a: Four, and I offer them in this order: go now and beat the weather; fly as far as the weather stays comfortably visual, land at a suitable field and arrange ground transport for the rest; go tomorrow morning; or do not go at all. If I were instrument rated and current and the airplane were equipped, filing is a fifth option, but that does not help in icing or convection. What I do not do is press on visually toward a valley field with no weather reporting because somebody has an appointment.

items.q: How do you assess risk for this flight?
items.a: With PAVE before the flight and IMSAFE for myself: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment and External pressures, against Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion. On this leg the pilot item is mountain experience, the aircraft item is a carbureted 160 horsepower single with no ice protection and a nose heavy loading, the environment item is terrain and a destination with no weather reporting, and the external item is the customer. I also use a written flight risk assessment tool with a score I will not exceed.

items.q: What are your personal minimums for this leg?
items.a: Mine are tighter than the regulations and I write them down before I look at the weather: ceilings at least 3,000 feet above the highest terrain on the route, visibility at least 6 statute miles, surface wind and crosswind limits I will not exceed, no flight into forecast moderate turbulence or mountain obscuration, an hour of fuel on board at landing, and wheels down at 1A3 at least an hour before sunset. A personal minimum written after the forecast is not a personal minimum.

items.q: When is sunset on the day of this flight, and why does it matter?
items.a: Look it up for the date and for the destination, not for the departure point: the sunrise and sunset tables in the back of the Chart Supplement, or a flight planning app set to 1A3. It matters because the field has no tower, no attendant, pilot activated lighting described as nonstandard, terrain around a one runway valley and no weather reporting. Late November gives short days, and a 2 hour 8 minute leg that departs late becomes an after dark arrival at a field I have never seen.

items.q: When does night begin, for logging, for currency, and for the lights?
items.a: Three different definitions. For the regulations generally, 14 CFR 1.1, General definitions, says night is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight as published in the Air Almanac. For passenger carrying recency, 14 CFR 61.57(b) uses the period from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise. For position lights, 14 CFR 91.209, Aircraft lights, uses sunset to sunrise.

items.q: If you do arrive at 1A3 after dark, what are the issues?
items.a: Pilot activated runway lighting described as nonstandard low intensity, terrain I cannot see, a right hand pattern on runway 20, displaced thresholds, wildlife on the runway, a 4 degree PAPI and no weather reporting to tell me what the valley is doing. Low intensity lights at a mountain field give very little cue to terrain, and the black hole effect on a dark approach causes pilots to fly low. If I cannot be on the ground in daylight, I do not go to 1A3.
