items.q: What is the specific weather trap at a destination with no reporting in the mountains?
items.a: Believing a nearby observation describes the field. With nothing reporting at 1A3, I can be legally and comfortably visual all the way and arrive to find the valley filled or the ridge obscured, with no way to know until I am there. The answer is to fly the leg with an alternate already chosen that does report, to set a fuel and time point at which I commit or divert, and to treat every arrival at 1A3 as one that may have to be abandoned.

items.q: How do the winds aloft over the ridges differ from the forecast?
items.a: They are stronger and less steady, because the terrain channels and accelerates the flow and because the forecast grid cannot resolve a valley. Expect the wind to speed up through gaps and over crests, to reverse in the lee, to produce shear layers at ridge top height, and to arrive at the surface at Copperhill from a direction the forecast never mentioned. That is why I compute crosswind components for both runway ends at 1A3 before I go, and why I overfly the field before descending.

items.q: What density altitude at 1A3 would make you cancel the departure home?
items.a: Whatever density altitude makes the book takeoff distance over a 50 foot obstacle, plus my fifty percent factor, exceed the 3,500 feet available, or makes the climb rate insufficient for the rising ground off the departure end. I compute it rather than guess it: pressure altitude from the actual altimeter setting, then 120 feet per degree Celsius above the 11.4 degree standard temperature for 1,789 feet, then into the Section 5 chart in VB-880. If I have to think hard about it, I offload fuel or wait for the cool of the morning.

items.q: What airspace do you expect at Walterboro, and how do you confirm it?
items.a: Read it off the sectional and confirm in the Chart Supplement; the chart symbol tells you everything. A dashed magenta line around the airport means Class E to the surface, a magenta vignette means Class E from 700 feet above ground, a dashed blue line means Class D, segmented magenta on the airport symbol means a non towered field. Check the airport data block on the chart and the Chart Supplement entry for a control tower, and check NOTAMs for any temporary change.

items.q: What airspace is over 1A3, and what does its having instrument approaches tell you?
items.a: Read the sectional, but expect the airspace to reflect the fact that 1A3 has RNAV GPS approaches to both runway ends. Published instrument approaches normally come with a Class E transition area lowering the Class E floor over the airport, usually to 700 feet above ground, shown as the inside edge of a magenta vignette. Do not assert the floor from the approaches alone; find the magenta or blue vignette around Copperhill on the chart and read the airspace from the symbol.

items.q: Class E starts at 700 AGL over an airport. What is the ceiling of that Class E?
items.a: 18,000 feet mean sea level, or more precisely up to but not including 18,000 feet. Class A begins at 18,000 feet MSL, so Class E runs from its 700 foot above ground floor all the way up to the base of Class A. The reason the answer is that simple is that everything above is controlled and nothing else intervenes over that airport. The common error is to answer 1,200 feet or 14,500 feet, which are floors of other Class E areas, not a ceiling.

items.q: Why does an airport get a 700-foot Class E floor rather than 1,200?
items.a: Because it has an instrument approach procedure, and the transition area lowers controlled airspace to protect arriving and departing instrument traffic closer to the ground. On the sectional that area is drawn as a magenta vignette whose soft inner edge marks where the Class E floor becomes 700 feet above ground. Outside it, Class E typically begins at 1,200 feet above ground, shown by the blue vignette edge. Below the Class E floor the airspace is Class G.

items.q: Give me the VFR cloud clearances in Class E below 10,000 feet.
items.a: 14 CFR 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums: 3 statute miles visibility, 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal from clouds. That applies day and night in Class E at less than 10,000 feet mean sea level. The same figures apply in Class C and Class D, and in Class B the requirement is 3 statute miles and clear of clouds. At and above 10,000 feet MSL in Class E it changes to 5 statute miles with 1,000 feet below, 1,000 above and 1 statute mile horizontal.

items.q: What about Class G at 3,000 feet over the mountains on this route?
items.a: It depends on height above the surface, not height above sea level, which is the trap over rising terrain. In Class G at or below 1,200 feet above ground, day, it is 1 statute mile and clear of clouds; at night, 3 statute miles with 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal. Above 1,200 feet above ground but below 10,000 feet MSL, day, it is 1 statute mile with 500, 1,000 and 2,000; at night 3 statute miles with the same clearances.

items.q: You decide to cruise at 10,500. What are your visibility and cloud clearances?
items.a: At and above 10,000 feet mean sea level, in Class E, 5 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontal from clouds. Note the threshold is 10,000 feet MSL and also more than 1,200 feet above the surface, so climbing through 10,000 changes the requirement. The horizontal clearance jumping from 2,000 feet to a full statute mile is the part people forget, and over mountain terrain a mile of lateral clearance can be hard to find.

items.q: What equipment does the airspace on this route require?
items.a: Check it against 14 CFR 91.215, ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use, and 14 CFR 91.225, Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use, after reading which airspace the course actually crosses. In broad terms a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required in Class A, B and C, within the 30 nautical mile Mode C veil around a Class B primary airport, above the Class B or C ceiling to 10,000 feet, and above 10,000 feet MSL excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet above ground.

items.q: Does this route take you anywhere ADS-B Out is required?
items.a: Work it from the chart rather than from memory: look for any Class B or C airspace near the course line and the Mode C veil ring, and decide what cruise altitude you will use. If you plan 10,500 feet, 14 CFR 91.225 applies at and above 10,000 feet MSL except in airspace at and below 2,500 feet above ground. At 6,500 or 8,500 away from Class B and C it generally does not. Either way the airplane's equipment list and the latest ADS-B performance report settle whether it is compliant.

items.q: How do you identify a military training route on the sectional?
items.a: They are drawn as thin gray lines labeled IR or VR with a route number. IR means operations are conducted under instrument flight rules and VR under visual flight rules. I note any that cross my course, check the Chart Supplement for the route description and the scheduling activity, and ask Flight Service or Atlanta Center whether the route is active. Military traffic on these routes can be fast and low, so seeing the line on the chart is only the first step.

items.q: What is the difference between IR1206 and IR206?
items.a: The number of digits tells you the altitude band. A four digit number, such as IR1206 or VR1207, identifies a route with no segment flown above 1,500 feet above ground. A three digit number, such as IR206 or VR207, identifies a route that includes one or more segments above 1,500 feet above ground. So a three digit route can reach my cruise altitude while a four digit route lives down where I would be in a descent or a diversion.

items.q: Your course crosses a military operations area. Can you fly through it?
items.a: Yes. A MOA is not prohibited to VFR traffic and no clearance is required, but it exists to separate military training from instrument traffic and the activity in it can be aggressive. Before entering I contact the controlling agency or Flight Service to find out whether it is active, I consider flying around or above it, and if I go through I keep a high level of vigilance and lights on. The hours, altitudes and controlling agency are printed on the chart margin panel.

items.q: What about a restricted area on your route?
items.a: A restricted area contains hazards to aircraft such as artillery, gunnery or guided missiles, and I may not enter it when it is active without permission from the using or controlling agency. The chart margin panel lists the designator, altitudes, times of use and the controlling agency. If it is cold I may transit, and the controlling agency or Flight Service will tell me. The safe planning answer on a route like this is to draw the course so it misses the area entirely.

items.q: What is an alert area and what is a warning area?
items.a: An alert area is airspace containing a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity; no clearance is required and both participating and transiting pilots are equally responsible for collision avoidance. A warning area is airspace from three nautical miles outward from the coast of the United States containing activity hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft; it may be over domestic or international waters, and its purpose is to warn pilots of the hazard.

items.q: How do you find out whether an MOA or a restricted area is hot?
items.a: Read the times of use in the chart margin panel, then confirm on the day. The panel gives the designator, the altitudes, the hours of operation and the controlling agency. For the day of flight I check NOTAMs, including special activity airspace NOTAMs, ask Flight Service during the briefing, and once airborne ask the controlling agency or Atlanta Center directly. Scheduled hours are the plan; the NOTAM and the controller are the fact.

items.q: What is the stadium symbol on the chart and why does it matter?
items.a: It marks a stadium that may be subject to a temporary flight restriction during an event. Under 14 CFR 91.145, Management of aircraft operations in the vicinity of aerial demonstrations and major sporting events, and the standing flight data center NOTAM, aircraft are prohibited below 3,000 feet above ground within a 3 nautical mile radius of stadiums seating 30,000 or more people, from one hour before until one hour after the event. The symbol is a reminder to check NOTAMs, since the restriction exists only when the event does.

items.q: What is a national security area, and what is a presidential TFR?
items.a: A national security area is airspace where there is a requirement for increased security of ground facilities; pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying through it, and it can be made regulatory by NOTAM. A presidential temporary flight restriction is issued under 14 CFR 91.141, Flight restrictions in the proximity of the Presidential and other parties, and it is not voluntary; it moves with the protected person and is published by flight data center NOTAM, so the only way to know is to check NOTAMs on the day.

items.q: What services does 1A3 have, and what does it not have?
items.a: It has 100LL by 24 hour credit card self service, a lighted wind indicator, a white and green rotating beacon from sunset to sunrise, pilot activated low intensity runway lights on CTAF 122.9, a two light PAPI at each end and RNAV GPS approaches to both runway ends. It does not have a control tower, a UNICOM, any weather reporting, or approach control on the field; approach and departure service comes from Atlanta Center on 133.1, and an instrument clearance is obtained by telephone.

items.q: What does 24-hour credit card self-service fuel mean for your planning?
items.a: It means fuel is theoretically available at any hour and practically available only if the pump and the card reader are working and my card is accepted. There is no attendant to help and no UNICOM to ask. I telephone the airport manager before departure to confirm the pump is serviceable and the price, check NOTAMs for a fuel outage, carry more than one card, and plan the fuel so I could leave again without buying any.

items.q: You land at 1A3 and the card reader is dead. Now what?
items.a: I should never be in a position where that strands me, which is why the leg is planned to arrive with usable fuel rather than reserve only. With 48 gallons usable and about 22 gallons planned for the leg, I land with enough to reach a field that does have fuel. On the day I would telephone the airport manager, whose number is in the Chart Supplement, look for a nearby field with attended fuel, and if nothing works, wait rather than depart on reserves into mountain terrain.

items.q: Describe the runway lighting at 1A3 and how you turn it on.
items.a: The Chart Supplement entry reads ACTVT NON STANDARD LIRL RWY 02/20 on CTAF, so the runway edge lights are low intensity, pilot controlled, and activated on 122.9, but the keying sequence is described as nonstandard. The usual pilot controlled lighting sequence is seven, five or three keys of the microphone within five seconds for high, medium or low intensity. Because this one is flagged as nonstandard, read the full Chart Supplement entry for the actual sequence before you depart.

items.q: The lighting remark says NON STANDARD. What should you do about that word?
items.a: Treat it as a direct instruction to go and read the full Chart Supplement entry for 1A3 and the AIM section on pilot control of airport lighting, because the normal three, five and seven click intensities may not apply. Nonstandard can mean a different keying sequence, a different number of clicks, a different on time or lights that do not step through three intensities. Find out on the ground; keying a microphone at a dark mountain field and getting nothing is not the moment to discover the sequence is different.

items.q: What does a white and green rotating beacon tell you, and what are the hours here?
items.a: Alternating white and green identifies a lighted land airport, and at 1A3 the beacon operates from sunset to sunrise. A beacon on during daylight hours in Class B, C, D or E surface airspace is a sign that the ground visibility is below 3 statute miles or the ceiling is below 1,000 feet, but at an uncontrolled field like 1A3 with no weather reporting that cue does not exist, because the beacon is simply on a sunset to sunrise schedule.

items.q: Who do you talk to at 1A3, and how do you announce yourself?
items.a: Nobody; it is self announce on CTAF 122.9, with no tower and no UNICOM listed. I announce the airport name first and last, give position and intentions ten miles out, entering the pattern, on downwind, base and final, and clear of the runway. In mountain terrain I also overfly the field well above pattern altitude to look for traffic and for the wind indicator, and I keep listening on 122.9 well before I arrive, since other traffic may be on the same shared frequency at nearby fields.

items.q: How would you get an IFR clearance out of 1A3?
items.a: By telephone, which is exactly what the Chart Supplement says: clearance delivery is by telephone and approach and departure service is from Atlanta Center. I would call the clearance delivery number before engine start, get the clearance and a void time, and depart to meet it. The practical point is that there is no clearance delivery frequency on the ground at a valley field, so the plan has to be made on the ramp with the engine shut down, not with the propeller turning.

items.q: What is 133.1 at Copperhill, and what is 342.425?
items.a: Approach and departure service from Atlanta Air Route Traffic Control Center through the Mount Oglethorpe remote communications air to ground site: 133.1 is the very high frequency civil frequency and 342.425 is the paired ultra high frequency used by military aircraft. That is my contact for flight following, for an instrument clearance in the air and for an emergency. Coverage depends on altitude, so if I cannot raise Atlanta down in the valley, the answer is to climb.

items.q: Where do you find NOTAMs for this trip, and what types are there?
items.a: From the FAA NOTAM search website, from a standard briefing through Flight Service on 1 800 WX BRIEF, or through a flight planning application; AIM, Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) System, describes the system. The types are NOTAM D, which covers navigation aids, public airports, services and hazards; flight data center NOTAMs, which cover regulatory matters such as temporary flight restrictions and changes to instrument procedures; pointer NOTAMs; special activity airspace NOTAMs; and military NOTAMs.

items.q: Which NOTAM would hurt this trip the most?
items.a: One that closes the runway or the fuel at 1A3, or an unlit obstruction or an out of service PAPI at a field with terrain on the approach and no weather reporting. On a route like this I also check for temporary flight restrictions, for special activity airspace, and for GPS interference testing NOTAMs, because the approaches at 1A3 are RNAV GPS and my navigation backup matters more over the mountains. I read them for both airports and along the route, not just the destination.

items.q: How do you confirm fuel and field condition before you go?
items.a: Chart Supplement entry first for the published services, NOTAMs second for what has changed, and then a telephone call to the airport manager, whose number is in the Chart Supplement. At a 24 hour self service field with no attendant and no UNICOM, the phone call is the only way to learn that the pump is down, the runway is being seal coated or the deer fence is broken. The Chart Supplement tells me what is supposed to be there; the phone call tells me what is there today.

items.q: What services would you look for at airports along the route, and where?
items.a: Fuel, runway length and surface, lighting, a tower or a common traffic advisory frequency, and whether anybody is on the field; the sectional gives me the quick version and the Chart Supplement gives me the detail. On the chart, the airport data block carries the field elevation, the longest runway, the CTAF and the lighting and fuel symbols, and a star on the symbol means rotating beacon operation. I write two or three such fields on the navigation log as my planned outs.

items.q: What do power lines, railroad tracks and a racetrack look like on a sectional?
items.a: Power transmission lines are drawn as a line with small towers along it, railroads as a line with cross ticks, and the various cultural features have their own symbols explained in the chart legend. Read the legend panel on the chart rather than guessing, because the symbols for a dual track railroad, an abandoned railroad, a power line and a pipeline are easy to confuse. Linear features like these make excellent checkpoints in the low country out of Walterboro.

items.q: Halfway along, Copperhill is going down. How do you pick a diversion field?
items.a: Fuel, weather, runway and terrain, in that order, and I picked the candidates before I took off. I want a field I can reach with reserve intact, that has reported weather I can actually see, with a runway long enough for the Warrior and terrain I can get into and out of. On this route that usually means a larger field back toward lower ground rather than another small strip deeper in the mountains. I write two or three candidate fields with frequencies on the navigation log.

items.q: Show me how you divert in the air with no GPS.
items.a: Fly the airplane, then turn toward the new field before doing anything else. Pick the field off the chart, turn to an approximate heading estimated from the chart, note the time and the fuel, then measure the distance and the course with a plotter or with the finger and the chart scale, compute groundspeed and time from the last known groundspeed, and refine the heading. Then tell ATC, get weather, and brief the arrival. The order matters: heading first, arithmetic second.

items.q: How do you estimate heading, time and fuel to a diversion field quickly?
items.a: Use round numbers. Measure the course against a line of longitude or with a plotter, apply the same wind correction angle you already know works for that general direction, and estimate the distance by eye against the chart scale or the latitude ticks, where one minute of latitude is one nautical mile. At 105 knots I cover 1.75 nautical miles per minute, so divide the distance by 1.75 for minutes, and multiply hours by 8.4 gallons for fuel. Refine once the airplane is pointed the right way.

items.q: What do you tell ATC when you divert?
items.a: Who I am, where I am, what I am doing and what I want. On this route that is Atlanta Center on 133.1: call sign, position, altitude, that I am diverting from 1A3 to the new field, and a request for any weather they have and for flight following to it. If I cannot reach them down low I climb, and if the diversion is because of weather closing in, I say so, because that changes the service they will try to give me.

items.q: What is your best glide speed, and is the number in your handbook the right one?
items.a: The best glide speed has to come from Piper Report VB-880 for serial 28-8116257, not from the 73 knots printed in the VB-1180 revision. That 73 knot figure and the glide chart it comes from are computed at 2,440 pounds, a weight this airplane cannot reach. Best glide speed decreases with weight, so at 2,277 pounds the correct speed is lower. I read the right book, and in the airplane I fly the speed on the placard and in the emergency checklist for this serial.

items.q: Engine failure over the ridges. Where do you go?
items.a: Downhill and downwind toward the valley floor, toward the largest clear area within glide, while I fly best glide and run the restart flow. Over forested ridges the realistic options are a river bank, a field in the valley bottom, a road, a clearcut or a lake shore. I turn toward lower ground immediately rather than spending altitude looking, because altitude over a ridge converts into reach only in the downhill direction, and the valley is where any flat ground will be.

items.q: How does rising terrain affect your glide footprint?
items.a: It cuts it, and it cuts it asymmetrically. The glide range is a ratio of height above the ground, not height above sea level, so flying toward terrain that rises 1,000 feet eats 1,000 feet of glide before I even start. Downhill the footprint stretches; uphill it collapses. That is the practical argument for crossing ridges high and at an angle, and for never routing along a valley at an altitude from which only the valley floor ahead is reachable.

items.q: What are your off-airport landing options over unbroken forest?
items.a: Plan for a controlled arrival into the tops rather than a landing, flown at minimum controllable airspeed, wings level, full flaps, fuel and ignition off, doors unlatched and harnesses tight. The aim is to use the canopy to dissipate energy and to protect the cabin. I look for a clearcut, a road, a river or a power line cut first; all of them beat trees. The passenger briefing before departure covers the harness, the doors and the fire extinguisher for exactly this reason.

items.q: Lost over the mountains with no GPS. Walk me through it.
items.a: The five Cs: climb, communicate, confess, comply and conserve. Climb for terrain clearance, radio range and radar coverage; communicate with Atlanta Center on 133.1 or Flight Service, or 121.5 if nothing else answers; confess that I am uncertain of my position; comply with the instructions I am given; and conserve fuel by setting an economical power setting and by not wandering. Before any of that, note the time and the heading so the dead reckoning position is not lost too.

items.q: Without talking to anyone, how would you fix your position using a VOR?
items.a: Tune and identify a VOR, center the needle with a FROM indication, and that radial is a line of position; where it crosses a road, a river or a ridge I can see on the chart is my position. A second VOR crossed with the first gives a fix without needing ground reference. The trap is the ambiguity between TO and FROM: a centered needle with TO gives the reciprocal radial, and plotting that outbound from the station puts you on exactly the wrong side of it.

items.q: How does terrain affect your radio and radar coverage on this route?
items.a: Both are line of sight, so a ridge between me and the antenna blocks them regardless of how close I am. Low in a valley at Copperhill I may not reach Atlanta Center at all, and radar coverage will be poor or absent. The remedy is altitude: climb before transmitting, and expect to lose both during the descent into 1A3. That is one more reason to tell Center my intentions before I start down rather than after I have lost them.

items.q: Who do you call in an emergency on this route, and on what frequency?
items.a: Atlanta Center on 133.1 if I am already in contact or can reach them, otherwise 121.5, the emergency frequency. I squawk 7700 on the transponder, which gets attention even where radio coverage is poor, and I use the word mayday for a distress situation or pan pan for urgency. On the Walterboro end I would use whatever approach control or center frequency I had been working, and near 1A3 I would also broadcast my intentions on CTAF 122.9 so that local traffic knows.

items.q: Would you fly into the valley at Copperhill at dusk with a lowering ceiling?
items.a: No, and I would make that decision long before I was over the valley. A one runway field at 1,789 feet with ridges on the approach and along the east side of the runway, a right hand pattern, no weather reporting, nonstandard pilot activated low intensity lighting and wildlife on the runway is a field to arrive at in good light and good weather. A lowering ceiling at dusk in mountain terrain removes every option at once, which is the definition of a trap.

items.q: What is your plan if you simply cannot get into 1A3?
items.a: Divert to the alternate I chose on the ground, with the fuel I planned for that purpose, and tell the customer. I pick an alternate that reports weather, has fuel and has a runway and terrain I can manage, and I set a decision point on the navigation log, defined by both position and fuel, at which I commit to 1A3 or turn. Deciding in advance is what keeps the decision from being made by the weather, the fuel gauge or the customer.

items.q: What do you brief your passenger before this flight?
items.a: Seat belts and harnesses, how the doors and the emergency exit work, the fire extinguisher location, no smoking, the sterile cockpit periods and when I need quiet, what to do if I become incapacitated, and that I would like to be told about any traffic, bird or hazard they see. On this trip I would add the route, the expected two hours and a bit, the turbulence likely near the mountains, and the plain statement that we may divert and that the decision is mine.

items.q: You clip a runway light landing at 1A3. Is that reportable, and where do you look?
items.a: Look in 49 CFR Part 830, Notification and Reporting of Aircraft Accidents or Incidents and Overdue Aircraft, and Preservation of Aircraft Wreckage, Mail, Cargo, and Records, not in the Federal Aviation Regulations. Part 830 defines an accident by death or serious injury or substantial damage to the aircraft, and 830.5 lists the serious incidents that require immediate notification of the National Transportation Safety Board. Damage to a runway light alone is not on that list; damage to the airplane may change the answer.

b: Classes, entry and equipment requirements, VFR minimums, special use airspace.

items.q: What are the four broad categories of airspace in the National Airspace System?
items.a: Controlled, uncontrolled, special use and other airspace. Controlled airspace is Classes A, B, C, D and E, where ATC service is available to IFR and, in varying degrees, to VFR flights. Uncontrolled is Class G. Special use airspace covers prohibited, restricted, warning and alert areas, MOAs, controlled firing areas and national security areas. Other airspace includes MTRs, TRSAs, ADIZs and parachute jump areas.

items.q: What does controlled airspace actually mean for a VFR pilot?
items.a: It means ATC service is available there and IFR traffic is being separated in it, so as a VFR pilot you are subject to higher cloud clearances and visibilities, and in some classes to communication, clearance and equipment requirements. Controlled does not mean you are controlled; outside Class B, ATC does not separate you from other VFR traffic.

items.q: What are the vertical limits of Class A airspace?
items.a: From 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600, that is 60,000 feet. Above FL600 the airspace is Class E. Below 18,000 the classes depend on location. Class A also overlies the waters within 12 nautical miles of the coast of the 48 contiguous states and Alaska.

items.q: How much airspace over water does Class A cover?
items.a: It includes the airspace overlying the waters within 12 nautical miles of the coast of the 48 contiguous states and Alaska, at and above 18,000 feet MSL. Beyond 12 NM the airspace is international and operated under ICAO rules, though US operating rules still bind US-registered aircraft.

items.q: What is required to operate in Class A airspace?
items.a: All operations must be conducted under IFR. You need an instrument rating, an instrument-rated and IFR-equipped aircraft, an ATC clearance, and two-way radio communication, plus a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out. This is 14 CFR 91.135 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Operations in Class A airspace). There is no VFR in Class A, so there are no VFR weather minimums.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class A airspace?
items.a: There are none, because VFR is not permitted. Every flight in Class A is conducted under instrument flight rules with an ATC clearance, so cloud clearance and visibility minimums do not apply. Altimeters are set to 29.92 inches of mercury at and above 18,000 feet, and altitudes are expressed as flight levels.

items.q: What are the typical dimensions and shape of Class B airspace?
items.a: It surrounds the nation's busiest airports and typically extends from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, drawn as an upside-down wedding cake in two or more layers of increasing radius with altitude. Every Class B is individually tailored, so the exact radii and shelf altitudes are unique to each airport and must be read from the chart.

items.q: What is the entry requirement for Class B airspace?
items.a: You must receive a specific ATC clearance to enter, and the words must be unambiguous: cleared into the Class Bravo. Radio contact alone is not enough, and an instruction to remain clear or a mere acknowledgement of your call sign does not authorize entry. This is 14 CFR 91.131 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Operations in Class B airspace).

items.q: What equipment is required to operate in Class B airspace?
items.a: An operable two-way radio, a transponder with Mode C altitude reporting, and ADS-B Out. Under 14 CFR 91.131 an IFR operation additionally requires an operable VOR or TACAN receiver, or a suitable RNAV system. The transponder and ADS-B requirements also apply within the 30 NM Mode C veil around the primary Class B airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL.

items.q: What pilot certification is required to fly in Class B airspace?
items.a: At least a private pilot certificate, or a student, sport or recreational pilot who holds the logbook endorsement required by 14 CFR 61.95 (Part 61, Subpart C, Student Pilots, Operations in Class B airspace and at airports located within Class B airspace) for that specific Class B area. At a small number of the busiest airports listed in Part 91 Appendix D, Section 4, student solo operations are prohibited entirely.

items.q: How is Class B airspace depicted on a sectional chart?
items.a: By solid blue lines around the primary airport, with each layer labeled by a pair of numbers in hundreds of feet giving the ceiling over the floor, for example 100 over 30 meaning 10,000 MSL down to 3,000 MSL. The surrounding 30 NM Mode C veil is shown as a thin solid magenta ring.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class B airspace?
items.a: 3 statute miles visibility and clear of clouds. There is no vertical or horizontal cloud clearance requirement because ATC is separating every aircraft in the airspace, so staying clear of cloud is enough. Note that clear of clouds means exactly that, with no defined buffer, so a VFR pilot must still avoid flying into anything.

items.q: What is the Mode C veil and what does it require?
items.a: The Mode C veil is the airspace within 30 nautical miles of a primary Class B airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, inside which you must have an operable transponder with automatic pressure altitude reporting and ADS-B Out. It is required by 14 CFR 91.215 and 14 CFR 91.225 whether or not you enter the Class B itself, and it is charted as a thin magenta ring. The same 30 NM ring is also the ADS-B Out veil of 14 CFR 91.225, and the chart shows both as a single thin solid magenta circle around the Class B primary airport.

items.q: What are the dimensions of Class C airspace?
items.a: An inner circle of 5 NM radius from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation, and an outer shelf from 5 to 10 NM radius extending from 1,200 feet AGL up to the same 4,000 foot ceiling. Charted altitudes are shown in hundreds of feet MSL. The shape is a two-tier version of the Class B wedding cake.

items.q: What is the Class C outer area and how does it differ from the outer shelf?
items.a: The outer area extends to about 20 NM radius and is where radar service is normally provided, but it is not charted, is not part of the Class C airspace, and carries no entry or equipment requirement. The 10 NM outer shelf is charted Class C and does carry the communication and equipment requirements.

items.q: What is the entry requirement for Class C airspace?
items.a: Two-way radio communication must be established before entering, which is satisfied when the controller uses your call sign without a restriction, for example November Three Four Five, standby. No clearance is required. If the reply is aircraft calling, remain clear of the Class Charlie, you have not established communication and may not enter. This is 14 CFR 91.130 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Operations in Class C airspace).

items.q: What equipment is required for Class C airspace?
items.a: An operable two-way radio, a transponder with Mode C altitude reporting, and ADS-B Out, required within and above Class C airspace up to 10,000 feet MSL under 14 CFR 91.215 and 14 CFR 91.225. There is no navigation equipment requirement for a VFR flight beyond that.

items.q: How is Class C airspace depicted on a sectional?
items.a: By solid magenta lines around the airport, with the ceiling over the floor of each ring shown in hundreds of feet MSL. The inner ring reads with SFC as the floor. It surrounds airports with an operating control tower serviced by radar approach control and a certain volume of traffic.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class C airspace?
items.a: 3 statute miles visibility, and cloud clearances of 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally. This is the standard set often remembered as three, one, five, two, and it applies in Class C, Class D and Class E below 10,000 feet MSL, under 14 CFR 91.155 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Basic VFR weather minimums).

items.q: What are the dimensions of Class D airspace?
items.a: A cylinder from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation, with a radius tailored to the instrument procedures at the field, commonly about 4 NM. The charted ceiling is the airport elevation plus 2,500, rounded up to the next 100 feet, shown in a dashed box in hundreds of feet MSL.

items.q: Why does Class D airspace often have extensions and what shape are they?
items.a: Because instrument approaches must be contained in controlled airspace. Extensions are keyhole-shaped arms that reach out along the final approach course. If an extension is 2 NM or less it remains Class D, drawn with the dashed blue line; if it is longer than 2 NM it becomes a Class E surface extension, drawn with a dashed magenta line.

items.q: What is the entry requirement for Class D airspace?
items.a: Two-way radio communication must be established with the tower before entering, and you must maintain it while in the airspace. No clearance is required to enter, though a clearance is required to take off or land. This is 14 CFR 91.129 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Operations in Class D airspace).

items.q: What equipment is required for Class D airspace?
items.a: Only an operable two-way radio. Class D carries no transponder or ADS-B requirement of its own, though those may still be required by the Mode C veil, by the airspace above 10,000 feet MSL, or by Class B or C airspace overlying the field. Confirm on the chart rather than assuming.

items.q: How is Class D airspace depicted and what are its VFR weather minimums?
items.a: By a dashed blue line around the airport, with the ceiling in a dashed box in hundreds of feet MSL. VFR minimums are 3 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontal cloud clearance, under 14 CFR 91.155 (Basic VFR weather minimums).

items.q: What happens to Class D airspace when the control tower closes?
items.a: It reverts to either Class E or Class G, depending on what the chart and the Chart Supplement say for that field. If it becomes Class E to the surface, the VFR minimums stay at 3 statute miles and the standard cloud clearances; if it becomes Class G, the lower Class G minimums apply. Either way there is no one to talk to, so use CTAF and the published times in the Chart Supplement.

items.q: What is Class E airspace?
items.a: All controlled airspace that is not Class A, B, C or D. It is where IFR traffic is being controlled but no communication or clearance is required of a VFR pilot. It covers the great majority of controlled airspace in the country, both at low level and en route.

items.q: What are the types of Class E airspace?
items.a: A surface area designated for an airport; an extension to a surface area; airspace used for transition to or from the terminal or en route environment; en route domestic areas; and federal airways. There is also Class E airspace above FL600 and Class E over the offshore areas. A Victor airway is one of the charted forms of Class E: it runs from 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 MSL, is 8 NM wide, and appears as a light blue centerline labeled with a V and a route number.

items.q: Where do the various floors of Class E airspace sit?
items.a: Unless otherwise designated, Class E begins at 14,500 feet MSL and runs up to but not including 18,000. Around airports the floor is lowered: 700 feet AGL where an instrument approach needs the protection, 1,200 feet AGL over most of the rest of the country, and the surface where a surface area is designated. Federal airways are Class E from 1,200 AGL to 18,000 MSL.

items.q: How is Class E airspace depicted on a sectional?
items.a: A dashed magenta line is a Class E surface area; a shaded, fuzzy magenta band marks where the floor drops to 700 feet AGL, with the Class E on the inside of the shading; a shaded blue band marks a 1,200 foot AGL floor where Class G extends higher on the other side; and a blue and magenta zipper line marks the boundary where Class E floors change or Class E ends. Read the vignette from its soft side: inside the magenta shading Class E starts at 700 feet AGL, outside it Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL, and Class G fills everything below.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class E below 10,000 feet MSL?
items.a: 3 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontal cloud clearance, under 14 CFR 91.155 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Basic VFR weather minimums). These are the same minimums as Class C and Class D.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class E at and above 10,000 feet MSL?
items.a: 5 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet above, 1,000 feet below and 1 statute mile horizontal cloud clearance, under 14 CFR 91.155. Note the qualifier: it applies at or above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL. The minimums increase because the 250 knot speed limit ends at 10,000, so closure rates are far higher.

items.q: Is any equipment or communication required to fly VFR in Class E airspace?
items.a: None for the airspace itself. No clearance, no radio call and no transponder are required by the class. Other rules still apply: a transponder and ADS-B Out are required at and above 10,000 feet MSL except below 2,500 AGL, and inside the Mode C veil, under 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.225.

items.q: What is Class G airspace and how far up does it extend?
items.a: Uncontrolled airspace, defined as any airspace that is not Class A, B, C, D or E. It extends from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E, which is typically 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, and in some remote areas up to 14,500 feet MSL. No ATC service is provided and nothing is required to enter it.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL by day?
items.a: 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds, under 14 CFR 91.155 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Basic VFR weather minimums). This is the lowest legal VFR weather anywhere in the system, and it is a long way from safe, since 1 mile at 100 knots is 36 seconds of forward warning.

items.q: What are the VFR weather minimums in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL at night?
items.a: 3 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontal cloud clearance, under 14 CFR 91.155. The night figures are the standard three, one, five, two set, because at night you cannot see the cloud you are about to enter.

items.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class G from 1,200 AGL up to but not including 10,000 MSL?
items.a: By day, 1 statute mile with 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontal cloud clearance. By night, 3 statute miles with the same cloud clearances. The visibility changes between day and night; the cloud clearances do not. This is 14 CFR 91.155 (Basic VFR weather minimums).

items.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class G at and above 10,000 MSL and more than 1,200 AGL?
items.a: 5 statute miles visibility with 1,000 feet above, 1,000 feet below and 1 statute mile horizontal cloud clearance, day or night, under 14 CFR 91.155. Both conditions must be met, so above 10,000 MSL but within 1,200 feet of the ground, as over high terrain, the lower figures still apply.

items.q: What is the night traffic pattern exception to the Class G visibility minimums?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.155(b) you may operate an airplane at night in Class G airspace at or below 1,200 feet AGL, within half a statute mile of the runway, with 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds, provided you remain in the traffic pattern of an airport. It exists so a pattern can be flown in marginal conditions at an uncontrolled field, not as a way to depart cross country.

items.q: What visibility and ceiling are needed to take off, land or enter the traffic pattern in a surface area?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.155(c) and (d), no one may operate under VFR beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface, or take off, land or enter the pattern there unless ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles, or if no ground visibility is reported, flight visibility is at least 3 statute miles. Otherwise you need Special VFR.

items.q: What is Special VFR and what does it require?
items.a: Special VFR is an ATC clearance to operate in a surface area below basic VFR minimums, requiring at least 1 statute mile flight visibility and remaining clear of clouds. You must request it; ATC will not offer it. At night both an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft are required. It is authorized by 14 CFR 91.157 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Special VFR weather minimums), and it is prohibited at certain airports listed in Part 91 Appendix D.

items.q: What is the maximum indicated airspeed below 10,000 feet MSL?
items.a: 250 knots indicated. Under 14 CFR 91.117 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Aircraft speed), no person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at more than 250 knots IAS. It is an MSL limit, so it applies over high terrain too, and it applies in all airspace, including inside Class B.

items.q: What is the speed limit at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport?
items.a: 200 knots indicated, under 14 CFR 91.117(b) (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Aircraft speed). It applies at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area, unless ATC authorizes otherwise.

items.q: What is the speed limit beneath a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor through Class B?
items.a: 200 knots indicated, under 14 CFR 91.117(c). It applies in the airspace underlying a Class B area and in any VFR corridor designated through Class B. Inside the Class B itself the limit is the general 250 knots below 10,000 feet, because ATC is separating that traffic.

items.q: What happens if the minimum safe airspeed for the operation is greater than the speed limit?
items.a: You may fly at that minimum safe speed. 14 CFR 91.117(d) allows an aircraft whose minimum safe airspeed for a particular operation exceeds the maximum prescribed by the section to be operated at that minimum safe speed, and the pilot must notify ATC. This is written for heavy or high-performance types on approach, not as a general excuse.

items.q: Is there a speed limit above 10,000 feet MSL?
items.a: There is no indicated airspeed limit above 10,000 feet MSL in Part 91 for civil aircraft, other than the prohibition on supersonic flight for civil aircraft over the United States. The 250 knot limit of 14 CFR 91.117 applies below 10,000 MSL, and the aircraft's own Vno and Vne limits, from the POH or AFM, always apply.

items.q: What is special use airspace?
items.a: Airspace where activities must be confined because of their nature, or where limitations are imposed on aircraft that are not part of those activities. The types are prohibited areas, restricted areas, warning areas, military operations areas, alert areas, controlled firing areas and national security areas.

items.q: Give a mnemonic for the types of special use airspace.
items.a: MC PRAWN: Military operations area, Controlled firing area, Prohibited area, Restricted area, Alert area, Warning area, National security area. A common alternative is WARMPC for the same list without national security areas. Knowing the list matters less than knowing the entry rule for each.

items.q: What is a prohibited area and what is the rule for entering one?
items.a: Airspace of defined dimensions within which flight is prohibited, established for security or national welfare reasons, such as over the White House or Camp David. Entry requires permission from the controlling agency, which is essentially never granted. It is charted with a blue hatched boundary and a P number, and the rule is the same VFR or IFR, under 14 CFR 91.133 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Restricted and prohibited areas). A prohibited area is charted as a blue hatched band with a P number inside, and its altitudes and times of use appear in the special use airspace table in the chart margin.

items.q: What is a restricted area and how do you enter one?
items.a: Airspace containing unusual, often invisible hazards such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery or guided missiles. Entry without the permission of the using or controlling agency is prohibited by 14 CFR 91.133. Charted with a blue hatched boundary and an R number, with times, altitudes and controlling agency listed in the chart panel. When it is not active you may be cleared through by the controlling agency; when it is active, IFR clearances are routed around it and VFR must stay out or get permission.

items.q: What is a warning area?
items.a: Airspace of defined dimensions extending from 3 nautical miles outward from the coast, containing activity that may be hazardous to non-participating aircraft. It exists because the activity is in international airspace where the United States cannot legally prohibit flight. It is charted with a blue hatched boundary and a W number. Entry is not prohibited, but you should contact the controlling agency before transiting.

items.q: What is an alert area and what is required to fly through it?
items.a: Airspace containing a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity, neither of which is inherently hazardous. It is charted with a blue hatched boundary and an A number. No permission is required and there is no entry restriction; both participating and transiting pilots are equally responsible for collision avoidance, so transit with full vigilance and, ideally, with flight following.

items.q: What is a military operations area and what is the rule for VFR and IFR flight through one?
items.a: An MOA is airspace established outside Class A to separate military training from IFR traffic and to tell VFR pilots where that training happens. It is charted with a magenta hatched boundary. VFR aircraft may enter without permission, and should contact the controlling agency for a traffic advisory and exercise extreme caution. IFR aircraft are cleared through only if separation can be provided, otherwise ATC routes them around. On the chart a MOA is a magenta hatched band labeled with its name, and its times, altitudes and controlling agency are listed in the special use airspace table in the chart margin.

items.q: What is a controlled firing area and why is it not charted?
items.a: An area where activities are conducted under conditions that eliminate the hazard to non-participating aircraft, using spotters, radar or ground observers who stop the activity the moment an aircraft approaches. Because the burden of avoidance falls entirely on the using agency and not on the pilot, no chart depiction and no entry restriction are needed.

items.q: What is a national security area?
items.a: Airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions established at ground facilities where there is a need for increased security. Pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying through it. When a greater level of security is needed, flight may be temporarily prohibited by regulation under 14 CFR 99.7, and that prohibition is published by NOTAM. On a sectional a national security area is a thick dashed magenta line with an explanatory note, and remaining clear is voluntary unless a NOTAM makes it mandatory.

items.q: Where do you find the operating times, altitudes and controlling agency for special use airspace?
items.a: In the special use airspace panel on the sectional, which lists each area by number with its altitudes, times of use, controlling agency and frequency. Times shown as intermittent or by NOTAM mean you must check NOTAMs before the flight, and the safest practical method is always to call the controlling agency on the listed frequency and ask whether it is hot.

items.q: What is a temporary flight restriction and why are TFRs established?
items.a: A TFR is a temporary regulatory restriction on flight in a defined area. The reasons are to protect persons and property from an existing or imminent hazard; to provide a safe environment for disaster relief aircraft; to prevent unsafe congestion of sightseeing aircraft over an incident; to protect declared national disaster areas for humanitarian reasons; to protect the President, Vice President and other public figures; and to provide a safe environment for space agency operations. See 14 CFR 91.137, 91.141 and 91.143.

items.q: How are TFRs published and how do you find out about one?
items.a: Through FDC NOTAMs, which are regulatory, and through a weather briefer or an approved briefing source. They are also depicted on the FAA TFR website and in most electronic flight bags. Because a TFR can be issued hours before departure and is never on your sectional, checking is a required part of preflight action under 14 CFR 91.103.

items.q: What does a Presidential TFR look like?
items.a: Typically a 30 nautical mile outer ring with a 10 nautical mile inner core, from the surface to 18,000 feet MSL, issued under 14 CFR 91.141 (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, Flight restrictions in the proximity of the Presidential and other parties). The inner core is closed to almost all general aviation; in the outer ring you generally need to be on an IFR or VFR flight plan with a discrete transponder code and in two-way contact with ATC. Read the actual NOTAM, since the terms vary.

items.q: What is a stadium TFR?
items.a: A standing restriction over major sporting events: no aircraft below 3,000 feet AGL within 3 nautical miles of any stadium with a seating capacity of 30,000 or more, from one hour before to one hour after the event, for major league baseball, NFL, NCAA Division I football and major motor speedway events. It is issued under 14 CFR 91.145 and published by NOTAM, and it applies whether or not you knew the game was on.

items.q: What are military training routes and how do you read their numbers?
items.a: MTRs are corridors flown at high speed, often below 10,000 feet MSL and at more than 250 knots. IR means IFR routes and VR means VFR routes. A route with a four-digit number, such as IR1006, is flown entirely at or below 1,500 feet AGL; a three-digit number, such as VR102, means one or more segments go above 1,500 feet AGL. They are charted as thin gray lines; contact Flight Service for the schedule.

items.q: What are the rules for flying over national parks, wildlife refuges and wilderness areas?
items.a: Pilots are requested to maintain at least 2,000 feet AGL over these areas, which are marked on sectionals by a blue dotted line. It is an advisory request under an FAA advisory circular rather than a regulation for most areas, but some parks have specific regulatory restrictions published by NOTAM, and the 91.119 minimum safe altitudes always apply.

items.q: What is an Air Defense Identification Zone and what does it require?
items.a: An ADIZ is airspace over land or water in which the ready identification, location and control of all aircraft is required in the interest of national security. Operating in or penetrating one generally requires a filed flight plan, a functioning two-way radio, an operating transponder with Mode C, and position reports. The Washington DC Special Flight Rules Area additionally requires a specific online training course.

items.q: When is a transponder with altitude reporting required?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.215 (Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use): in all Class A, B and C airspace; within the 30 NM Mode C veil of a Class B primary airport; above the ceiling of and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or C up to 10,000 MSL; and at and above 10,000 feet MSL over the 48 states, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL.

items.q: Does the 200-knot restriction near a Class C or D primary airport apply inside Class B airspace?
items.a: No. The 200-knot rule expressly does not apply within a Class B airspace area; operations there revert to the general limit of 250 knots indicated below 10,000 feet MSL. The restriction also yields when ATC otherwise authorizes or requires a different speed. This is 14 CFR part 91, subpart B (Flight Rules), General, section 91.117, Aircraft speed, which caps indicated airspeed at 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 NM of the primary Class C or D airport.

items.q: Are there any entry or equipment requirements to fly VFR in Class G airspace?
items.a: None at all. Class G is uncontrolled, so no clearance, no radio contact and no transponder is required by the airspace itself, and ATC provides no separation service. Only the visibility and cloud clearance values of 14 CFR 91.155 (Part 91, Subpart B - Basic VFR weather minimums) and the aircraft equipment rules constrain you.

items.q: What are the minimum safe altitudes for VFR flight?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B - Minimum safe altitudes: General): anywhere, an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface; over congested areas, 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet; over other than congested areas, 500 feet above the surface; and takeoff and landing are excepted.

items.q: How does the 500-foot rule differ over open water and sparsely populated areas?
items.a: There is no altitude floor at all: over open water or sparsely populated areas the airplane simply may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure, under 14 CFR 91.119 (Part 91, Subpart B - Minimum safe altitudes: General). Over other than congested areas the rule is instead 500 feet above the surface, and the emergency landing standard always applies.

items.q: You lose the radio inbound to a towered field. What do the light gun signals mean in flight?
items.a: Steady green is cleared to land; flashing green means return to the airport for landing, with a steady green to follow at the right moment; steady red means give way to other traffic and continue circling; flashing red means the airport is unsafe, do not land; alternating red and green is a general warning to exercise extreme caution. See 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B (Flight Rules, General), section 91.125 ATC light signals.

items.q: What do the tower light gun signals mean to an aircraft on the ground?
items.a: Steady green is cleared for takeoff; flashing green means cleared to taxi; steady red means stop; flashing red means taxi clear of the runway in use; flashing white means return to your starting point on the airport; alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution. The signals are listed in 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B (Flight Rules, General), section 91.125 ATC light signals.

items.q: Which light gun signal means the same thing in the air and on the ground, and which one is ground only?
items.a: Alternating red and green is a general warning meaning exercise extreme caution, and it carries that same meaning whether you are flying or taxiing. Flashing white is the ground only signal, telling you to return to your starting point on the airport, and it has no meaning in flight. Every other color changes meaning between the two situations, so you must know which set applies to you.

items.q: Two airplanes are approaching head on. What does each pilot do?
items.a: Each pilot alters course to the right. Neither aircraft has the right of way, so both must turn, and the turn should be made early and be large enough that the other pilot can plainly see it. This is 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B (Flight Rules, General), section 91.113 Right-of-way rules: Except water operations, the rule deciding who gives way when aircraft converge.

items.q: Two aircraft are converging at about the same altitude. Who has the right of way?
items.a: The aircraft to the other's right has the right of way, so if the traffic is off your right side you give way. That applies between aircraft of the same category; otherwise an aircraft in distress comes first, then a balloon, a glider, an airship, an aircraft towing or refueling another, and last a plain airplane or rotorcraft. From 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B (Flight Rules, General), section 91.113 Right-of-way rules: Except water operations.

items.q: What are the rules when you overtake another aircraft?
items.a: The aircraft being overtaken has the right of way. The overtaking aircraft, whether climbing, descending or level, must alter course to the right and pass well clear. The same keep to the right habit applies when you are following a road, river, canyon or shoreline, so opposing traffic passes down your left. From 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B (Flight Rules, General), section 91.113 Right-of-way rules: Except water operations.

items.q: Under a Class B shelf, how do you work out every layer of airspace above a nontowered airport?
items.a: Read upward from the ground. With a magenta vignette over a field at 535 MSL and a shelf from 3,000 to 11,000: Class G from the surface to 699 AGL, Class E from 700 AGL to 2,999 MSL, Class B 3,000 to 11,000, Class E from 11,000 up to 18,000, then Class A from 18,000 MSL to FL600.

items.q: What is the airspace stack above a Class D airport that lies under a Class B shelf?
items.a: From the surface up: Class D from the surface to its charted ceiling, say 2,900 MSL; Class E from 2,900 to the floor of the shelf at 4,000; Class B from 4,000 to 11,000; Class E from 11,000 up to 18,000; and Class A above that to FL600. The sliver of Class E between the Class D top and the shelf is the layer pilots forget.

items.q: Must you report weather to ATC under IFR, and which weather?
items.a: Yes. You must report any unforecast weather conditions encountered, per 91.183(c), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications.' That includes unexpected icing, turbulence, thunderstorms or conditions that differ from the forecast you planned against. This report is required at all times, radar contact or not.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: any unforecast weather conditions

items.q: What must you tell ATC when you leave an assigned altitude under IFR?
items.a: Report vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level for a newly assigned altitude or flight level, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports, which applies at all times whether or not you are in radar contact. The standard phrasing is 'Warrior four five bravo leaving six thousand for four thousand.'
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level

items.q: What do you report when you arrive at a holding fix or clearance limit?
items.a: The time and altitude or flight level upon reaching a holding fix or the point to which you were cleared, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times, in radar contact or not, because ATC uses it to protect the airspace and plan your onward clearance.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: time and altitude or flight level upon reaching a holding fix

items.q: What report is required when you leave a holding fix?
items.a: Report leaving any assigned holding fix or point, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports, required at all times whether or not in radar contact. Together with the report on reaching the fix, it brackets your time in the hold for ATC.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: leaving any assigned holding fix or point

items.q: What are compulsory reporting points, and when must you report over them?
items.a: They are fixes shown on en route charts as solid triangles, and a position report is required over them when you are not in radar contact, per 91.183(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications,' and AIM 5-3-2. Open triangles are on-request reporting points. The report contains identification, position, time, altitude, type of flight plan and ETA for the next fix.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: compulsory reporting points

items.q: When must you tell ATC about your climb or descent rate?
items.a: Whenever you are unable to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times. On a warm day at gross weight a Warrior II can easily fall below 500 feet per minute in the climb through the mid-altitudes, so this report comes up in real life; check the POH climb performance chart before accepting a high altitude.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: unable to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute

items.q: What must you report if you go missed?
items.a: Report when an approach has been missed, and request clearance for specific action, for example another approach or clearance to the alternate, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times, in radar contact or not.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: executing a missed approach

items.q: When does a change in true airspeed have to be reported to ATC?
items.a: When the average true airspeed at cruising altitude varies by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from that filed in the flight plan, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times. For a Warrior II filed at 110 knots true, 10 knots is the greater figure, so a sustained change of 10 knots or more is reportable.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: change in average true airspeed at cruise of 5 percent or 10 knots

items.q: What must you report if navigation or communication equipment fails under IFR?
items.a: You must report any loss of VOR, TACAN, ADF, low frequency navigation receiver capability, GPS anomalies while using installed IFR-certified GPS, complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability, or impairment of air-ground communications, per 91.187, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports.' Include aircraft identification, the equipment affected, the degree of impairment, and the assistance you want.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: loss of navigation capability

items.q: Is there a catch-all IFR reporting item?
items.a: Yes. You must report any information relating to the safety of flight, per 91.183(c), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications.' If something is happening that ATC would want to know about to keep you or anyone else safe, tell them; this is the clause that covers everything the specific items do not.
items.concept: Mandatory IFR report: any information relating to the safety of flight

items.q: Which IFR reports are required only when you are not in radar contact?
items.a: Three: leaving the final approach fix or outer marker inbound on final approach; a corrected estimate whenever a previously submitted estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes; and position reports over compulsory reporting points, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. In the North Atlantic the corrected estimate threshold is 3 minutes. Everything else on the list is required at all times.
items.concept: Which IFR reports are required only when not in radar contact

items.q: Where do you look up the full list of required IFR reports?
items.a: AIM paragraph 5-3-3, 'Reports,' in Chapter 5, En Route Procedures, which splits them into reports required at all times and reports required only when not in radar contact. The regulatory hooks are 91.183, Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications,' and 91.187, 'Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports.'
items.concept: AIM 5-3-3 as the source for IFR position and additional reports

items.q: What does a steady green light mean to a vehicle or ground personnel on the movement area?
items.a: It means cleared to cross, proceed or go. The vehicle or person may cross the runway or taxiway or continue along the route they were waiting on. The signal parallels the takeoff clearance given to an aircraft, which is why a pilot should know the ground columns as well: if you see a vehicle receive a steady green while you are holding, expect it to move onto the surface ahead of you. See 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, section 91.125.
items.concept: Steady green - vehicles, equipment and ground personnel

items.q: What does a flashing green light mean to a vehicle or ground personnel?
items.a: Nothing; the cell is not applicable. Flashing green is a signal aimed at aircraft only, meaning cleared to taxi on the ground or return for landing in the air, so the light gun table assigns it no meaning for vehicles, equipment or personnel on the movement area. A driver who sees it should not move and should await a signal that does apply. Per 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, section 91.125, ATC light signals.
items.concept: Flashing green - vehicles, equipment and ground personnel (not applicable)

items.q: What does a steady red light mean to a vehicle or ground personnel?
items.a: It means stop, exactly as it does for an aircraft on the ground. The vehicle or person must halt where they are and hold position until another signal is given, and must not cross or enter the runway or taxiway. Steady red is one of the signals that carries the same plain meaning in both ground columns, which makes it easy to remember. Per 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, section 91.125, ATC light signals.
items.concept: Steady red - vehicles, equipment and ground personnel

items.q: What does a flashing red light mean to a vehicle or ground personnel?
items.a: It means clear the taxiway or runway immediately. Unlike steady red, which says stop and hold, flashing red tells the driver or person to get off the movement area at once, normally because an aircraft needs that surface. A pilot should know this so that on a nonradio arrival he can predict what the vehicles he can see will do. From 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, section 91.125, ATC light signals.
items.concept: Flashing red - vehicles, equipment and ground personnel

items.q: What does a flashing white light mean to a vehicle or ground personnel?
items.a: It means return to your starting point on the airport, the same as it does for an aircraft on the ground. The driver or person is to go back to where they entered the movement area and hold there. Flashing white is the only signal whose two ground columns read identically while having no meaning at all in flight. Reference: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, section 91.125, ATC light signals.
items.concept: Flashing white - vehicles, equipment and ground personnel

items.q: How do you acknowledge a light gun signal from the tower?
items.a: In daylight, by rocking your wings; at night, by flashing your landing light or navigation lights once. On the ground, move the ailerons or rudder during daylight hours, or flash the taxi or landing light at night. The tower has no other way of knowing you saw and understood the signal, so the acknowledgment matters. If a nonradio arrival is planned, call the tower by telephone beforehand where practical.
items.concept: Acknowledging a light gun signal

items.q: You see a stadium symbol on the sectional. What does it mean to you?
items.a: That there is a large stadium there, charted as a visual landmark, and that it carries a standing flight restriction whenever a qualifying sporting event is in progress. The chart does not draw the restricted airspace, because the restriction only exists while the event is on, so the symbol is a prompt to check NOTAMs for the day rather than an airspace boundary.

items.q: State the standing sporting event flight restriction.
items.a: No aircraft below 3,000 feet AGL within a 3 nautical mile radius of any stadium with a seating capacity of 30,000 or more people during a qualifying event, effective from one hour before the scheduled event time until one hour after the end of the event. It is published as a standing FDC NOTAM rather than being charted, and it is reissued and renumbered periodically.

items.q: Which events trigger the stadium restriction?
items.a: Major League Baseball, National Football League and NCAA Division One football games, and major motor speedway events such as NASCAR Sprint, Indy Car and Champ series races, at stadiums or speedways seating 30,000 or more. A high school game, a minor league game, a concert or a Division Two football game does not trigger it, though a separate TFR can always be issued for any of them.

items.q: What is the regulatory basis for the stadium restriction and for sporting event TFRs generally?
items.a: The standing stadium NOTAM is issued as a special security instruction under 14 CFR 99.7, Special security instructions. Separately, 14 CFR 91.145, Management of aircraft operations in the vicinity of aerial demonstrations and major sporting events, is the rule the FAA uses to put temporary restrictions around air shows and major sporting events by NOTAM. Cite both and say which one the stadium NOTAM uses.

items.q: Who may operate inside a stadium restriction?
items.a: Only the operations the NOTAM allows. Typically that is law enforcement and military aircraft supporting the event, air ambulance flights, aircraft operating under an ATC clearance for arrival or departure at an airport inside the restricted area, and approved event-related operations such as a broadcast or banner operator with a waiver. A transient VFR airplane without a reason to be there has none.

items.q: You are a commercial pilot and someone offers you money to tow a banner over a game. What is your answer?
items.a: That the stadium restriction forbids it unless the operation is specifically approved, so I would need the event's approval and an FAA waiver before I accepted the job. Banner towing is otherwise an operation a commercial pilot can be paid for without a Part 119 certificate, under the exception in 14 CFR 119.1(e), but the airspace restriction is a separate problem and the money does not solve it.

items.q: How do you find out whether a stadium restriction is active on your route today?
items.a: Check NOTAMs in the preflight briefing and look at the graphical TFR depiction, and read the FDC NOTAMs, not just the local field ones. The stadium restriction is time-based and tied to the event schedule, so you have to know when the game is. On a route that passes a charted stadium, the safe planning move is to route around it or above 3,000 feet AGL and not depend on the timing being what you expected.

items.q: What happens if you blunder through an active stadium restriction?
items.a: You may be intercepted, and you can expect a certificate action: a special security instruction issued under 14 CFR 99.7 has the force of a regulation, and 14 CFR 91.103, Preflight action, required you to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight. The defense that you did not know is the admission that you did not check NOTAMs. Squawk, listen on 121.5 and comply if you are intercepted.

items.q: What exactly is a MOA, and may you fly through one?
items.a: A military operations area is airspace of defined vertical and lateral limits established outside Class A to separate certain nonhazardous military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR aircraft may fly through one without a clearance or permission at any time, active or not, but should exercise extreme caution and should check with the controlling agency. IFR traffic is cleared through only if ATC can provide separation; otherwise you get rerouted.

items.q: The examiner points at a prohibited area on the chart and asks what it is. What do you say?
items.a: That it is a prohibited area, identified by its P number, that flight within it is prohibited under 14 CFR Part 73, and that I would read the special use airspace panel on the chart for the altitudes, times and controlling agency and check NOTAMs rather than rely on memory for what that particular one protects. If I do not know what is under it, I say so; being certain about the rule matters more than naming the site.

items.q: What is specifically prohibited inside the outer ring of a presidential TFR?
items.a: Flight training, practice instrument approaches, aerobatics, glider and parachute operations, banner towing, sightseeing, model aircraft, and anything else the NOTAM names, even though transit is allowed on a flight plan with a discrete code. Read the NOTAM text itself rather than assuming the standard template, because the dimensions and the exceptions change with the visit and sometimes mid-visit.

items.q: Name the Part 91 rules under which temporary flight restrictions are issued.
items.a: 14 CFR 91.137, Temporary flight restrictions in the vicinity of disaster/hazard areas; 91.138, for national disaster areas in Hawaii; 91.139, Emergency air traffic rules; 91.141, for the President and other parties; 91.143, Flight limitation in the proximity of space flight operations; and 91.145, Management of aircraft operations in the vicinity of aerial demonstrations and major sporting events. Security restrictions come separately under 14 CFR 99.7.

items.q: Sort these for me: MOA, restricted, prohibited, alert, warning, national security area.
items.a: MOA separates military training from IFR traffic and VFR may enter. Restricted contains invisible hazards and needs permission when active. Prohibited is closed outright. An alert area simply warns of a high volume of training and carries no entry restriction at all, with both pilots responsible for collision avoidance. A warning area is the same kind of hazard as a restricted area but begins 3 nautical miles out over international water. A national security area asks you to stay out voluntarily.

b: Density altitude, weight and balance, V-speeds, aerodynamics and load factor.

items.q: What is Vso and where do you find the number for your aircraft?
items.a: Vso is the stalling speed, or minimum steady flight speed, in the landing configuration, that is gear down and full flaps at maximum landing weight. It is the bottom of the white arc on the airspeed indicator. The actual figure is type-specific and must be read from the POH or AFM for the aircraft being flown.

items.q: What is Vs1 and how does it differ from Vso?
items.a: Vs1 is the stalling speed in a specified configuration, normally clean, meaning flaps and gear up. It is higher than Vso because without flaps the wing produces less lift at a given speed. Vs1 is the bottom of the green arc. Both figures are published in the POH or AFM for the aircraft you are flying and both are quoted at maximum weight.

items.q: What is Vx and what does it buy you?
items.a: Vx is the best angle of climb speed, giving the greatest gain in altitude in the shortest horizontal distance. It is the speed for clearing an obstacle off the end of the runway. It is flown at the airspeed where excess thrust is greatest. It is slower than Vy, so it gives worse engine cooling and poorer visibility over the nose, and should be held only as long as the obstacle requires.

items.q: What is Vy and when do you use it?
items.a: Vy is the best rate of climb speed, giving the greatest gain in altitude in the shortest time. It is the speed for the normal climb to cruise once obstacles are behind you, and it is the speed flown at the airspeed where excess power is greatest. Use the number in the POH or AFM for the aircraft being flown, corrected for weight and altitude where the manual gives that correction.

items.q: How do Vx and Vy change with altitude?
items.a: Vx increases and Vy decreases with altitude, and they converge at the absolute ceiling, where the only remaining climb speed produces zero rate of climb. Both are indicated airspeeds, so the true airspeeds are climbing faster than the indicated figures suggest. This convergence is why climb performance falls away sharply at high density altitude.

items.q: What is best glide speed and how does it change with weight?
