items.a: Best glide is the speed that gives the greatest distance for altitude lost, which is the speed for the maximum lift-to-drag ratio. It decreases as weight decreases. A lighter aircraft glides at a lower airspeed but achieves the same glide ratio and the same distance; a heavier aircraft glides at a higher speed over the same distance, arriving sooner. Published figures are at maximum gross weight, so reduce slightly when light.

items.q: What is Vfe and what marks it on the airspeed indicator?
items.a: Vfe is the maximum flap extended speed, the highest speed at which the flaps may be flown in the extended position. It is the top of the white arc. Many aircraft publish more than one figure, a higher speed for the first small increment of flap and a lower speed for the larger settings, so read the specific limits from the POH or AFM.

items.q: Why do some aircraft publish more than one flap limiting speed?
items.a: Because the aerodynamic load on the flap and its structure rises steeply with deflection. A small first setting adds mostly lift with a modest load, so it can be carried at a higher speed; the large settings add a great deal of drag and bending load, so they carry a lower limit. Where the manual publishes staged limits, the top of the white arc reflects the highest of them, and the lower limits are placarded.

items.q: What is Vno and what does the yellow arc mean?
items.a: Vno is the maximum structural cruising speed, the top of the green arc and the start of the yellow arc. Below it the aircraft can withstand a full sharp-edged gust. The yellow arc between Vno and Vne is the caution range: it may be used only in smooth air, and even then with caution, because a gust encountered there can overstress the airframe.

items.q: What is Vne and how is it marked?
items.a: Vne is the never exceed speed, marked by the red line at the top of the airspeed indicator. It must never be exceeded in any operation. Beyond it structural failure or control flutter becomes possible. It is normally set at 90 percent of the speed demonstrated in flight test, and the actual value comes from the POH or AFM for the aircraft flown.

items.q: What is Va, design maneuvering speed?
items.a: Va is the maximum speed at which full, abrupt deflection of a single flight control may be made without exceeding the limit load factor. At or below Va the wing stalls before the structure breaks. Above it, full control deflection or a strong gust can overstress the airframe. Va is not marked on the airspeed indicator; it is a placard or POH figure, and it varies with weight.

items.q: Why does Va increase with weight?
items.a: Because a heavier aircraft stalls at a higher airspeed. The protection Va gives works by letting the wing stall and shed the load before the structure is overloaded. At high weight the wing needs a higher speed to reach the critical angle of attack, so the speed at which stall protects the structure is also higher. At low weight the wing stalls sooner, so Va comes down. The same reasoning applies to the other weight-dependent airspeeds, not just maneuvering speed: stall speeds and best glide rise with weight too.

items.q: If Va is published at maximum gross weight, what do you fly at a lower weight?
items.a: You fly a lower speed. Va decreases with weight, so an aircraft below maximum gross must use a reduced maneuvering speed. Many manuals publish Va at two or three weights; interpolate between them, or use the rule of thumb that Va varies with the square root of the weight ratio. Getting this wrong the safe way means going slower than necessary, which costs nothing.

items.q: What are Vle and Vlo?
items.a: Vle is the maximum landing gear extended speed, the highest speed at which the aircraft may be flown with the gear down and locked. Vlo is the maximum landing gear operating speed, the highest speed at which the gear may be moved in transit; some aircraft publish separate extension and retraction figures. Neither is marked on the airspeed indicator, and both come from the POH or AFM.

items.q: What does the white arc on the airspeed indicator represent?
items.a: The flap operating range. Its bottom is Vso, the stalling speed in the landing configuration at maximum weight, and its top is Vfe, the maximum flap extended speed. Anywhere inside the arc it is legal to have flaps extended; the flaps must be retracted before accelerating past the top of it.

items.q: What does the green arc on the airspeed indicator represent?
items.a: The normal operating range. Its bottom is Vs1, the stalling speed clean at maximum weight, and its top is Vno, the maximum structural cruising speed. The whole arc may be used in any conditions, including turbulence, because within it the structure can take a full sharp-edged gust.

items.q: Which V-speeds are marked on the airspeed indicator and which are not?
items.a: Marked: Vso and Vfe as the ends of the white arc; Vs1 and Vno as the ends of the green arc; the yellow caution arc from Vno to Vne; and Vne as the red line. Not marked: Va, Vx, Vy, best glide, Vle and Vlo. Those are found in the POH or AFM and on placards, which is exactly why they are the ones pilots forget.

items.q: What is density altitude?
items.a: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature: the altitude in the standard atmosphere at which the air has the density you are actually flying in. It is the altitude the airplane and engine think they are at. It has no direct use for terrain clearance; it is purely a performance figure, and it is the entry argument for most takeoff, climb and landing charts.

items.q: What three conditions increase density altitude?
items.a: High temperature, high altitude and high humidity. Each of these thins the air. Remember that high density altitude means low air density and poor performance. Hot, high and humid is the classic accident setup, because all three degrade takeoff and climb at the same time, and the pilot sees a normal indicated airspeed while the aircraft is nowhere near normal performance.

items.q: What three conditions decrease density altitude?
items.a: Low temperature, low altitude and low humidity. Cold, low and dry air is dense air, which gives more lift for the same indicated airspeed, more power from the engine and more thrust from the propeller, so takeoff rolls shorten and climb rates improve. A cold morning at sea level is the best performance the aircraft will ever give you.

items.q: Why does humid air have a lower density than dry air?
items.a: Because a water molecule is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules it displaces. Adding water vapor to a given volume at a given pressure and temperature pushes out heavier molecules, so the mixture weighs less. The effect is smaller than temperature or altitude but it is real, and it is worst on the hot, humid days when performance is already marginal.

items.q: How does high density altitude affect the wing?
items.a: The thin air produces less lift at any given true airspeed, so the wing must move faster through the air to generate the lift needed for flight. The indicated airspeed for lift-off, stall and climb is unchanged, but the true airspeed and therefore the groundspeed at those indicated speeds are higher. That is why the takeoff roll is longer and the landing roll is longer.

items.q: How does high density altitude affect the engine?
items.a: The engine produces less power because it takes in less mass of air per cycle. A normally aspirated engine loses roughly 3 percent of its power per thousand feet of density altitude, and the mixture goes progressively richer if left alone, further reducing power. The remedy for the mixture is to lean, but nothing recovers the lost mass flow. A turbocharged engine holds power to its critical altitude.

items.q: How does high density altitude affect the propeller?
items.a: The propeller produces less thrust because each blade is an airfoil working in thin air. Fewer air molecules pass over the blade per second, so it produces less aerodynamic force for the same rotational speed and blade angle. The propeller is therefore less efficient, and this loss compounds with the engine power loss: the engine turns the propeller more weakly and the propeller converts that into less thrust.

items.q: Summarize the three ways an aircraft is degraded as air density falls.
items.a: Power, thrust and lift all decrease. Power falls because the engine takes in less air. Thrust falls because the propeller is less efficient in thin air. Lift falls because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils. The result is a longer takeoff roll, a shallower climb angle, a lower rate of climb, a reduced service ceiling and a longer landing roll.

items.q: How do you compute density altitude in the aircraft?
items.a: Set 29.92 in the altimeter to read pressure altitude, then correct it for temperature with a flight computer, the chart in the POH, or the rule of thumb of adding about 120 feet of density altitude for every degree Celsius the outside air is above the standard temperature for that pressure altitude. Standard is 15 degrees Celsius at sea level, falling about 2 degrees per thousand feet.

items.q: What is pressure altitude?
items.a: The height above the standard datum plane, the theoretical level where the pressure is 29.92 inches of mercury. You read it by setting 29.92 in the altimeter, or by applying the correction printed in the Chart Supplement. It is the entry argument for almost every performance chart, and it is the first step toward density altitude. You can compute it on the ground without touching the altimeter: 29.92 minus the setting, times 1,000, added to the field elevation.

items.q: What is indicated altitude and what makes it accurate?
items.a: What you read on the altimeter with the current local altimeter setting in the Kollsman window. It is accurate only if the setting is current and from a station within 100 nautical miles, and only if the temperature is close to standard. Flying from high pressure to low pressure, or from warm to cold air, without resetting leaves the aircraft lower than indicated. The altimeter is also susceptible to temperature error, not only to a stale setting: flying into lower pressure or lower temperature it reads higher than true altitude, which is the point of high to low, look out below.

items.q: What is true altitude?
items.a: The actual vertical distance above mean sea level. Airport elevations, terrain and obstruction heights, and most airway and chart figures are expressed as true altitude in MSL. Indicated altitude equals true altitude only when standard temperature and pressure conditions exist; in cold air true altitude is lower than indicated.

items.q: What is absolute altitude?
items.a: The height above the ground, in AGL. It is what a radar altimeter reads and it changes constantly as the terrain beneath you rises and falls. Pattern altitudes, minimum safe altitudes over non-congested areas and cloud bases in reports are all expressed in AGL, so mixing AGL and MSL is a common and dangerous planning error.

items.q: What is indicated airspeed and what is calibrated airspeed?
items.a: Indicated airspeed is what the airspeed indicator reads, driven by the difference between pitot and static pressure. Calibrated airspeed is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error, which is largest at low speed and high angle of attack. The correction table is in the POH or AFM for the aircraft flown.

items.q: What is true airspeed and how does it relate to indicated airspeed as you climb?
items.a: True airspeed is the speed of the aircraft through the air mass around it. As you climb into thinner air the indicator under-reads, so true airspeed becomes progressively higher than indicated, by very roughly 2 percent per thousand feet. That is why the same indicated approach speed at a high field means a much higher groundspeed and a longer landing roll.

items.q: What is groundspeed and how is it derived?
items.a: True airspeed corrected for wind, which is how fast the aircraft is moving over the ground. It is the only speed that determines how long a leg takes and therefore how much fuel it consumes. A headwind reduces it, a tailwind increases it, and a crosswind component reduces it slightly through the wind correction angle.

items.q: When are calibrated, true and ground speed all the same number?
items.a: At sea level in the standard atmosphere with no wind. Under those conditions calibrated airspeed equals true airspeed because the air density is the standard reference density, and true airspeed equals groundspeed because there is nothing pushing the aircraft off its path. Any departure from standard density or any wind breaks the equality.

items.q: What are the four forces acting on an airplane in flight?
items.a: Lift, weight, thrust and drag. Lift acts perpendicular to the relative wind, weight acts vertically downward through the center of gravity, thrust acts forward along the propeller axis and drag acts rearward parallel to the relative wind. In unaccelerated straight and level flight they are in equilibrium, that is lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Thrust equal to drag is specifically the condition for constant speed, and it applies in a climb or descent, not only in level flight. Lift equal to weight means a steady climb or descent rate, not necessarily level flight; lift greater than weight increases the rate of climb and lift less than weight decreases it. Weight is the only one of the four forces that always points at the center of the earth, and in maneuvering flight it is mass times gravity times load factor.

items.q: What is the lift equation and what does each term tell you?
items.a: Lift equals the coefficient of lift times one half the air density times velocity squared times wing area. The coefficient of lift is set by angle of attack and flap setting and is the pilot's main control; density is set by density altitude; velocity is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the lift; wing area is fixed except for flaps. It explains why a small speed change has such a large effect on lift. Beyond the four terms of the equation, this sheet lists the levers separately: angle of attack, air density, wing surface area, airfoil efficiency, camber and true airspeed, with camber the one the pilot changes by lowering flaps.

items.q: What is an airfoil and which parts of the aircraft are airfoils?
items.a: An airfoil is any surface designed to produce useful aerodynamic force from its motion through the air. On an airplane the wings, the horizontal tail surfaces, the vertical tail surface and the propeller blades are all airfoils. That last one matters: the propeller produces thrust by producing lift, which is why it loses effectiveness in thin air exactly as a wing does.

items.q: What is angle of incidence?
items.a: The angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the wing's chord line and the airplane's longitudinal axis: it is the angle at which the wing is bolted to the fuselage. It is a design value chosen by the manufacturer and the pilot cannot change it. It is not angle of attack, which is measured against the relative wind and changes constantly in flight.

items.q: What is angle of attack?
items.a: The angle between the wing chord line and the relative wind. It is directly controlled by the pilot and it is the variable that determines the coefficient of lift. A wing stalls at one particular angle of attack, the critical angle, regardless of airspeed, weight, bank angle or attitude, which is why a wing can stall at any speed and in any attitude.

items.q: What is relative wind?
items.a: The direction of the airflow with respect to the wing. It is always parallel and opposite to the flight path of the aircraft through the air mass. In a climb the relative wind comes from below the flight path, in a descent from above, and in a stall recovery the pilot changes the angle of attack by changing the relationship between the chord line and this airflow.

items.q: State Bernoulli's principle and how it applies to a wing.
items.a: The pressure of a fluid decreases where the speed of the fluid increases. Air accelerating over the curved upper surface of a wing arrives at a lower static pressure than the slower air beneath, and that pressure difference is a large part of the lift. High speed flow means low pressure; low speed flow means high pressure.

items.q: How does Newton's third law explain lift?
items.a: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The wing deflects a mass of air downward, and the reaction to that downward acceleration is an upward force on the wing. Bernoulli and Newton are two descriptions of the same event, not competing theories; both are needed for a complete picture of how a wing works.

items.q: What are the three axes of an airplane and which control surface moves it about each?
items.a: The longitudinal axis, nose to tail, is rolled by the ailerons; the lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip, is pitched by the elevator; the vertical axis, top to bottom, is yawed by the rudder. All three axes pass through the center of gravity, which is why moving the CG changes the effectiveness of every control.

items.q: What is induced drag and what causes it?
items.a: Induced drag is the drag penalty that comes with producing lift. High pressure under the wing spills around the tip into the low pressure above it, setting up wingtip vortices; those vortices push the air behind the wing downward. That downwash tilts the total lift vector rearward, and the rearward component of it is induced drag. It is greatest at high angle of attack and low airspeed, and it varies inversely with the square of the airspeed.

items.q: What is parasite drag and what are its three types?
items.a: Parasite drag is the drag from the aircraft moving through the air that is not associated with producing lift. The three types are form drag, from the shape of parts sticking into the airflow such as the pitot tube, antennas and tires; interference drag, where two airflows meet and interfere, as at a wing root; and skin friction drag, from the air dragging on the imperfectly smooth surface of the aircraft.

items.q: How do induced and parasite drag vary with airspeed, and what is L over D max?
items.a: Induced drag decreases with airspeed and parasite drag increases with the square of airspeed. Their sum, total drag, is a U-shaped curve with a minimum where the two are equal. That minimum is the maximum lift-to-drag ratio, L over D max, which is the best glide speed and, in level flight, the speed for maximum endurance of range depending on the aircraft.

items.q: What is the region of reversed command?
items.a: The range of airspeeds below L over D max where more power is required to fly slower, because induced drag is climbing steeply as speed decreases. In this region the aircraft is behind the power curve: a nose-up correction reduces speed and increases the power needed, so the aircraft settles further. It is where a low, slow, high-drag approach becomes unrecoverable, and the fix is to lower the nose and add power together.

items.q: What do flaps do, and what do they not do?
items.a: Flaps increase the lift and the drag of the wing at any given angle of attack, which lets the aircraft fly slower and descend more steeply without increasing speed, and gives a better view over the nose on approach. They lower the stall speed. They do not increase angle of attack, and they do not by themselves increase the wing's structural strength, which is why Vfe exists.

items.q: What is ground effect and when does it occur?
items.a: Ground effect is the reduction in induced drag when the wing is within about one wingspan of the surface, because the ground interferes with the formation of the wingtip vortices and reduces downwash. It is strongest at a height of about a quarter of the wingspan. On takeoff it can allow the aircraft to become airborne below safe flying speed and then settle back; on landing it produces the float during the flare.

items.q: What are the four left-turning tendencies?
items.a: P-factor, torque, gyroscopic precession and spiralling slipstream. All four act to yaw a single-engine airplane with a clockwise-turning propeller to the left, and all four are strongest in the same condition: high power, low airspeed and high angle of attack, which is exactly the takeoff and climb. Right rudder is the answer to all of them.

items.q: What is P-factor?
items.a: Asymmetric propeller loading. At a high angle of attack the descending blade on the right side meets the relative wind at a higher angle of attack and takes a bigger bite of air than the ascending blade on the left, so it produces more thrust. The thrust line moves to the right of center and the aircraft yaws left. It is negligible in cruise and strong in slow flight, climb and takeoff.

items.q: How does engine torque produce a left turning tendency?
items.a: By Newton's third law: the engine and propeller turn clockwise as seen from the cockpit, so the airframe is pushed counterclockwise, rolling to the left. In flight this shows as a left roll tendency. On the ground the rolling moment presses the left main wheel down harder, giving it more friction than the right, and the airplane veers left during the takeoff roll.

items.q: How does gyroscopic precession cause a left yaw?
items.a: A spinning propeller behaves like a gyroscope, in which a force applied to the rim is felt 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation. Raising the tail on takeoff applies a forward force to the top of the propeller disc; 90 degrees around a clockwise rotation, that force is felt on the right side, which yaws the nose left. It is most pronounced in tailwheel aircraft as the tail comes up.

items.q: What is spiralling slipstream and when is it strongest?
items.a: The air accelerated by the propeller travels back around the fuselage in a corkscrew path and strikes the left side of the vertical fin and rudder, pushing the tail right and yawing the nose left. It is most noticeable when the propeller is turning fast and the aircraft is moving slowly, that is at high power and low airspeed on takeoff and in the climb.

items.q: What is adverse yaw and what causes it?
items.a: Adverse yaw is the tendency of the nose to yaw opposite to the direction of roll. Rolling right, the left aileron goes down, which increases that wing's lift and therefore its induced drag, while the right aileron goes up, reducing lift and induced drag on that side. The extra drag on the rising wing drags the nose left just as you roll right. It is worst at low speed and high angle of attack, when induced drag dominates.

items.q: What design features reduce adverse yaw?
items.a: Differential ailerons, where the up-going aileron deflects further than the down-going one so the drag is more balanced; Frise-type ailerons, whose leading edge protrudes into the airflow below the up-going wing to add drag there; coupled rudder and aileron systems; and drooped or upturned wingtip designs that alter the tip vortex. None of them removes the need for rudder.

items.q: What is load factor?
items.a: Load factor is the ratio of the total load supported by the wings to the actual weight of the airplane, expressed in Gs. In unaccelerated level flight it is 1G. Any maneuver or gust that bends the flight path away from a straight line requires the wings to make more lift than weight, and that extra lift is a structural load. It is a ratio, not a force, which is why it does not depend on how heavy the airplane is.

items.q: How does load factor vary with bank angle in a level turn?
items.a: It increases with the bank angle and is independent of airspeed and aircraft weight. It equals one divided by the cosine of the bank angle, so it rises slowly at first and then very steeply. At 30 degrees it is 1.15 G, at 45 degrees 1.41 G, at 60 degrees 2.0 G, and at 75 degrees it is 3.86 G. Beyond 60 degrees a small increase in bank is a large increase in load. The mechanism is worth stating: in the bank the vertical component of lift falls below weight and the airplane descends unless a higher angle of attack restores it, and that extra lift is exactly what drives load factor above one.

items.q: How does load factor affect stall speed?
items.a: As load factor increases, stalling speed increases, in proportion to the square root of the load factor. At 2 G, in a 60 degree level bank, the stall speed is about 1.41 times the wings-level figure, a 41 percent increase. This is why an accelerated stall is possible at seemingly safe airspeeds, and why the base-to-final overbank is so lethal. The two figures to have ready for a level 60-degree bank are a load factor of 2 g and a 40 percent increase in stall speed.

items.q: What is centrifugal force in a turn and how does it relate to lift?
items.a: Centrifugal force is the equal and opposite reaction of the airplane to the change of direction, acting outward and opposite to the horizontal component of lift. In a level turn the vertical component of lift must still equal weight while the horizontal component turns the aircraft, so the total lift, and therefore the load factor, must increase as bank increases.

items.q: Does an aircraft stall at a particular airspeed or a particular angle of attack?
items.a: At a particular angle of attack, the critical angle of attack, always. The published stall speed is simply the airspeed at which, at maximum gross weight, wings level and 1 G, the wing happens to reach that angle. Change the weight, the load factor or the configuration and the stall speed changes, but the critical angle of attack does not.

items.q: What are basic empty weight and useful load?
items.a: Basic empty weight is the airframe, engine, all permanently installed equipment, unusable fuel and full operating fluids, including full engine oil in most modern manuals. Useful load is maximum ramp or gross weight minus basic empty weight, that is the total of usable fuel, occupants, baggage and cargo you may carry. Both figures come from the current weight and balance record for the specific aircraft.

items.q: Define datum, station, arm and moment.
items.a: The datum is an imaginary vertical reference plane chosen by the manufacturer from which all horizontal distances are measured. A station is a location along the fuselage expressed as its distance from the datum. The arm is the horizontal distance from the datum to the center of gravity of an item. The moment is weight multiplied by arm, and it is what actually gets summed in a weight and balance computation.

items.q: How do you compute the center of gravity of a loaded aircraft?
items.a: Multiply each item's weight by its arm to get its moment, sum all the weights and sum all the moments, then divide total moment by total weight. The result is the CG expressed as inches from the datum. Compare it with the forward and aft limits in the POH or AFM at that weight, and check both the takeoff and the landing condition after fuel burn.

items.q: How do you compute a weight shift?
items.a: Use the proportion: weight shifted divided by total weight equals change in CG divided by the distance the weight was moved. Rearranged, the CG change equals weight moved times the distance moved, divided by total weight. Moving weight aft moves the CG aft, and the same is true of adding weight aft of the current CG.

items.q: What does a forward center of gravity do to the aircraft?
items.a: It makes it more stable in pitch but less controllable. The tail must produce more downforce, so the wing carries more load and the aircraft effectively flies heavier: a higher stall speed, a higher approach speed, a longer takeoff roll from the greater back pressure needed, more drag and a lower cruise true airspeed, and a harder flare. Stall recovery is better because the nose drops readily.

items.q: Why is a forward CG associated with being easier to stall?
items.a: Because the extra tail downforce adds to the effective load the wing must lift, so at any given airspeed the wing is at a higher angle of attack, and therefore closer to the critical angle. It also raises the stall speed. The compensation is that once the wing does stall, the nose-heavy aircraft pitches down of its own accord, which is what recovery requires.

items.q: What does an aft center of gravity do to the aircraft?
items.a: It makes the aircraft less stable in pitch and harder to recover from a stall. The tail downforce needed is smaller, so the wing carries less load: a lower stall speed, less drag and a higher cruise true airspeed. But the shorter arm to the tail reduces elevator authority, the aircraft is twitchy in pitch, and stall and spin recovery become difficult or, past the aft limit, impossible.

items.q: Why is the aft CG limit the dangerous one?
items.a: Because it removes the aircraft's own tendency to recover. A forward CG costs performance but the nose still drops at the stall. Behind the aft limit, longitudinal stability is lost: the nose does not pitch down, the elevator may lack the authority to lower it, and a stall can develop into a flat spin from which recovery is not possible. The penalty for being forward is money; the penalty for being aft is the airplane.

items.q: How does fuel burn move the center of gravity in flight?
items.a: It depends on where the tanks are relative to the CG. If the fuel is forward of the CG the aircraft moves aft as it burns, and if it is aft the CG moves forward. In many light aircraft the wing tanks sit close to the CG so the shift is small, but it is never zero. Check the CG at both takeoff and zero-fuel or landing weight, because a legal takeoff loading can become an illegal landing loading.

items.q: How does operating at a heavier weight affect takeoff and climb?
items.a: Longer ground roll, higher lift-off speed, reduced rate and angle of climb, reduced maneuverability, and a higher stall speed. The wing must reach a higher angle of attack for the same airspeed, so it flies closer to the critical angle; it produces more induced drag, so cruise true airspeed falls; and the extra weight on the nosewheel affects handling on the ground.

items.q: How does a lighter weight affect performance?
items.a: Shorter ground roll, lower lift-off and stall speeds, better climb rate and angle, and a higher cruise true airspeed, because a lower angle of attack is needed for level flight so there is less induced drag. The wing is further from the critical angle of attack at any given speed. The trade is that Va and best glide speed both come down, and the ride in turbulence is rougher.

items.q: How does runway surface affect takeoff and landing distance?
items.a: A soft or rough surface such as grass, sand, mud or snow increases the takeoff distance, sometimes by 25 percent or more, because rolling resistance and wheel drag are much greater. The same surface generally shortens the landing roll for the same reason, though it costs braking control. Standing water or slush adds impingement drag on takeoff and can cause hydroplaning on landing. Apply the corrections given in the POH or AFM. The chart notes quantify it: dry grass adds about 15 percent to the takeoff ground roll and about 45 percent to the landing ground roll, and a tailwind adds 10 percent per 2 knots.

items.q: How does runway gradient affect takeoff and landing distance?
items.a: An upslope increases the takeoff distance and decreases the landing distance, because the aircraft must climb the hill while accelerating and the same hill helps decelerate it. A downslope does the opposite. A 1 to 2 percent gradient is enough to matter at a short field. Gradient is published in the Chart Supplement, and at a one-way strip it, not the wind, may decide which direction you use.

items.q: What are the limitations of the performance charts in the pilot's operating handbook?
items.a: They were produced with a brand-new airplane, flown by an experienced factory test pilot, in ideal conditions, on a smooth, dry, level, paved runway with a perfectly executed technique. Your aircraft has a worn engine, a rigged-out airframe and dirty surfaces, and you are not that pilot. Treat chart numbers as the best possible case, never as a prediction.

items.q: What safety margin should you apply to book takeoff and landing distances?
items.a: A common and defensible practice is to add at least 50 percent to the chart figure, that is require a runway of at least 1.5 times the computed distance, and more for a soft surface, an obstacle, a marginal density altitude, or an aircraft you do not know well. The chart figure is a legal reference under 14 CFR 91.103; the margin is what makes it survivable.

items.q: What are the VFR fuel requirements, and how do they change at night?
items.a: Enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, plus a reserve computed at normal cruise consumption of 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night, under 14 CFR 91.151 (Part 91, Subpart B - Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions). The reserve is a legal floor rather than a plan; most operators set a personal minimum of one hour on landing.

items.q: What preflight information are you required to gather before a flight?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B - Preflight action) you must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight: NOTAMs; weather reports and forecasts; known traffic delays advised by ATC; runway lengths at the airports of intended use; alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed as planned; fuel requirements; and takeoff and landing distance data.

items.q: Which parts of the preflight action rule apply to every flight?
items.a: Runway lengths at the airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data apply to any flight, while weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available, and any known traffic delays are required for IFR flights and for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, under 14 CFR 91.103 (Part 91, Subpart B - Preflight action). The distance data must come from the approved flight manual.

items.q: What happens to lift in a stall?
items.a: Lift is drastically reduced but it is not zero. Past the critical angle of attack the airflow separates from the upper surface, so the wing loses most of its lift and gains a great deal of drag, but it keeps producing some lift; that is why a stalled airplane descends rather than drops. The recovery is to reduce the angle of attack, which reattaches the flow.

items.q: What is a skidding turn, and how do you correct it?
items.a: A skid is too much rudder for the bank: the nose is pointed too far inside the turn, the tail slides outward, and the ball goes to the outside of the turn. The correction is less rudder in the direction of turn, or more bank. A skid at low speed and high power is the classic entry to a spin off the base-to-final turn.

items.q: What is a slipping turn, and how do you correct it?
items.a: A slip is too little rudder for the bank: the nose points outside the turn, the airplane slides toward the low wing, and the ball goes to the inside of the turn. The correction is more rudder in the direction of the turn, or less bank. A slip flown deliberately, with crossed controls, is a useful way to lose altitude or hold the centerline in a crosswind.

items.q: What is Mach number and why would a piston pilot care about it?
items.a: The ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound. The speed of sound falls with temperature, so the same true airspeed is a higher Mach number when it is cold or high. Light piston airplanes never approach it and turbine types are limited by Mmo, but the same physics sets the propeller tip speed limit on any airplane.

items.q: With 4,000 indicated, an altimeter setting of 29.49 and an OAT of 20 degrees C, what are the other altitudes?
items.a: Pressure altitude is about 4,400, since 29.49 is 0.43 inches below standard and each hundredth is worth about 10 feet. The warm air pushes density altitude to roughly 4,800. Over terrain at 1,000 MSL absolute altitude is 3,000 AGL, and true altitude is near 4,000, in fact slightly higher because the air is warmer than standard.

items.q: Which regulation sets IFR fuel requirements, and what is its official title?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.167, Part 91, Subpart B, titled 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' In plain English, no person may operate a civil aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first airport of intended landing, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, and then for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. Helicopters use 30 minutes instead of 45.
items.concept: 91.167 IFR fuel requirements rule

items.q: What is the first of the three IFR fuel legs?
items.a: Enough fuel to complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather, per 91.167(a)(1), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' That means the fuel to fly the filed route and the expected approach, not the great circle distance.
items.concept: IFR fuel: fuel from departure to the first airport of intended landing

items.q: What is the second IFR fuel leg, and when does it apply?
items.a: Fuel to fly from that airport to the most distant alternate airport listed in the flight plan, per 91.167(a)(2), Part 91, Subpart B. It applies only if an alternate is required or filed. If you file two alternates you must carry fuel to reach the farther one.
items.concept: IFR fuel: fuel from the destination to the most distant alternate

items.q: What is the IFR fuel reserve, and how is it calculated?
items.a: 45 minutes at normal cruising speed, after the destination and any alternate, per 91.167(a)(3), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' It is a time reserve computed at normal cruise fuel flow and altitude, not a fixed gallon figure, and unlike the VFR rule it is 45 minutes day or night.
items.concept: IFR fuel: plus 45 minutes at normal cruising speed

items.q: When is an IFR alternate not required?
items.a: When the destination has a standard instrument approach procedure and, for at least 1 hour before through 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the forecast ceiling is at least 2,000 feet above airport elevation and visibility at least 3 statute miles, per 91.167(b), Part 91, Subpart B. That is the 1-2-3 rule. Alternate airport weather minimums themselves are in 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
items.concept: The alternate fuel leg applies only if an alternate is required: the 1-2-3 rule

items.q: How do you turn the 91.167 fuel rule into gallons in your Warrior II?
items.a: Take the planned cruise fuel flow from the POH cruise performance tables, typically around 8 to 9 gallons per hour for a 160 horsepower Lycoming O-320 at a normal cruise power setting, and multiply by the time to destination, plus time to the alternate if required, plus 0.75 hour for the 45-minute reserve. Add taxi, runup, climb and any approach allowance, then compare against usable fuel, which is 48 gallons on most Warrior IIs; confirm your airplane's usable fuel and fuel flow against the POH.
items.concept: Applying 91.167 to the PA-28-161 Warrior II

items.q: Are NOTAMs part of the required preflight action, and which ones matter?
items.a: Yes, they fall under all available information concerning that flight in 91.103, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' Check NOTAMs for departure, destination and alternate airports, for navigation aids and GPS outages along the route, and for temporary flight restrictions. Get them from an official source such as the FAA NOTAM search or an approved briefing provider, and remember a TFR can be issued after you depart.
items.concept: NW KRAFT N: NOTAMs

items.q: What weather must you obtain before a flight under 91.103?
items.a: Weather reports and forecasts for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' That means the current and forecast conditions at departure, en route, destination and alternates: METARs, TAFs, area forecasts or graphical forecasts, winds aloft, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, PIREPs and icing and turbulence products, all from a source approved for preflight briefing.
items.concept: NW KRAFT W: weather reports and forecasts

items.q: What does the known traffic delays item require?
items.a: Any known traffic delays of which the pilot in command has been advised by ATC, for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' Delays matter because holding burns the fuel you planned as reserve, which is why this item sits next to the fuel requirement in the same paragraph.
items.concept: NW KRAFT K: known traffic delays

items.q: What does the alternatives item of 91.103 require you to think about?
items.a: Alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' This is more than an IFR alternate airport: it is the set of diversion fields, routes and turnback points you identified before departure, with their weather, runway lengths, fuel availability and hours. Picking them on the ground is the antidote to deciding under pressure in the air.
items.concept: NW KRAFT A: alternatives available

items.q: What performance data must you have before every flight?
items.a: Takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, or other reliable data for an aircraft without one, per 91.103(b), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' For the Warrior II use the POH takeoff and landing distance charts for the day's weight, pressure altitude, temperature, wind and runway surface, then add a margin, because the book numbers were flown by a test pilot in a new airplane on a dry paved runway.
items.concept: NW KRAFT T: takeoff and landing performance data

items.q: What is VF, and how does it differ from VFE?
items.a: VF is the design flap speed, a certification speed the manufacturer uses when stressing the flap structure during design. VFE is the operating limit shown to the pilot: the maximum flap extended speed, marked as the top of the white arc. You fly to VFE; VF sits behind it in the certification basis and is not a cockpit number. Take VFE from your Warrior II's indicator and POH rather than guessing either one.
items.concept: V-speed: VF, design flap speed

items.q: What is VREF?
items.a: The calculated final approach speed, the reference speed flown across the threshold, conventionally about 1.3 times VSO at the actual landing weight. Transport and turbine aircraft publish a VREF table that varies with weight. A light trainer like the 1981 Warrior II generally does not; its POH gives normal and short field approach speeds instead. Use the POH approach speeds and apply the handbook's gust correction.
items.concept: V-speed: VREF, calculated final approach speed

items.q: What is equivalent airspeed?
items.a: Calibrated airspeed corrected for compressibility error. Air behaves as effectively incompressible at low speeds, so below roughly 200 knots and 10,000 feet, equivalent and calibrated airspeed are the same number and a Warrior II pilot never sees a difference. The correction matters to high speed and high altitude aircraft. EAS is the formal step between calibrated and true airspeed.
items.concept: Type of speed: equivalent airspeed (EAS), CAS corrected for compressibility error

items.q: What is critical Mach number?
items.a: The lowest Mach number at which airflow over any part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound. The airplane as a whole is still subsonic, but a local region over the thickest part of the wing has gone sonic. Above it a shock wave forms, bringing buffet, a pitch change and loss of control effectiveness. It is a jet and high performance concern rather than a Warrior one, but it is examinable.
items.concept: Type of speed: critical Mach, lowest Mach number at which airflow over any part of the aircraft reaches the speed of sound

items.q: Explain the low speed stall.
items.a: As airspeed decreases, the angle of attack must be increased to retain the lift required to maintain altitude. Eventually an angle of attack is reached at which the wing is not producing enough lift to support the aircraft, and it stalls. This is the classic straight-ahead power-off stall, and it is the case the published stall speed in the handbook describes.
items.concept: Low speed stall - as airspeed decreases the angle of attack must increase to hold altitude until the wing can no longer support the aircraft

items.q: What is static stability?
items.a: Static stability is the initial tendency, the direction of movement, that an aircraft displays toward or away from its original state of equilibrium immediately after it is disturbed. It describes only that first reaction in the first instant; it says nothing about what the motion does afterward, which is the job of dynamic stability.
items.concept: Static stability - the initial tendency, or direction of movement, back to equilibrium

items.q: What is positive static stability?
items.a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to return to its original state of equilibrium after being disturbed. Displace the nose with a bump and the airplane starts straight back toward the trimmed attitude on its own. Airplanes certificated in the normal category are required to show it about all three axes within the normal operating envelope.
items.concept: Positive static stability - the initial tendency to return to the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed

items.q: What is neutral static stability?
items.a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to remain in the new condition after its equilibrium has been disturbed. It neither moves back toward the original state nor further away from it, but simply stays where the disturbance left it. A ball resting on a flat tabletop is the usual picture.
items.concept: Neutral static stability - the initial tendency to remain in the new condition after equilibrium has been disturbed

items.q: What is negative static stability?
items.a: The initial tendency of the aircraft to continue away from the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed, so the displacement grows from the first instant. It is static instability, and the usual picture is a ball balanced on top of a dome, which rolls away once nudged. Loading the center of gravity aft of the limit moves an airplane in this direction.
items.concept: Negative static stability - the initial tendency to continue away from the original state of equilibrium after being disturbed

items.q: What is dynamic stability?
items.a: Dynamic stability describes the motion an aircraft displays over time after being disturbed from its trimmed condition, in other words what happens to the oscillation once the initial tendency has acted. The two forms are independent: an airplane can be positively statically stable and still have negative dynamic stability, giving oscillations that grow with each cycle.
items.concept: Dynamic stability - the behavior over time after being disturbed from the trimmed condition

items.q: What is positive dynamic stability?
items.a: Over time the motion of the displaced object decreases in amplitude and the object returns toward the equilibrium state, each oscillation smaller than the one before it until the motion dies out. A trimmed airplane whose phugoid damps out over a few cycles after a disturbance is showing it, and it is what makes an airplane restful to fly hands off.
items.concept: Positive dynamic stability - over time the motion decreases in amplitude and the object returns toward equilibrium

items.q: What is neutral dynamic stability?
items.a: Once displaced, the object neither decreases nor increases in amplitude, so the oscillation simply continues at the same size indefinitely. A worn automobile shock absorber exhibits this tendency: the car keeps bouncing after a bump instead of the motion dying away.
items.concept: Neutral dynamic stability - once displaced the motion neither decreases nor increases in amplitude; a worn automobile shock absorber

items.q: What is negative dynamic stability?
items.a: Over time the motion of the displaced object increases in amplitude and becomes more divergent, each oscillation larger than the last, until the pilot intervenes or the structure is overstressed. It is dynamic instability, and it is not acceptable in a certificated airplane in any mode the pilot is expected to control.
items.concept: Negative dynamic stability - over time the motion increases and becomes more divergent

items.q: Which handbook actually applies to this airplane?
items.a: Piper Report VB-880. This airplane is serial 28-8116257, which falls in TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300, and that block is covered by VB-880. The handbook circulating online for the Warrior II is VB-1180, which covers serials 28-8316001 and up. It is the right model but the wrong revision, so the systems carry across and the weights and the speeds that depend on weight do not.

items.q: What is the maximum takeoff weight of this airplane?
items.a: 2325 pounds in the normal category and 2020 pounds in utility, from FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, the item whose serial range contains 28-8116257. The widely circulated Warrior II handbook prints 2440 pounds, but that is the later serial block from 28-8316001 up and it is not this airplane. I would confirm it against Section 2 of the book actually in the airplane.

items.q: Someone hands you a Warrior II POH that says 2440 pounds. What do you say?
items.a: That it is the right model and the wrong serial block. 2440 pounds belongs to serials 28-8316001 and up, covered by report VB-1180; this airplane is 28-8116257 and TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A gives 2325 pounds normal. Everything that scales with weight goes with it: maneuvering speed, the stall speeds behind the airspeed indicator arcs, the climb and approach speeds, and all of Section 5.

items.q: What is the maximum ramp weight of this airplane?
items.a: I would take that from Section 2 of the airplane's own handbook, because it is not published anywhere I can verify. The TCDS gives no ramp weight, and the 2447 pounds in the later handbook is simply that book's 2440 pound gross plus the 7 pound start, taxi and run-up fuel allowance. I could do the same arithmetic on 2325 pounds, but the answer would be my arithmetic rather than a published limit.

items.q: Is the maximum landing weight the same as the takeoff weight?
items.a: On the later serials it is: that handbook prints the same figure for both, so there is no reduced landing weight on this type. For this airplane the likely answer is that takeoff and landing weight are both 2325 pounds, but applying that convention to a different serial block is an assumption, so I would confirm it in Section 2 of this airplane's own handbook rather than state it flatly.

items.q: What is maneuvering speed on this airplane?
items.a: It has to come from this airplane's own handbook, because maneuvering speed is quoted at a gross weight and this airplane's gross weight is not the one in the circulating book. That book gives 111 KIAS at 2440 pounds and 88 KIAS at 1531 pounds, with linear interpolation permitted; interpolating to 2325 pounds gives about 108 knots, which the square root of weight rule agrees with, but that is derived, not published.

items.q: What does the maneuvering speed placard in the cockpit say?
items.a: On the later serials it reads Va equals 111 KIAS at 2440 pounds, see POH. The placard physically in this airplane will name a different weight and a different speed, because its gross weight is 2325 pounds, so I would read my own placard and quote that. Pointing out that the printed placard in the common handbook belongs to a different serial block is a good way to show I understand applicability.

items.q: What is turbulent air operating speed, and how does it relate to Va?
items.a: They are the same speed under two names. The handbook lists turbulent air operating speed in Section 4 and refers you straight back to the design maneuvering speed paragraph in Section 2. So it carries exactly the same weight dependence, and the figure for this airplane has to come from its own book rather than from the 2440 pound number printed in the later handbook.

items.q: How many markings are on this airspeed indicator, and is one of them blue?
items.a: Four markings and no blue line: one red radial at 160 KIAS, a yellow arc 126 to 160, a green arc 50 to 126 and a white arc 44 to 103. A blue radial is single-engine best rate of climb on a twin, so it does not belong on a Warrior. The caution is that three of those four endpoints are weight dependent and were set at a heavier gross weight than this airplane's.

items.q: Where does the handbook print Vso and Vs1?
items.a: It does not print them as named speeds at all. The stall speeds come out of the arcs and out of one sentence in Section 4: the gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS, which is also the bottom of the white arc, and 50 KIAS at the bottom of the green arc is Vs1 by convention. Both are gross weight figures at 2440 pounds, so this airplane stalls slower and its own book gives the numbers.

items.q: What are Vx and Vy on this airplane?
items.a: The circulating handbook gives best rate of climb at 79 KIAS and best angle at 63 KIAS, both explicitly at gross weight, and adds that at lighter than gross weight these speeds are reduced somewhat. Gross weight in that book means 2440 pounds, which is not this airplane's, so I would fly the speeds from this airplane's own handbook and expect them to be a little lower.

items.q: What approach speeds does the handbook give?
items.a: An initial approach speed of about 70 KIAS and a final approach speed of 63 KIAS with flaps extended to 40 degrees, with flaps able to be lowered at speeds up to 103 KIAS. Section 4.5 says plainly that the Section 4 speeds are for standard airplanes flown at gross weight under standard conditions at sea level, and that gross weight is 2440 pounds, so this airplane's own figures will be a little lower.

items.q: What glide ratio does this airplane have?
items.a: No glide ratio is published anywhere in the handbook. What is published is a glide performance chart at 73 KIAS with the propeller windmilling, flaps up and no wind, and the chart's own worked example loses 3000 feet of altitude over 5.6 nautical miles. I would present that as reading the chart rather than as a published ratio, and I would say that the chart itself is drawn at a weight this airplane does not operate at.

items.q: What is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component?
items.a: 17 knots, printed in Section 4.5 and on the cockpit placard as DEMO. X-WIND 17 KTS. It is a demonstrated value rather than a limitation, so it is what a test pilot showed on a particular day, not a line the airplane cannot cross. Whether I would accept 17 knots depends on my currency and the runway, and the handbook's crosswind technique is a faster approach with partial or no flaps.

items.q: What are the baggage limits?
items.a: 200 pounds in the normal category and zero in utility. The baggage door placard says BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS and then UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION, NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. The 200 pounds is a structural limit, so it is the same across the Warrior II serial range, but on a 2325 pound airplane you run out of gross weight long before you run out of baggage allowance.

items.q: Where is the datum on this airplane?
items.a: 78.4 inches ahead of the wing leading edge at the inboard intersection of the straight and tapered section, which is a geometric definition and so is the same whatever the gross weight. The loading arms are geometry too and carry across: pilot and front passenger 80.5 inches, rear seats 118.1, fuel 95.0 and baggage 142.8, all aft of datum.

items.q: What are the center of gravity limits?
items.a: The rearward limit is 93.0 inches aft of datum throughout, and the forward limit varies with weight: 83.0 inches at 1950 pounds and less, with straight line variation above that. The upper anchor printed in the circulating handbook is 88.3 inches at 2440 pounds, which is not this airplane's gross weight, so the whole upper part of its envelope comes from its own book. The utility rows are 83.8 at 2020 pounds and 83.0 at 1950 and below.

items.q: Does the handbook publish a moment limit table?
items.a: No. Section 2 gives the CG limits in inches only, and Section 6 works in weight and arm with a loading graph and a graphical center of gravity envelope. There is no moment envelope with inch-pound limits anywhere in the handbook, so any table in that form has come from another source and I would check it against the airplane's own weight and balance data before trusting it.

items.q: What maneuvers are prohibited in the normal category?
items.a: Section 2.15: all acrobatic maneuvers including spins are prohibited in the normal category. The in-full-view-of-pilot placard says the same thing twice over, that no acrobatic maneuvers are approved for normal category operations and that spins are prohibited for normal and utility category. So the commercial maneuvers that need more than 60 degrees of bank have to be flown in the utility category.

items.q: What maneuvers are approved in the utility category?
items.a: Three, for bank angles exceeding 60 degrees: steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles. Those three carry across to this airplane. What does not carry is the entry speed, because the 111 KIAS printed beside them in the circulating handbook is maneuvering speed at 2440 pounds; this airplane's entry speed is lower and comes from its own book and its own placard.

items.q: What else does utility category operation require?
items.a: No aft passengers and no baggage, per the baggage door placard and the utility category placard, which also raises the positive limit load factor from 3.8 G to 4.4 G. Spins stay prohibited in both categories. In practice that means the commercial maneuvers are flown with two people in the front, nothing in the back, and a center of gravity inside the utility envelope.

items.q: What are the flight load factors?
items.a: Section 2.17: positive 3.8 G in the normal category and 4.4 G in utility. For negative G the handbook does not print a number at all; it writes no inverted maneuvers approved across both columns. It also publishes no separate flaps-up and flaps-down load factors, so the commonly taught 2.0 G flaps-down figure is from the certification rule and not from this handbook.

items.q: What kinds of operation is this airplane approved for?
items.a: Section 2.19: day or night VFR and day or night IFR, when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable. There is no icing approval stated anywhere in Section 2, so flight into known icing is not approved. The handbook also carries an MEL statement, that certain operations may be authorized with listed equipment inoperative under a current FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List dated concurrently with or after the handbook.

items.q: What equipment does the handbook require for day VFR in this airplane?
items.a: Twelve items in Section 2.19: airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer, oil pressure indicator, oil temperature indicator, fuel pressure indicator, fuel quantity indicator for each tank, volt-ammeter, elevator and rudder trim indicator, alternator, and a safety restraint for each occupant. The two people forget are the fuel pressure indicator and the volt-ammeter, and that list is a better answer for this airplane than reciting the regulation.

items.q: What is added for night VFR, and for IFR?
items.a: Section 2.19: night VFR adds position lights, instrument lights and anti-collision strobe lights to the day VFR list. Day IFR adds a vacuum pump and a gyro suction indicator, which is why the vacuum system being optional on this type matters. Night IFR is simply everything required for day and night VFR plus everything required for day IFR.

items.q: If the handbook lists required equipment, why does 91.205 still matter?
items.a: Because the handbook says so. The NOTE at the end of Section 2.19 reads that the above system and equipment list does not include specific flight instruments and communication and navigation equipment required by the FAR Part 91 and 135 operating requirements. So the POH list is the type certification basis and the operating rule sits on top of it; I need both to be satisfied before the airplane is legal.

items.q: Can you use the Section 5 performance charts out of the common handbook?
items.a: No. Every chart in that section is computed for a 2440 pound airplane, including takeoff ground roll and distance, climb, cruise, landing distance, glide and the stall speed chart, whose weight axis is drawn to maximum weight 2440 pounds. This airplane plans from its own book. Some of those charts do read down to lighter weights, so entering them at 2325 pounds is not nonsense, but they are not approved data for this airplane.

items.q: What is the wing loading and power loading of this airplane?
items.a: The handbook prints 14.4 pounds per square foot and 15.3 pounds per horsepower, but both are computed at 2440 pounds and are therefore not this airplane's. At 2325 pounds they work out around 13.7 and 14.5, but those are derived figures and are not published anywhere, so I would offer them as arithmetic rather than quote them as handbook values.

items.q: How do you do a short field takeoff in this airplane?
items.a: Here is the trap: the handbook's plain short field takeoff is accomplished without flaps, by applying full power before brake release, lifting off at 40 to 52 KIAS depending on weight and climbing out at 79 KIAS. It is the short field with an obstacle that uses 25 degrees, the second notch. Those speed bands are quoted at a heavier gross weight, so I would take the numbers from this airplane's own book.

items.q: How do you do a soft field takeoff?
items.a: Both soft field cases use 25 degrees of flap, the second notch. The technique is to accelerate and lift the nose gear off as soon as possible, lift off at the lowest possible airspeed, and then with an obstacle accelerate just above the ground to 52 KIAS to climb past it, or without an obstacle accelerate just above the ground to the best rate of climb speed, retracting the flaps slowly while climbing out.

items.q: What is the handbook's technique for a short field landing?
items.a: Section 4.31: the best technique for short and slow landings is to use full flap and enough power to maintain the desired airspeed and approach flight path, with mixture full rich, fuel on the fullest tank and the electric fuel pump on. Reduce speed during the flare and contact the ground close to the stalling speed, hold the nose wheel off as long as possible, then lower it gently and brake.

items.q: How does the handbook want a crosswind landing flown?
items.a: Section 4.31: in high wind conditions, particularly in strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach the ground at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps. That trades the lower touchdown speed for better control authority and less weathercocking, and it sits alongside the handbook's general guidance to vary the flap setting and touchdown speed with the surface, the wind and the loading.

items.q: Give me the power off landing procedure.
items.a: Section 3.3: locate a suitable field, establish a spiral pattern, be 1000 feet above the field at the downwind position for a normal landing approach, and when the field can easily be reached slow to the shortest-landing speed. Touch down at the lowest possible airspeed with full flaps. When committed, ignition off, master off, fuel selector off, mixture to idle cut-off and belts and harnesses tight.

items.q: How do you lose extra height on a forced landing in this airplane?
items.a: Section 3.13: excess altitude may be lost by widening your pattern, using flaps or slipping, or a combination of these. The caution that goes with slipping is Operating Tip 10.3(i): prolonged slips or skids resulting in more than 2000 feet of altitude loss can uncover the fuel outlet and interrupt the fuel flow when the tank in use is not full, which matters if the engine is still running.

items.q: The engine fails just after takeoff. What does the handbook actually say?
items.a: Section 3.3: if sufficient runway remains for a normal landing, land straight ahead; if not, maintain a safe airspeed, make only a shallow turn to avoid obstructions and use flaps as the situation requires. If enough altitude has been gained to attempt a restart: fuel selector to a tank containing fuel, electric fuel pump check on, mixture check rich, carburetor heat on, primer locked. There is no turn-back option in the book.

items.q: The engine fails in cruise. Walk me through it.
items.a: Section 3.3: fuel selector to a tank containing fuel, electric fuel pump on, mixture rich, carburetor heat on, engine gauges checked for the cause, primer checked locked, and if no fuel pressure is indicated check the selector is on a tank with fuel in it. If power returns, carb heat and pump off. If not, prepare for a power off landing and trim for best gliding angle, taking the speed from this airplane's own handbook.

items.q: Is there a spin recovery procedure, and what is the order?
items.a: Intentional spins are prohibited in this airplane, but there is a recovery: throttle idle, ailerons neutral, rudder full opposite to the direction of rotation, control wheel full forward, then rudder neutral when rotation stops and control wheel as required to smoothly regain level flight. Note Piper's order, with throttle and ailerons first, and note the word smoothly, which is there to avoid a secondary stall or an overspeed.

items.q: What does the category placard in full view of the pilot say?
items.a: THIS AIRPLANE MUST BE OPERATED AS A NORMAL OR UTILITY CATEGORY AIRPLANE IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE OPERATING LIMITATIONS STATED IN THE FORM OF PLACARDS, MARKINGS AND MANUALS. ALL MARKINGS AND PLACARDS ON THIS AIRPLANE APPLY TO ITS OPERATION AS A UTILITY CATEGORY AIRPLANE. FOR NORMAL AND UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION, REFER TO THE PILOT'S OPERATING HANDBOOK. NO ACROBATIC MANEUVERS ARE APPROVED FOR NORMAL CATEGORY OPERATIONS. SPINS ARE PROHIBITED FOR NORMAL AND UTILITY CATEGORY.

items.q: What does the placarded takeoff checklist say, word for word?
items.a: TAKEOFF CHECKLIST: Fuel on proper tank; Seat backs erect; Electric fuel pump on; Fasten belts/harness; Engine gauges checked; Trim tab set; Flaps set; Controls free; Carb. heat off; Door latched; Mixture set; Air conditioner off; Primer locked. It is a two-column placard in full view of the pilot, and note that electric fuel pump on appears there, which makes the pump rule a placarded item rather than advice.

items.q: What does the placarded landing checklist say, word for word?
items.a: LANDING CHECKLIST: Fuel on proper tank; Flaps set (White Arc); Mixture rich; Fasten belts/harness; Electric fuel pump on; Air conditioner off; Seat backs erect. Flaps set, white arc, is the placarded way of saying do not exceed the flap limiting speed of 103 KIAS. A footnote under both placards says the air conditioner off item is mandatory for air conditioned aircraft only.

items.q: What does the baggage compartment placard say?
items.a: BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS. UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION - NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. NORMAL CATEGORY OPERATION - SEE PILOT'S OPERATING HANDBOOK WEIGHT AND BALANCE SECTION FOR BAGGAGE AND AFT PASSENGER LIMITATIONS. It is on the inside of the baggage compartment door, and the 200 pound limit is structural, so it is the same for this serial as for any other Warrior II.

items.q: What does the utility category placard say?
items.a: UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION ONLY. (1) NO AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. (2) ACROBATIC MANEUVERS ARE LIMITED TO THE FOLLOWING: SPINS PROHIBITED; STEEP TURNS; LAZY EIGHTS; CHANDELLES, each with an entry speed printed beside it. The three maneuvers carry across to this airplane; the entry speeds printed in the common handbook are maneuvering speed at 2440 pounds, so this airplane's placard will show its own, lower figure.

items.q: What does the oil cooler winterization placard say?
items.a: OIL COOLER WINTERIZATION PLATE TO BE REMOVED WHEN AMBIENT TEMPERATURE EXCEEDS 50 DEGREES F. It is in full view of the pilot when the winterization kit is installed, and Section 7.5 describes the plate as provided to restrict air during winter operation. For a late November checkride I would look for the plate on the preflight and know the removal rule.

items.q: What does the air conditioner placard say, and when does it apply?
items.a: WARNING - AIR CONDITIONER MUST BE OFF TO INSURE NORMAL TAKEOFF CLIMB PERFORMANCE. It is in full view of the pilot near the air conditioner control panel, and only applies when air conditioning is installed. The matching footnote under the takeoff and landing checklist placards says the air conditioner off item in those checklists is mandatory for air conditioned aircraft only.

items.q: What does the fuel filler placard on this airplane say?
items.a: FUEL - 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE, adjacent to the fuel filler caps. The handbook prints a second, graphic AVGAS ONLY placard with GRADE 100LL and GRADE 100 lines, but restricts it to serial numbers 28-8316037 and up, and this airplane is 28-8116257, so it gets the first version. That is a case where the handbook does the serial-block reasoning for you.

items.q: Summarize the general limitations statement in Section 2.
items.a: Section 2.1: this airplane must be operated as a normal or utility category airplane in compliance with the operating limitations stated in the form of placards and markings and those given in this section and handbook. The point for the oral is where limitations live: not only in Section 2 but in the placards and the instrument markings as well, and all three have to agree with the airplane in front of you.

items.q: What are the power plant instrument markings, all of them?
items.a: Tachometer, green arc 500 to 2700 RPM with the red line at 2700. Oil temperature, green 75 to 245 degrees F, red line 245. Oil pressure, green 60 to 90 PSI, yellow 25 to 60 at idle, a second yellow 90 to 100 for ground warm-up, red lines at 25 and 100. Fuel pressure, green .5 to 8 PSI with red lines at .5 and 8. Those are the figures an examiner can ask for one at a time.

items.q: With a checkride in late November, which limitations would you check first?
items.a: The ones the season touches. Whether the oil cooler winterization plate is fitted, and its 50 degrees F removal rule; the oil grade for the temperature, which in the 0 to 70 degrees F row is SAE 30 straight or 30, 40 or 20W-40 ashless dispersant; carburetor ice, since the handbook's band of minus 5 to 20 degrees C covers a November morning exactly; and the weight the airplane plans to, which is 2325 pounds and not 2440.

items.q: What is the datum on N84054 and where is it physically?
items.a: It is a reference point 78.4 inches ahead of the wing leading edge at the inboard intersection of the straight and tapered wing section, so it hangs in empty space out in front of the spinner. Nothing is bolted there. Every arm in Section 6 is measured aft of it, which is why all the arms on this airplane are positive numbers.

items.q: What is an arm?
items.a: The horizontal distance in inches from the datum to the center of a load. On this airplane the front seats are at 80.5 inches, the rear seats 118.1, the fuel 95.0 and the baggage 142.8. An arm is a fixed property of where the seat or tank is, not of what you put in it, which is why the arms are the same on every Warrior II regardless of gross weight.

items.q: What is a moment and why do you work with it instead of just arms?
items.a: A moment is weight times arm, in inch-pounds - a measure of turning effect about the datum. You use it because moments add and arms do not. Two 100 lb loads at 80.5 and 142.8 are not a 200 lb load at 111.65 by luck; you add their moments and divide by total weight. For the real load that total is 199,118 in-lb, and 199,118 divided by 2,276.99 lb gives the CG.

items.q: How do you find the CG from a completed loading form?
items.a: Divide total moment by total weight. For the real checkride load, 199,118.1 in-lb divided by 2,276.99 lb gives a CG of 87.45 inches aft of datum. Then you check that single number against two limits: the forward limit interpolated at that same total weight, and the aft limit. Weight and CG must both pass; passing one proves nothing about the other.

items.q: What is your airplane's maximum takeoff weight, and why is it not the 2,440 lb in the handbook?
items.a: 2,325 lb normal category. The POH in the airplane is Piper report VB-1180, written for serials 28-8316001 and up, which is TCDS 2A13 item XVI-B at 2,440 lb. Serial 28-8116257 falls in item XVI-A, serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300, which is certificated at 2,325 lb normal and 2,020 lb utility. The book in the cockpit is for a heavier airplane.

items.q: How do you know which TCDS item your airplane falls under?
items.a: By serial number, not by year or model name. Serial 28-8116257 lies between 28-7716001 and 28-8216300, which is TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A at 2,325 lb. The 1982 break at 28-8316001 starts item XVI-B at 2,440 lb. The FAA registry confirms the serial and the 1981 build. When the TCDS and a handbook disagree, the TCDS governs.

items.q: What is the aft CG limit on your airplane and where does it come from?
items.a: 93.0 inches aft of datum, and it is constant at every weight from 1,200 lb to gross. It is read straight off the POH's own Figure 6-15 as the vertical line marked AFT LIMIT 93, it is printed in POH 2.13(a), and the TCDS gives the same figure for item XVI-A. Because it does not depend on gross weight, this one carries across from the 2,440 lb book unchanged.

items.q: What is the forward CG limit on your airplane?
items.a: It is a sloped line: 83.0 inches at 1,950 lb and anything lighter, moving aft in a straight line to 87.0 inches at 2,325 lb. The 83.0 end is read off the POH chart and printed in POH 2.13(a). The 87.0 end is from TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, because the POH's line ends at 88.3 inches at 2,440 lb, which is not this airplane's gross weight.

items.q: Which parts of the POH CG envelope apply to your airplane and which do not?
items.a: The aft limit of 93.0 inches and the forward limit of 83.0 inches at 1,950 lb and below apply, and so does the whole bottom half of the chart. The top does not: Figure 6-15 is captioned 2440 MAX. GROSS WT. and its forward line runs to 88.3 inches at 2,440 lb. Above 2,325 lb the chart describes an airplane that is not his, so the envelope has to be cut off there.

items.q: Does using the POH's forward line instead of the TCDS one change your answer?
items.a: Barely, and it is a useful cross-check. The POH's line runs 83.0 at 1,950 lb to 88.3 at 2,440 lb, a slope of 0.01082 in/lb; extended down to 2,325 lb it reads 87.06 inches against the TCDS's 87.0. They describe the same physical line, and his envelope is that line truncated at 2,325 lb. At the real load the two differ by 0.05 inch of margin and change no verdict.

items.q: How do you interpolate the forward limit at a weight between the published points?
items.a: Straight-line, as POH 2.13 NOTES instructs: Straight line variation between points given. The slope is 4.0 inches over 375 lb, which is 0.01067 inch per pound. So forward limit equals 83.0 plus 0.01067 times weight minus 1,950. At 2,276.99 lb that is 83.0 plus 3.49, giving 86.49 inches. Below 1,950 lb it is flat at 83.0.

items.q: Why does the forward CG limit slope aft as weight increases?
items.a: Because it is a stabilator authority limit, not a balance limit. At the forward CG the stabilator has to produce enough download to raise the nose at rotation and to hold the flare. The heavier the airplane, the more download is needed, and at some point the tail runs out of authority. So the allowable forward CG has to retreat aft as weight rises - 4.0 inches of retreat over the last 375 lb on this airplane.

items.q: Why is the aft limit a straight vertical line when the forward limit slopes?
items.a: Because the aft limit is set by longitudinal stability and spin recovery, and those are governed by how far the CG sits ahead of the neutral point, which does not move with gross weight. Static margin is a geometry question, so the answer is the same 93.0 inches at 1,200 lb as at 2,325 lb. The forward limit is a control-power question, and control power does depend on weight.

items.q: What happens if you load forward of the forward CG limit?
items.a: The airplane gets nose-heavy and the stabilator may not have enough authority to rotate on takeoff or to complete the flare, so you arrive flat or on the nosewheel. Stall speed rises because the tail download adds to the lift the wing must make, takeoff and landing distances grow, climb suffers, and cruise is slower from the extra trim drag. On this load the worst case is only 0.96 inch of forward margin.

items.q: What happens if you load aft of the aft CG limit?
items.a: Longitudinal stability falls away. The airplane becomes twitchy in pitch, may rotate prematurely on takeoff or pitch up in the climb, stall warning and buffet arrive later or not at all, and - the part the POH calls out by name - spin recovery becomes more difficult and may become impossible. The POH's exact words are that it can lead to inadvertent stalls and even spins. The limit is 93.0 inches.

items.q: Which way does the CG move as fuel burns on this airplane, and why?
items.a: Forward. The fuel sits at 95.0 inches, which is aft of the loaded CG of about 87.4, so removing it takes away an aft-of-CG weight and the CG creeps forward. On the real load it moves from 87.45 inches full to 86.35 inches dry - 1.1 inches across all 48 gallons, which is why the POH can say fuel burn-off does not significantly affect the center of gravity.

items.q: If burning fuel moves the CG forward, is landing the critical case on your flight?
items.a: No, and this is the trap. The CG does move forward, but the forward limit drops faster. Each gallon burned moves the CG forward about 0.020 inch while dropping the forward limit 0.064 inch, so the margin grows about 0.044 inch per gallon. Forward margin goes from 0.96 inch at brake release to 1.69 inches after two hours and 2.94 inches dry. Takeoff binds.

items.q: So which end of the flight do you have to check on this loading?
items.a: Takeoff, at full fuel. That is where total weight is highest, the forward limit is furthest aft, and the margin is smallest at +0.96 inch. On an airplane whose fuel is aft of the CG you still check both ends, because a load that is aft-limit-critical at takeoff could in principle run forward in flight - but on this nose-heavy load every gallon burned helps.

items.q: Why are two adults of your size in the front seats the hard case on this airplane?
items.a: Because 500 lb goes in at 80.5 inches, the most forward station that carries people, and it does two bad things at once. It drags the CG toward the forward limit, and it adds weight, which drives the forward limit aft to meet it. Nothing else on the airplane loads that far forward. Four average adults are easier on CG than two heavy ones up front.
