items.q: Is the real checkride load legal at full fuel?
items.a: Yes, on the assumed empty weight. Takeoff weight 2,276.99 lb against a 2,325 lb limit, so 48.01 lb spare, with the CG at 87.45 inches against a forward limit of 86.49 and an aft limit of 93.0 - inside by 0.96 inch forward and 5.55 inches aft. That verdict rests on an assumed empty weight and must be recomputed from the airplane's own record.

items.q: Counter-intuitively, does taking the 25 lb bag out help or hurt?
items.a: It hurts the CG. The bag sits at 142.8 inches, well aft, so removing it pulls the CG forward toward the limit: margin falls from 0.96 inch with the bag to 0.61 inch without it. It does buy 25 lb of gross-weight headroom. On a nose-heavy Warrior the baggage compartment is an ally, so leave the bag in and secure it.

items.q: What is the baggage limit and what does the placard say?
items.a: 200 lb in normal category at an arm of 142.8 inches, and zero in utility. The baggage door placard reads BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS, and the utility placard reads UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION - NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. The 200 lb figure is a structural and volume limit on the floor and the tiedowns, not something derived from gross weight, so it is the same on his airplane as on the 2,440 lb one.

items.q: Can you ever reach the 200 lb baggage limit with this load?
items.a: No, and that is the point of checking both limits. With 500 lb up front and full fuel you have only 48 lb of gross-weight margin left, so weight stops you at about a quarter of the placarded baggage allowance. A placard being satisfied never means the loading is legal - the 200 lb baggage limit, the 2,325 lb gross and the CG envelope are three separate tests.

items.q: What does utility category allow on this airplane, and what does normal allow?
items.a: Utility allows steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles beyond 60 degrees of bank, but only 2,020 lb, two occupants both at 80.5 inches, no baggage and no rear passengers, with a forward limit of 83.8 inches at 2,020 lb. Normal allows four seats, 200 lb of baggage and 2,325 lb, but prohibits all acrobatic manoeuvres including spins and bank beyond 60 degrees.

items.q: Can you fly the commercial manoeuvres in utility category with this loading?
items.a: No. Pilot and examiner alone are 500 lb, and with the assumed empty weight the airplane is already at 1,963.99 lb dry. Full fuel puts it at 2,251.99 lb, which is 231.99 lb over the 2,020 lb utility maximum; even bone dry it only just fits. Chandelles and lazy eights at these weights have to be flown inside normal-category bank limits, or with a much lighter airplane.

items.q: What is a ramp weight allowance, and does your airplane have one?
items.a: It is permission to be heavier at engine start than at brake release, covering the fuel burned in start, taxi and run-up - on the 2,440 lb Warrior that is 7 lb, which is exactly why its ramp weight is 2,447 lb. For serial 28-8116257 no ramp weight is published anywhere available, so assume none: be at or under 2,325 lb at engine start, not just at brake release.

items.q: Where would 2,332 lb come from, and may you quote it as your ramp weight?
items.a: It is 2,325 plus the 7 lb start, taxi and run-up allowance from the Section 6 loading form, and no, you may not quote it. TCDS item XVI-A publishes a 2,332 lb ramp weight for the Cadet only, not the Warrior II, and VB-1180's 2,447 lb belongs to the heavier airplane. Until VB-880 Section 2.11 says otherwise, that number is arithmetic, not a limitation.

items.q: What is your maximum landing weight?
items.a: Not separately published, so plan on 2,325 lb, the same as takeoff. VB-1180 1.11(c) sets landing weight equal to takeoff weight on the 2,440 lb airplane, and TCDS 2A13 publishes no reduced landing weight for any PA-28-161, so this airframe almost certainly follows the same convention. Confirm it in VB-880 Section 2 rather than asserting it.

items.q: How do you use the Loading Graph, Figure 6-13?
items.a: Enter on the left at the weight of one item, run across to that item's diagonal line, then down to read moment over 1000 in pound-inches. Repeat for each station, add the moments to the empty moment, and divide by total weight. The four lines are pilot and front passenger, fuel labelled 6 lb/gal, aft passengers and baggage - steepest to shallowest, because a steeper line means a shorter arm.

items.q: What is basic empty weight and what is already included in it?
items.a: The weight of the airplane as it sits with all permanently installed equipment, full oil, and the 2.0 gallons of unusable fuel - one gallon in each wing. POH 6.3 has you drain the tanks, put the unusable fuel back and fill the oil before weighing, and the Figure 6-5 footnote says so. So oil and unusable fuel are never separate lines on the loading form, and never subtracted.

items.q: What is the difference between standard empty weight and basic empty weight?
items.a: Standard empty weight is the bare airplane with full oil and unusable fuel but no optional equipment; basic empty weight is that plus the optional equipment actually installed. Piper published about 1,353 lb standard for a 1981 Warrior II, but a real equipped trainer runs 100 to 170 lb heavier. Only basic empty weight, from this airplane's own record, is any use for loading.

items.q: What empty weight and empty CG are you using, and are they this airplane's?
items.a: No, they are assumed. The figures used are 1,463.99 lb at 87.39 inches, which belong to N3572M, a 1978 PA-28-161 Warrior II at the same 2,325 lb gross, taken from a published flying club weight and balance summary. They were chosen because they are the only verified equipped 2,325 lb Warrior II with both a real weight and a real CG. N84054's own record replaces them.

items.q: What empty weight would make this loading stop working?
items.a: On weight alone, 1,512 lb: 2,325 minus 500 lb of occupants, 288 lb of fuel and 25 lb of bags. Drop the bags and it becomes 1,537 lb. But the CG fails first on an airframe whose empty CG is forward, and as empty weight rises the empty CG has to be further aft to pass: at 1,464 lb it must be aft of 85.90 inches, at 1,512 lb aft of 86.70 inches.

items.q: What do you do if the real numbers come back and the airplane is nose-heavy at full fuel?
items.a: Take fuel out before you reach for ballast. Dropping weight lowers the forward limit by 0.064 inch per gallon while moving the CG forward only 0.020 inch, so you gain margin. On the worked nose-heavy case, going from 48 to 30 gallons turns 0.58 inch outside into 0.12 inch inside. Baggage ballast also works but eats gross weight and must be secured against a hard landing.

items.q: Does the POH define a tab quantity for partial fuel on this airplane?
items.a: No. VB-1180 mentions no filler-neck tab anywhere, the Loading Graph runs only to 48 gallons and Section 8 gives no partial-fill mark. So tabs is not a POH quantity on a Warrior II, and any tab figure comes from the operator or from looking into the tank. If N84054's tanks are tabbed, measure the quantity and treat it as a local number, not a handbook one.

items.q: How much fuel can you actually carry, and how does that compare with what weight allows?
items.a: 48 usable gallons of 50 total, 2.0 unusable, which is 288 lb at 95.0 inches. Weight would allow more: with the occupants and bags aboard the airplane is 336 lb under gross, which is 56 gallons' worth. The tanks run out before the gross weight does, so on this flight fuel capacity binds, not weight - you simply cannot overfill yourself into an overweight airplane.

items.q: How does CG position affect stall speed?
items.a: Forward CG raises it, aft CG lowers it. A forward CG needs more tail download to trim, and that download is extra weight the wing must carry, so the wing reaches its stalling angle at a higher airspeed. At the aft limit the download shrinks and the airplane stalls slower - but it also gives less warning. Note the POH's 44 KIAS VSO is a 2,440 lb figure and is not his.

items.q: How does CG position affect cruise speed?
items.a: Aft CG is faster. Moving the CG aft reduces the tail download needed to trim, so the wing carries less effective load, flies at a lower angle of attack and makes less induced drag, and the stabilator makes less trim drag. The gain is small on a Warrior - a knot or two over the whole 10-inch envelope - but the direction is always the same: aft is faster, forward is safer.

items.q: How does CG position affect longitudinal stability?
items.a: The further forward the CG, the more statically stable the airplane: a bigger arm between CG and the tail means stronger restoring pitch moments, heavier stick forces and a stronger tendency to return to trimmed speed. Moving aft shrinks that static margin until the airplane is neutral and then divergent. That is what the 93.0 inch aft limit protects, and why spin recovery degrades beyond it.

items.q: What must you get from the airplane before any of this is a real weight and balance?
items.a: Its current signed Weight and Balance Record - basic empty weight, empty CG arm and empty moment - plus the date of that record and any Form 337 since, because new avionics, an ADS-B install or a removed interior all move both numbers. Also the equipment list, VB-880 itself for the printed envelope and ramp weight, and the STC list in case of a gross-weight increase.

items.q: Which term in the lift equation is the pilot's primary, immediate control?
items.a: The coefficient of lift, through angle of attack. Pitch is a direct and instantaneous control over the coefficient of lift, available in every regime; velocity responds more slowly and only through power and gravity; density is the atmosphere's choice on the day; and wing area moves only when the flaps do. It is also why the right answer to almost any question beginning 'why did the airplane do that' starts with angle of attack.

items.q: Of airspeed and angle of attack, which one actually stalls a wing?
items.a: Angle of attack, and only angle of attack. A wing stalls when the airflow separates at the critical angle of attack, which for a given wing is a fixed number, typically in the region of sixteen to eighteen degrees, regardless of airspeed, weight, bank, attitude, power setting or density altitude. Every stall is the same event; the only thing that varies is the airspeed at which you happen to arrive at that angle.

items.q: Then why do we talk about stall speed at all?
items.a: Because for one particular set of conditions, airspeed is a convenient stand-in for angle of attack. At a given weight, load factor and configuration there is exactly one speed at which level flight demands the critical angle of attack, and that is the published stall speed. Change the weight, the load factor or the flaps and the speed moves while the angle does not, so a published stall speed is valid only at the conditions printed beside it.

items.q: Why does stall speed rise with weight, and by how much?
items.a: Because a heavier airplane needs more lift for level flight, and at the critical angle of attack the only way to get more lift is more speed. Stall speed varies with the square root of the weight, so taking a 2,325 pound airplane down to 1,900 pounds, a ratio of 0.817, multiplies the stall speed by 0.90: about ten percent slower. It is also why a published stall speed belongs only to the weight printed with it.

items.q: Does the critical angle of attack change with weight, altitude, bank or power?
items.a: No. It is a property of the shape of the airfoil and nothing else, so it is the same at 2,325 pounds and at 1,600, at sea level and at ten thousand feet, wings level and in a sixty degree bank, at idle and at full throttle. Extending the flaps changes it, because that changes the shape of the wing. Everything else only changes the airspeed at which you arrive there.

items.q: Why does stall speed rise in a turn if the wing does not know it is turning?
items.a: Because the wing is being asked for more lift. In a level turn the lift must exceed weight by one over the cosine of the bank, which is the load factor, and making that lift at a given speed requires a higher angle of attack, so the critical angle arrives at a higher speed. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: seven percent at 30 degrees, nineteen at 45, twenty-five at 50 and forty-one at 60.

items.q: Is the load factor in a 50 degree bank different for a heavy airplane and a light one?
items.a: No. Load factor is a ratio, the lift being made divided by the airplane's weight, so both are at 1.56 g in a level 50 degree bank. What differs is the absolute load: at 2,325 pounds the wings carry about 3,620 pounds, and at 1,800 pounds about 2,800. The lighter airplane also has a lower stall speed, so the same bank angle leaves it a wider margin, which is why the same maneuver feels easier light.

items.q: In a steady climb, is lift greater than weight?
items.a: No; it is slightly less. In a steady climb at a constant airspeed the weight vector is no longer perpendicular to the flight path, so lift has to balance only the component of weight perpendicular to the path, which is weight times the cosine of the climb angle, while thrust carries the component along it. What makes an airplane climb is excess thrust, not excess lift, which is the single most useful correction to make to a student's mental model.

items.q: Where is lift-to-drag maximum, and what is special about that point?
items.a: It is the angle of attack at which induced and parasite drag are equal, so total drag is at its minimum for the lift being made. That one angle of attack gives the best glide ratio and the flattest glide, defines the boundary of the region of reversed command, and is the reference from which best glide speed is published. It is an angle of attack first and a speed second: the speed that corresponds to it moves with weight.

items.q: What is the difference between thrust required and power required, and why do Vx and Vy follow from it?
items.a: Thrust required is the drag the airplane must overcome; power required is that drag multiplied by the speed at which it is overcome. The greatest excess of thrust gives the best angle of climb, Vx, and the greatest excess of power gives the best rate, Vy. Because power is drag times speed, the power-required curve bottoms out at a higher speed than the drag curve, which is why Vy is always the faster of the two in a propeller airplane.

items.q: Why do Vx and Vy move toward each other as you climb?
items.a: Because the engine makes less power and the propeller less thrust as the air thins, so both the excess thrust and the excess power shrink. In indicated terms Vx increases slightly while Vy decreases, and at the absolute ceiling they meet at the one speed at which the airplane can just maintain altitude with no excess of either. In true airspeed both of them increase, which is a distinction worth being able to make out loud.

items.q: Rate of turn and radius of turn: what changes each?
items.a: Both are set by bank angle and true airspeed and by nothing else. Rate of turn equals g times the tangent of the bank divided by the airspeed, so it increases with bank and decreases with speed. Radius equals airspeed squared divided by g times the tangent of the bank, so it decreases with bank and increases with the square of speed. Weight, wing loading and horsepower appear in neither expression.

items.q: How do you recognize a skid without looking at the ball?
items.a: By your body. In a coordinated turn the resultant of lift and inertia presses you straight down into the seat; in a skid you are pushed toward the outside of the turn, the way a car slides you across the seat in a fast corner, and in a slip you lean toward the inside, toward the low wing. The ball does exactly the same thing, because it is simply a weight in a curved tube obeying the same resultant that you are.

items.q: Why does maneuvering speed fall as the airplane gets lighter?
items.a: Because the protection it offers works through the stall. Maneuvering speed is the speed at which the wing reaches its critical angle of attack at exactly the limit load factor, so the wing gives way before the structure does. A lighter airplane reaches that limit load factor with less lift, so it stalls at a lower speed, and the speed at which the stall protects the airframe comes down with it, in proportion to the square root of the weight ratio.

items.q: Why is this airplane's maneuvering speed not the number printed in the common handbook?
items.a: Because maneuvering speed is quoted at a gross weight, and this airplane's maximum takeoff weight is 2,325 pounds from the type certificate data sheet, not the 2,440 pounds in the circulating book. A lower gross weight means a lower maneuvering speed. The right answer on the ride is to read the placard and the handbook that belong to this serial number rather than quoting a figure from a later serial block.

items.q: What is the resultant that the wing actually has to support in a turn?
items.a: The vector sum of weight, acting straight down, and the inertial reaction to the turn, acting horizontally outward. That resultant is longer than weight alone and tilted outward, and the wing must produce lift equal and opposite to it, which is why total lift in a level turn exceeds weight by one over the cosine of the bank. The ratio of that resultant to the airplane's weight is precisely what load factor means.

items.q: How does the airplane's weight affect its glide ratio?
items.a: It does not. The glide ratio is the lift-to-drag ratio, which is a function of angle of attack and configuration alone, so a heavy airplane and a light one glide the same distance from the same height in still air. What changes is the speed at which that angle of attack occurs, which varies with the square root of weight, so the heavy airplane arrives sooner at a higher speed and a higher rate of descent.

items.q: What does a fixed-pitch propeller do to the power available at low airspeed?
items.a: It reduces it. The blade angle is set for one compromise condition, so at a low forward speed the blades meet the air at too large an angle, the propeller loads up, rpm falls and the engine cannot develop its rated power. That is why full-throttle static rpm on this airplane is specified well below the 2,700 rpm rated speed, and why slow, high-power flight regimes have less thrust available than the horsepower figure suggests.

items.q: Why does induced drag dominate at low speed and parasite drag at high speed?
items.a: Because they depend on speed in opposite ways. Induced drag is the price of making lift, and at low speed the wing needs a high angle of attack and makes strong tip vortices, so it varies inversely with the square of airspeed. Parasite drag is the cost of pushing the airframe through the air and varies with the square of airspeed. Their sum is a U-shaped curve whose minimum is lift-to-drag maximum, which is where the two are equal.

items.q: What is actually happening at the wing when it stalls?
items.a: The boundary layer can no longer follow the increasingly adverse pressure gradient over the upper surface, so the airflow separates and the low pressure region over the wing collapses. Lift falls sharply, drag rises sharply, and the separated wake over the tail produces the buffet that warns you. Nothing about airspeed is involved in the definition; the separation happens at the critical angle of attack whatever the airplane is doing.

items.q: Why does a wing's maximum lift coefficient put an absolute limit on turn performance?
items.a: Because the lift needed in a level turn goes up as one over the cosine of the bank, without limit, while the lift available at a given speed is capped by the maximum lift coefficient. Where the two meet is the steepest level turn the airplane can make at that speed, and it is set by the stall, not by the structure or the engine. Going steeper from there requires more airspeed, and eventually the structural limit becomes the binding one.

items.q: How does extending flaps change the lift curve and the stall?
items.a: Flaps increase the camber of the wing, which raises the lift coefficient at every angle of attack and raises the maximum lift coefficient, so the wing can carry its weight at a lower airspeed. They also reduce the angle of attack at which the stall occurs, measured against the original chord line, which is why the nose attitude at the stall is lower with flaps out. The later settings add far more drag than lift.

items.q: Does the ball tell you anything about the airplane's angle of attack?
items.a: No, and conflating the two is dangerous. The ball reports only whether the lateral forces are in balance, that is whether the airplane is slipping or skidding; it is blind to angle of attack, load factor and how near the wing is to stalling. A perfectly centered ball at the critical angle of attack is still a stall, and an uncoordinated one simply decides which wing will drop when that stall arrives.

items.q: Read me the day VFR equipment list out of your handbook.
items.a: Airspeed indicator; altimeter; magnetic compass; tachometer; oil pressure indicator; oil temperature indicator; fuel pressure indicator; fuel quantity indicator for each tank; volt-ammeter; elevator and rudder trim indicator; alternator; and a safety restraint for each occupant. Twelve items, and note that fuel pressure and the volt-ammeter are on this list even though 91.205 does not ask for them.

items.q: How do you compute crosswind and headwind components from the wind and the runway?
items.a: Find the angle between the wind direction and the runway heading, then crosswind equals wind speed times the sine of the angle and headwind equals wind speed times the cosine. Thirty degrees gives half the wind as crosswind, forty-five gives about 70 percent, sixty gives about 90 percent, and beyond sixty treat it as nearly all crosswind. The POH chart does the same thing graphically.

items.q: Wind 095 at 22 knots, runways 05 and 14. Work both.
items.a: Runway 05 is 050 magnetic, so the wind is 45 degrees off to the right; runway 14 is 140, so the wind is 45 degrees off to the left. Sine and cosine of 45 are both 0.707, so each runway sees a 15.6-knot crosswind and a 15.6-knot headwind. The wind genuinely splits them, so the decision has to come from the gust, the runway lengths, the obstacles and the side you want the crosswind on.

items.q: Wind 095 at 22 gusting 30, runway 05. Does the gust change your decision?
items.a: Yes, and it is the number that decides the flight. At 30 knots the crosswind component becomes 30 times 0.707, which is 21.2 knots, well above this airplane's 17-knot demonstrated crosswind. The gust, not the steady wind, is what you will be flying in the flare. I would say no to a departure that commits me to that crosswind on the return, and wait for it to come down or move the flight.

items.q: Wind 200 at 16, runway 05. What are the components?
items.a: Runway 05 is 050 and the wind is from 200, so the angle is 150 degrees, which means the wind is largely behind you. Crosswind is 16 times the sine of 150, which is 16 times 0.5, or 8 knots of crosswind and 13.9 knots of tailwind. A 14-knot tailwind is a long way outside what a Warrior's takeoff chart covers, so that runway is out; take the reciprocal.

items.q: Wind 040 at 20 on runway 36. Work it, and tell me what it means.
items.a: Forty degrees off the nose to the right. Crosswind is 20 times the sine of 40, which is 20 times 0.643, or 12.9 knots; headwind is 20 times the cosine of 40, which is 20 times 0.766, or 15.3 knots. So about 13 knots of crosswind and 15 knots of headwind. The crosswind is inside the 17-knot demonstrated figure, the headwind shortens the takeoff roll, and that runway is a reasonable choice.

items.q: How much does a tailwind hurt, and what does the handbook assume?
items.a: A great deal, and it is not symmetric with a headwind. The general planning rule is that a 10 percent tailwind component relative to liftoff speed increases the takeoff distance by roughly 20 percent, and landing distance grows the same way. The handbook's takeoff and landing charts are built for headwind components and usually only cover a small tailwind if any, so beyond that you are extrapolating, which you should not do.

items.q: How do you read a time, fuel and distance to climb chart?
items.a: It is not a single lookup. The chart gives the time, fuel and distance accumulated in a climb from sea level at standard conditions up to the altitude you enter with, so you read it twice: once at the departure airport's pressure altitude and temperature, once at your cruise altitude and the temperature up there, and subtract the first set of numbers from the second. The difference is what the climb costs you.

items.q: Work an example of a climb computation for me.
items.a: Say the chart gives 4 minutes, 1.0 gallon and 6 nautical miles at the departure field's conditions, and 15 minutes, 3.2 gallons and 24 nautical miles at cruise altitude. Subtract: 11 minutes, 2.2 gallons and 18 nautical miles for the climb segment. Then add the handbook's allowance for start, taxi and run-up, which on this airframe is the 7-pound fuel allowance, a little over a gallon, on top of that.

items.q: Why do you have to subtract rather than just read the cruise altitude line?
items.a: Because the chart is cumulative from sea level and standard temperature, not from your airport. If you depart from a field at 3,000 feet and read only the 8,000-foot line, you have charged yourself for 3,000 feet of climb you never flew, which overstates time, fuel and distance. On a short leg out of a high airport that error is large enough to change the altitude you pick.

items.q: What does temperature do to the climb numbers?
items.a: Hot air raises density altitude, which costs you both lift and power, so the rate of climb falls and time, fuel and distance to climb all increase. Most charts give a correction, typically a percentage increase in time, fuel and distance for each given number of degrees above standard; some are plotted with temperature lines you enter directly. If the chart has no correction for your temperature you must not extrapolate past it.

items.q: What does altitude itself do to the climb?
items.a: Rate of climb decreases steadily with altitude as the normally aspirated engine loses power and the wing needs a higher true airspeed for the same indicated airspeed, so each successive thousand feet takes longer, burns more and covers more ground. Vx and Vy converge as you climb, and they meet at the absolute ceiling where rate of climb is zero. The service ceiling is where the best rate has fallen to 100 feet per minute.

items.q: What are the chart's assumptions, and what do you do about them?
items.a: A climb at the published climb speed, full throttle, mixture leaned per the handbook, a clean airplane, no wind, a level hard surface runway and a new airplane flown by a test pilot. Your airplane is 40 years old, you are not a test pilot, and the chart distance is still air distance. Add a margin, correct the distance for wind using groundspeed, and treat the result as a plan, not a promise.

items.q: The climb chart says 18 nautical miles in 11 minutes. There is a 20-knot headwind. Now what?
items.a: That 18 miles is a still air distance. Work it in groundspeed instead: at a climb speed of, say, 85 knots true with a 20-knot headwind, groundspeed is 65 knots, so 11 minutes covers 65 times 11 over 60, which is 11.9 nautical miles. The fuel and time do not change, but you are 6 miles short of where the chart put you, which matters when the first checkpoint is inside the climb.

items.q: Your loading is legal on weight but the CG is close to the forward limit. What are your options?
items.a: Move weight aft or add weight aft. In order of preference: put the baggage in the baggage compartment instead of the back seat; move a passenger from the front to the rear seats; add ballast in the baggage compartment; or reduce weight that is forward of the CG. On this airplane the baggage compartment arm is 142.8 inches, far aft of everything else you can load, so it is the strongest lever you have.

items.q: Why is the baggage compartment such a powerful lever on this airplane?
items.a: Because of how far aft it is. The loading arms are 80.5 inches for the front seats, 118.1 for the rear seats, 95.0 for fuel and 142.8 for baggage, and the aft CG limit is 93.0 inches. Baggage sits almost 50 inches behind the aft limit, so every pound you put there moves the CG aft several times as effectively as the same pound in the back seat.

items.q: Work it: 1,900 pounds, CG at 83.2 inches, you add a 25-pound bag in the baggage compartment.
items.a: Old moment is 1,900 times 83.2, which is 158,080 inch-pounds. The bag adds 25 times 142.8, which is 3,570. New weight 1,925 pounds, new moment 161,650, and new CG is 161,650 divided by 1,925, which is 83.97 inches. That is 0.77 inches further aft, and at 1,925 pounds the forward limit is still 83.0 inches, so the loading now has nearly an inch of margin instead of two tenths.

items.q: At 2,000 pounds with the CG at 84.0 inches, how much ballast in the baggage compartment moves the CG aft half an inch?
items.a: Set the new CG to 84.5 and solve. Two thousand times 84.0 plus w times 142.8, all over 2,000 plus w, equals 84.5. That gives 168,000 plus 142.8w equals 169,000 plus 84.5w, so 58.3w equals 1,000 and w is about 17 pounds. Seventeen pounds in the baggage compartment buys half an inch, which tells you how little ballast it takes and how much a forgotten bag back there matters.

items.q: How much does moving a passenger from the front to the back seat change things?
items.a: A lot. A 170-pound passenger moving from the front seats at 80.5 inches to the rear seats at 118.1 inches shifts 37.6 inches. In a 2,200-pound airplane that is 170 times 37.6 divided by 2,200, which is 2.9 inches aft. That is the biggest single lever on the airplane, so if the CG is forward, seat the heavier people in the back before you reach for ballast, and then check the aft limit.

items.q: What has to be checked after you add weight aft to fix a forward CG?
items.a: Three things. That the new gross weight is still within 2,325 pounds for this serial number; that the baggage does not exceed the 200-pound placarded limit and is secured; and that you have not now gone past the aft limit of 93.0 inches, in either the takeoff or the landing condition. Also confirm that you are still in the category you intend, since utility category on this airplane allows no baggage and no aft passengers.

items.q: Does fuel burn help you with a forward CG problem on this airplane?
items.a: No, it makes it worse. The fuel arm is 95.0 inches, which is aft of the aft CG limit of 93.0 and aft of any realistic loaded CG, so burning fuel moves the center of gravity forward. That means the landing condition, not the takeoff condition, is the critical one when you are tight against the forward limit, and you must run the numbers for both.

items.q: What does a forward CG actually do to the airplane?
items.a: It increases longitudinal stability and makes the airplane feel heavy in pitch. The tail carries a larger download, so the wing must produce more lift, which raises the stall speed and increases cruise drag, costing you speed and range. The nose is harder to raise in the flare and on a soft field takeoff, and at the extreme you may not be able to round out at all. The upside is docile stall behavior and easier recovery.

items.q: Could you simply put ballast in the back seat instead of the baggage compartment?
items.a: You could, and it is legal if it is properly secured and within the seat's structural limit, but it is less effective: the rear seat arm is 118.1 against the baggage compartment's 142.8. You need roughly twice as much weight in the back seat to achieve the same CG shift once you account for the distance from the CG. Secure it either way, because unsecured ballast becomes a projectile and a moving CG.

b: Steep turns, steep spiral, chandelle, lazy eight, eights on pylons, the power-off 180, and the short and soft field work.

items.q: What do you do before starting any of the commercial performance maneuvers?
items.a: Clear the area and complete the checklist. Select an altitude that lets you finish the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL; make at least two 90 degree clearing turns or one 180, scanning above, below and behind; choose an area clear of towns, congested areas and other traffic; note the wind direction; and confirm you have a landing option if the engine quits.

items.q: Where does the entry airspeed for a chandelle, lazy eight or steep turn come from?
items.a: From the airplane's handbook. The ACS calls for the manufacturer's recommended entry airspeed, and if none is published, a safe airspeed not to exceed VA at the current weight. Read the recommended maneuvering entry speed or VA from the POH or AFM and reduce VA for weights below maximum gross. Never fly a memorized number from a different airplane.

items.q: Why do you set up with the wind perpendicular to your flight path before a chandelle or lazy eight?
items.a: So drift does not distort the symmetry of the maneuver and so you have a usable visual reference. These are attitude maneuvers, not ground track maneuvers, but entering with the wind on the beam and turning into it keeps you inside the practice area and puts a prominent 90 degree reference off the wingtip to judge the turn against.

items.q: Which commercial maneuvers are graded on ground track and which are graded on attitude and energy?
items.a: Ground reference: the steep spiral and eights on pylons, where wind correction and the path over the ground are the point. Attitude and energy: steep turns, chandelles and lazy eights, which are flown to the horizon and the instruments and are not corrected for drift. Confusing the two is a common error, so do not chase a ground track in a chandelle or a lazy eight.

items.q: What is a steep turn and what is it meant to demonstrate?
items.a: A steep turn is a level 360 degree turn at a high bank angle, flown in each direction. At the commercial level the bank is 50 degrees. It demonstrates smooth coordinated control at increased load factor, holding altitude and airspeed while the vertical component of lift is reduced, division of attention between outside references and instruments, and recognition of the overbanking tendency.

items.q: State the ACS completion standards for commercial steep turns.
items.a: Roll into a coordinated 360 degree steep turn at 50 degrees of bank, then perform the task in the opposite direction, maintaining the entry altitude plus or minus 100 feet, airspeed plus or minus 10 knots, bank plus or minus 5 degrees, and rolling out on the entry heading plus or minus 10 degrees. Entry speed is the manufacturer's recommendation or a safe speed not exceeding VA.

items.q: At what altitude should steep turns be flown?
items.a: High enough to recover safely. The Airplane Flying Handbook recommends performing them at an altitude that allows completion no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, and 14 CFR 91.119 minimum safe altitudes apply regardless. Unlike the chandelle, lazy eight and steep spiral tasks, the ACS steep turn task does not itself publish a minimum altitude, but the same practice is expected.

items.q: How do you fly a steep turn, step by step?
items.a: Clear the area, slow to the entry speed and trim. Pick a reference on the horizon and note the heading. Roll smoothly to 50 degrees, adding back pressure as the bank passes about 30 degrees and adding power to hold airspeed. Hold the pitch picture outside and cross-check the altimeter and VSI. Begin the rollout about 25 degrees before the entry heading, releasing back pressure and power as the wings come level.

items.q: Why must you add back pressure and power as you roll into a steep turn?
items.a: Because banking tilts the lift vector. At 50 degrees of bank only part of the total lift opposes weight, so total lift must increase to hold altitude, which means more angle of attack and more back pressure. That extra lift brings extra induced drag, which slows the airplane, so power must come in to hold airspeed. A level 50 degree turn loads the airplane to about 1.56 g.

items.q: What is the overbanking tendency and how does it show up in a steep turn?
items.a: The outside wing travels a larger arc than the inside wing, so it moves faster, makes more lift, and the bank tends to steepen by itself. Past roughly 30 degrees of bank you must hold opposite aileron to keep the bank constant, with rudder as needed for coordination. Relax and the bank increases, the nose drops, and the turn tightens into a descending spiral.

items.q: You are 150 feet low and still in the steep turn. How do you fix it?
items.a: Reduce the bank first, then pitch. Pulling harder at 50 degrees of bank mostly tightens the turn and adds load factor and drag rather than raising the nose. Shallow the bank by 5 to 10 degrees so more lift acts vertically, raise the nose to recover the altitude, then re-establish exactly 50 degrees. Catch deviations early, because the standard allows only plus or minus 100 feet.

items.q: How much do you lead the rollout from a steep turn and why?
items.a: Lead by roughly half the bank angle, about 25 degrees before the entry heading, because rolling out from 50 degrees takes several seconds and the airplane keeps turning the whole time. Release back pressure and reduce power as the wings come level so the nose does not balloon and the airspeed does not run outside the plus or minus 10 knot tolerance.

items.q: What are the common errors in a steep turn?
items.a: Not clearing the area; rolling in too abruptly or too slowly; failing to add back pressure and power together, so altitude is lost immediately; letting the bank creep outside plus or minus 5 degrees through overbanking tendency; pulling instead of shallowing when low; uncoordinated rudder; fixating on the instruments; and a late rollout that misses the entry heading by more than 10 degrees.

items.q: What is a steep spiral and what does it demonstrate?
items.a: A steep spiral is a gliding constant radius turn of at least three complete 360 degree turns around a ground reference point with the engine at idle. It demonstrates power-off gliding control, wind drift correction, orientation and planning, and the ability to lose a large amount of altitude over a fixed point, which is exactly what you do circling down to a forced landing field.

items.q: What airspeed do you fly in a steep spiral and what is the tolerance?
items.a: The airspeed the handbook recommends for the maneuver, normally the published best glide speed at the current weight; read it from the POH or AFM. The ACS requires the specified airspeed to be held within plus or minus 10 knots throughout, which is the hardest part of the maneuver because the pitch attitude required changes continuously as the bank changes around each turn.

items.q: How steep may the bank get in a steep spiral?
items.a: The ACS limits it to not more than 60 degrees at the steepest point. That steepest bank occurs on the downwind side of the circle where groundspeed is highest. If holding a constant radius would require more than 60 degrees, you have chosen too small a radius or too much wind, so widen the circle or pick a different reference point before you start.

items.q: Where in a steep spiral is the bank steepest and where is it shallowest?
items.a: Steepest directly downwind, shallowest directly upwind. Bank must track groundspeed to hold a constant radius: highest groundspeed downwind demands the tightest turn, lowest groundspeed upwind the shallowest. Between those points the bank changes continuously, so in any real wind the bank angle should never be constant at any moment of the maneuver.

items.q: What must you do with the engine during a steep spiral and why?
items.a: Clear it. With the throttle closed for several turns the engine cools, plugs can foul and the carburetor can ice, so advance the throttle briefly at least once each 360 degree turn and use carburetor heat as the handbook directs. Clearing also confirms the engine will make power when you level off and limits shock cooling of the cylinders.

items.q: What are the ACS completion standards for the steep spiral?
items.a: At least three complete 360 degree turns holding a constant radius around the point, bank not exceeding 60 degrees at the steepest point, the specified airspeed plus or minus 10 knots, coordinated flight and proper division of attention throughout, and roll out toward a specified object or heading plus or minus 10 degrees. The maneuver must be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.

items.q: How do you choose the entry altitude and entry point for a steep spiral?
items.a: Work backwards from the bottom. Three full turns plus the rollout must finish at or above 1,500 feet AGL, so estimate the altitude lost per turn in the glide and add it up, which usually means entering several thousand feet AGL. Pick a point with open landing areas nearby, arrive abeam it at the planned altitude, then close the throttle abeam the point and establish the glide.

items.q: How is a steep spiral different from a spiral dive?
items.a: A steep spiral is a controlled, coordinated, constant airspeed gliding turn at a bank you selected. A spiral dive is a loss of control in which bank and back pressure feed each other so bank, airspeed, load factor and descent rate all increase together. The defining difference is that in a steep spiral you hold a constant airspeed with pitch and never let the bank exceed what you chose.

items.q: What are the common errors in a steep spiral?
items.a: Not clearing the area or the engine; too small a radius so the bank exceeds 60 degrees downwind; holding a constant bank so the circle becomes an egg shape drifting downwind; letting airspeed wander outside plus or minus 10 knots as the bank changes; skidding with rudder instead of banking; fixating on the point; and finishing the maneuver below 1,500 feet AGL.

items.q: What is a chandelle and what is it meant to demonstrate?
items.a: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180 degree climbing turn that begins near cruise or maneuvering speed and finishes with the wings level on the reciprocal heading at an airspeed just above a stall. It demonstrates the airplane's maximum climb performance for a given bank, smooth coordinated control through a wide speed range, and planning and division of attention. It is a performance maneuver, not a turn.

items.q: What are the entry configuration and airspeed for a chandelle?
items.a: Clean unless the handbook says otherwise, straight and level and trimmed, at the manufacturer's recommended entry airspeed, or if none is published a safe speed not exceeding VA at the current weight, taken from the POH or AFM. Enter at an altitude that lets the maneuver be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, with the wind on the beam from the side you will turn toward.

items.q: How is a chandelle flown from entry to the 90 degree point?
items.a: Roll smoothly to approximately 30 degrees of bank, then simultaneously begin a continuous increase in pitch and apply the recommended climb power. From entry to the 90 degree point the bank stays constant at 30 degrees while pitch increases steadily and airspeed decays steadily. The maximum pitch attitude is reached exactly at the 90 degree point and the bank has not yet changed.

items.q: How is a chandelle flown from the 90 degree point to the 180 degree point?
items.a: Pitch is now held constant and the bank is rolled out at a constant rate so the wings arrive level exactly at the 180 degree point. Airspeed continues to decay toward just above the stall, so right rudder must be increased steadily to hold coordination. Do not let the nose fall as bank is removed, and do not add or take away power partway through.

items.q: What airspeed should the airplane be at when the chandelle is complete?
items.a: Just above a stall, held momentarily without stalling, with the wings level. The ACS asks for the rollout to be complete at the 180 degree point plus or minus 10 degrees at an airspeed just above stall, maintained for a moment, followed by a return to straight and level flight with a minimum loss of altitude. A stall, or a stall warning that develops into one, is unsatisfactory.

items.q: What is the only numeric tolerance the ACS puts on a chandelle?
items.a: The rollout must be complete at the 180 degree point plus or minus 10 degrees. There is no numeric altitude or airspeed tolerance. The rest of the standard is qualitative: approximately 30 degrees of bank held constant to the 90 degree point, constant pitch and a constant rate rollout from there, an airspeed just above stall at completion without stalling, coordination throughout, and minimum altitude loss on recovery.

items.q: Why does a chandelle need steadily increasing right rudder?
items.a: Because airspeed is falling while power is high and angle of attack is rising, so the left turning tendencies grow throughout. Slipstream, torque and P-factor all strengthen as the airplane slows at high power, so rudder pressure must increase continuously and is greatest at the very end of the maneuver, where the airplane is slowest. Coordination is graded for the whole maneuver.

items.q: What power setting do you use for a chandelle?
items.a: The climb power the handbook specifies for the maneuver. With a fixed pitch propeller you normally advance the throttle to full or to the recommended setting as the pitch begins to increase and then leave it there. With a constant speed propeller, set the recommended manifold pressure and RPM and leave them alone. Adding or reducing power partway through the maneuver is a common error.

items.q: How do you identify the 90 degree and 180 degree points in a chandelle?
items.a: Choose them before entry. With the wind on the beam, pick a prominent ground feature or section line abeam the wingtip on the side you will turn toward and make it your 90 degree point. The exit heading is the entry heading plus 180, and the original reference will sit off the opposite wingtip at completion. Cross-check the heading indicator, but fly the maneuver visually.

items.q: What are the common errors in a chandelle?
items.a: Too much or too little initial bank; changing bank before the 90 degree point; pitch that stops increasing, or increases so fast the airplane stalls early; not holding pitch constant during the rollout so the nose falls; a rollout rate that is not constant, finishing early or late; poor coordination as speed decays; stalling; and finishing more than 10 degrees off the 180 degree point.

items.q: What is a lazy eight and what does it demonstrate?
items.a: A lazy eight is a pair of symmetrical 180 degree climbing and descending turns in opposite directions in which pitch and bank change continuously and the nose traces a lazy figure eight against the horizon. It demonstrates mastery of the airplane through constantly changing airspeed, attitude and load factor with smooth coordinated control, and precise planning of a maneuver that never reaches a steady state.

items.q: What is the entry configuration and airspeed for a lazy eight?
items.a: Clean, straight and level and trimmed, at the manufacturer's recommended entry airspeed, or in its absence a safe speed not exceeding VA at the current weight, taken from the POH or AFM. Set cruise or the recommended power and leave it there for the whole maneuver. Enter at an altitude that allows completion no lower than 1,500 feet AGL with the wind perpendicular to the entry heading.

items.q: What happens at the 45, 90, 135 and 180 degree points of a lazy eight?
items.a: At 45 degrees of turn the pitch attitude is at its maximum nose up and the bank is about 15 degrees and still increasing. At 90 degrees the pitch is passing level through the horizon, the bank is steepest at about 30 degrees, the altitude is highest and the airspeed is lowest. At 135 degrees the pitch is maximum nose down with the bank decreasing. At 180 degrees the airplane is level again at entry altitude and airspeed on the reciprocal heading.

items.q: State the ACS tolerances for a lazy eight.
items.a: Approximately 30 degrees of bank at the steepest point, a constant change of pitch and roll rate and airspeed throughout, coordinated flight, and at the 180 degree point altitude plus or minus 100 feet from the entry altitude, airspeed plus or minus 10 knots from the entry airspeed, and heading plus or minus 10 degrees. Continue through the number of symmetrical loops the evaluator specifies.

items.q: Where is the airspeed lowest in a lazy eight and how slow should it get?
items.a: At the 90 degree point, where pitch is passing through level, bank is steepest and altitude is highest. It should reach a genuine minimum there, comfortably above a stall but slow enough that the maneuver reads as a maximum performance climbing turn rather than a gentle wander. Airspeed then builds back to the entry value by the 180 degree point, within plus or minus 10 knots.

items.q: What does constant change mean in a lazy eight, and why does the examiner care?
items.a: It means pitch, bank, airspeed and altitude are changing at every instant, with no pauses and no segments of constant bank. Continuously varying control pressure is the entire point of the maneuver, so a lazy eight flown as a climbing turn, then a level segment, then a descending turn is unsatisfactory even if the numbers at the 180 degree point are within tolerance.

items.q: How do you set up the visual references for a lazy eight?
items.a: Before entry, with the wind perpendicular to the nose, pick a prominent horizon reference abeam the wing for the 90 degree point and a second reference roughly diagonal ahead for the 45 degree point. Note the entry heading, altitude and airspeed. Fly the maneuver against those outside references and the horizon; the heading indicator and altimeter are a cross-check, not the primary reference.

items.q: How is a lazy eight different from a chandelle?
items.a: A chandelle is a single 180 degree maximum performance climbing turn with a constant 30 degree bank to the 90 degree point that ends slow, high and on a new heading. A lazy eight is a pair of symmetrical climbing and descending 180 degree turns that returns to the entry altitude and airspeed at each 180 degree point, with pitch and bank changing continuously and never held constant.

items.q: What are the common errors in a lazy eight?
items.a: Too much pitch or bank early, so the airplane runs out of energy before the 90 degree point; holding a constant bank instead of changing it continuously; letting the nose slice through the 90 degree point instead of arriving level there; halves that are not symmetrical; poor coordination at the slow steep 90 degree point; adding or removing power; and being outside plus or minus 100 feet at the 180 degree point.

items.q: What are eights on pylons and what do they demonstrate?
items.a: Eights on pylons is a figure eight flown around two ground reference points while an imaginary line from your eye through a fixed wingtip reference stays pinned to each pylon. It demonstrates the relationship between groundspeed and pivotal altitude, precise division of attention at low altitude, and coordinated control, because the pylon is held with altitude rather than with yaw.

items.q: What is pivotal altitude?
items.a: Pivotal altitude is the height at which, for a given groundspeed, the airplane's rate of turn exactly matches the rate at which the line of sight to the pylon sweeps, so the wingtip reference appears fixed on the pylon. Above it the pylon appears to move behind the reference; below it the pylon appears to move ahead. It depends only on groundspeed, not on bank angle or on radius.

items.q: What is the formula for pivotal altitude in knots? Work an example.
items.a: Pivotal altitude in feet AGL equals groundspeed in knots squared divided by 11.3. At 90 knots groundspeed, 90 squared is 8,100; 8,100 divided by 11.3 is 717 feet AGL. If the pylons sit at 400 feet MSL, that is 717 plus 400, or 1,117 feet MSL on the altimeter. Recompute for the groundspeed you actually expect and always add the pylon elevation to convert to MSL.

items.q: What is the pivotal altitude formula if your groundspeed is in miles per hour?
items.a: Pivotal altitude in feet equals groundspeed in miles per hour squared divided by 15. At 105 mph, 105 squared is 11,025, divided by 15 is 735 feet AGL. Use 11.3 as the divisor for knots and 15 for miles per hour, and be certain which unit your groundspeed is in before dividing, because mixing the two puts you a long way off the correct altitude.

items.q: Where does the divisor 11.3 come from?
items.a: From the geometry of a level turn: pivotal altitude equals velocity squared divided by the acceleration of gravity, with velocity in feet per second and g about 32.2 feet per second squared. One knot is 1.69 feet per second, so squaring gives 2.85, and 32.2 divided by 2.85 is about 11.3. That derivation is also why bank angle never appears in the formula; only groundspeed matters.

items.q: Why does the pivotal altitude change during eights on pylons?
items.a: Because groundspeed changes as the airplane turns through the wind while the airspeed stays constant. Turning downwind the groundspeed rises and pivotal altitude rises with the square of it, so you must climb; turning upwind the groundspeed falls and you must descend. That continuous, gentle climbing and descending to hold the pylon is the maneuver itself.

items.q: How do you work out the groundspeed to use before flying eights on pylons?
items.a: Estimate it from the airspeed you plan to fly and the reported wind, then compute a starting altitude. A practical shortcut is to use the average of the highest and lowest groundspeeds you expect, which is close to your true airspeed. Then refine it in flight: enter the turn and see whether the pylon creeps ahead or behind, and adjust. The computed number is only a starting point.

items.q: How do you establish the wingtip reference line?
items.a: Set the computed pivotal altitude, roll into a medium bank turn around the pylon, and note where the pylon sits against a fixed point on the airplane in line with your eye, typically a spot along the wing or wingtip. That becomes your reference for the whole maneuver. It must be a fixed point, and your head must stay still; leaning to make the pylon line up is the classic self-deception.

items.q: The pylon appears to move ahead of your reference line. What is wrong and what do you do?
items.a: You are below pivotal altitude, so the airplane is turning faster than the line of sight is sweeping. Climb slightly to reach the pivotal altitude for your current groundspeed and the pylon will drift back onto the reference line. Do not yaw the airplane with rudder to chase it, and do not change bank to fix it; the correction for this maneuver is altitude.

items.q: The pylon appears to move behind your reference line. What is wrong and what do you do?
items.a: You are above pivotal altitude, so the line of sight is sweeping faster than the airplane is turning. Descend slightly and the pylon will move forward onto the reference line. As when low, the correction is made with small, smooth pitch changes; power stays set and the bank stays where the ground track and the wind require it to be.

items.q: Why must you never use rudder to hold the pylon?
items.a: Because yawing the airplane to slide the reference onto the pylon puts it in a slip or a skid, banked and distracted at low altitude, which is the classic stall and spin setup. The ACS specifically requires the pylon position be maintained while avoiding slips and skids. Correct with altitude and keep the ball centered; if that will not work, your altitude or groundspeed assumption is wrong.

items.q: What bank angle should eights on pylons be flown at?
items.a: Approximately 30 to 40 degrees at the steepest point, which the ACS uses as the entry criterion and which drives how far apart the pylons must be. You do not fly a fixed bank; it varies through each turn as the wind changes the ground track. Pylons too close together force an excessive bank, and pylons too far apart give a bank too shallow to be a meaningful exercise.

items.q: How do you choose the two pylons?
items.a: Pick two prominent, easily identified objects at similar elevation, clear of congested areas and with usable emergency landing options nearby, spaced so a short straight and level diagonal of a few seconds fits between the turns and the steepest bank stays near 30 to 40 degrees. Put the line between them roughly perpendicular to the wind so the entry diagonal is flown downwind.

items.q: How do you enter and fly eights on pylons?
items.a: Compute pivotal altitude, then enter diagonally downwind between the pylons at that altitude and the planned airspeed. Turn toward the first pylon and place the reference line on it, holding it with small pitch changes. Roll out as the wing comes off the pylon, fly the short diagonal to the second pylon so it passes abeam, turn the opposite direction around it, then repeat or roll out on the assigned heading.

items.q: Where in eights on pylons is your altitude lowest and where is it highest?
items.a: Lowest where groundspeed is lowest, when the airplane is headed most nearly into the wind, and highest where groundspeed is highest, headed most nearly downwind. Because pivotal altitude varies with the square of groundspeed, a strong wind makes that altitude swing large, and the lowest point of the maneuver is what sets your real clearance from terrain and obstacles.

items.q: What are the ACS completion standards for eights on pylons?
items.a: Determine the approximate pivotal altitude; select suitable pylons that permit straight and level flight between them and account for the wind; enter at the appropriate altitude and airspeed with approximately 30 to 40 degrees of bank at the steepest point; apply the corrections needed to keep the line of sight reference on the pylon; divide attention between airplane control and outside references; and hold pylon position avoiding slips and skids. This task publishes no numeric altitude or airspeed tolerance.

items.q: What altitude limits apply to eights on pylons in practice?
items.a: Pivotal altitude sets the working height, often a few hundred to about a thousand feet AGL, but 14 CFR 91.119 still governs. Away from congested areas you may not operate closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure, and over open water or sparsely populated areas the same 500 foot rule applies. Choose pylons in open country so the computed altitude is both legal and survivable.

items.q: What are the common errors in eights on pylons?
items.a: Miscomputing pivotal altitude or using airspeed in place of groundspeed; using rudder to hold the pylon; moving your head to make the reference line up; correcting with bank instead of altitude; abrupt, oversized pitch corrections; badly chosen or badly spaced pylons; losing coordination in the turn; and fixating on the pylon instead of scanning for traffic, terrain and obstructions.

items.q: What is the power-off 180 degree accuracy approach and landing?
items.a: It is a landing flown from the downwind leg with the throttle closed abeam a chosen touchdown point and no power used again. It demonstrates judgment of a power-off glide, energy management with pattern shape, flaps and slips, and the precision that defines a commercial certificate: putting the airplane exactly where you intended without power available to correct your errors.

items.q: Where do you set up for the power-off 180 and at what altitude?
items.a: On the downwind leg, parallel to the landing runway, at not more than 1,000 feet AGL, which the ACS specifies. Fly pattern spacing corrected for the wind, complete the before landing checklist and make the appropriate radio calls, select and aim for a suitable touchdown point considering wind, landing surface and obstructions, and close the throttle abeam that point.

items.q: What is the touchdown tolerance for the power-off 180?
items.a: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 200 feet beyond the specified touchdown point. Landing before the point does not meet the standard, so plan to arrive a little long and bring it back with flaps and a slip. The airplane must also touch down with the crosswind corrected, no side drift, and the longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline.

items.q: What airspeed and configuration do you use in the power-off 180 glide?
items.a: Close the throttle abeam the point and establish the best glide speed from the POH or AFM, then transition to the recommended approach speed as you configure, or in the absence of a published figure not more than 1.3 VSO, plus 10 or minus 5 knots with the gust factor applied. Add flaps in stages only once the landing is clearly assured; early flaps throw away glide you cannot get back.

items.q: How do you tell during the glide whether you will make your touchdown point?
items.a: Watch the aim point in the windscreen. A point that stays fixed relative to the airframe is where you will arrive; one that moves down and away from you means you will overshoot it, and one that rises toward you means you will land short. Check it continuously from the moment you close the throttle and correct with pattern shape, flaps or a slip while you still have energy to trade.

items.q: You are high on the power-off 180. What are your options, in order?
items.a: Trade the excess energy, starting with what you can undo. Widen or extend the base slightly, then add the next stage of flaps, and if still high use a forward slip, which increases drag and steepens the path without building airspeed. Hold the target airspeed throughout. Do not use full flaps and a full slip at the same time until the touchdown point is clearly made.

items.q: You are low on the power-off 180. What do you do?
items.a: Tighten the pattern and cut the corner toward the runway immediately, do not add any further flaps, and hold the target airspeed rather than trying to stretch the glide with pitch, which only steepens the descent. If the touchdown point still cannot be reached safely, go around. An unsatisfactory landing distance is a retest item; an unsafe attempt to stretch a glide is a disqualifying one.

items.q: When would you use a forward slip versus a sideslip on the power-off 180?
items.a: A forward slip is a drag device used to lose altitude with the longitudinal axis angled away from the ground track; a sideslip is the crosswind technique that keeps the axis aligned with the runway. The ACS asks you to correlate the crosswind with the direction of the forward slip and to transition to a sideslip for landing so touchdown occurs with no drift and the axis aligned.

items.q: How does the wind change the way you fly the power-off 180?
items.a: A strong headwind on final shortens the glide over the ground, so fly the downwind closer in and delay flaps; light wind means the glide carries farther, so widen out or plan to slip. Wind also changes your groundspeed on downwind and therefore the timing to the abeam point. Judge it from the aim point behavior rather than from a memorized pattern, because the wind is different every day.

items.q: What are the common errors on the power-off 180?
items.a: Downwind too high, too wide or above 1,000 feet AGL; closing the throttle late or not abeam the point; not trimming for the glide; full flaps early followed by a landing short; stretching the glide with pitch and letting airspeed decay; not slipping when a slip was needed; drift or side load at touchdown; and touching down short of the point or beyond the 200 foot tolerance.

items.q: How is the power-off 180 different from a simulated engine failure approach?
items.a: The power-off 180 is a precision maneuver flown from a known downwind at a known altitude to a specified point on a runway, graded on touching down within 200 feet beyond that point. The simulated emergency approach may begin at any altitude anywhere, is graded on field selection, best glide within 10 knots, planning and checklist discipline, and is normally terminated with a go around rather than a landing.

items.q: What is a short-field takeoff and maximum performance climb for?
items.a: It is the technique for getting airborne in the least ground roll and clearing a 50 foot obstacle in the shortest horizontal distance, used when runway length or obstacles are limiting. It demonstrates that you can extract book performance from the airplane, which requires the handbook's exact flap setting, liftoff speed and obstacle clearance speed rather than an improvised technique.

items.q: How do you fly a short-field takeoff?
items.a: Use every available foot: taxi to the very beginning of the usable surface and align with the centerline. Set the flap configuration the handbook specifies. Hold the brakes, apply takeoff power, and confirm full power and normal engine indications before brake release. Rotate at the recommended liftoff speed, accelerate to and hold VX until the obstacle is cleared or you are 50 feet up, then accelerate to VY.

items.q: What airspeeds does the ACS grade on a short-field takeoff?
items.a: The recommended obstacle clearance airspeed or VX until the obstacle is cleared or the airplane is 50 feet above the surface, then VY for the remainder of the climb, both taken from the POH or AFM. The commercial airspeed tolerance is tighter than the private standard, so read the exact figure in the current ACS Task CA.IV.E rather than assuming the private plus 10 minus 5 knots.

items.q: When do you retract the gear and flaps after a short-field takeoff?
items.a: Retractable gear comes up when there is no usable runway left to land on, or as the handbook directs, since gear is only drag once you are committed. Flaps stay at the takeoff setting until the obstacle is cleared and you have accelerated toward a safe climb speed, then come up in stages while you lower the nose enough to hold airspeed, because retracting flaps costs lift immediately.

items.q: What are the common errors on a short-field takeoff?
items.a: Not using the full runway; the wrong flap setting; releasing the brakes before full power is set and verified; rotating early so the airplane mushes in ground effect; over rotating and settling back; climbing at the wrong speed, especially slower than VX, which costs climb angle and stall margin at once; retracting flaps or gear too early; and drifting off the centerline in a crosswind.

items.q: What is a short-field approach and landing meant to achieve?
items.a: Touchdown at the slowest safe speed on a precise point with the shortest possible ground roll, so the airplane can be landed over an obstacle and stopped in minimum distance. It is a steep, stabilized, power-controlled approach at the handbook's short-field speed and flap setting, followed by a firm touchdown with minimal float and immediate maximum braking.

items.q: What approach speed do you fly for a short field, and what is the tolerance?
items.a: The manufacturer's published short-field approach speed, or in its absence not more than 1.3 VSO, held to plus 10 or minus 5 knots with the gust factor applied. Take VSO or the published speed from the POH or AFM. Excess speed is the enemy of this maneuver, because every extra knot turns into float and runway consumed, and the touchdown tolerance is unforgiving.

items.q: What is the touchdown tolerance for a commercial short-field landing?
items.a: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 100 feet beyond the specified point, threshold markings or landing zone, with no side drift and with the longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline or landing path. That is half the private pilot allowance. The tolerance runs from the specified point forward only, so touching down short of it is also unsatisfactory.

items.q: Describe the technique for a short-field landing.
items.a: Fly a stabilized approach at the recommended flap setting and speed, controlling the descent path with power and the airspeed with pitch so the airplane arrives at the aim point on speed. Reduce power in the roundout so float is minimal, and touch down firmly on the mains at minimum controllable airspeed. Then retract flaps if the handbook calls for it, hold the yoke aft, and brake firmly without skidding.

items.q: Where should you aim on a short-field landing if you must touch down on a specified point?
items.a: Aim short of the touchdown point by about the distance the airplane travels during the roundout, so the flare uses up the difference and the wheels arrive on the point. Practice tells you that distance for your airplane. With 100 feet of tolerance beyond the point and none before it, the safer error is a slightly late touchdown, never an approach that lands short of the threshold.

items.q: Why do you carry power on a short-field approach rather than gliding it?
items.a: Because the approach is flown near 1.3 VSO, slow and draggy on the back side of the power curve where the sink rate is high. Power gives precise control of the descent path and an immediate escape if the sink rate builds. Closing the throttle early produces a hard arrival short of the point; on this approach the throttle is the glidepath control and pitch holds the speed.

items.q: What are the common errors on a short-field landing?
items.a: Approaching fast so the airplane floats past the point; an unstabilized approach with the power chasing the path; flaring high; holding off for a soft touchdown instead of accepting a firm one; not braking promptly; braking hard enough to skid or lock a wheel; letting the yoke come forward during braking; drift at touchdown; and missing the 100 foot touchdown tolerance.

items.q: What is a soft-field takeoff and what problem does it solve?
items.a: It is the technique for departing grass, sand, mud or snow, where the wheels sink and rolling resistance is high. The object is to transfer weight from the wheels to the wings as early as possible, lift off at the lowest possible airspeed, and accelerate in ground effect. It is about surface drag and protecting the nosewheel, not about obstacle clearance.

items.q: How do you fly a soft-field takeoff?
items.a: Set the flap configuration the handbook specifies before taxiing onto the surface and keep the airplane rolling onto the runway without stopping. Hold full aft elevator to keep weight off the nosewheel, apply takeoff power smoothly, then relax back pressure just enough to keep the nose from coming up too far. Lift off at the lowest possible speed, level off in ground effect, accelerate, then climb.

items.q: Why must you level off in ground effect after a soft-field liftoff?
items.a: Because the airplane leaves the surface below the speed at which it can climb out of ground effect. Induced drag is reduced close to the ground, so the wing will fly at a speed that will not sustain a climb once clear of it. Staying low to accelerate to VX or VY prevents settling back onto the surface or a stall just above it.

items.q: What climb speed do you use after a soft-field takeoff and how is it graded?
items.a: VX if an obstacle must be cleared, otherwise VY, both from the POH or AFM, established once you have accelerated in ground effect. The commercial standard on the climb airspeed is tighter than the private plus 10 minus 5 knots, so read the exact figure in the current ACS Task CA.IV.C. Directional control and wind drift correction are graded throughout the takeoff and climb.

items.q: Why do you avoid stopping the airplane on a soft field?
items.a: Because the wheels sink into the surface as soon as they stop rolling, and breaking out again can take more power than the airplane has, or outside help. Complete the run-up and checklists on a firm surface, keep the yoke full aft, and taxi onto the runway in one continuous rolling turn that flows straight into the takeoff roll.

items.q: What are the common errors on a soft-field takeoff?
items.a: Stopping on the soft surface; not holding full aft elevator during the taxi and initial roll; over rotating so the tail strikes or the airplane leaps off and settles back; failing to relax back pressure after liftoff so the airplane never accelerates in ground effect; climbing away before reaching VX or VY; the wrong flap setting; and poor directional control in a crosswind.

items.q: What is the objective of a soft-field landing?
items.a: To touch down at the lowest possible sink rate and airspeed and keep the nosewheel off the surface as long as possible, so the airplane does not dig in or nose over on soft or rough ground. Weight is transferred gradually from the wings to the wheels, and the airplane is kept rolling after touchdown rather than braked to a stop.

items.q: What approach speed and configuration do you use for a soft-field landing?
items.a: The manufacturer's recommended approach speed, or in its absence not more than 1.3 VSO, held to plus 10 or minus 5 knots with the gust factor applied, at the flap setting the handbook specifies, usually full. Take the numbers from the POH or AFM. The approach itself is a normal approach; the whole difference lies in the roundout, the touchdown and the rollout.

items.q: Describe the roundout and touchdown for a soft-field landing.
items.a: Carry a small amount of power into the flare and hold the airplane just off the surface, increasing back pressure as the speed decays, so it settles onto the main wheels with almost no sink rate. Keep adding back pressure to hold the nosewheel clear for as long as elevator authority lasts, reduce power smoothly, and let the airplane roll with little or no braking.

items.q: What is the touchdown point tolerance for a commercial soft-field landing?
items.a: The ACS sets no distance tolerance for the soft-field landing. The graded standard is touchdown at a proper pitch attitude with a minimum descent rate, no side drift, and the longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline or landing path, together with correct approach airspeed control and correct handling of the nosewheel after touchdown.

items.q: Why do you avoid braking after a soft-field landing?
items.a: Because the soft surface already supplies heavy rolling resistance, and braking loads the nosewheel and can dig the mains in or nose the airplane over. Hold the yoke full aft, add power as needed to keep taxiing without stopping, and let the surface slow you. The examiner watches your elevator position through the rollout as closely as the touchdown itself.

items.q: What are the common errors on a soft-field landing?
items.a: Approaching too fast; removing all power in the flare so the airplane drops on; flaring high and settling hard; letting the nosewheel down early or letting it fall as the speed decays; using the brakes; drift at touchdown; and relaxing the aft elevator during the rollout, which is what actually damages airplanes operating off soft ground.

items.q: What is an emergency descent and when would you use one?
items.a: It is a maximum rate descent flown to get the airplane down quickly while remaining fully under control. Typical reasons are an in-flight fire, smoke or fumes in the cabin, a medical emergency on board, a loss of cabin pressurization, or any situation in which the time spent at altitude is itself the hazard. It is flown to the configuration and airspeed the handbook publishes.

items.q: What configuration and airspeed do you use for an emergency descent?
items.a: Whatever the POH or AFM specifies, typically power to idle, propeller full forward, and drag added with the landing gear and any flap setting the handbook permits. The airspeed is the handbook figure, bounded by VNE, VLE or VFE for whatever is extended. Never exceed a structural or configuration limit speed to descend faster, and never fly a remembered number from another airplane.

items.q: Why is an emergency descent flown in a bank?
items.a: A bank of 30 to 45 degrees keeps a positive load factor on the airplane, prevents the nose from dropping too far, and produces a steep descent path without letting the airspeed run away. It also improves the view of the ground and helps keep you over the area you want. The ACS requires the bank angle to stay between 30 and 45 degrees during the descent.

items.q: State the ACS tolerances for the emergency descent.
items.a: Establish the configuration and airspeed the handbook specifies for the scenario; use a bank angle between 30 and 45 degrees to maintain positive load factors; maintain the appropriate airspeed plus 0 or minus 10 knots; level off at the specified altitude plus or minus 100 feet; maintain orientation, divide attention appropriately and plan a smooth recovery; and complete the appropriate checklist.

items.q: Why is the emergency descent airspeed tolerance plus 0 and minus 10 knots?
items.a: Because the target airspeed sits close to a structural or configuration limit, so there is no allowance for being fast. You may be up to 10 knots slow and still meet the standard, but exceeding the target risks exceeding VNE, VLE or VFE. That asymmetry is a favorite oral question and the reason to set the descent up deliberately rather than simply shoving the nose down.

items.q: How do you actually enter an emergency descent?
items.a: Close the throttle and set the propeller as the handbook directs, then roll into a bank of 30 to 45 degrees while lowering the nose to the target airspeed. Add the gear and any permitted flaps as drag. Keep the airplane coordinated, clear the path below visually, watch the airspeed against the limit, and start the level off early enough to arrive at the target altitude within 100 feet.

items.q: What must you watch out for during an emergency descent?
items.a: Exceeding VNE, VLE or VFE; shock cooling the engine, which the handbook procedure is written to limit; traffic and terrain below, since the descent rate is very high and forward visibility is reduced; disorientation; an overshoot at the level off; and, when the cause is fire, following the handbook fire checklist exactly rather than improvising with heat and ventilation controls.

items.q: What are the common errors on an emergency descent?
items.a: Pushing the nose over with no bank, which unloads the airplane and floats loose objects and the pilot; letting the airspeed pass the target; using a bank outside the 30 to 45 degree band; forgetting the gear or the propeller control; failing to clear the area below; skipping the checklist; and starting the recovery so late that the level off misses the plus or minus 100 foot tolerance.

items.q: The engine quits. What is the very first thing you do?
items.a: Pitch for the airplane's best glide speed and trim, because airspeed is the only thing that buys you time and distance and it decays within seconds. The ACS requires you to establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed within plus or minus 10 knots. Only after that do you turn toward a field, attempt a restart, and configure for landing.

items.q: What is the correct order of actions in a simulated engine failure?
items.a: Airspeed, field, checklist, radio, secure, land.
