items.a: Because every one of them rolls at a low airspeed and a high angle of attack, which is when adverse yaw is at its worst. The down-going aileron adds lift and with it induced drag to the rising wing, yawing the nose away from the roll, and induced drag is the dominant drag at low speed. Steep turns, chandelles, lazy eights and the pylon entries all begin and end with such a roll, so rudder goes in with the aileron and comes off with it.

items.q: How do you tell adverse yaw apart from a left-turning tendency when you feel it?
items.a: By what each one depends on. Adverse yaw exists only while the ailerons are deflected and always opposes the direction of roll, so it reverses when you reverse the roll and vanishes when the ailerons are neutral. The propeller effects are always to the left and depend on power, airspeed and angle of attack, not on aileron position. Rolling left at the apex of a lazy eight you are fighting both at once, in opposite directions.

items.q: You are 400 pounds under gross for the ride. What does that do to your lazy eight entry speed?
items.a: It lowers it. Maneuvering speed falls with the square root of the weight ratio, so at 1,925 pounds against this airplane's 2,325 pound maximum, the ratio is 0.828 and its square root is 0.91, meaning the entry should be about nine percent below the gross-weight figure. Entering at the book number when light puts you above maneuvering speed, where an abrupt pull can exceed the limit load factor before the wing stalls.

items.q: Why is maneuvering speed the right entry speed for these maneuvers rather than a comfortable cruise?
items.a: Because it is the fastest speed at which the airplane is protected from the pilot. These maneuvers involve large, sometimes hurried pitch and bank inputs at a varying load factor, and below maneuvering speed a full deflection of one control in one direction stalls the wing before it overstresses the airframe. It is also fast enough to carry the kinetic energy the maneuver has to trade for altitude and heading change.

items.q: What does the handbook actually approve this airplane to do among these maneuvers?
items.a: It approves steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles, listing them under utility category operation for bank angles exceeding 60 degrees, where the limit load factor is 4.4 g rather than the normal category's 3.8. Utility on this airplane means a reduced weight, no baggage and no rear seat occupants. Spins are prohibited in both categories, so stall margin is something you preserve rather than something you recover from.

items.q: Why does induced drag matter so much more in these maneuvers than in cruise?
items.a: Because every one of them is flown slow, at a high angle of attack, or at an elevated load factor, and induced drag varies with the square of the lift coefficient and inversely with the square of airspeed. In cruise it is a small part of total drag; at the apex of a lazy eight or the completion of a chandelle it is most of it. That is why these maneuvers bleed speed so fast and why any slip or skid, which only adds more drag, is costly.

items.q: What is the region of reversed command, and which of these maneuvers put you in it?
items.a: It is the band of speeds below the lift-to-drag maximum where total drag rises as the airplane slows, so more power is needed to fly slower. The chandelle completion, the apex of a lazy eight, the soft-field climb-out and the short-field approach all sit in it. The symptom is that pulling back makes the airplane go down, and the fix is always lowering the nose and adding power together, never pitching for altitude.

items.q: Why can't the airspeed indicator alone tell you how close you are to a stall in these maneuvers?
items.a: Because it knows nothing about load factor. A given indicated airspeed is comfortable at one g and stalled at two, and in a lazy eight the load factor runs from below one g at the apex to well above one in the recovery. Only the angle of attack is the same at every stall, so you judge the margin by the feel of the controls, the buffet, and the horn, which on this airplane sounds between five and ten knots above the stall.

items.q: Does the stall warning horn still work properly in a 50 degree bank?
items.a: Yes, and it warns at the right moment, because the detector is an angle of attack sensor rather than an airspeed sensor: a tab in the wing leading edge lifted by the airflow as the stagnation point moves toward the stall position. In the turn it will sound at a much higher indicated airspeed than the published stall speed, which is exactly correct. Remember it is electrical, and it is dead with the master switch off.

items.q: Why is coordination more than a style point in these maneuvers?
items.a: Because an uncoordinated airplane is both a draggy one and a dangerous one. A slip or a skid presents the fuselage to the airflow, adding parasite drag you cannot afford at low speed, and it makes the two wings fly at different angles of attack. Near the stall, that difference decides which wing drops and how violently. The ACS grades coordination throughout for that reason, not because a centered ball looks tidy.

items.q: What is the single thing these commercial maneuvers are testing aerodynamically?
items.a: That you can predict what the airplane is about to do and lead it rather than react to it. Each maneuver puts the airplane at a specific place on the curves of lift, drag and power and asks you to move along them smoothly: energy traded for altitude in a lazy eight, bank traded for climb in a chandelle, altitude traded for distance in the power-off 180. The tolerances exist to prove the prediction, not the reflexes.

items.q: How does a high density altitude change the way these maneuvers fly?
items.a: It cuts the density term in the lift equation, so at a given indicated airspeed the true airspeed is higher, which means a larger turn radius and a slower rate of turn at the same bank, and a higher groundspeed and pivotal altitude on the pylons. The engine makes less power and the propeller less thrust, so the chandelle climbs less and the soft field takes longer. Indicated stall speed is unchanged; true stall speed goes up.

items.q: The examiner says to treat him as your client. What do you brief before takeoff?
items.a: Everything you would brief a paying passenger, out loud and in order: belts and harnesses, door and exits, fire extinguisher location, vents and sick bags, ELT, what the flight will involve, sterile cockpit periods and when I want quiet, and an invitation to speak up immediately about any hazard he sees, such as birds or traffic. Then the departure briefing: runway, expected performance, and what I will do if the engine quits.

items.q: Give me your departure briefing.
items.a: Runway in use and expected takeoff distance against the runway available; the airspeeds I will use and the initial heading and altitude; the departure route and first frequency. Then the abort and emergency plan: what will make me abort on the ground, and if the engine fails after takeoff with runway remaining I land straight ahead, and above a safe altitude I turn only to a chosen field. Passengers are briefed to stay quiet until I say otherwise.

items.q: When do you give the passenger briefing in an emergency descent to a forced landing?
items.a: After the memory items and once the airplane is established, not before. The order is fly the airplane, best glide and a field, memory items for the engine, then brief the passengers while you are set up and before you are busy again on short final, then back to the checklist to confirm nothing was missed. Tell them to tighten belts, show them the door latch, have them unlatch it before touchdown, and say where to meet.

items.q: What do you tell a passenger about the controls and the sterile cockpit?
items.a: That the yoke and pedals on their side move with mine and they should keep hands and feet clear unless I ask, and that bags and feet stay away from the control column and flap handle. For quiet: no conversation from taxi through 1,000 feet after takeoff, and from the descent through the landing and taxi clear, except to tell me about a hazard, which I always want to hear immediately.

items.q: Your passenger starts chatting on short final. What do you do?
items.a: Say 'standby' once, firmly and without heat, and keep flying the airplane. Do not negotiate and do not look at him. If it continues and it is degrading the approach, go around and sort it out with altitude under you. Then debrief it after landing. Having briefed the sterile period before takeoff is what makes the single word work; if you never briefed it, the fault is yours.

items.q: What is the one thing a passenger should always interrupt you for?
items.a: A hazard. Traffic, birds, smoke, a warning light, an open door, or anything that looks wrong outside. Brief it that way: 'if you see something that worries you, say it immediately, even if I am busy'. The risk of an unnecessary call is trivial; the risk of a passenger who saw the other airplane and waited for a quiet moment is not.

items.q: You change a frequency while crossing a runway and drift off the centerline. What went wrong?
items.a: In substance, yes. Changing a frequency while crossing a runway is doing two things at once in a critical phase, and the airplane drifted while the pilot was heads-down. The fix is sequencing: stop the airplane, or finish crossing and stop clear, before you touch a radio. Taxi is a critical phase in both 121.542 and 135.100 for exactly this reason, and runway incursions are overwhelmingly a distraction problem.

items.q: Why would you ever fly a no-flap landing?
items.a: Because the flaps failed, because the system is jammed or asymmetric, or because you chose to. The handbook itself says that in high wind conditions, particularly strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps. Other reasons: a known electrical or mechanical problem, an airplane you do not want to slow down in turbulence, and practice so that the first one is not for real.

items.q: How does the approach differ without flaps?
items.a: It is flatter and faster. Without flaps the airplane's lift to drag ratio is better, so for the same power the descent path is shallower; you must start down earlier and plan a longer, lower final rather than trying to force the normal picture. Power controls the path and attitude controls the speed exactly as before, but you will carry less power, and you need a longer runway and no obstacle on the approach end.

items.q: How does the sight picture change on a no-flap landing?
items.a: The nose sits higher for the same airspeed because the wing needs a higher angle of attack without the flaps, so you see less of the runway over the cowl and the aiming point appears to be further down the glareshield. The approach angle itself is shallower, so the runway looks flatter and further away. Expect both, trust the airspeed and the aiming point, and do not chase the unfamiliar picture with pitch.

items.q: What speed do you fly on a no-flap approach?
items.a: A little faster than the full-flap figure, because the clean stall speed is higher than the full-flap stall speed. The handbook publishes 63 knots as the final approach speed with 40 degrees of flap, so without flaps I fly several knots above that, and I add half the gust factor if it is gusty. What I do not do is drag it in slowly; the flaps-up margin above the stall is what I am protecting.

items.q: Describe the roundout and touchdown without flaps.
items.a: Begin the roundout a little higher and more gradually, because the shallower approach path means less attitude change is needed between the approach and the landing attitude. Then expect to hold it off for a long time: the airplane is faster and cleaner, so it floats. Keep the aiming point and the centerline, let the speed bleed, and touch down on the main wheels with the nose high but short of the full-flap attitude.

items.q: How much more runway does a no-flap landing need?
items.a: Materially more, and the handbook does not publish a figure for it. The float is longer because of the extra speed and the better lift to drag ratio, and the touchdown is faster, so the ground roll is longer too. A planning rule of adding at least half again to the book landing distance is reasonable and conservative. Pick a long runway, land on the numbers you can actually make, and go around early if it is not working.

items.q: What are the common errors on a no-flap landing?
items.a: Flying the normal flap sight picture and ending up high and fast; chopping the power to make the normal descent angle and arriving low and slow; forcing the airplane onto the runway during the long float, which causes a bounce or a wheelbarrow on the nosewheel; floating past the planned touchdown point and landing long; and failing to brief the passengers or tell the tower that the landing will be a long one.

items.q: Name the three stages of a stall.
items.a: Approaching the stall, the full stall, and the recovery. The first is the approaching or imminent stall, where the angle of attack is nearing critical and the airplane gives you the warning signs; the second is the full stall, where the critical angle of attack has been exceeded; the third is the recovery back to unstalled, controlled flight. Describe what happens in each rather than fighting over the vocabulary.

items.q: Describe the first stage, the approaching stall.
items.a: The angle of attack is approaching critical but has not reached it. You get the cues: the stall warning horn, which on this airplane sounds five to ten knots above the stall, aerodynamic buffet as separated air from the wing root strikes the tail, mushy and ineffective controls, a high nose attitude for the airspeed, and a decaying airspeed with a high sink rate. The wing is still flying and recovery costs almost no altitude.

items.q: Describe the full stall.
items.a: The critical angle of attack has been exceeded, airflow over the upper surface has separated, and the wing is producing less lift than it was a moment ago even though the angle of attack has increased. The airplane pitches down as the center of pressure moves aft and the tail download is lost, the sink rate increases sharply, and any yaw at that moment drops a wing and starts a spin. Controls are sloppy and the ailerons are untrustworthy.

items.q: Describe the recovery stage.
items.a: The stage where the angle of attack is reduced below critical and the wing starts flying again. Reduce the angle of attack first, by releasing back pressure or pushing, because nothing else recovers a stall. Then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, add power smoothly as needed, and return to the desired flight path with the minimum loss of altitude, retracting flaps and gear on schedule rather than all at once.

items.q: Someone answers 'incipient' for the first stage. Is that wrong?
items.a: It is the wrong word in the wrong place rather than a wrong idea. Incipient is the word the FAA uses for the second phase of a spin, between the stall break and a fully developed spin, not for the approach to a stall; the stall itself is normally described as approaching or imminent, then full, then recovery. The examiner is checking that you understand the progression, so describe what the airplane is doing at each point.

items.q: What is a secondary stall, and where does it fit?
items.a: A second stall caused by the recovery itself: the pilot raises the nose again before the wing has regained flying speed, exceeds the critical angle of attack a second time, and stalls. It is not one of the stages; it is a recovery error, and it is the commonest one on a checkride. The fix is patience, letting the airspeed build before you raise the nose, and avoiding an abrupt pull in the pitch-up after adding power.

items.q: What is an accelerated stall?
items.a: A stall that occurs at a load factor greater than one, and therefore at a higher airspeed than the published one-g stall speed. Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so at 45 degrees of bank, 1.41 g, the stall speed rises about 19 percent, and at 60 degrees, 2 g, about 41 percent. The wing has not changed its mind about the critical angle of attack; only the speed at which you reach it has changed.

items.q: How does an accelerated stall feel different from a normal one?
items.a: It is faster and sharper. The break comes with little warning at a speed that feels perfectly safe, the buffet is more pronounced and the roll-off tendency is stronger, and the airplane can be banked, turning, and at a low pitch attitude when it happens. That is why it is the stall behind the base-to-final accident: nose low, speed apparently adequate, and a tightening skidding turn.

items.q: How is the accelerated stall flown on the commercial checkride?
items.a: Clearing turns, then set up at or below maneuvering speed in the configuration the examiner specifies, roll into a coordinated turn of about 45 degrees of bank and increase back pressure smoothly and firmly until the stall warning or buffet, keeping the ball centered. Recover at the first indication by reducing angle of attack, level the wings and add power. Pick the entry altitude so that recovery is complete no lower than 3,000 feet AGL.

items.q: Why does the ACS set a higher recovery altitude for the accelerated stall?
items.a: Because the break is abrupt and the airplane can roll substantially before you catch it, so you need more room than for a straight-ahead power-off stall. Plan for recovery to be complete no lower than 3,000 feet AGL, against 1,500 feet for the other stalls. It is also the reason you keep the entry speed at or below maneuvering speed: an abrupt pull above Va can overstress the airframe before it stalls.

items.q: What is maneuvering during slow flight meant to demonstrate?
items.a: Control of the airplane at an airspeed where any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor or reduction in power would produce a stall warning, while flying it accurately. It shows that you can feel the airplane in the region of reversed command, that you lead with rudder, that you use power for altitude and pitch for speed, and that you are not startled by sloppy controls and a high nose.

items.q: Fly me slow flight with a turn and a climb, then the other way with a descent. What are you watching?
items.a: Airspeed first, because everything else follows it. Right rudder increases with power and decreases as the bank reverses, and the stall speed rises with bank angle, so I keep the bank shallow, lead the roll-in with rudder and keep the ball centered. In the climb I watch that the nose does not come up as power goes in, and in the descent that I do not let the speed increase out of the slow flight regime.

items.q: What tolerances does the commercial standard hold you to in slow flight?
items.a: Tighter than private: altitude within 50 feet, heading within 10 degrees, bank within 5 degrees, and airspeed plus 5 and minus 0 knots. The minus zero is the one that bites, since it means you may be fast but never slow, so set the speed a touch above the target rather than hunting for it from below. Clearing turns before entry and a positive recovery are part of the task, not optional extras.

b: Physiology, illusions, decision making, and the things that impair a pilot.

items.q: What does the IM SAFE checklist stand for and when do you run it?
items.a: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion (or Eating). It is a personal pre-flight self-assessment run before every flight, and again before any leg after a long day. Each letter is a go/no-go item about you rather than the airplane; a single honest failure is grounds to cancel, because unlike a broken radio there is no minimum equipment list for the pilot.

items.q: Under the Illness item of IM SAFE, what should stop you flying?
items.a: Any condition that degrades performance or could incapacitate you: fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, a head cold or blocked sinuses, ear infection, sore throat, dizziness, pain, or anything that distracts. A cold matters far more in the air than on the ground because blocked eustachian tubes and sinuses cannot equalize on the descent and can rupture an eardrum.

items.q: How should a pilot treat medication under IM SAFE?
items.a: Assume both the drug and the underlying condition are disqualifying until you have checked. Prescription drugs need clearance from an Aviation Medical Examiner. For over-the-counter drugs the standard guidance is to wait at least five maximum dosing intervals after the last dose before flying, so a drug labeled every four to six hours means roughly 30 hours grounded. Sedating antihistamines, sleep aids and anything warning about drowsiness are no-go.

items.q: What kinds of stress affect a pilot and why does stress matter in the cockpit?
items.a: Physiological stress such as fatigue, illness, heat, noise or missed meals; psychological stress such as work or family pressure, grief or financial worry; and environmental stress such as turbulence, vibration, glare or a hot cockpit. Stress narrows attention, so a stressed pilot fixates on one problem and stops flying the airplane. Stress is cumulative, so several small ones add up to one large one.

items.q: What are the exact alcohol limits for acting as a required crewmember?
items.a: No flying within 8 hours of the last drink, with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or more, or while under the influence at all, under 14 CFR 91.17 (Part 91, Subpart A — General; Alcohol or drugs). The same section bars using any drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety, bars carrying an obviously intoxicated passenger except a medical patient under care, and requires you to submit to a blood or breath test on request.

items.q: Is being legal on the 8-hour and 0.04 percent rule the same as being fit to fly?
items.a: No. Those are minimum legal thresholds, not a fitness standard. A hangover leaves impaired judgment, dehydration, headache and reduced tolerance to hypoxia long after blood alcohol reads zero, and 14 CFR 91.17 still prohibits flying while under the influence regardless of the number. The practical personal minimum most pilots adopt is 24 hours from bottle to throttle.

items.q: How does alcohol interact with altitude and hypoxia?
items.a: Alcohol both intensifies and mimics hypoxia. It causes histotoxic hypoxia by preventing cells from using the oxygen delivered to them, so the physiological effect of one ounce of alcohol is roughly equivalent to an additional 2,000 feet of altitude. Judgment, reaction time, night vision and vestibular tolerance all degrade, and the two impairments compound rather than simply add.

items.q: What is the difference between acute and chronic fatigue, and what fixes each?
items.a: Acute fatigue is short-term, from a long day, missed sleep, dehydration or a hard workout, and is cured by rest, food and fluid. Chronic fatigue builds over weeks from continuous stress or inadequate recovery and is not fixed by one good night's sleep; it needs a break from the cause and often medical help. Fatigue is insidious because it degrades your ability to judge how degraded you are.

items.q: What does the Emotion item of IM SAFE ask you to check?
items.a: Whether anything emotionally significant has happened that will occupy your attention in the cockpit: an argument, a bereavement, a job loss, or even good news that has you distracted. Emotion drives the mental workload up before the engine starts. Some versions of the mnemonic use Eating instead, in which case it asks whether you are properly fed and hydrated, since low blood sugar mimics the early symptoms of hypoxia.

items.q: What does PAVE stand for, and what is it used for?
items.a: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures. It is a pre-flight risk-identification checklist that sorts hazards into four buckets so none is overlooked, and it is used to set personal minimums before you launch. Each element is assessed against the specific flight, and the risks are considered together rather than one at a time, because several yellow items make a red flight.

items.q: What goes into the Pilot element of PAVE?
items.a: Your health, recency and currency, total and recent experience in type, proficiency in the maneuvers and conditions planned, fatigue and emotional state, and whether you are legal and current for the operation. IM SAFE is the tool used inside this element. Ask specifically whether you have flown this route, this aircraft and this weather recently, not merely whether the paperwork is valid.

items.q: What goes into the Aircraft element of PAVE?
items.a: Airworthiness, inspection status and required documents, equipment fit and whether it suits the flight, fuel on board, weight and balance, performance for the runway and density altitude, and your familiarity with the systems and avionics installed. The documents that must be aboard are remembered as ARROW: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio station license if international, Operating limitations, and Weight and balance data.

items.q: What goes into the enVironment element of PAVE?
items.a: Weather now and forecast, including ceilings, visibility, winds, icing, thunderstorms and density altitude; terrain along the route; airspace and any temporary restrictions; airports, runway lengths, surfaces and lighting; day or night; and NOTAMs. It also covers the alternates available if the plan fails, since the environment decides whether you have an out.

items.q: What are external pressures in PAVE and why are they the most dangerous element?
items.a: They are the reasons you feel you must complete the flight: a passenger's schedule, a business meeting, an aircraft booking, the cost already spent, wanting to look competent, or get-home-itis. They are dangerous because they do not appear on any instrument and they quietly bias every other judgment, turning a marginal weather call into a launch. The mitigation is to plan an out in advance and tell passengers the trip may not happen.

items.q: What are the five hazardous attitudes, and what mnemonic captures them?
items.a: Anti-authority, Impulsivity, Invulnerability, Macho and Resignation, remembered by the phrase I'M A Raging Idiot. They are unconscious thought patterns that precede poor decisions. The technique is to recognize the thought as it occurs, name which attitude it is, and then deliberately recite the specific antidote before acting.

items.q: What is the anti-authority attitude and its exact antidote?
items.a: Anti-authority is the thought Don't tell me — resentment of rules, procedures and anyone telling you what to do, expressed as skipping a checklist or busting a regulation you consider pointless. The prescribed antidote, word for word, is Follow the rules. They are usually right.

items.q: What is the impulsivity attitude and its exact antidote?
items.a: Impulsivity is the thought Do something quickly — the urge to act immediately on the first idea that comes to mind, without pausing to identify the best option, typically after an engine problem or an unexpected clearance. The prescribed antidote, word for word, is Not so fast. Think first.

items.q: What is the invulnerability attitude and its exact antidote?
items.a: Invulnerability is the thought It won't happen to me — accepting known risk because accidents are things that happen to other pilots, which leads to flying into marginal weather or stretching fuel. The prescribed antidote, word for word, is It could happen to me.

items.q: What is the macho attitude and its exact antidote?
items.a: Macho is the thought I can do it — trying to prove ability, impress passengers or better someone else, which shows up as low passes, tight patterns or pressing on when others have turned back. It is not limited to men. The prescribed antidote, word for word, is Taking chances is foolish.

items.q: What is the resignation attitude and its exact antidote?
items.a: Resignation is the thought What's the use? — believing the outcome is out of your hands, so you stop flying the airplane, defer to a passenger or controller, or go along with whatever happens. It often follows a compounding series of problems. The prescribed antidote, word for word, is I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.

items.q: What is aeronautical decision making?
items.a: A systematic approach to the mental process a pilot uses to determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It is deliberate rather than instinctive: it replaces the reflex answer with a structured sequence of gathering information, weighing alternatives against risk, choosing, acting and then checking the result. It is taught because most accidents follow a chain of poor decisions rather than a single mechanical failure.

items.q: What are the six steps of the DECIDE model?
items.a: Detect that a change has occurred; Estimate the need to counter or react to it; Choose a desirable outcome for the flight; Identify actions that will successfully control the change; Do take the necessary action; and Evaluate the effect of that action. The last step closes the loop, which is what makes it a continuous process rather than a single decision.

items.q: How is risk formally assessed, and what are the two variables?
items.a: By likelihood and severity. Likelihood ranges from probable through occasional and remote to improbable; severity ranges from catastrophic through critical and marginal to negligible. Plotting the two on a matrix converts a vague worry into a rating of high, serious, medium or low, and anything catastrophic or critical demands mitigation or cancellation however unlikely it seems.

items.q: What is single-pilot resource management?
items.a: The art of managing all available resources — onboard equipment, charts, checklists, air traffic control, flight service, passengers and your own attention — when there is no other crewmember. It bundles aeronautical decision making, risk management, task management, automation management, controlled flight into terrain awareness and situational awareness into one discipline, and it is what replaces crew resource management in a single-pilot cockpit.

items.q: What does good automation management require of a single pilot?
items.a: Knowing what the autopilot and navigator are doing, why, and what they will do next, and being willing to turn them off. The rules are to select the level of automation appropriate to the workload, verify every entry against the chart or clearance before executing it, monitor the result rather than assume it, never program while maneuvering at low altitude, and hand-fly the moment the box does something unexpected.

items.q: What is situational awareness and what most commonly destroys it?
items.a: The accurate perception of all the factors affecting the flight — aircraft state, position, terrain, traffic, weather, airspace, fuel, time and your own condition — plus a projection of where they will be shortly. It is most commonly destroyed by fixation on one problem or one instrument, by task saturation, by fatigue and complacency, and by an unresolved disagreement between what the instruments say and what you feel.

items.q: What is hypoxia?
items.a: A state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair function. It covers not only breathing too little oxygen but inadequate transport of oxygen in the blood and the inability of the tissues to use the oxygen delivered. Because the brain is the first organ affected and judgment is the first faculty lost, the dangerous feature of hypoxia is that the victim usually feels fine and does not recognize it.

items.q: What are the symptoms of hypoxia?
items.a: Impaired judgment and euphoria first, then a false sense of wellbeing, drowsiness, headache, dizziness, tingling in the fingers and toes, visual impairment starting with night vision and peripheral vision, slowed reaction and poor coordination, and finally cyanosis — a blue tinge to the lips and fingernails. Onset is insidious and the symptoms are individual, which is why an altitude chamber or a personal pulse oximeter is valuable.

items.q: What is hypemic hypoxia and what causes it?
items.a: Hypemic means not enough blood: the blood cannot take up and carry sufficient oxygen to the cells even though the lungs are receiving plenty. Causes include carbon monoxide poisoning, which is the most common form in aviation, anaemia, blood loss from severe bleeding, blood donation, and certain blood disorders. Descending helps only partly, because the carrying capacity itself is reduced.

items.q: What is hypoxic hypoxia and why does it occur at altitude?
items.a: Hypoxic hypoxia is insufficient oxygen reaching the blood in the first place, from a blocked airway, drowning, or most relevantly the reduced partial pressure of oxygen at altitude. The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere stays at about 21 percent all the way up; what falls is the pressure, so there are fewer molecules per breath and too little pressure to drive them across the lung membrane into the blood.

items.q: What is stagnant hypoxia?
items.a: Stagnant means not flowing: oxygen-rich blood is not being moved to the tissues. Causes include excessive G loading pooling blood away from the brain, cold constricting the peripheral circulation, a limb crossed or compressed until it falls asleep, shock, and heart failure. The oxygen is present and correctly carried; the pump or the plumbing is the problem.

items.q: What is histotoxic hypoxia?
items.a: Histotoxic hypoxia is the inability of the cells to use the oxygen delivered to them, remembered as a history of drugs and alcohol. Alcohol, narcotics, cyanide and certain poisons block the cellular enzymes that consume oxygen. Breathing supplemental oxygen does not fix it, because the delivery system is working perfectly and the fault is in the tissue itself.

items.q: What is time of useful consciousness, and what are the figures at altitude?
items.a: The time from the loss of an oxygen supply until a pilot can no longer take corrective action — not the time to unconsciousness. Typical values for a rested pilot at rest are about 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 feet, 10 minutes at 22,000, 3 to 5 minutes at 25,000, 2.5 to 3 minutes at 28,000, 1 to 2 minutes at 30,000, 30 to 60 seconds at 35,000, and 15 to 20 seconds at 40,000. Rapid decompression roughly halves these.

items.q: What do you do if you suspect hypoxia in flight?
items.a: Put on supplemental oxygen at 100 percent immediately if available, and start a descent to a lower altitude without waiting to confirm the diagnosis; below about 10,000 feet the symptoms resolve quickly. Reduce workload, check for a cabin heat or exhaust source of carbon monoxide, declare an emergency if you need priority to descend, and land and be examined if the symptoms do not clear.

items.q: What are the Part 91 supplemental oxygen requirements?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.211 (Part 91, Subpart C — Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements; Supplemental oxygen): the required flight crew must use oxygen for that part of a flight above 12,500 feet MSL lasting more than 30 minutes, must use it at all times above 14,000 feet MSL, and above 15,000 feet MSL every occupant must be provided with oxygen. Pressurized aircraft above FL250 must additionally carry at least a 10-minute supply for each occupant.

items.q: What is hyperventilation and what causes it?
items.a: An excessive rate and depth of breathing that washes carbon dioxide out of the blood faster than the body produces it, upsetting blood chemistry. It is usually triggered by an unexpectedly stressful situation — turbulence, an emergency, first solo, inadvertent instrument conditions — where anxiety drives the breathing rate up, and it can also occur when consciously overbreathing at high altitude. The problem is too little carbon dioxide, not too much oxygen: the excess breathing blows off carbon dioxide the body needs to regulate breathing.

items.q: What are the symptoms of hyperventilation?
items.a: Lightheadedness and dizziness, tingling in the fingers, toes and around the mouth, hot and cold sensations, visual impairment, muscle spasm and cramping of the hands, a sense of suffocation, and eventually unconsciousness — at which point normal breathing resumes on its own and recovery begins. The symptoms deliberately overlap those of hypoxia, which is what makes the pair a favorite examiner question.

items.q: How do you treat hyperventilation?
items.a: Slow the breathing rate down consciously and restore carbon dioxide. Practical methods are to talk aloud — reading a checklist or making a radio call forces a normal breathing pattern — to breathe into a paper bag or into cupped hands so exhaled carbon dioxide is rebreathed, and to breathe slowly and deliberately for several breaths. Reassuring the affected person and reducing the stressor is part of the fix. Talking aloud or laughing is an effective in flight technique because it forces slow controlled exhalation and rebuilds carbon dioxide.

items.q: How do you distinguish hypoxia from hyperventilation, and why does it matter?
items.a: They present almost identically, so the safe rule is to assume hypoxia first: put on 100 percent oxygen and descend, then slow the breathing rate. If it was hypoxia, oxygen fixes it; if it was hyperventilation, oxygen does no harm and controlled breathing on the mask resolves it. Clues are altitude and cyanosis for hypoxia, and a recent fright with tingling and muscle spasm at low altitude for hyperventilation.

items.q: Where does carbon monoxide in a light aircraft cabin come from?
items.a: From engine exhaust gases leaking into the cabin, most often through a crack or hole in the exhaust muffler or the shroud around it. Cabin heat in most piston singles is produced by ducting fresh air over that muffler shroud and into the cabin, so a cracked muffler feeds exhaust straight into the heat supply. Leaks around firewall penetrations, worn door and window seals and open cowl gaps can also let it in.

items.q: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous physiologically?
items.a: Because haemoglobin binds carbon monoxide roughly 200 to 250 times more readily than oxygen, so even a trace concentration progressively takes the blood's carrying capacity out of service. The result is hypemic hypoxia at any altitude, including sea level. The gas is colorless, odourless and tasteless, and once absorbed it can take many hours — up to about 48 — to clear from the body.

items.q: What are the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning in flight?
items.a: Headache first, then drowsiness, dizziness, sluggishness, a feeling of warmth, blurred vision, impaired judgment, loss of muscle power, throbbing in the temples, and in severe cases nausea, convulsions and unconsciousness. A smell of exhaust in the cabin is a strong clue even though the gas itself has no odour. Symptoms typically appear soon after the cabin heat is turned on.

items.q: What is spatial disorientation and what causes it?
items.a: The inability to correctly perceive aircraft attitude, altitude or motion relative to the earth. It arises when the three orientation systems disagree: vision, reliable but useless without a horizon; the vestibular system of the inner ear, which senses only changes and is easily fooled; and the kinesthetic sense, which cannot tell gravity from acceleration. The cure is to obtain visual reference or trust the instruments, keep head movements small, and if overwhelmed engage the autopilot and ask for help.

items.q: What causes motion sickness and how is it managed in flight?
items.a: Conflict between what the eyes see and what the inner ear senses, made worse by anxiety, turbulence, heat, poor ventilation and stale air. Symptoms are general discomfort, then nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating and vomiting. Manage it by opening fresh air vents, having the affected person look at a fixed point on the horizon outside, avoiding unnecessary head movement, flying smoothly, and if it is you, transferring the controls or landing.

items.q: What is an ear block and why is it worse on descent than on climb?
items.a: Trapped air in the middle ear cannot equalize with the outside pressure. On the climb, expanding middle-ear air escapes easily down the eustachian tube, which vents outward like a one-way flutter valve. On the descent the higher outside pressure tends to hold that tube shut, so air must be forced back up into the ear, and if a cold or infection has swollen the tube it cannot be — producing severe pain, hearing loss and possible eardrum rupture.

items.q: How do you clear an ear block, and what if it will not clear?
items.a: Swallow, yawn, chew, or use the Valsalva maneuver — pinch the nostrils shut, close the mouth and blow gently against them. If it will not clear on the descent, climb back to an altitude where the pain eases, try again, and then descend at a much slower rate. Decongestant sprays or drops approved for pilots may help. Persistent blockage after landing needs a doctor.

items.q: What is a sinus block and how does it differ from an ear block?
items.a: The same trapped-gas problem in the frontal or maxillary sinuses when the small openings that vent them are swollen shut by a cold, allergy or infection. It produces severe pain over the eyebrow or in the upper cheek and teeth, and sometimes a bloody nose, and it can occur on the climb as well as the descent. It cannot be relieved by the Valsalva maneuver, so slowing the rate of change and levelling off is the only in-flight remedy.

items.q: Why should you not fly with a cold?
items.a: Because blocked eustachian tubes and sinus openings cannot equalize the pressure changes of a climb or descent, which can produce extreme pain, temporary or permanent hearing loss, vertigo and a ruptured eardrum. A cold also brings fatigue and degraded concentration, and the decongestants used to treat it can themselves be disqualifying or cause drowsiness and a rebound block in flight. The answer is simply not to fly until it has cleared.

items.q: What causes decompression sickness?
items.a: A reduction in barometric pressure that allows nitrogen dissolved in the body's tissues and fluids to come out of solution and form bubbles. If the pressure drops faster than the lungs can offload the gas, the bubbles lodge in joints, the bloodstream, the lungs, the spinal cord or the brain. Risk rises with altitude, with a rapid climb or decompression, and enormously with a recent scuba dive that has supersaturated the tissues with nitrogen.

items.q: What are the symptoms of decompression sickness?
items.a: The most common is deep, boring joint pain, classically in the shoulders, elbows and knees, known as the bends. Other forms are the chokes, with chest pain and a burning cough; the creeps, with itching and mottled skin; and neurological effects with headache, visual disturbance, confusion, numbness or paralysis. Symptoms may not appear until hours after returning to the ground.

items.q: What actions do you take if decompression sickness occurs in flight?
items.a: Put on 100 percent oxygen, descend and land as soon as possible, and keep the affected person still, since movement circulates the bubbles. On the ground seek an FAA medical officer, an Aviation Medical Examiner or an emergency room without delay, as definitive treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber. Do not fly again or ascend, and remember that delayed symptoms can appear hours later on the ground.

items.q: How long must you wait after scuba diving before flying?
items.a: For flight up to and including 8,000 feet cabin altitude, wait at least 12 hours after a dive that did not require a controlled ascent, and at least 24 hours after a dive that did require a controlled decompression ascent. For any flight above 8,000 feet, wait at least 24 hours after any dive. The waits apply to passengers as well as pilots, and unpressurized light aircraft routinely exceed 8,000 feet en route over terrain.

items.q: Why does scuba diving before flight create such a large risk?
items.a: Because breathing air at depth exposes the body to pressures well above sea level, which drives far more nitrogen into solution in the tissues and fluids than normal. The body offloads that excess only slowly through the lungs. Climbing to altitude soon afterwards subtracts pressure from an already supersaturated body, so bubbles form at altitudes that would be entirely harmless to someone who had not dived.

items.q: What is dehydration, what are its symptoms, and how much water is needed?
items.a: A critical loss of body water, brought on in aviation by dry cabin air, high altitude, heat, wind, sun through the canopy, and drinking coffee or alcohol rather than water. Symptoms are headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness, dizziness and poor concentration — easily mistaken for hypoxia. Drink about 2 to 4 quarts of water every 24 hours, and carry water on the airplane rather than waiting until you feel thirsty.

items.q: What is heatstroke and how do you guard against it?
items.a: Heatstroke is the failure of the body to control its own temperature, usually following untreated dehydration and heat exhaustion, and it presents as collapse with hot dry skin, confusion and a very high body temperature. It is a medical emergency. Guard against it with ventilation, loose porous clothing, shade over the cockpit while waiting, plenty of water, and by not sitting in a closed cabin on a hot ramp.

items.q: What does 14 CFR 91.19 prohibit?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.19 (Part 91, Subpart A — General; Carriage of narcotic drugs, marihuana, and depressant or stimulant drugs or substances) makes it illegal to operate an aircraft within the United States knowing that any such substance is carried aboard, unless the carriage is authorized by a federal or state statute or agency. Note that it applies to knowledge of the cargo, not to the pilot's own condition, which is 91.17 — and a violation can cost the certificate outright.

items.q: What does 14 CFR 61.53 say about flying with a medical deficiency?
items.a: 14 CFR 61.53 (Part 61, Subpart A — General; Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency) forbids acting as pilot in command or as a required crewmember while you know of any medical condition, or any worsening of one, that would make you unable to meet the requirements of your medical certificate — even though the certificate itself has not expired. It also applies when operating under BasicMed or in operations needing no medical at all, where the standard is being able to operate safely.

items.q: What is the ICEFLAGS mnemonic for and what does each letter cover?
items.a: It lists the illusions that lead to spatial disorientation: Inversion, Coriolis, Elevator, False horizon, Leans, Autokinesis, Graveyard spiral, Somatogravic. The first five plus the graveyard spiral come from the vestibular system of the inner ear being fooled by sustained or unusual accelerations, while the false horizon and autokinesis are visual illusions that occur when the eyes are given misleading or insufficient reference.

items.q: What causes the leans and what wrong input does it invite?
items.a: A gradual, prolonged roll into a turn — below the roughly 2 degrees per second threshold the inner ear can detect — goes unnoticed, so when the pilot then rolls abruptly back to level the ear registers only that second roll and reports a turn in the opposite direction. The pilot feels banked the wrong way and leans bodily to compensate, and the invited input is to roll back into the original unwanted bank while believing the wings are level.

items.q: What is the Coriolis illusion and why is it so incapacitating?
items.a: After a turn has been held long enough for the fluid in the semicircular canals to catch up and move at the same rate as the canal, the ear reports no turn at all. A sudden head movement in a different plane — looking down at a chart or up at a switch — then sets that fluid moving in other canals at once, producing an overwhelming sensation of rotating or tumbling on an entirely different axis. The pilot maneuvers violently to stop a rotation that is not happening and can lose control.

items.q: What is the graveyard spiral and how does it kill?
items.a: In a prolonged, coordinated, constant-rate turn the ear stops sensing the rotation and the pilot believes the wings are level. Noticing a loss of altitude he pulls back, which in a bank only tightens the spiral and increases the descent rate. If he does level the wings the ear reports a turn the other way, so he rolls back in. The fatal input is pulling harder in the bank, which steepens the descent until impact or structural failure.

items.q: What is the inversion illusion and what does it make a pilot do?
items.a: An abrupt change from a climb to straight and level flight — the sudden reduction in vertical acceleration — over-stimulates the otolith organs and creates the sensation of tumbling backwards. The instinctive correction is to push the nose sharply down to stop the perceived backward tumble, which puts the airplane into a steep nose-low attitude and can lead to a rapid loss of altitude at exactly the wrong moment.

items.q: What is the elevator illusion?
items.a: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, typically from an updraft, stimulates the otolith organs into reporting a climb, and the pilot pushes the nose down to correct a climb that is not occurring. An abrupt downward acceleration in a downdraft produces the opposite illusion of descending, tempting the pilot to pull the nose up. Both are why an attitude indicator must be believed over the seat of the pants in turbulence.

items.q: What is the somatogravic illusion and why is a go-around so dangerous?
items.a: A rapid forward acceleration pushes the otoliths back exactly as a nose-up pitch would, producing a powerful false sensation of pitching up. On a go-around at night or in poor visibility the pilot applies full power, feels the airplane rearing up, and pushes the nose down to correct — flying a low, accelerating airplane into the ground. A rapid deceleration produces the reverse illusion of pitching down and tempts an excessive pull-up into a stall.

items.q: What is the false horizon illusion?
items.a: The pilot aligns the airplane with something that is not the true horizon: a sloping cloud deck, an obscured or indistinct horizon, the aurora borealis, a dark night scene in which ground lights and stars merge into a single field, or a lit sloping shoreline. The airplane ends up in a banked or pitched attitude the pilot believes is level. The defense is to cross-check the attitude indicator whenever the natural horizon is not sharp and unmistakable.

items.q: What is autokinesis and how do you defeat it?
items.a: Staring at a single stationary light against a dark, featureless background for several seconds makes that light appear to move on its own, because the eye has no reference against which to hold it steady. The pilot may maneuver to align with or avoid the apparently moving light and lose control or depart the intended attitude. Defeat it by keeping the eyes moving in a normal scan, avoiding a fixed stare, and referring to the flight instruments.

items.q: You land after a flight in which you suspected decompression sickness, but now you feel fine. What do you do?
items.a: Seek medical evaluation anyway, because signs and symptoms of decompression sickness can be delayed for hours after returning to the ground. Contact an aviation medical examiner or an FAA regional flight surgeon, describe the flight profile and any recent diving, stop flying and avoid any further altitude exposure, rest and hydrate, and be ready for hyperbaric chamber treatment if joint pain, rash, or neurological signs appear later.

items.q: Why does blocking one eye create a blind spot, and what does that mean in the cockpit?
items.a: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, and normally binocular vision fills the gap because the two eyes see it in different places. If a door post, a wing, a passenger's head or sunglasses block one eye, that gap is no longer covered and an airplane can sit in it unseen. A consistent scan and moving your head defeat it.

items.q: How do you protect your night vision before a night departure?
items.a: Adapt to the dark first. Full dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes, so avoid bright white light for at least half an hour before takeoff, and use dim red or low white lighting in the cockpit afterward. A single flash of a landing light, a ramp floodlight or a bright phone screen undoes the adaptation and it takes the full 30 minutes to rebuild.

items.q: What are the two kinds of stress a pilot has to watch for?
items.a: Acute and chronic. Acute stress is the immediate, short-term response to a present demand, and it ends when the demand ends. Chronic stress is a continuing level of demand that the person cannot resolve, carried for weeks or months. Some texts split out a third, episodic or intermittent stress, for recurring bouts of acute stress. The PHAK's aeronautical decision making chapter covers both.

items.q: Give me a real example of acute stress in the cockpit.
items.a: An alternator light on a night cross country; a runway change on short final; a passenger getting sick; the gust that drops a wing in the flare. Each is a single, identifiable demand that arrives and then passes. In small doses acute stress sharpens you, raising heart rate and attention; in large doses it narrows attention to one thing and you stop flying the airplane while you solve the problem.

items.q: Give me a real example of chronic stress in a pilot's life.
items.a: A marriage coming apart, a job in doubt, money trouble, a sick parent, or a certificate program you are behind on and paying for. None of it is in the airplane and all of it comes with you. Chronic stress is corrosive because it has no end point, it degrades sleep, and the pilot stops noticing it, which is exactly why IMSAFE asks the question out loud instead of leaving it to feel.

items.q: How does acute stress change the way you fly?
items.a: It triggers the fight-or-flight response: heart rate and breathing rise, blood sugar rises, attention narrows. A moderate amount improves reaction time; past that the effects are attention tunneling, fixation on one instrument or one problem, and loss of the big picture. Classic symptoms are task saturation, missed radio calls, and reverting to the first action that comes to mind rather than the right one.

items.q: How does chronic stress change the way you fly?
items.a: It shows up as fatigue, poor sleep, irritability, slow decisions, and a flat, indifferent approach to risk, and it lowers the amount of acute stress you can absorb before you are overloaded. A pilot carrying chronic stress has used up most of his margin before he gets to the airport, so a routine diversion or a stuck alternator pushes him straight into saturation.

items.q: How do the two kinds of stress interact?
items.a: They stack. Chronic stress consumes the reserve you need for the acute events of a flight, so the same alternator failure that a rested pilot handles as a nuisance becomes an emergency for a pilot who has not slept properly in a month. The dangerous combination is chronic stress plus a new acute demand, which is the pattern behind a lot of loss of control accidents that read on paper as pilot error.

items.q: Where does stress sit in the IMSAFE check?
items.a: S is for stress, and the question is not whether you feel stressed but whether anything is occupying attention that belongs to the flight. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue and emotion in the same checklist all feed stress, so a yes on any of them is usually a yes on S too. IMSAFE is a go/no-go check on the pilot and it has only one output: fly, or do not fly.

items.q: What do you actually do about stress before a flight?
items.a: Treat it as a hazard with mitigations rather than a mood. Remove sources you can remove, build margin into the flight, add fuel and time, brief yourself on the things most likely to go wrong, and set the no-go criteria before you are under pressure rather than during. If the stress is chronic, the honest mitigation is to stop flying for a period and deal with the cause; a commercial pilot who cannot say that out loud will eventually say it to an investigator.

items.q: Why is stress more dangerous to a commercial pilot than to a private pilot?
items.a: Because a commercial pilot is paid, and payment adds external pressure to every other source of stress: a customer waiting, a schedule, a reputation, an income. The stress and the external pressure feed each other, and the result is a pilot who launches into weather he would have declined as a private pilot. Naming the pay as a hazard on the PAVE checklist is the professional move.

items.q: How does stress relate to the hazardous attitudes?
items.a: Stress is the fuel; the hazardous attitudes are how it comes out. A stressed pilot reaches for impulsivity because deciding fast ends the discomfort, or resignation because nothing he does seems to matter. The antidotes still work but you have to remember them, which is harder under load, so the defense is to run the checklist rather than rely on judgment when you can feel yourself under pressure.

items.q: What is the sterile cockpit rule?
items.a: The requirement that no flight crewmember perform any duty during a critical phase of flight other than those required for the safe operation of the aircraft, and no non-essential conversation take place. The rules are 14 CFR 121.542, Flight crewmember duties, and 14 CFR 135.100, Flight crewmember duties. Both define critical phases of flight as all ground operations involving taxi, takeoff and landing, and all other operations below 10,000 feet except cruise flight.

items.q: Does the sterile cockpit rule bind you on a Part 91 flight?
items.a: No. 121.542 and 135.100 apply to air carriers and commercial operators under Parts 121 and 135; there is no equivalent sterile cockpit regulation in Part 91. You should say that plainly rather than pretend it is binding. Then say that you brief and fly it anyway, because the accident record behind the rule is a single-pilot problem even more than an airline one.

items.q: Why brief it anyway if it does not apply to you?
items.a: Because a single pilot has no one to catch the item he drops while answering a question. The workload peaks that the rule was written around are exactly the phases where a light single kills people: taxi, takeoff and initial climb, the pattern, the approach and the landing roll. Briefing it turns a passenger from a distraction into another set of eyes, and tells him when his input is welcome and when it is not.

items.q: When are your high-workload periods on a typical flight?
items.a: Taxi, including every runway crossing; the takeoff and initial climb to about 1,000 feet AGL; the departure and frequency changes; arrival into the terminal area and the descent checklist; the traffic pattern, the approach and the landing; and the roll-out and taxi clear. Add any abnormal, which makes whatever phase you are in a critical one. The debrief item from the last candidate's ride was taxi, and that is not an accident.

items.q: You cannot tell whether it is hypoxia or hyperventilation. What do you actually do?
items.a: Treat it as hypoxia first, because hypoxia is the one that kills you quickly. Put on oxygen at 100 percent flow and descend; if there is no oxygen, descend immediately. If the symptoms do not improve with oxygen, or you are at a low altitude where hypoxia is implausible, switch to the hyperventilation treatment: consciously slow the breathing rate, talk aloud, and breathe into a bag or cupped hands to restore carbon dioxide.

items.q: What is physically happening in hyperventilation?
items.a: You are breathing faster or deeper than the body needs, and blowing off carbon dioxide faster than you produce it, which raises blood pH. Oxygen is not the problem; the chemistry is. The result is dizziness, tingling in the fingers, toes and around the mouth, visual disturbance, cool clammy skin, muscle spasm, and eventually unconsciousness, at which point normal breathing resumes on its own.

items.q: Your passenger is panicking and breathing fast at 6,000 feet. Walk me through it.
items.a: Fly the airplane, then take charge of him. Get him to slow his breathing and talk to you, counting out loud or reading the checklist aloud, which forces a slower rate better than any instruction to relax; have him breathe into a paper bag or cupped hands if that is not enough. At 6,000 feet with no oxygen equipment in use, hypoxia is unlikely, but descend anyway and land if he does not settle.

items.q: Why does stress sit at the root of hyperventilation?
items.a: Because the trigger is almost always emotional rather than physical: fear, anxiety, or the sudden onset of an abnormal situation. That is also why it bites pilots at the worst time, during an emergency, when they are already loaded. The pilot who hyperventilates during an emergency makes the emergency worse by becoming a second problem, which is one more reason to brief, rehearse and slow yourself down deliberately when things go wrong.

items.q: Your cross country forecast is likely IFR and you are VFR only. What are your options?
items.a: Three, and I would name all three to the customer up front. Go IFR if I am rated, current and the airplane is equipped. Go part way, to the last field that is comfortably VFR, and arrange a car or an airline for the rest. Or do not go, and reschedule. Having the alternatives ready before the weather turns is what stops the pressure from producing a bad decision at the hold short line.

items.q: Name an accident that shows external pressure at work.
items.a: The Kobe Bryant helicopter accident in January 2020 is the obvious one: a charter flight continuing into deteriorating visibility toward a destination that a high-profile client expected to reach, ending in spatial disorientation and a loss of control in instrument conditions. The pattern is older than that accident and it is the same every time: a pilot who would have turned back on a personal flight pressing on because someone was waiting.

items.q: How do you mitigate external pressure before it reaches you?
items.a: Decide and publish the rules while you are calm. Set personal minimums in writing and tell the customer about them before you accept the job; build the alternatives into the plan so turning back is a plan rather than a failure; refuse to quote an arrival time you cannot guarantee; carry fuel; and agree in advance who pays for a night on the road. Then the hard conversation has already happened.

items.q: How is get-there-itis different from external pressure?
items.a: Get-there-itis, or plan continuation bias, is the internal version: the pilot's own fixation on completing the original plan even as the evidence changes. External pressure is the push from outside. They reinforce each other, and the combination is what carries a VFR pilot into instrument conditions. The defense is the same for both: pre-set go/no-go gates tied to observable facts, checked out loud at fixed points in the flight.

b: Why spins happen, the phases, and the recovery.

items.q: What is a spin?
items.a: An aggravated stall in which the airplane descends in a downward corkscrew path while autorotating. It is, in short, an uncoordinated stall: a stall accompanied by yaw. Both the essential ingredients must be present — the wing must be beyond the critical angle of attack and there must be yaw at the moment of the stall — which is why a wings-level, coordinated stall does not spin.

items.q: In a spin, is only one wing stalled?
items.a: No. Both wings are stalled, but one is more deeply stalled than the other. The inner, descending wing is at a higher angle of attack, well past the critical angle, producing less lift and much more drag; the outer, rising wing is at a lower angle of attack, still stalled but less so, producing more lift and less drag. That difference is what sustains the roll and yaw.

items.q: Explain aerodynamically why one wing stalls more than the other in a spin.
items.a: Yaw makes the two wings fly at different speeds and different angles of attack. The retreating, inner wing slows down and its downward motion increases its angle of attack further past the critical angle, so its lift falls and its drag rises. The advancing, outer wing speeds up, its upward motion reduces its angle of attack, so it keeps more lift and less drag. The result is a rolling moment toward the inner wing and a yawing moment that keeps the yaw going.

items.q: How is a spin entered deliberately?
items.a: It is set up like a power-off stall: power to idle, hold the airplane straight and level and let the speed decay, raising the nose to maintain altitude. As the stall breaks, apply full rudder in the desired direction of the spin, bring the yoke fully aft, and keep the ailerons neutral. Hold all three inputs. Never do this except in an airplane approved for spins, within its weight and center of gravity limits and per the POH or AFM.

items.q: What are the four phases of a spin?
items.a: Entry, incipient, developed and recovery. Entry is the pilot's action of stalling with yaw applied. The incipient phase runs from the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully established. The developed phase is a stabilized corkscrew descent. Recovery is the phase in which the angle of attack goes below critical, the rotation stops and the airplane is flown out of the resulting dive.

items.q: What happens during the incipient phase and how long does it last?
items.a: It is the transitional period between the stall with rotation and the fully developed spin, typically the first two turns or about four to six seconds in a light single, during which the attitude, rate of rotation and airspeed are all still changing and are not yet stable. Most inadvertent spins in training are caught here, and recovery in the incipient phase is usually immediate because the aerodynamic forces have not stabilized.

items.q: What characterizes the developed phase of a spin?
items.a: The rotation has stabilized: angular rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed are approximately constant, and the flight path is nearly vertical in a steady downward corkscrew. The airspeed is low and steady — often near or below the stalling speed — and the controls feel soft and ineffective. The altitude loss per turn is now predictable and large, which is why altitude for recovery must be planned in advance.

items.q: What defines the recovery phase of a spin?
items.a: It begins when the angle of attack of the wings falls below the critical angle and the rotation slows. The nose steepens as the wings begin flying again, the rotation stops, and the airplane is left in a steep nose-down dive from which it must then be recovered. Recovery is not complete when rotation stops — the dive recovery that follows is part of it, and is where the airframe can be overstressed.

items.q: What are the standard spin recovery steps, in order?
items.a: Power idle; ailerons neutral; full rudder opposite the direction of rotation; yoke briskly forward to break the stall. Hold those inputs until rotation stops. Once it stops, neutralize the rudder immediately and make a smooth recovery from the resulting dive, adding power once the wings are flying and the nose is coming up. Always use the procedure in the POH or AFM for the airplane being flown, which takes precedence over any generic method.

items.q: What does the memory aid PARE stand for in spin recovery?
items.a: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder full opposite, Elevator forward — the same four actions in the same order. The order matters: power first because thrust and slipstream can flatten the spin, ailerons before rudder because a deflected aileron aggravates the rotation, rudder before elevator because stopping the yaw first prevents the spin re-establishing as the wing unstalls.

items.q: Why must the power be reduced to idle before anything else in a spin recovery?
items.a: Because thrust aggravates and can flatten the spin. Power at the nose raises the nose attitude, which keeps the angle of attack high, and the propeller slipstream over the tail plus the gyroscopic and slipstream yawing effects increase the rate of rotation. A flatter spin makes the rudder less effective because the fuselage blankets it, and a flat spin in some airplanes is unrecoverable.

items.q: Why must the ailerons be neutral in a spin, and what happens if you use them?
items.a: Because aileron deflection changes the angle of attack of each wing at exactly the wrong time. Applying aileron against the rotation lowers the aileron on the already deeply stalled inner wing, raising its angle of attack further, deepening its stall and increasing its drag, which accelerates the rotation rather than stopping it. It can also flatten the spin. Neutral ailerons keep the wings symmetrical while the rudder does the work.

items.q: What are the two mistakes to avoid during the dive recovery after the rotation stops?
items.a: Pulling too hard and pulling too gently. Pulling abruptly can exceed the load factor limit or trigger a secondary stall at high speed, since the wing is still near the critical angle of attack. Pulling too gently allows the airspeed to build past Vne and wastes a great deal of altitude. The technique is smooth, progressive back pressure that keeps the airplane below the maneuvering speed and load limit while arresting the descent.

items.q: How do you tell a spin from a spiral dive?
items.a: By the airspeed above all. In a spin the wing is stalled, the airspeed is low and steady at or near the stall, the rotation rate is constant, the controls feel soft, and the load factor is around one G. In a spiral dive the wing is not stalled: the airspeed increases rapidly and continuously, the bank and rate of turn steepen, the load factor builds, and the controls are firm and effective.

items.q: Why does applying spin recovery inputs in a spiral dive make things worse?
items.a: Because the wing is not stalled, so pushing the elevator forward is exactly wrong: it accelerates an already accelerating airplane straight toward Vne, and full opposite rudder at high speed can overstress the fin. The spiral recovery is the opposite in emphasis — reduce power, roll the wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, and only then apply smooth back pressure to raise the nose, watching the airspeed and load factor throughout.

items.q: What is the difference between a slipping and a skidding turn?
items.a: In a skidding turn there is too much rudder for the bank, so the tail swings out and the nose yaws toward the inside of the turn; the ball is on the outside of the turn, away from the low wing. In a slipping turn there is too little rudder for the bank, or top rudder is held, so the airplane slides toward the low wing; the ball is on the inside, toward the low wing. In both, the ball tells you which rudder is needed: step on the ball.

items.q: Which is worse at the stall, a skid or a slip, and exactly why?
items.a: A skid is far worse. Skidding yaw puts the inside wing on the retreating side at a higher angle of attack while the outside wing advances at a lower one, so the inside wing stalls first and the airplane rolls rapidly and violently toward the inside of the turn, over the top, straight into a spin entry. A slipping stall tends to drop the nose and roll the airplane toward wings-level or the outside, with much less tendency to autorotate.

items.q: Why does the pilot's instinctive reaction make a skidding stall worse?
items.a: Because the skid causes the outside wing to overbank, the natural correction is opposite aileron to hold the bank. That lowers the aileron on the inside wing, increasing its angle of attack still further at the moment it is closest to the stall, so it stalls first and hardest. The other instinct — pulling back to stop the nose dropping — also raises the angle of attack. Both instincts together are the classic entry to a stall-spin.

items.q: Why is the base-to-final turn the classic stall-spin accident?
items.a: Because it combines every ingredient at an altitude too low to recover. Overshooting the centerline tempts the pilot to add bottom rudder to tighten the turn without more bank, which skids; the bank is then held off with opposite aileron; the nose drops so back pressure is added; and the airplane is already slow, low and configured. The fix is to accept the overshoot, go around, and never use rudder to tighten a turn.

items.q: How does load factor in a turn change the stalling speed, and why does that matter near the ground?
items.a: Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so a 30-degree bank raises it about 7 percent, a 45-degree bank about 19 percent, and a 60-degree bank about 41 percent. In the pattern the margin above the stall is already small, so a steep or tightened turn to correct an overshoot can raise the stalling speed above the speed being flown while the pilot's attention is entirely outside on the runway.

items.q: What must you check in the POH or AFM before any intentional spin?
items.a: Whether the airplane is approved for intentional spins at all, and in which category and configuration. Check the placards and the certification category — many airplanes are approved for spins only in the utility category, which restricts weight, center of gravity and often forbids baggage or rear-seat occupants. Confirm the manufacturer's entry and recovery procedure, flap and power restrictions, and the altitude loss to expect per turn.

items.q: In which three flight situations is the critical angle of attack most commonly exceeded?
items.a: Low speed, high speed and turning flight. In each of them the pilot asks the wing for more lift than it can give at that angle of attack: slowing until the angle needed to hold altitude reaches the critical angle; pulling abruptly while fast; or loading the wing in a bank. Knowing all three stops a pilot from assuming the airplane is safe merely because the airspeed is high.
items.concept: Three flight situations in which the critical angle of attack is most commonly exceeded: low speed, high speed and turning flight

items.q: Why does coordination matter so much at the stall?
items.a: Because a stall with yaw is a spin entry. If the ball is out at the break, the outside wing is moving faster and the inside wing is at a higher angle of attack and more deeply stalled, so it drops and autorotation begins. A skid is worse than a slip, and the instinctive correction, picking the dropping wing up with aileron, deepens the stall on that wing. Keep the ball centered with rudder through the whole maneuver.

items.q: Describe a stall from entry through recovery, as you would fly it for the examiner.
items.a: Clearing turns, then configure and set power, raise the nose to the stall attitude and hold it, keeping the ball centered with rudder and the wings level with aileron. Call the cues aloud as the horn, the buffet and the mushy controls arrive, and then the break itself. Recover by reducing angle of attack, leveling the wings, adding full power, retracting flaps on schedule, and returning to altitude and heading without a secondary stall.

b: What to carry and what the regulations require.

items.q: What emergency or survival equipment does Part 91 actually require in a light airplane?
items.a: Very little. The only universal item is an emergency locator transmitter under 14 CFR 91.207. There is no federal requirement under Part 91 for a fire extinguisher, first aid kit, survival kit, water or rations in an ordinary land-based light airplane in the lower 48 states. Everything beyond the ELT is a matter of good practice and of the operator's own standards, not regulation.

items.q: What does 14 CFR 91.207 require about emergency locator transmitters?
items.a: 14 CFR 91.207 (Part 91, Subpart C — Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements; Emergency locator transmitters) requires most US-registered civil airplanes to carry an automatic-type approved ELT, attached as far aft as practicable and armed. It must be inspected every 12 calendar months for proper installation, battery corrosion, controls and audible signal, with the inspection recorded in the maintenance records.

items.q: May you fly with the ELT removed?
items.a: Yes, for limited purposes. 14 CFR 91.207 permits operation for up to 90 days with the ELT removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement, provided the aircraft records show the removal with the date, and a placard reading ELT not installed is displayed in view of the pilot. The section also exempts ferry flights to a place of installation and certain training, agricultural and single-seat operations.

items.q: What is the difference between a 121.5 MHz and a 406 MHz ELT?
items.a: The 406 MHz unit transmits a digital, registered identification and, in GPS-equipped versions, a position, and it is the only type still monitored by the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system — satellite monitoring of 121.5 ended in February 2009. A 121.5 MHz-only ELT still meets the letter of 14 CFR 91.207 but is heard only by overflying aircraft and ground stations. A 406 unit must be registered with NOAA, and the registration kept current.

items.q: How and when may an ELT be tested, and how do you check yours is not transmitting?
items.a: Tests are made only during the first five minutes after the hour and limited to three audio sweeps. Coordinate with the tower or flight service if on an airport. As a routine habit, monitor 121.5 MHz on the radio after a hard landing and before shutting down, and again after engine shutdown, so an inadvertently triggered ELT is found by you rather than by search and rescue.

items.q: What over-water equipment does Part 91 require, and when does it apply?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.205(b)(12) (Part 91, Subpart C; Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements), an airplane operated for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore must carry approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device. For non-commercial private flights Part 91 requires none of it, which does not make going without it sensible.

items.q: What should be carried for a private over-water flight even though the regulation does not demand it?
items.a: An approved life vest for every occupant, worn or immediately within reach — not in the baggage compartment — a life raft with its own survival pack for anything beyond a short crossing, a 406 MHz personal locator beacon carried on the body, waterproof handheld radio, signaling mirror, whistle, strobe and flares, and immersion suits where the water is cold. Never inflate a life vest inside the cabin; inflate it only after leaving the aircraft.

items.q: What does a sensible general survival kit contain for flight over remote terrain?
