items.a: Water and a means to purify more, such as filtration or purification tablets; high-energy food; a reflective space blanket and warm clothing suited to the terrain in winter, not summer; fire-starting means; a knife or multi-tool; a first aid kit; a signaling mirror, whistle and strobe; a headlamp with spare batteries; sun protection and insect repellent; a charged phone and, most valuably, a 406 MHz personal locator beacon.

items.q: Why is a personal locator beacon better than relying on the aircraft ELT?
items.a: Because it is on your body rather than in the tail. An aircraft ELT can be destroyed by the impact, submerged, or its antenna broken, and it does you no good if you have walked away from the wreck. A registered 406 MHz personal locator beacon with GPS is activated deliberately by you, reports your identity and position within roughly 100 meters, and works away from the airplane.

items.q: What should you do after an off-airport landing in remote terrain?
items.a: Stay with the aircraft unless it is unsafe or you are certain of reaching help. An airplane is a far larger search target than a person, provides shelter, and holds your supplies. Activate the ELT and any personal locator beacon, use the radio and transponder on 7700 while battery power lasts, treat injuries, get out of the wind and off the cold ground, make ground-to-air signals, and ration water rather than food.

items.q: What kind of fire extinguisher belongs in a cockpit, and how is it used?
items.a: A hand-held Halon or Halotron unit, mounted where the pilot can reach it from the seat with the belts on, and checked for charge and date during preflight. Dry chemical is a poor cockpit choice because the powder obscures vision and damages avionics. Aim at the base of the fire, discharge in short bursts, and ventilate the cabin afterwards, since Halon products of combustion are toxic in a closed cockpit.

items.q: What changes for survival preparation when flying in Alaska or over mountainous or remote terrain?
items.a: The exposure is far higher, and the local rules are stricter — Alaska state law imposes its own survival equipment list, so check the current Alaska statute and the Chart Supplement before flying there. In all remote areas, file a flight plan and use flight following, plan routes along roads and valleys with landing options, carry seasonal clothing and shelter, and tell someone your route and expected arrival time.

items.q: How do you decide what survival equipment a particular flight needs?
items.a: By assessing the flight rather than the regulation: the terrain overflown, the season and temperature, the distance from help, and the time it would take rescue to reach you. A summer flight between towns needs little; the same route in winter, at night, or over water, mountains or desert needs shelter, water, warmth and a locator beacon. Pack for the worst conditions along the route, and check the gear is present and serviceable during the preflight rather than assuming it is.

items.q: Show me the emergency and survival equipment carried on board and tell me exactly what is in it.
items.a: Know the stowage location and the full contents before every flight and brief passengers on them. A typical kit stowed in the baggage area holds water and purification tablets, a reflective emergency blanket, a first aid kit, a signaling mirror and whistle, a flashlight with spare batteries, fire starting material and high energy food. You must be able to find and identify each item in the dark, so inventory the kit during preflight and confirm nothing is expired or missing.

items.q: What are the water purification tablets in the survival kit for, and how do you use them?
items.a: They make questionable surface water safe to drink after a forced landing, which matters because a person survives only about three days without water. Strain the clearest water you can find through cloth, add the number of tablets the label specifies for that volume, usually one or two per liter, then wait the stated time, normally about thirty minutes, before drinking; cold or cloudy water needs longer. Tablets expire, so check the date whenever the kit is inspected.

items.q: What is the reflective emergency blanket for, and how do you use it after an off-airport landing?
items.a: It prevents hypothermia, which is the most common cause of death among survivors of a forced landing in cold or wet conditions. The metallized sheet reflects radiated body heat back to the occupant and blocks wind and rain while weighing almost nothing. Wrap up with insulation such as seat cushions or brush underneath you, since most heat is lost to the cold ground, and use the bright surface as a signaling panel for search aircraft.

items.q: What does Part 830 require you to do with the wreckage?
items.a: 49 CFR 830.10, Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo and records, makes the operator responsible for preserving the wreckage, cargo, mail and all records until the NTSB takes custody. You may disturb it only to rescue people, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury, and if you do move anything you should make sketches, notes and photographs first.

items.q: You have just walked away from an off-airport landing. First actions?
items.a: People first, then the airplane, then the phone calls. Account for everyone and treat injuries; get clear of fuel; shut off the master, magnetos and fuel selector before you leave the cockpit; make sure the ELT is transmitting or switch it on manually; stay with the airplane, which is far easier to find than you are. Then notify the nearest NTSB office if 49 CFR 830.5 requires it, and tell the operator and your insurer.

items.q: How do you declare an emergency, and what do you say?
items.a: Say mayday three times on the frequency in use, or 121.5 if you have nobody, then who you are, where you are, what is wrong, what you intend to do, souls on board and fuel remaining. Squawk 7700. 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, lets you deviate from any rule to the extent required to meet the emergency, and may require a written report afterwards on request.

items.q: Why do controllers want souls on board and fuel remaining?
items.a: Souls on board tells the rescue services how many people to look for and is a number nobody can reconstruct afterwards; fuel remaining, stated in time rather than gallons, tells the controller how long you can stay airborne and how much fire risk there is at the scene. Give both unprompted when you declare, because once the workload rises you may not get the chance.

items.q: What do you do about the ELT in an emergency landing?
items.a: Nothing in the air, and then check it on the ground. A modern 406 MHz ELT fires automatically on impact through its g-switch and transmits your registration and position to the satellite system. If you have a cockpit remote switch you can turn it on manually before touchdown or after; after a landing, confirm it is transmitting by listening on 121.5, and leave it on. If it was not a real emergency, turn it off and tell Flight Service.

items.q: After an in-flight fire you land safely with the airplane scorched. Any reporting obligation?
items.a: Yes. An in-flight fire is on the immediate notification list in 49 CFR 830.5 regardless of damage or injuries, so the operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately by the most expeditious means available. Whether a written report follows depends: if the fire caused substantial damage it is an accident and the 10-day Form 6120.1 is due; if not, you file only if the Board asks.

b: Vision, lighting, equipment and the differences that matter after dark.

items.q: How is night defined for the purpose of logging night flight time?
items.a: Night is the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time — the definition in 14 CFR Part 1.1 (General definitions). Flight time in that window is what may be logged as night under 14 CFR 61.51 (Part 61, Subpart A — General; Pilot logbooks), and it is what satisfies the night aeronautical experience for the private and commercial certificates.

items.q: What period counts for night takeoff and landing currency?
items.a: From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise, under 14 CFR 61.57(b) (Part 61, Subpart A — General; Recent flight experience: Pilot in command). To carry passengers at night you must have made three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days in that window, in the same category, class and type if a type rating is required. Touch and goes do not count at night.

items.q: What period governs when position lights must be on?
items.a: From sunset to sunrise, under 14 CFR 91.209 (Part 91, Subpart C — Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements; Aircraft lights), which prohibits operating an aircraft during that period without lighted position lights. The same section prohibits parking or moving an aircraft in a night operating area of an airport unless it is lighted or marked by obstruction lights. In Alaska a separate visibility-based definition applies.

items.q: When can you legally carry passengers at night without being night current?
items.a: In the window between the end of evening civil twilight and one hour after sunset, and correspondingly between one hour before sunrise and the beginning of morning civil twilight. It is technically night for logging purposes under Part 1.1, but the 61.57(b) currency requirement does not begin until an hour after sunset, so passengers may be carried without the three recent full-stop night landings.

items.q: What are the rules for anticollision lights?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.209, an aircraft equipped with an anticollision light system may not be operated day or night unless those lights are lighted. The pilot in command may switch them off when, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so — the standard examples being strobes reflecting off cloud or fog at night, and turning them off on the ramp when they would blind other people. Anticollision lights are required equipment on small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, and on any anticollision light system initially installed after August 11, 1971.

items.q: What equipment is required for night VFR flight, and what mnemonic covers it?
items.a: FLAPS: Fuses — one spare set or three of each kind required, accessible in flight; Landing light, if the aircraft is operated for hire; Anticollision lights; Position lights; and an adequate Source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment. These are added to the day VFR list by 14 CFR 91.205(c) (Part 91, Subpart C; Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements).

items.q: Is a landing light legally required for night flight?
items.a: Only if the aircraft is operated for hire. 14 CFR 91.205(c) qualifies the landing light requirement that way, so a private night flight in your own airplane is legal with the landing light inoperative provided 14 CFR 91.213 (Part 91, Subpart C; Inoperative instruments and equipment) is complied with — placarded, deactivated and recorded. Legal and wise are different things: a landing light matters for obstacle and animal detection on the runway.

items.q: Why are spare fuses required for night flight, and what if the aircraft has circuit breakers?
items.a: Because an electrical failure at night takes the instrument lights, radios and navigation lights with it, and a blown fuse is a repairable failure only if you have a spare within reach. 14 CFR 91.205(c) requires one spare set of fuses, or three of each kind required, accessible in flight. Aircraft using resettable circuit breakers instead of fuses satisfy the requirement without carrying spares.

items.q: What personal equipment should a pilot carry for a night flight?
items.a: At least one reliable flashlight plus spare batteries, and preferably two flashlights so a failure is not a crisis; a red or dim white light for use inside the cockpit; a brighter white light for the walkaround and any outside work; current sectional charts including those for adjacent areas, plus the chart supplement; and a means of holding or mounting the light so both hands stay free. Check the batteries before the flight, not after takeoff.

items.q: Why a red light inside the cockpit and a white light outside?
items.a: Red light does not bleach the rhodopsin in the rods, so dark adaptation is largely preserved, which is why it is traditional for cockpit use; white light of any brightness destroys adaptation in seconds. The drawback is that red light makes anything printed in red on a chart disappear and reduces contrast on fine detail, so low-intensity white light is often preferred for chart reading. Outside, on the preflight, a strong white light is needed to see the airframe properly.

items.q: What do the cones in the eye do, and what are their limitations at night?
items.a: The cones provide all color vision and fine detail, and are concentrated in the fovea at the center of the retina, which is why you read and identify things by looking straight at them. They need relatively bright light to work, so they effectively shut down at night. The result is that in darkness the very center of your visual field goes blind and you lose color perception almost entirely. The rods sit off center and give peripheral and night vision, which is why off center viewing is the technique for seeing anything at night.

items.q: What do the rods in the eye do?
items.a: The rods handle peripheral vision, movement detection and vision in dim light. They lie outside the fovea, give no color and poor detail, but are about 10,000 times more sensitive to light than the cones. They take much longer to adapt to darkness than the cones do. At night they are the only part of the eye still working, and they are best at detecting a light or a movement out to the side rather than dead ahead.

items.q: What is rhodopsin and why does it matter after dark?
items.a: Rhodopsin, or visual purple, is the light-sensitive chemical in the rods that makes night vision possible. It builds up slowly in darkness and gives the eye its sensitivity, but exposure to bright light bleaches it almost instantly and it must be regenerated. That is the physiological reason a single glance at a landing light, a phone screen or a lightning flash can undo half an hour of dark adaptation.

items.q: How long does dark adaptation take, and how quickly is it lost?
items.a: The rods take about 30 minutes to adapt fully to darkness, with most of the useful gain in the first 20. It can be lost within seconds of exposure to bright light. Practically this means avoiding bright ramp lights before departure, keeping the cockpit lighting at the lowest usable level, using red or dim white light for charts, and turning away from strobes and landing lights on the ground.

items.q: What is the night blind spot and how do you work around it?
items.a: Because the cones at the center of the retina stop working in darkness, a blind spot of roughly 5 to 10 degrees forms in the exact center of the visual field at night. An object stared at directly can disappear entirely — an airplane on a collision course at a mile or more can vanish. The workaround is off-center viewing: look about 5 to 10 degrees to one side of the object and use peripheral vision, and keep the eyes moving.

items.q: How should a pilot scan for traffic, and how does the technique change at night?
items.a: Move the eyes in a series of short, regularly spaced steps of about 10 degrees, pausing 1 to 2 seconds in each block so the eye can focus, working systematically across the windscreen; a common taught pattern is top to bottom in sectors of about 30 degrees, holding each for 2 to 3 seconds. At night the same discipline applies but with off-center viewing, because the target will only be seen out of the corner of the eye and will disappear if looked at directly.

items.q: How does oxygen affect vision, and what oxygen practice is recommended at night?
items.a: Vision is the first sense to suffer from a lack of oxygen, because the retina is extremely oxygen-hungry. Night vision measurably degrades from about 5,000 feet and the loss grows quickly above that, well below the altitudes at which supplemental oxygen becomes legally required. The recommended practice is to use supplemental oxygen above about 5,000 feet at night, and to remember that smoking and alcohol shift the effective altitude higher still.

items.q: What is empty field myopia and how do you avoid it?
items.a: On a dark or featureless night, with nothing for the eye to focus on, the eye relaxes to a resting focus of about 10 to 30 feet and you effectively stare at nothing while believing you are looking outside. Traffic and terrain simply are not seen. Avoid it by deliberately focusing on a distant light, a star or a ground feature every so often, and by including the flight instruments in the scan to keep the eyes working.

items.q: What causes a false horizon at night, and what does it make a pilot do?
items.a: A sloping cloud deck, an obscured or invisible horizon, the aurora borealis, or a dark scene in which scattered ground lights merge with the stars. The pilot aligns the wings with the false reference and ends up flying in a bank or a nose-high or nose-low attitude while believing it is level. It is a leading cause of loss of control on dark nights, and the defense is to trust the attitude indicator over the outside picture whenever the horizon is not sharp.

items.q: How does autokinesis appear at night and what should you do about it?
items.a: A single stationary light stared at for several seconds against a black background appears to move of its own accord. On a dark night the light might be a star, a tower light, or another aircraft, and the pilot may maneuver to follow, avoid or line up with an object that never moved, departing the intended attitude. Do not fix the gaze: keep the eyes sweeping, cross-check the instruments, and use off-center viewing.

items.q: What is the black hole approach and where does it occur?
items.a: A night approach over featureless, unlit terrain — water, snow, desert, forest or open fields — with only the runway lights visible ahead and no ground lighting, no horizon and no visual cues between you and the threshold. It is the most dangerous of the night visual illusions. It typically occurs approaching a lit runway in an otherwise dark area, and it is a form of the featureless terrain illusion.

items.q: Why is the black hole approach so lethal, and what does the pilot do wrong?
items.a: The absence of intervening cues makes the pilot feel higher than he actually is, so he flies a progressively lower and flatter approach, descending below the safe path and often levelling into a shallow drag-in. He then strikes terrain, trees or obstacles short of the runway while believing the picture looks normal. The illusion also tends to draw the airplane into a constantly steepening descent as the runway lights fill more of the view.

items.q: How do you defend against the black hole approach?
items.a: Use a VASI or PAPI wherever one is available and stay on it. Fly the electronic glidepath — an ILS, LPV or LNAV/VNAV — or an approach with a published vertical path even in visual conditions. Cross-check the altimeter against the published altitudes and distances, monitor the vertical speed rather than the picture, keep the landing light and instrument scan in use, and if the approach ever feels uncertain, go around rather than continue.

items.q: What is the runway width illusion?
items.a: A runway narrower than usual makes the pilot feel higher than he actually is, so he flies a lower approach and risks striking obstacles or undershooting, and may flare late and land hard. A runway wider than usual makes him feel lower than he is, so he flies too high, flares high and can drop the airplane in or overrun. Look up the runway dimensions before arrival and fly the approach on instruments and the glidepath rather than the picture.

items.q: What is the runway slope illusion and how does terrain around the airport add to it?
items.a: An upsloping runway makes the pilot feel higher than he is, so he flies a lower and flatter approach. A downsloping runway makes him feel lower than he is, so he flies too high. Upsloping terrain in the approach path produces the same effect as an upsloping runway, and downsloping terrain the same as a downsloping runway. Check the chart supplement for runway gradient, and use the glidepath indications rather than the visual picture.

items.q: How do rain, haze and atmospheric conditions distort the approach picture at night?
items.a: Rain on the windscreen makes the runway appear lower than it is, tempting a steeper than normal approach and a hard landing or overrun. Haze, smoke or a shallow fog makes the runway seem farther away and higher, so the pilot flies lower and can descend into obstacles, and it also makes lights appear dimmer and more distant. Penetrating fog on the approach can make the airplane appear to pitch up and induce a push over.

items.q: What extra precautions apply to clearing the propeller and starting at night?
items.a: Look carefully for people and objects that will not be seen in the dark, and call out clearly before turning the key. Switch on the rotating beacon or flash the position lights to warn anyone nearby that the engine is about to start. Turn the landing light on before beginning to taxi, and use it as necessary, remembering that a person in the dark near the ramp may not have seen you at all.

items.q: What is the downside of running lights on the ground at night?
items.a: They place an excessive drain on the electrical system at low engine rpm when the alternator is producing little output, and a landing light can overheat when there is no airflow over it, shortening its life or burning it out. They also dazzle other pilots and ground crew. Use them where they buy safety — on entering a runway, at intersections, when anyone is nearby — and be considerate elsewhere.

items.q: How should you taxi at night to avoid a runway incursion?
items.a: Taxi slowly and rely on taxiway lighting and signage rather than memory, keeping the airport diagram out and following your position on it. Stop before every hold short line and read the sign. Hold the brakes firmly or lock them when stopped, since it is hard to see slow forward creep at night. Turn the landing and taxi lights on when taxiing onto or crossing a runway, so other aircraft and the tower can see you.

items.q: Why can aircraft lights be mistaken for stars at night, and what should you look for?
items.a: Because a distant aircraft at night is nothing more than a point of light against a field of other points of light, and at your own altitude it will sit near the apparent horizon among them. Look for movement relative to the background, and for a flashing or colored element — a strobe or the red and green position lights — and remember that a light showing no relative motion is the one on a collision course with you.

items.q: How bright should cockpit lighting be at night, and why?
items.a: At the minimum brightness that still allows the instruments to be read. Bright panel and dome lighting bleaches the rhodopsin in the rods, destroys dark adaptation and reflects off the inside of the windscreen, which both hides outside traffic and creates false images. Dim it after start, keep the instrument scan active because the outside picture is unreliable, and avoid phones and tablets at full brightness.

items.q: How should you identify an airport at night when approaching from a distance?
items.a: Look first for the rotating beacon and fly toward it, and do not begin any descent or approach until the runway lights themselves have been positively identified. Lighted airports away from cities stand out clearly; those inside a lit urban area can disappear into the surrounding lights, so know the airport's exact position relative to its city before you go. Use the GPS, a VOR radial or a distance readout to confirm, and check the frequency and lighting status beforehand.

items.q: What do the different rotating beacon colors and flash patterns mean?
items.a: Alternating white and green is a lighted civilian land airport; alternating white and yellow is a lighted civilian water airport; two quick white flashes alternating with green is a military airport; flashing red marks obstructions or hazardous areas for air navigation; and steady red marks an obstruction on or near an airport. Green alone alternating with two whites is the pattern to watch for if you must avoid landing at a military field by mistake.

items.q: What does an airport beacon operating during daylight hours mean?
items.a: In Class B, C, D and E surface areas it usually indicates that the ground visibility is less than 3 statute miles or the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet, so a special VFR clearance would be required to operate in the surface area. It is only an advisory: there is no regulatory requirement to switch the beacon on for that purpose, so its absence in daylight does not prove the field is VFR. Obtain the actual weather before relying on it.

items.q: How does pilot-controlled lighting work and what do the clicks do?
items.a: Key the microphone on the published common traffic advisory or dedicated lighting frequency: seven clicks within five seconds gives highest intensity, five clicks medium, and three clicks low. Always key seven first, even if you want it dim, because that turns every system on and resets the timer; then reduce. The lights normally stay on for 15 minutes, so re-key on the downwind or before the final approach so they are not lost during the flare.

items.q: What color are runway edge lights, and what does a change of color mean?
items.a: Runway edge lights are white. On instrument runways, yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 feet, or half the runway length, whichever is less, forming a caution zone that warns of the approaching end during the landing rollout. Edge lights come in high, medium and low intensity systems, and the intensity of many of them can be adjusted by the tower or by pilot-controlled lighting.

items.q: What colors are taxiway edge and centerline lights?
items.a: Taxiway edge lights, marking the edges of taxiways and ramp areas, are blue. Taxiway centerline lights are green. Some airports also use clearance bar lights, which are three in-pavement yellow lights at a hold point, and runway guard lights, a pair of flashing yellow lights either side of a taxiway at a runway holding position, marking the point beyond which you must not go without a clearance.

items.q: What do runway centerline lights tell you about the distance remaining?
items.a: They are white from the threshold, then alternating white and red from 3,000 feet to 1,000 feet remaining, then red for the last 1,000 feet. They are spaced at 50-foot intervals along the centerline. The color change is a direct distance-remaining cue during the rollout at night or in low visibility, and reaching solid red means only 1,000 feet of runway is left in front of you.

items.q: What color are the threshold and runway end lights?
items.a: They are on a single bar of lights at each end of the runway that shows green outward to arriving aircraft as the threshold, and red inward as the runway end to aircraft on the runway. Green means the landing threshold when seen from the approach; red seen ahead from the runway means the pavement is about to run out. Some runways also have runway end identifier lights, a pair of synchronized flashing white strobes either side of the threshold to make it stand out.

items.q: How do you read a VASI?
items.a: A standard two-bar VASI gives red over white means on the correct glide path; white over white means too high; red over red means too low — remembered as red over red, you're dead. It provides a normal glide path of about 3 degrees and safe obstruction clearance within 10 degrees either side of the extended centerline out to 4 nautical miles. It is usable to about 4 miles in the day and up to 20 miles at night.

items.q: How do you read a PAPI?
items.a: A PAPI is a single row of usually four lights beside the runway. Two white and two red is on the glide path; three white and one red is slightly high; four white is too high; one white and three red is slightly low; and four red is too low. Each light unit changes from white to red as you pass through its angle, so the count tells you how far off the path you are, not merely which side of it.

items.q: What extra attention should the preflight inspection get at night?
items.a: Do it with a good white flashlight and take longer over it. Check every light — position, anticollision, strobe, landing, taxi, instrument and interior — actually works, and tap the lenses: a light that blinks when tapped has a loose connection or a failing bulb. Check the fuel visually and by taste and smell rather than color alone, look carefully for leaks and damage that shadow hides, and walk the taxi route or examine it for bumps, potholes and obstructions that will not be visible from the cockpit.

items.q: What weather items deserve particular attention when planning a night flight?
items.a: The temperature and dewpoint spread above all — a small and closing spread means radiation fog is likely to form after sunset, and fog can cover an airport in minutes. Also check the wind, whose direction and speed are much harder to judge at night because the usual surface clues are invisible; cloud bases you will not be able to see; and the fact that you cannot see build-ups or an approaching line of weather in the dark.

items.q: How should the chart and route be prepared for a night cross-country?
items.a: Draw the course line boldly in black so it is readable under dim red or white light, and mark it up more heavily than you would by day. Choose checkpoints that are prominently lit: cities and towns, large highways, airport rotating beacons, lit towers and bridges. Note frequencies, minimum safe altitudes and airport lighting details on the chart itself, and carry the adjacent sectionals as well as the one for the route.

items.q: Why do navigation aids and flight following matter more at night?
items.a: Because the visual checkpoints that carry a daytime flight largely disappear, so the electronic picture becomes the primary means of navigation rather than the backup. Being fluent with VORs, GPS and flight following increases both safety and efficiency, keeps you clear of terrain and airspace you cannot see, and gives someone who knows where you are if the engine stops. Set up and brief the navigation before it is dark and busy, not during the descent.

items.q: How does a night takeoff differ from a day takeoff?
items.a: There is no visible horizon, so the attitude indicator becomes the primary pitch reference from rotation onward, cross-checked with airspeed, vertical speed and altimeter. Line up on the centerline lights or markings and note the heading indicator agrees with the runway. Expect the initial climb to feel nose-high, resist the urge to lower the nose, and climb straight ahead to a safe altitude before turning, because obstacles and terrain off the departure end are invisible.

items.q: How does a night landing differ from a day landing?
items.a: Depth perception is poor and the flare is the hard part, so use the glidepath indications and a stabilized approach rather than the visual picture, and fly a normal approach speed and profile without dragging it in. Use the landing light for the flare where it helps, but be ready for it to be useless in fog or over a dark surface, and judge the height by the runway lights on either side moving into the peripheral vision. Expect the flare a little higher than it feels and hold the attitude.

items.q: How should route and altitude selection change for a night cross-country?
items.a: Fly higher than you would by day — it increases glide range, radio and navigation coverage, and terrain clearance you cannot see. Choose routes over lit areas, roads and valleys with airports along them rather than the shortest line over unlit terrain or water. Know the maximum elevation figures for every quadrant on the route, and set a personal minimum altitude well above them. Note which airports along the way have lighting and how it is activated.

items.q: Before a night flight, how do you find out what lighting your destination has and whether it is working?
items.a: Check the Chart Supplement entry for the airport and read the NOTAMs. The Chart Supplement lists runway edge and approach lighting, visual glideslope indicators such as VASI or PAPI, beacon operating hours, and any pilot controlled lighting frequency and click sequence, while NOTAMs report lights that are out of service or beacons inoperative. Reviewing all available information, NOTAMs included, is required by 14 CFR 91.103, Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules General, titled Preflight action.

items.q: Which runway and taxiway signs and markings matter most at night, and why are they harder to use then?
items.a: The mandatory instruction signs, which are white lettering on a red background, and the runway holding position markings they accompany, which are two solid and two dashed yellow lines with the solid lines on the taxiway side. At night painted markings show only in the taxi or landing light and can be worn or masked by rain, so rely on the internally lighted signs: red with white letters for mandatory, yellow with black letters for direction, and black with yellow letters for location.

items.q: How should your personal minimums change for a night flight?
items.a: Raise them, and operate only within your demonstrated abilities and the airplane's limitations. Reasonable night minimums include higher ceiling and visibility than the legal VFR values, a wider temperature and dewpoint spread to guard against ground fog, lower crosswind limits, alternates with lighted runways, higher en route altitudes for terrain and engine failure options, and recent night landing practice before carrying passengers. Set them in writing before the flight, not in the airplane.

items.q: What does the source of power item require at night?
items.a: An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment, per 91.205(c)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. In a Warrior II that is the engine-driven alternator with the battery as the reserve. If the alternator fails at night, shed load immediately to lights and one radio; expect well under an hour of useful battery time, and confirm the POH electrical failure checklist.
items.concept: FLAPS S: source of electrical power

items.q: Define morning and evening civil twilight.
items.a: Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise. Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun reaches 6 degrees below the horizon. It usually lasts between 20 and 35 minutes, longer at high latitudes and in winter, and the times are published in the Air Almanac for your location.
items.concept: Definition of civil twilight - morning begins at 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise; evening begins at sunset and ends at 6 degrees below; usually 20 to 35 minutes

items.q: What exactly is sunset?
items.a: Sunset occurs when the upper limb of the sun, that is its upper edge, sinks just under the horizon. It is not the moment the sun's center crosses, and it is not when the sky goes dark. Sunset is the instant evening civil twilight begins, and it is the instant your position and anticollision lights must be on.
items.concept: Definition of sunset - the upper edge of the sun, the upper limb, sinks just under the horizon

items.q: What exactly is sunrise?
items.a: Sunrise occurs when the upper limb of the sun, that is its upper edge, rises just above the horizon. It marks the end of morning civil twilight, and it is the moment at which the position lights and anticollision lights may be turned off.
items.concept: Definition of sunrise - the upper limb rises just above the horizon

b: The questions he was actually asked, with the answers worked out.

items.q: What are the three types of parasite drag?
items.a: Form, interference and skin friction. Parasite drag is every bit of drag that is not a by-product of lift, and it comes from the airframe simply being pushed through the air. All three grow with the square of the airspeed, so they dominate at cruise and high speed and are almost irrelevant at low speed.

items.q: What is skin friction drag and how do designers reduce it?
items.a: The air in the boundary layer sticks to the surface and is dragged along with it, so every square foot of skin resists the airflow. No surface is perfectly smooth; rivet heads, screws, paint texture, dirt, bugs and frost all roughen it and thicken the boundary layer. It is reduced with flush riveting, smooth paint, careful sealing of gaps, and keeping the airplane clean and free of frost.

items.q: What is interference drag and where on an airplane does it show up?
items.a: Where two airflows from different parts of the airframe meet and mix, the combined flow is more turbulent and more draggy than the sum of the two separately. The classic location is the wing root, where flow over the wing meets flow around the fuselage; also the tail junction, strut ends and gear fairings. It is reduced with fillets and fairings that blend one surface smoothly into the other.

items.q: What is form drag and how is it reduced?
items.a: Form drag is the pressure drag caused by the shape of a body disrupting the airflow and leaving a low-pressure turbulent wake behind it: struts, fixed landing gear, the pitot tube, antennas, steps, an open cowl flap, anything sticking into the airstream that is not producing lift. Streamlining, fairings and retracting the gear cut it dramatically, because a streamlined shape lets the flow close in behind rather than separating.

items.q: How does parasite drag change with airspeed?
items.a: It increases with the square of the airspeed, so doubling the speed roughly quadruples parasite drag. Nothing about the airframe changes, but each part is disturbing four times the mass of air per second at twice the speed. This is why parasite drag is the dominant term at cruise and is almost negligible near the stall.

items.q: How does induced drag change with airspeed?
items.a: It decreases with the square of the airspeed. In level flight, lift must equal weight; the faster you fly, the lower the angle of attack needed to make that lift, so the spanwise pressure difference and the vortices are weaker and the downwash is smaller. Induced drag is therefore the dominant term at slow speed and near the stall, and the small term at cruise.

items.q: How does total drag change with airspeed, and what is significant about its lowest point?
items.a: Total drag is the sum of a curve rising with the square of speed and one falling with the square of speed, so it forms a U. The bottom of the U is where parasite and induced drag are equal; that is the maximum lift-to-drag speed (L/Dmax), which is best glide and the speed for maximum endurance in a glide and maximum range in a jet. Above that speed total drag rises steeply because parasite drag takes over.

items.q: What is the region of reversed command and why does it matter?
items.a: It is the range of speeds slower than L/Dmax, where total drag increases as you slow down, so more power is required to fly slower. It is the back side of the power curve. It matters on short final, in slow flight and during a soft-field takeoff, because a speed loss increases drag, which loses more speed unless you add power. Recovery is power plus a lowered nose, not pitch alone.

items.q: What is wake turbulence and how is it formed?
items.a: Wake turbulence is the disturbed air left behind an airplane, and its main component is a pair of counter-rotating wingtip vortices. Because the wing makes lift by holding higher pressure below and lower pressure above, air spills around each tip from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side and rolls up into a horizontal tornado trailing from each tip. It is a direct by-product of lift, and therefore of induced drag.

items.q: When is an airplane generating the strongest wake turbulence?
items.a: When it is heavy, clean and slow. Heavy means a lot of lift is being produced; clean and slow mean it is being produced at a high angle of attack with a large pressure difference across the tips and no flaps to spread the load. Those are exactly the conditions just after rotation and on short final, which is why the worst wake encounters happen in the airport environment.

items.q: Once shed, how do wingtip vortices move?
items.a: They sink at roughly 300 to 500 feet per minute and level off about 900 feet below the generating aircraft's flight path, so staying at or above that path keeps you clear. In still air they also spread outward at about 5 knots each. Near the ground they cannot sink further, so they roll sideways and drift with the wind, which is why a light quartering tailwind of 3 to 7 knots is the worst case: it holds a vortex over the touchdown zone.

items.q: How do you avoid wake turbulence behind a heavier aircraft on takeoff and on landing?
items.a: Landing behind a larger airplane, stay at or above its approach path and touch down beyond its touchdown point. Departing behind one, rotate before its rotation point and climb above and upwind of its path. Behind a departing aircraft on an intersecting runway, avoid crossing below its path. If you are unsure, ask for and accept the wake turbulence separation rather than a visual approach and a waiver of it.

items.q: What is ground effect?
items.a: Ground effect is the change in the airflow around a wing operating within about one wingspan of the surface, and it is strong within half a span. The ground interrupts the formation of the wingtip vortices and reduces the upwash and downwash behind the wing. With less downwash the lift vector tilts less rearward, so at a given coefficient of lift there is a large reduction in induced drag. It is not a cushion of compressed air, although it feels like one.

items.q: What happens as you leave ground effect on a takeoff?
items.a: Induced drag increases sharply, so the airplane needs a higher angle of attack and more thrust to hold the same speed and climb. There is a nose-up change in pitching moment as the downwash on the tail is restored, a decrease in stability, and a change in the static source pressure that shows as a slight increase in indicated airspeed. If you lifted off below flying speed you can settle back onto the runway here.

items.q: What are the practical hazards of ground effect on takeoff and on landing?
items.a: On takeoff, the reduced drag lets the airplane become airborne below a safe flying speed; climb out of ground effect and it can sink back or fail to climb, especially at high density altitude or over obstacles. On landing, the same drag reduction makes the airplane float and refuse to settle, eating up runway; the answer is a stabilized approach at the right speed rather than carrying extra knots.

items.q: How does an elevator trim tab work?
items.a: The trim tab is a small hinged surface on the trailing edge of the elevator, and it deflects opposite to the way you want the elevator to go. For nose-up trim the tab moves down; the air pushes the tab up, and because the tab is behind the elevator hinge line, that force levers the elevator trailing edge up, holding the elevator up without any pressure from you. Think of it as a small elevator that flies the big one.

items.q: What does trim actually do for the pilot, and what does it not do?
items.a: It relieves the control pressure needed to hold a given attitude, and in doing so it sets an airspeed: a properly trimmed airplane will return to that speed after a disturbance if power is unchanged. It does not change control authority, it does not fly the airplane, and it is not a substitute for pitch input. Correct technique is pitch to the attitude, hold it, then trim the pressure off.

items.q: Explain the difference between static and dynamic stability.
items.a: Static stability is the initial tendency an airplane shows the instant it is displaced from equilibrium in pitch, roll or yaw. Dynamic stability is what it does over time after that first response. The two are separate: an airplane can be statically positive but dynamically negative, meaning it starts back toward equilibrium but the oscillations grow instead of dying out.

items.q: What do positive, neutral and negative stability mean?
items.a: Positive: it initially heads back toward equilibrium, and over time the oscillations damp out and it settles. Neutral: it stays wherever the disturbance left it, and any oscillation neither grows nor decays. Negative: it initially moves further away from equilibrium, and over time the motion diverges and grows. Certificated airplanes are required to be statically positive in all three axes.

items.q: What design features give an airplane lateral stability?
items.a: Dihedral is the main one, plus sweepback, keel effect from the fuselage side area above the CG, and the high-wing pendulum effect of hanging the weight below the wing. All of them work the same way: they turn a sideslip into a rolling moment that lifts the low wing back toward level.

items.q: How does dihedral actually produce lateral stability?
items.a: Dihedral is the upward angle of the wings from root to tip, and it works through sideslip, not bank alone. When a wing drops, the airplane slides toward the low wing; that sideways relative wind meets the upward-angled low wing at a higher angle of attack and the raised wing at a lower one. The low wing makes more lift and rolls the airplane back to level, which is positive static lateral stability.

items.q: What are the drawbacks of dihedral?
items.a: Because the wings are tilted up, some of each wing's lift acts sideways rather than vertically, so a little lift is wasted. More importantly, the same restoring moment that levels the wings resists the pilot's roll inputs, so the airplane is more sluggish in roll and less crisp to maneuver. Strong dihedral also couples roll with yaw and can produce Dutch roll. Stability and maneuverability are always traded against each other.

items.q: What is keel effect?
items.a: Keel effect is the lateral stability contributed by the side area of the fuselage and vertical fin above the center of gravity. In a sideslip, the relative wind striking that large area above the CG pushes the top of the airplane away, which levers the low wing back up, just like the keel and sail of a boat. On a high-wing airplane the weight slung below the wing adds a pendulum effect in the same direction.

items.q: What provides longitudinal stability, and what is the role of the CG?
items.a: The horizontal stabiliser, working with a CG located ahead of the center of lift. The nose-heavy couple is balanced by a download on the tail; if the nose pitches up the wing's angle of attack increases, lift increases, and the nose-down couple grows, pushing the nose back down. Moving the CG aft shortens the tail arm and weakens this, which is why an aft CG limit exists.

items.q: What provides directional stability?
items.a: The vertical stabiliser, plus the fuselage side area behind the CG. If the airplane yaws, the fin meets the relative wind at an angle of attack and generates a side force that swings the nose back into the wind, like a weathervane. Sweepback also helps, because the forward-going wing presents more span to the airflow and generates more drag.

items.q: If you put a heavy suitcase in the back seat, what changes aerodynamically?
items.a: The CG moves aft. Longitudinal stability decreases, so the airplane is twitchier in pitch and less inclined to return to trimmed speed. Less tail download is required, so the wing carries less load: stall speed drops slightly and cruise speed increases slightly for the same power. The stall break is sharper, and recovery from a stall or spin becomes harder because the elevator has less leverage to lower the nose.

items.q: Why does an aft CG make stall and spin recovery harder?
items.a: Recovery needs a nose-down pitching moment, which the elevator produces by pushing the tail up about the CG. Moving the CG aft shortens the arm between the CG and the tail, so the same elevator deflection generates a smaller moment. At the same time the natural nose-down restoring couple from the wing is weaker. Loaded beyond the aft limit the elevator may not be able to break the stall at all.

items.q: Which is worse, a skidding turn or a slipping turn, and why?
items.a: A skid is far worse, because it is how a low-altitude spin starts. In a skid there is too much rudder into the turn; the outside wing speeds up and lifts, so the airplane overbanks and the pilot holds opposite aileron. That lowered aileron increases the inside wing's angle of attack while the yaw already has it flying slower, so the inside wing stalls first and the airplane snaps over into the turn.

items.q: Why is the base-to-final skid the classic spin scenario?
items.a: The pilot overshoots the centerline, is reluctant to steepen the bank so low, and adds bottom rudder to swing the nose around. That skids the airplane, and the back pressure being held to stop the nose dropping raises the angle of attack. The inside wing stalls first with yaw already established, so the airplane rolls rapidly into the turn and toward inverted, from a height where there is no room to recover.

items.q: What happens if a wing stalls in a slipping turn instead?
items.a: A slip is the safer of the two. With too little rudder for the bank, the nose points outside the turn and the outside wing is the one flying slower; the airplane tends to roll back toward wings level rather than snap into the turn. The stall is still a stall and must be recovered, but it does not have the built-in yaw that drives autorotation, so it rarely develops into a spin.

items.q: What is P-factor and when is it strongest?
items.a: P-factor is asymmetric propeller thrust at high angles of attack. With the nose up, the descending blade on the right side meets the air at a higher angle of attack and at a slightly greater speed than the ascending blade on the left, so it produces more thrust. The thrust line is effectively displaced to the right of center, yawing the airplane left. It is strongest slow, at high power and high angle of attack: climb, go-around and takeoff.

items.q: Explain torque as a left-turning tendency.
items.a: Newton's third law. With a propeller turning clockwise from the cockpit, the reaction on the airframe is a roll to the left. In flight this must be countered with aileron or built-out rigging. On the ground the left roll puts extra weight on the left main wheel, which increases its rolling friction, and the airplane veers left. Torque is greatest at high power and low airspeed.

items.q: Explain spiralling slipstream.
items.a: The propeller does not throw air straight back; it throws it back in a corkscrew. That rotating tube of accelerated air wraps around the fuselage and strikes the left side of the vertical fin and rudder, pushing the tail right and yawing the nose left. It is most pronounced when the propeller is turning fast and the airplane is moving slowly, since the helix is then tightly wound: full power at low speed.

items.q: What is gyroscopic precession and when does a single-engine pilot feel it?
items.a: A spinning propeller is a gyroscope, so a force applied to it takes effect 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation. Raising the tail on a tailwheel takeoff applies a forward force at the top of the disc, which is felt at the right side of the disc and yaws the nose left. In any airplane it appears whenever pitch or yaw changes rapidly, such as during a stall break or a nose-up entry into a maneuver.

items.q: What are the three broad categories of aircraft icing?
items.a: Structural icing, which forms on the airframe and lifting surfaces; induction icing, which blocks the engine's air supply, including carburettor ice and air-filter ice; and instrument icing, which blocks the pitot tube, static ports, fuel vents or the stall warning vane. All three can happen on the same flight and each needs a different response.

items.q: Describe clear ice: how it forms and why it is the most dangerous.
items.a: Clear ice forms roughly between 0 and -10 degrees Celsius from large supercooled droplets. The droplet only partly freezes on impact and the rest runs back before freezing, so the ice forms as a smooth, hard, glassy sheet that spreads well aft of the leading edge. It is the heaviest type, the hardest to see, the hardest to shed, and it can build behind the reach of any de-ice boot.

items.q: Describe rime ice.
items.a: Rime forms roughly between -15 and -20 degrees Celsius from small supercooled droplets that freeze instantly on contact. Because they freeze before they can spread, air is trapped between them, giving a rough, opaque, milky, brittle deposit built forward off the leading edges. It is lighter than clear ice and breaks off more readily, but its rough shape spoils the leading-edge airflow and cuts maximum lift quickly.

items.q: What is mixed icing?
items.a: Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime, formed roughly between -10 and -15 degrees Celsius where both large and small supercooled droplets are present. It takes on the worst of both: rough, irregular shapes like rime with hard, spreading clear ice mixed in, and it accumulates quickly. It is the most common form of airframe icing found in convective and frontal cloud.

items.q: What two conditions must exist together for structural icing to form?
items.a: Visible moisture such as cloud, rain or drizzle, and an aircraft surface temperature at or below freezing. Both are needed: freezing air in clear sky will not ice you, and cloud well above zero will not either. Note the surface temperature can be below the outdoor air temperature, and freezing rain or freezing drizzle can ice an airplane very rapidly even in air slightly above zero at flight level.

items.q: How does structural icing degrade aircraft performance?
items.a: It changes the shape of the aerofoil and roughens the surface, so maximum lift falls and the stall occurs at a lower angle of attack and higher airspeed with little or no buffet warning. Drag rises sharply, weight increases, control surfaces can jam or their balance change, and the stall warning system may be iced and silent. Antennas, propeller blades and windshields ice too. The response is to leave the icing conditions.

items.q: What is induction icing and what protects against it?
items.a: Induction icing blocks the engine's air supply, either as ice on the air filter and inlet or as carburettor ice in the venturi. The protection is an alternate air source that bypasses the blocked filter and draws warm air from inside the cowling, usually through a spring-loaded door that opens automatically or by a cockpit control, and carburettor heat in a carburetted engine. Check the arrangement in the POH for the airplane flown.

items.q: In what conditions does carburettor ice form, and what are the symptoms?
items.a: Fuel vaporization and the venturi pressure drop can cool the carburettor by 30 to 40 degrees Celsius, so ice can form with outside air anywhere from about -7 to +21 degrees Celsius and relative humidity above 80 percent, even on a warm hazy day. In a fixed-pitch airplane the symptom is a gradual loss of rpm and rough running; with a constant-speed propeller it is a loss of manifold pressure at constant rpm.

items.q: What is instrument icing and what does it do to your indications?
items.a: Ice blocks the pitot tube, static ports or fuel vents. A blocked pitot with a clear drain makes the airspeed fall toward zero; a blocked pitot and drain turns the airspeed indicator into an altimeter that over-reads in a climb and under-reads in a descent. Blocked static ports freeze the altimeter, kill the vertical speed indicator, and make airspeed read low in a climb and high in a descent. Pitot heat and the alternate static source are the fixes.

items.q: What is Va, and give both of the standard definitions.
items.a: Va is design maneuvering speed. Practically, it is the highest speed at which full, abrupt deflection of a single flight control in one direction will not overstress the airframe. Aerodynamically, it is the speed at which the wing reaches its critical angle of attack and stalls at exactly the limit load factor, so the wing lets go before the structure does. The value at gross weight is in the POH or AFM and on a placard.

items.q: What does Va not protect you against?
items.a: It protects a single full control input in one direction. It does not cover rapid reversals, such as full left then full right rudder, which can overload the tail even below Va, and it does not cover simultaneous inputs on two axes. It also does not guarantee protection from every gust; for rough air use the turbulent air penetration speed in the POH, which may differ from Va.

items.q: Why does Va change with weight, and which way does it move?
items.a: Va decreases as weight decreases, in proportion to the square root of the weight ratio: Va equals the gross-weight value times the square root of actual weight divided by maximum gross weight. Load factor is lift divided by weight, so a lighter airplane reaches its limit load factor with less lift; it must therefore be slowed down so that the wing stalls and sheds that lift before the limit is reached.

items.q: Define Vso, Vs and Vr.
items.a: Vso is the stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration, gear and flaps down, and it marks the bottom of the white arc. Vs or Vs1 is the stall speed in a specified configuration, normally clean, and it marks the bottom of the green arc. Vr is rotation speed, the speed at which back pressure is applied on the takeoff roll. Take the actual numbers from the POH for the airplane you are flying.

items.q: Define Vx and Vy, and how do they change with altitude?
items.a: Vx is best angle of climb: the most altitude gained per unit of horizontal distance, used to clear an obstacle. Vy is best rate of climb: the most altitude gained per unit of time. Vx increases slightly with altitude and Vy decreases with altitude, so the two converge and meet at the absolute ceiling, where the only remaining climb speed gives zero rate of climb. Take the values from the POH.

items.q: Define Vfe, Vno and Vne, and what the arcs and lines on the airspeed indicator mean.
items.a: Vfe is maximum flap extended speed, the top of the white arc, and many airplanes have a higher limit for a partial flap setting; Vno is maximum structural cruising speed, the top of the green arc, above which you fly only in smooth air and with caution; Vne is never exceed, the red line. The yellow arc between Vno and Vne is the caution range. All values come from the POH and the placards.

items.q: What is maximum demonstrated crosswind component, and is it a limitation?
items.a: It is the strongest 90-degree crosswind in which the manufacturer's test pilot actually demonstrated a satisfactory takeoff and landing during certification. For most normal category airplanes it is not a certificated limitation, so exceeding it is not illegal, but it was flown by a professional in a new airplane and it is a sensible personal limit. Check the POH, since some airplanes do publish it as a limit.

items.q: Why does an airplane keep rotating in a spin instead of just recovering?
items.a: It is autorotation, and it is self-sustaining. The down-going wing meets the relative wind at an even higher angle of attack, so it is more deeply stalled, producing less lift and much more drag; the up-going wing is at a lower angle of attack, producing more lift and less drag. The lift difference keeps rolling it and the drag difference keeps yawing it, and the two feed each other until the angle of attack is reduced.

items.q: Describe the entry and incipient phases of a spin.
items.a: The entry is the pilot's action or the circumstances that stall the airplane while it is yawing, deliberately or otherwise. The incipient phase runs from the stall until the spin is fully developed, typically the first two to four turns; the aerodynamic and inertial forces are still changing, the attitude is not yet stabilized, airspeed settles low and constant, and the turn coordinator shows the direction of rotation. Most inadvertent spins are recovered here.

items.q: Describe the developed and recovery phases of a spin.
items.a: In the developed phase the rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed are stabilized on a near-vertical flight path; aerodynamic and inertial forces are in balance and the motion is constant or repeating, so the spin is in equilibrium and will continue until acted upon. The recovery phase begins when rotation stops and the angle of attack drops below critical; it may take a quarter turn or several turns depending on the airplane and spin mode.

items.q: What does PARE stand for and why is each step in that order?
items.a: Power idle, to remove the yawing effects of slipstream and P-factor and to avoid over-speeding in the dive. Ailerons neutral, because aileron into or out of the spin changes wing angles of attack and can flatten or tighten it. Rudder full opposite to the direction of rotation, which is what stops the yaw driving autorotation. Elevator briskly forward to break the stall. Always fly the manufacturer's procedure from the POH.

items.q: What is the two-step elevator technique in a spin recovery?
items.a: Move the elevator briskly forward to below the critical angle of attack, hold it until rotation stops and the wings are flying, then gradually ease back to level flight from the ensuing dive. Both halves matter: a timid forward input leaves the wing stalled and the spin continues, while a snatched pull-out overstresses the airframe or triggers a secondary stall. Neutralize the rudder as rotation stops so you do not spin the other way.

items.q: What is a stall?
items.a: A stall is the loss of lift and increase in drag that occurs when the smooth airflow over the wing separates. It happens when the angle of attack, the angle between the chord line and the relative wind, exceeds the wing's critical angle of attack, typically around 16 to 20 degrees. It is entirely a matter of angle of attack, not of speed, weight or attitude.

items.q: Can an airplane stall at any airspeed and any attitude?
items.a: Yes. A wing stalls only when the critical angle of attack is exceeded, and that can be done at any airspeed, any weight, any bank angle and any pitch attitude. A high-speed pull-up will exceed it at cruise speed, and a wing can be stalled pointing straight down. The published stall speed applies to one condition: unaccelerated flight, wings level, at gross weight, in the stated configuration.

items.q: What raises density altitude?
items.a: High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity. Rising temperature makes air expand and thin; falling pressure removes molecules; water vapor is lighter than dry air, so humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure. Temperature is the dominant everyday factor: a hot afternoon at a modest field elevation can easily produce a density altitude thousands of feet above the airport.

items.q: How does a high density altitude affect takeoff and landing distance?
items.a: Both get longer. The wing needs the same mass of air over it, so it must reach a higher true airspeed for the same indicated speed, which takes more runway to accelerate to and produces a higher groundspeed at touchdown to dissipate. At the same time the engine makes less power and the propeller less thrust, so acceleration is worse. Climb rate and climb gradient fall, and the service ceiling comes down.

items.q: What is the Vg diagram?
items.a: The Vg or V-n diagram is the graph of an airplane's flight operating strength: airspeed on the horizontal scale against load factor on the vertical. Curved lines on the left are the aerodynamic stall limits, horizontal lines top and bottom are the positive and negative limit load factors, and the vertical line on the right is Vne. Where the stall curve meets the positive limit load line is Va. Each airplane has its own, and it changes with weight and altitude.

items.q: What is the load factor in a level 30, 45 and 60 degree banked turn?
items.a: Roughly 1.15G at 30 degrees, 1.41G at 45 degrees and 2.0G at 60 degrees, because load factor in a level turn equals one divided by the cosine of the bank angle. It depends only on bank angle in level flight, not on airspeed or weight. Beyond 60 degrees it climbs steeply: 75 degrees is about 3.9G, and past that a normal category airplane is at its limit.

items.q: What is the difference between limit load and ultimate load?
items.a: Limit load is the maximum load expected in service; up to it the structure suffers no permanent deformation, and beyond it the airplane may be permanently bent even if it holds together. Ultimate load is limit load times a 1.5 safety factor, and it is where structural failure is expected. The airplane must withstand ultimate load for at least three seconds without failing, but it will not be flyable afterwards.

items.q: What are the limit load factors for the normal, utility and acrobatic categories?
items.a: Normal category: +3.8 and -1.52G, and it permits no aerobatics or intentional spins. Utility: +4.4 and -1.76G, allowing limited maneuvers including spins if approved. Acrobatic: +6.0 and -3.0G. Many light airplanes are certificated in more than one category depending on weight and loading, so check the POH limitations section and the weight and CG for the category you intend to use.

items.q: What are the privileges of a commercial pilot certificate?
items.a: You may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and you may be paid to act as pilot in command, under 14 CFR 61.133 (Part 61, Subpart F, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations: General). The certificate also requires that the flight itself complies with whatever operating rule applies to it, so the commercial certificate qualifies the pilot, not the operation.

items.q: What limitation is placed on a commercial pilot with a single-engine airplane rating but no instrument rating?
items.a: The certificate is issued with the limitation that the carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights of more than 50 nautical miles, or at night, is prohibited, under 14 CFR 61.133(b) (Part 61, Subpart F, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations). It is removed when you add an instrument rating in the same category and class; until then it restricts passengers for hire, not your own or non-revenue flying.

items.q: What design features counteract adverse yaw?
items.a: Differential ailerons, where the up-going aileron deflects further than the down-going one so that the extra parasite drag on the descending wing balances the extra induced drag on the rising wing. Frise-type ailerons, whose up-deflected leading edge projects into the airflow below the wing to add drag on the descending wing side. Some airplanes also interconnect rudder and aileron. None of these is a substitute for coordinated rudder.

items.q: What is a runway incursion and what are the three types?
items.a: A runway incursion is any incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface used for takeoff and landing. The three causes are pilot deviations, operational incidents or deviations by air traffic control, and vehicle or pedestrian deviations. The FAA also classifies each event for severity from category A, a near collision, down to category D, which meets the definition but has no immediate safety consequence.

items.q: What practices prevent runway incursions?
items.a: Have the airport diagram out and in view before taxi; write down and read back every hold short instruction with your call sign; keep a sterile cockpit while taxiing; know the signage and hold position markings; stop and ask if you are unsure of your position; scan the final approach path before crossing or entering any runway; and never begin a takeoff roll without hearing an explicit clearance and confirming you are on the assigned runway.

items.q: What annunciators would you expect in a modern light single, and when do they illuminate?
items.a: Typically low and high oil temperature and oil pressure, low and high voltage, low fuel quantity for each tank, alternator or standby alternator failure, standby battery status, starter engaged, pitot heat, and in some installations a carbon monoxide warning. Each has its own trigger threshold and its own required response, and both the list and the thresholds are aircraft specific: read them from the POH or AFM for the airplane being flown.

items.q: You find an instrument or item of equipment inoperative during preflight. What is the decision path?
items.a: Work through 14 CFR 91.213 (Part 91, Subpart C, Inoperative instruments and equipment). First, does the aircraft have an approved Minimum Equipment List? If so, the MEL is the sole authority and you follow it. If not, the item may be left inoperative only if it is not required by the equipment list or kinds of operations list for VFR-day type certification, not required by an airworthiness directive, not required by 91.205 for the flight, and not required by any other rule. Then deactivate or remove it, placard it INOPERATIVE, and determine it is not a hazard.

items.q: Where is the relative wind coming from in a spin?
items.a: From below. In a developed spin the flight path is nearly straight down, so the air arrives almost vertically from underneath the airplane, giving both wings an angle of attack far beyond critical, often 20 to 45 degrees. Because the airplane is also rolling, the down-going wing sees the relative wind from further below still, so its angle of attack is higher and it is more deeply stalled, which is what drives autorotation.

items.q: What is the difference between angle of attack and pitch attitude?
items.a: Angle of attack is the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind; pitch attitude is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon. There is no fixed relationship between them. You can hold a high nose attitude at a low angle of attack in a steep climb, or be pitched well down at the critical angle of attack in a spin or a descending accelerated stall.

items.q: What are wingtip vortices?
items.a: They are the rotating cores of air that trail from each wingtip whenever the wing is producing lift. High pressure below the wing spills around the tip into the low pressure above, and that spanwise flow rolls up into a horizontal vortex turning inward over the top. They are the physical cause of induced drag and of wake turbulence, and their strength rises with weight and angle of attack and falls with speed and span.

items.q: What is the benefit of a slotted flap over a plain flap?
items.a: A slotted flap leaves a gap between the wing trailing edge and the flap, so high-pressure air from beneath the wing accelerates through the slot and re-energizes the boundary layer over the top of the flap. That delays airflow separation, so the flap gives a much larger increase in maximum lift for the drag it adds, and it lets the wing keep flying to a higher angle of attack.

items.q: What is a microburst and how strong can it be?
items.a: A microburst is a small, intense downdraft from a convective cell, typically less than 1 nautical mile across, that spreads out radially when it hits the ground. Downdrafts can reach 6,000 feet per minute, and the horizontal outflow can produce a headwind-to-tailwind shear of 45 knots or more, an airspeed swing of up to 90 knots. It usually lasts only 2 to 5 minutes but can persist longer, and a dry microburst may show only virga.

items.q: Would you rather have a headwind shift to a tailwind or a tailwind shift to a headwind, and why?
items.a: A tailwind shifting to a headwind, every time: that is performance increasing, and it gives you airspeed and lift when you need them. The headwind-to-tailwind shift is what kills people. The initial headwind raises indicated airspeed, the pilot reduces power to hold the target speed, then the airplane passes into the downdraft and out into the tailwind, low, slow and with the power back. Caught in one, apply full power and fly straight ahead; do not turn.

items.q: What is the jet stream and why is it stronger in winter?
items.a: The jet stream is a narrow, meandering band of very strong winds near the tropopause, defined as 50 knots or more, that forms where a sharp horizontal temperature gradient exists between air masses. The polar jet lies broadly between 30 and 60 degrees latitude. In winter the contrast between polar and tropical air is greatest, so the jet is faster and shifts further toward the equator. Expect clear air turbulence near it.

items.q: Which cylinders on a horizontally opposed engine generally run hottest, and why?
items.a: Generally the rear cylinders, because cooling air entering the front of the cowling has already been warmed by the forward cylinders and its flow is more restricted by the time it reaches the back. The front cylinders normally show the lowest cylinder head temperatures. Which cylinder is actually hottest varies with baffling, cowl flap position and installation, so use the engine monitor and the POH limits for the airplane.

items.q: What engine parameters does an integrated engine indicating system typically display?
items.a: Typically engine rpm and, on a constant-speed installation, manifold pressure; fuel flow and fuel quantity per tank; oil pressure and oil temperature; cylinder head temperature and exhaust gas temperature for each cylinder; and bus voltage and alternator or battery current. Many also compute fuel used and fuel remaining. The exact set is installation specific, so confirm it in the POH or the avionics supplement.

items.q: What is the difference between AC and DC, and how does an alternator supply a DC aircraft?
items.a: Direct current flows in one direction, as from a battery; alternating current reverses direction many times a second. An alternator generates AC, which is converted to DC by a bank of diodes acting as a rectifier inside the alternator, so the bus sees DC. An inverter does the reverse, making AC from DC for equipment that needs it. Light aircraft use a DC bus so the battery can both power it and be charged from it.

items.q: How do you decide whether to treat a passenger for hypoxia or hyperventilation?
items.a: The symptoms overlap almost completely: headache, dizziness, tingling, visual changes and poor judgment appear in both. Hyperventilation is driven by stress and rapid breathing, often with tingling around the mouth and muscle spasm; hypoxia brings cyanosis, blue lips and fingernails, and euphoria. If in any doubt at altitude, treat it as hypoxia first: oxygen and descend. If oxygen makes no difference, slow their breathing and get them talking.

items.q: Where do spins most often occur?
items.a: Close to the ground, at low airspeed, with high power and the airplane uncoordinated at a high angle of attack. The classic case is the skidded base-to-final turn after overshooting the centerline. Others are the botched go-around, where full power and a nose-up trim state combine with uncorrected left-turning tendencies; an uncoordinated power-on stall; and the attempted turn back to the runway after an engine failure on climb-out.

items.q: How long should you wait to fly after donating blood?
items.a: There is no regulation, but donation reduces blood volume and haemoglobin, which lowers your tolerance to altitude and to hypoxia, and can leave you light-headed for some time. FAA guidance on fitness for flight in AIM Section 8-1-1 is to avoid flying until you have fully recovered, with at least 24 hours as the usual minimum and longer if you feel any effect. Check AIM 8-1-1 and ask an aviation medical examiner if in doubt.

items.q: What is an embedded thunderstorm and why is it so dangerous?
items.a: An embedded thunderstorm is a cell hidden inside other cloud, in a stratiform layer, haze or fog, so it cannot be seen and circumnavigated visually. You can be in the cell before you know it exists. It is the reason for onboard or datalink weather radar, for the standard 20 nautical mile avoidance from any cell, and for treating a forecast of embedded thunderstorms as a reason not to launch a light single into IMC.

items.q: What are the transponder modes and what does each provide?
items.a: Mode A replies with the four-digit identification code only. Mode C adds automatic pressure altitude reporting. Mode S adds a unique 24-bit aircraft address so it can be interrogated selectively rather than by every radar, plus datalink capability; it is the basis of traffic collision avoidance and of 1090ES ADS-B Out. All modes also transmit ident when the button is pressed.

items.q: Where is a Mode C transponder required?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.215 (Part 91, Subpart C, ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use), you need an operable coded transponder with automatic altitude reporting in all Class A, B and C airspace; within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, the so-called Mode C veil; above the ceiling of and within the lateral limits of Class B or C up to 10,000 MSL; and generally at and above 10,000 feet MSL except below 2,500 feet AGL.

items.q: What does best glide speed mean, and how is it affected by weight and wind?
items.a: Best glide is the speed for the maximum lift-to-drag ratio, which gives the greatest distance over the ground per foot of altitude lost. It is not the minimum sink speed, which is slower and gives the most time aloft. Best glide decreases as weight decreases, roughly with the square root of the weight ratio, though the glide ratio itself is unchanged. Into a headwind, fly a little faster; with a tailwind, a little slower.

items.q: How can the FAA WINGS program satisfy a flight review?
items.a: Satisfactory completion of one or more phases of the FAA-sponsored WINGS pilot proficiency award program relieves you of the flight review, under 14 CFR 61.56(e) (Part 61, Subpart A, Flight review). A phase requires a set of knowledge credits and flight activity credits, with the flight activities validated by an authorized instructor, so the flying is done and logged the same way; completing the phase simply substitutes for the review.

items.q: What must you have done to carry passengers at night?
