items.a: Within the preceding 90 days you must have made three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop, as sole manipulator of the controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and if required type, and those takeoffs and landings must have been done between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise. This is 14 CFR 61.57(b) (Part 61, Subpart A, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command). Without it you may fly at night yourself, just not with passengers.

items.q: What are the three different definitions of night, and what does each one govern?
items.a: Sunset to sunrise is when position lights must be on, under 14 CFR 91.209 (Part 91, Subpart C, Aircraft lights). The end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight is what may be logged as night flight time, under 14 CFR 61.51 (Part 61, Subpart A, Pilot logbooks). One hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise is the window for night takeoff and landing currency to carry passengers, under 14 CFR 61.57(b). Learn them separately and you will not make a logging or currency error.

items.q: What spare electrical parts must be carried for night VFR?
items.a: One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, accessible to the pilot in flight, under 14 CFR 91.205(c) (Part 91, Subpart C, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements). The full night VFR additions are remembered as FLAPS: fuses, landing light if operated for hire, anti-collision lights, position lights and an adequate source of electrical power. Airplanes with circuit breakers instead of fuses do not need spares.

items.q: What does an L in the airport data on a sectional chart tell you about lighting?
items.a: A plain L means runway lighting is available from sunset to sunrise. An asterisk before the L means lighting limitations exist, for example pilot-controlled lighting, part-time operation or lighting only on part of the runway, and you must check the Chart Supplement for the details. Absence of an L means no runway lighting at all. Pilot-controlled lighting keying sequences are published in the Chart Supplement, not on the chart.

items.q: Describe the dimensions of Class C airspace and when you must establish communications.
items.a: Typically a 5 nautical mile inner core from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation, and a shelf from 5 to 10 nautical miles from 1,200 feet to 4,000 feet. Beyond that is a 20 nautical mile outer area where radar service is available on request. Entry requires an operable Mode C transponder, ADS-B Out, and two-way radio communication established, which means the controller has used your call sign without a restriction, before you cross the boundary.

items.q: What are the maximum airspeeds in the various airspace?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.117 (Part 91, Subpart B, Aircraft speed): 250 knots indicated below 10,000 feet MSL; 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace; and 200 knots in a VFR corridor through, or in the airspace underlying, Class B. Nobody may exceed Mach 1. If the minimum safe speed for the operation exceeds one of these, you may fly that minimum safe speed.

items.q: May you fly through a National Security Area?
items.a: Yes. A National Security Area is airspace where pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying over sensitive ground facilities; the request is advisory, not regulatory, so transit is legal. When more is needed, flight through an NSA can be temporarily prohibited by regulation and the prohibition is published by NOTAM, so check NOTAMs before assuming it is still voluntary.

items.q: What is true airspeed and how does it relate to indicated airspeed?
items.a: True airspeed is the airplane's actual speed through the air mass: calibrated airspeed corrected for air density, that is for pressure altitude and temperature. Because thin air produces less dynamic pressure, TAS exceeds IAS by roughly 2 percent per 1,000 feet of altitude at standard temperature. TAS combined with the wind gives groundspeed. The airplane always stalls and maneuvers by indicated airspeed, but navigates by TAS.

items.q: On a soft-field takeoff, the mains touch back down after liftoff. Is that acceptable?
items.a: Yes, provided the nosewheel does not touch back down. The technique is to lift off as early as possible in ground effect, then lower the nose slightly and accelerate in ground effect to a safe climb speed; a light touch of the mains during that acceleration is normal and harmless. Letting the nosewheel drop back into soft ground is the failure, because it can dig in and it defeats the entire purpose of the technique.

items.q: When should you make the approach minimums callout on an instrument approach?
items.a: Call 100 feet above the decision altitude or minimum descent altitude, using the correct term for the approach: DA on a precision or approach with vertical guidance, MDA on a non-precision approach. Then call minimums at the altitude itself, with either the runway environment in sight and a landing decision, or a go-around. Using the right term shows you know which type of approach you are flying and what protection it gives.

items.q: What does the DECIDE model stand for?
items.a: Detect that a change has occurred; Estimate the significance of the change; Choose a desirable outcome; Identify actions that will achieve it; Do the action; Evaluate the result and start again. It is a continuous loop rather than a one-time procedure, and its value is that the final step forces you to check whether your action actually improved the situation.

items.q: What is the 3P model, and what are its companion checklists?
items.a: Perceive, Process, Perform. Perceive the circumstances of the flight using PAVE: pilot, aircraft, environment and external pressures. Process them for risk using CARE: consequences, alternatives, reality and external pressures. Perform risk management using TEAM: transfer, eliminate, accept or mitigate the risk. Then run the loop again, because the situation keeps changing.

items.q: What are the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes?
items.a: Anti-authority, don't tell me, antidote: follow the rules, they are usually right. Impulsivity, do something quickly, antidote: not so fast, think first. Invulnerability, it won't happen to me, antidote: it could happen to me. Macho, I can do it, antidote: taking chances is foolish. Resignation, what's the use, antidote: I'm not helpless, I can make a difference. The skill is recognizing the thought in yourself and saying the antidote out loud.

items.q: What two subject areas must a flight review cover, and what is the minimum time?
items.a: A minimum of 1 hour of ground training and 1 hour of flight training, covering a review of the current general operating and flight rules of Part 91, and a review of those maneuvers and procedures that in the instructor's discretion are necessary for the pilot to exercise the privileges of the certificate. This is 14 CFR 61.56 (Part 61, Subpart A, Flight review), required within the preceding 24 calendar months.

items.q: Who can give a flight review, and what else can substitute for one?
items.a: An authorized instructor, meaning a CFI with the appropriate category and class ratings on their flight instructor certificate. Under 14 CFR 61.56 you also need no review if within the preceding 24 calendar months you passed a practical test for a certificate, rating or operating privilege, completed an approved pilot proficiency check, or completed a phase of the FAA WINGS program. The review is not a test and is not passed or failed; it is either logged as satisfactory or it is not.

items.q: When may you fly an aircraft without an emergency locator transmitter?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.207 (Part 91, Subpart C, Emergency locator transmitters), the ELT may be removed for inspection, repair or replacement and the aircraft flown for up to 90 days, provided the records show the removal and a placard visible to the pilot reads ELT NOT INSTALLED with the date, make and model. The section also exempts ferrying a new aircraft for installation and training within 50 nautical miles of the airport. Otherwise it is inspected every 12 calendar months, and the battery is replaced after 1 cumulative hour of use or at 50 percent of useful life.

items.q: What are the types of NOTAM and what does each carry?
items.a: NOTAM D covers airport and facility information: runway and taxiway closures, lighting, navaids, services. FDC NOTAMs come from the Flight Data Center and are regulatory: amendments to instrument procedures and charts, and temporary flight restrictions. Pointer NOTAMs highlight and cross-reference another NOTAM so it is not missed. Military NOTAMs cover military airports and navaids. There are also SAA NOTAMs for special activity airspace and international NOTAMs.

items.q: What are the functions of Class E airspace?
items.a: Per AIM 3-2-6, Class E is used as a surface area for an airport, as an extension to a surface area, as transition areas beginning at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL to contain arriving and departing IFR aircraft, as en route domestic areas, as federal airways, and as offshore airspace areas. Unless otherwise designated, Class E also exists from 14,500 feet MSL up to but not including 18,000 MSL, and again above FL600.

items.q: What happens to the airspace at a Class D airport when the tower closes?
items.a: It reverts to either a Class E surface area or, where there is no weather reporting and observer, to Class G up to 700 or 1,200 feet AGL with Class E above. Which one applies at a given airport is published in the Chart Supplement under that airport's airspace entry, and it changes the weather minimums and the communication requirements, so look it up before planning a night arrival after tower hours.

items.q: Walk through the vestibular and visual illusions summarized as ICEFLAGS.
items.a: Inversion, an abrupt level-off after climb feeling like tumbling backwards; Coriolis, head movement during a prolonged turn producing violent false rotation; Elevator, an updraft feeling like a climb; False horizon, sloping cloud or ground lights mistaken for the horizon; Leans, a slow roll going unnoticed so that level feels banked; Autokinesis, a static light appearing to move when stared at; Graveyard spiral, a descending turn that feels level; Somatogravic, acceleration felt as a pitch-up.

items.q: How is a wing designed so that it stalls at the root before the tip?
items.a: Mainly by washout, a built-in twist that sets the tip at a lower angle of incidence than the root, so the root reaches the critical angle of attack first. Some wings also use a different, more stall-resistant aerofoil at the tip, or stall strips on the inboard leading edge to trip the root early. The point is to keep the ailerons flying and roll control available at the stall, and to give buffet warning from disturbed air over the tail.

items.q: What does a full-flow oil filter mean, and what does the oil system actually do?
items.a: Full-flow means all the oil passes through the filter before reaching the engine bearings, with a bypass valve so a clogged filter cannot starve the engine. Most light airplanes use a wet sump, where the oil is carried in the crankcase; a dry sump uses a separate tank and scavenge pumps. The oil lubricates, cools, cleans by carrying contaminants to the filter, seals the piston rings, cushions the bearings and inhibits corrosion, and on a constant-speed installation it also drives the propeller governor.

items.q: What instruments show a pressurized cabin's status?
items.a: A cabin differential pressure gauge, showing the difference in psi between cabin and outside pressure, often combined on one dial with a cabin altimeter, showing the pressure altitude the occupants are experiencing; and a cabin rate of climb indicator, showing how fast the cabin altitude is changing. Together they tell you whether the system is holding schedule and give the first warning of a slow loss of pressurization.

items.q: What are the light gun signals to an aircraft in flight?
items.a: Steady green: cleared to land. Flashing green: return for landing, to be followed by a steady green at the appropriate time. Steady red: give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red: airport unsafe, do not land. Alternating red and green: general warning, exercise extreme caution. Flashing white has no meaning in flight. Acknowledge by rocking the wings by day or flashing the landing light at night.

items.q: What are the light gun signals to an aircraft on the ground?
items.a: Steady green: cleared for takeoff. Flashing green: cleared to taxi. Steady red: stop. Flashing red: taxi clear of the runway in use. Flashing white: return to your starting point on the airport. Alternating red and green: general warning, exercise extreme caution. Acknowledge by moving the ailerons or rudder by day, or flashing the taxi or landing light at night.

items.q: What are the issue times and valid periods of a METAR and a TAF?
items.a: A METAR is a routine surface observation issued once an hour, usually between 55 and 59 minutes past the hour, and is treated as current until the next one; a SPECI is issued in between when conditions change significantly. A TAF is a forecast for within 5 statute miles of the airport, issued four times a day at roughly 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800Z, valid for 24 hours, and for 30 hours at some larger airports, amended as needed.

items.q: How is the maximum elevation figure calculated, and does it differ for a man-made obstacle?
items.a: The MEF is printed in each quadrangle in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL. For natural terrain it is the highest elevation in the quadrangle, plus the vertical error of the source data, plus a 200-foot allowance for vegetation and unmapped obstructions, rounded up to the next 100 feet. For a man-made obstacle it is the top of the obstacle plus the vertical error, rounded up, with no 200-foot allowance added, because the obstacle height is already known.

items.q: What is your immediate action for an alternator failure or a low-voltage annunciation?
items.a: Run the POH abnormal checklist: usually confirm the annunciation against the ammeter and voltmeter, cycle the alternator side of the master or the field circuit breaker once to try a reset, and if it does not restore, shed all non-essential electrical load to conserve the battery, keep the radios and one navigation source, tell ATC, and land as soon as practical. Assume you have well under an hour of battery, and remember the magnetos keep the engine running regardless.

items.q: What does IMSAFE stand for?
items.a: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion, sometimes shown as Eating. It is a personal pre-flight self-assessment of the pilot, run before every flight and again before any later leg of a long day. It is the pilot half of the PAVE checklist, and unlike the airplane there is no minimum equipment list for you, so a single honest failure is a reason to cancel.

items.q: Name the classic operational pitfalls.
items.a: Peer pressure; mind set, refusing to reconsider the plan; get-there-itis; duck-under syndrome, descending below minimums to break out; scud running; continuing VFR into instrument conditions; getting behind the aircraft; loss of positional or situational awareness; operating without adequate fuel reserves; descent below the minimum en route altitude; flying outside the envelope; and neglecting flight planning, preflight inspections and checklists. They are all pressure to press on rather than errors of skill.

items.q: What color are taxiway centerline lights, and what are the other airport lighting colors?
items.a: Taxiway centerline lights are green and taxiway edge lights are blue. Runway edge lights are white, turning amber for the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less. Runway centerline lights are white, then alternating red and white from 3,000 to 1,000 feet remaining, then red for the last 1,000 feet. Thresholds are green from the approach side and red from the runway side, and runway guard lights are flashing yellow.

items.q: In a chandelle, how should the bank angle change through the maneuver?
items.a: Establish about 30 degrees of bank and hold it constant through the first 90 degrees of turn while pitch is increased steadily to the highest attitude. Through the second 90 degrees the pitch attitude is held and the bank is rolled out slowly and continuously to zero, so the wings arrive level exactly as the airplane completes 180 degrees of turn at an airspeed just above a stall.

items.q: What do you do with the flaps during a short-field landing rollout?
items.a: Retract them right after touchdown, without an announcement. Raising the flaps dumps wing lift onto the wheels, which puts weight on the tires and makes maximum braking effective, and it removes flap drag that would otherwise mask brake feel. Identify the flap control by feel and position rather than calling out flaps identified; never move it in the flare, and only shorten the rollout this way when the runway actually requires it.

items.q: What is a full-flow oil system, and how does it differ from a continuous-flow system?
items.a: Full flow means all of the oil passes through the filter and the pressurized galleries before it reaches the bearings, so indicated oil pressure rises and falls with engine rpm. A continuous or constant-flow arrangement instead holds a steady pressure regardless of rpm and routes only part of the oil through the filter. Read the oil system description, quantity and pressure limits for your airplane from the POH or AFM.

items.q: What true airspeed do you use for the climb leg of a navigation log, and where does it come from?
items.a: Take it from the cruise-climb or time-to-climb table in the POH or AFM: read the recommended indicated climb speed, then convert it to true airspeed at the average of the departure and cruise altitudes with the forecast temperature, which in a light trainer works out near 85 knots. Apply the winds aloft for that mean altitude to get climb ground speed, and use the table for time, fuel and distance to climb.

items.q: The examiner asks where you would look up accident reporting in the airplane. What do you say?
items.a: That the rule is 49 CFR Part 830 and I carry it on my tablet, and that the AIM repeats the substance of it in the safety of flight chapter, which is where it turns up if you search the FAR/AIM app. I would name 49 CFR Part 830 first and the AIM second, because an examiner asking this question is usually checking that you know the reporting rule is not in Part 91 at all.

items.q: The crosswind works out near 15 knots, gusting over 20. Would you be comfortable departing?
items.a: I would compute the components first and say the number out loud. With a steady crosswind near 15 knots and gusts putting it above the airplane's 17-knot demonstrated figure, my answer is no, for three reasons: the gust spread, not the steady wind, is what I have to fly; the same crosswind is waiting for me if I have to come straight back; and I have not flown a crosswind that strong recently enough to call myself proficient in it.

items.q: Give me the passenger briefing you would use with a paying client.
items.a: SAFETY, delivered before boarding and again at the airplane. Seat belts and harnesses, how to fasten and unfasten; air vents and sick bags; fire extinguisher location; exits, the single right-side door and its latch, plus the ELT and survival gear; traffic and talking, meaning the sterile cockpit periods and the standing invitation to call out any hazard; and your questions. Only the seat belt item is actually required, by 14 CFR 91.107.

items.q: You are crossing a runway and the controller gives you a frequency change. What do you do?
items.a: Finish crossing, get clear of the hold short line, stop the airplane, and then touch the radio. Acknowledge the instruction but do not start head-down work in a critical phase. Taxi is a critical phase of flight in both 14 CFR 121.542 and 135.100, and runway incursions are overwhelmingly a distraction problem. This is exactly the item the last candidate was debriefed on: too many things at once, a drift off the centerline, then a recovery.

b: The questions he and his instructor singled out as needing more than a one-line answer.

items.q: What is the difference between currency, recency of experience and a flight review?
items.a: A flight review under 14 CFR 61.56 (Part 61, Subpart A, Flight review) keeps the certificate usable at all: without one in the preceding 24 calendar months you may not act as pilot in command of anything. Recent flight experience under 14 CFR 61.57 (Recent flight experience: Pilot in command) is narrower and limits only what you may do: takeoffs and landings to carry passengers, and instrument experience to fly in instrument conditions. You can be current and overdue for a review, or reviewed and not current.

items.q: What must you have done to carry passengers by day?
items.a: Within the preceding 90 days you must have made three takeoffs and three landings as sole manipulator of the controls in an aircraft of the same category, class and, if a type rating is required, type, under 14 CFR 61.57(a) (Part 61, Subpart A, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command). By day the landings need not be to a full stop, except in a tailwheel airplane, where all three must be to a full stop.

items.q: Who can give a flight review?
items.a: An authorized instructor: a flight instructor whose CFI certificate carries the category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft used, under 14 CFR 61.56 (Part 61, Subpart A, Flight review). A ground instructor cannot, and a commercial pilot friend cannot. The review is logged as satisfactory or not logged at all; it is not a practical test and there is no failure to report, though the instructor may simply decline to endorse and recommend more training.

items.q: What is required to be current to fly in instrument conditions?
items.a: Within the preceding 6 calendar months, in the appropriate category of aircraft, a flight simulator or an approved training device, you must have performed and logged, in actual or simulated instrument conditions, six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses using navigational electronic systems. This is 14 CFR 61.57(c) (Part 61, Subpart A, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command).

items.q: What happens if your instrument currency lapses?
items.a: You get a further 6 calendar months in which to regain it on your own, by flying the same six approaches, holding and course tracking in actual or simulated conditions. If that grace period also runs out, so twelve calendar months from the end of currency, you may no longer regain it alone: you must pass an instrument proficiency check given by an examiner, an authorized instructor or an approved person, under 14 CFR 61.57(d).

items.q: Where does it say you may use a safety pilot to regain instrument currency after the first six months?
items.a: In 14 CFR 61.57(c) itself. It allows the six approaches, holding and tracking to be done in simulated instrument conditions as well as actual, and simulated instrument flight in an aircraft requires a safety pilot under 14 CFR 91.109(c). Nothing in 61.57 makes the grace period different, so the same simulated-conditions option applies right up until 61.57(d) demands an instrument proficiency check at twelve months.

items.q: What is required of a safety pilot?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.109(c) (Part 91, Subpart B, Flight instruction; simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests), the safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft, and must have adequate vision forward and to each side; the aircraft must have fully functioning dual controls. A safety pilot is a required crewmember, so a current medical certificate is needed, and the two pilots must agree beforehand who is acting as pilot in command.

items.q: What are the four elements of common carriage, and what does holding out mean?
items.a: From AC 120-12A, Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property: a holding out of a willingness to, transport persons or property, from place to place, for compensation or hire. All four must be present. Holding out is any signal to the public that you will carry all comers: advertising, a website, business cards, word of mouth, an agent, or simply a reputation for being available. Common carriage requires certification under Part 119 and operations under Part 135 or 121.

items.q: What is private carriage, and how does it differ from common carriage?
items.a: Private carriage is carriage for compensation or hire without holding out: the operator serves only one or a very few select customers under long-term contracts, usually accepted as no more than one to three, and does not offer service to the public at large. It still normally requires a Part 119 certificate and operations under Part 135, but it is not common carriage. The distinguishing element is holding out, not the number of passengers or the size of the airplane.

items.q: A salaried pilot flies his employer's aircraft carrying company staff on company business under Part 91. Why is that legal?
items.a: Because the flying is incidental to the company's business and there is no carriage for compensation or hire. The company is not in the transport business; it owns or leases the airplane, keeps operational control, and carries its own people on its own business, charging nobody for the ride. The pilot draws a salary as an employee, which 14 CFR 61.133 (Part 61, Subpart F, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations) permits, not a fee for transporting anyone. No holding out and no compensation for carriage means no common carriage and no Part 119 certificate.

items.q: What would push that corporate operation over the line into needing an air carrier certificate?
items.a: Anything that turns transportation itself into the product: charging the passengers or another company for the flight, carrying non-employees or third-party customers for a fee, carrying property for hire, or advertising the airplane's availability. Then all four elements of common carriage are met and Part 119 certification with Part 135 or 121 operations is required. 14 CFR 91.501 (Part 91, Subpart F, Applicability) allows a narrow set of cost-reimbursement, time-sharing and interchange arrangements, but only for large and turbojet airplanes.

items.q: When does a medical certificate expire?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 61.23 (Part 61, Subpart A, Medical certificates: Requirement and duration), all classes expire at the end of the last day of the month. A first class is good for first class privileges for 12 calendar months if you were under 40 at the exam, 6 if 40 or over; a second class, which commercial privileges require, is 12 calendar months at any age; a third class is 60 calendar months if under 40, 24 if 40 or over. A lapsed higher class does not vanish, it steps down to the lower class privileges for the remaining time.

items.q: What are the current BasicMed limits, and can you use BasicMed for commercial flying?
items.a: BasicMed covers aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 pounds or less carrying no more than 7 occupants, that is six passengers, flown below 18,000 feet MSL at no more than 250 knots indicated, and not for compensation or hire. It requires having held a medical after 14 July 2006, a physician exam on the checklist every 48 months and the online course every 24 calendar months. Because commercial operations need at least a second class medical, BasicMed cannot be used to exercise commercial privileges.

items.q: Going through the maintenance logs, what are you actually checking?
items.a: Three sets of records, for the airframe, engine and propeller. Confirm the last annual and, where required, the last 100-hour; the pitot-static, altimeter and transponder checks; the ELT inspection and battery date; the airworthiness directive compliance list with recurring ADs and their next due times; any Form 337 major repairs and alterations; the current weight and balance and equipment list; time in service and time since overhaul; and any open discrepancy that has not been signed off.

items.q: What inspections must be current for the flight you are about to make?
items.a: Remembered as AV1ATE: Airworthiness Directives as they come due; VOR check within 30 days for IFR; 100-hour if required; Annual within 12 calendar months; Transponder within 24 calendar months; ELT within 12 calendar months. For IFR add the altimeter and static system check within 24 calendar months. Which apply depends on the operation, but the annual and the ADs apply to every flight.

items.q: May a 100-hour inspection be overflown?
items.a: Only by up to 10 hours, and only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, under 14 CFR 91.409(b). The excess time must then be subtracted from the next 100 hours, so flying 6 hours over means the next inspection is due at 94. There is no equivalent allowance for the annual: on the first day of the thirteenth calendar month the aircraft is simply unairworthy until inspected.

items.q: What are the pitot-static, altimeter, transponder and VOR check requirements?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.411 (Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests), the static system, altimeter and altitude reporting equipment must have been tested within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR in controlled airspace. Under 14 CFR 91.413 (ATC transponder tests and inspections), the transponder must be tested within the preceding 24 calendar months for any use. Under 14 CFR 91.171 (VOR equipment check for IFR operations), IFR VOR navigation requires a check within the preceding 30 days.

items.q: What documents must be on board, and how long is the registration good for?
items.a: Remembered as ARROW: Airworthiness certificate, displayed and readable, valid as long as the aircraft is maintained; Registration certificate, now valid for 7 years and renewable; Radio station license, only for international flight; Operating limitations, meaning the AFM or POH with placards, markings and supplements; and Weight and balance data with the current equipment list. 14 CFR 91.203 (Part 91, Subpart C, Civil aircraft: Certifications required) requires the airworthiness and registration certificates aboard.

items.q: What must a maintenance record entry contain, and who may approve a return to service?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 43.9 (Part 43, Content, form, and disposition of maintenance records), the entry must give a description of the work, the date completed, the name of the person doing it, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving return to service. 14 CFR 43.7 (Persons authorized to approve aircraft for return to service) lists who may give that approval. 14 CFR 91.417 makes the owner or operator responsible for keeping the records.

items.q: What maintenance may a pilot legally perform?
items.a: A pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate may perform the preventive maintenance listed in Appendix A to Part 43 on an aircraft they own or operate, provided it is not operated under Part 121, 129 or 135, under 14 CFR 43.3(g) (Part 43, Persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations). The list includes changing engine oil, servicing tires and struts, replacing safety belts, bulbs and reflectors, cleaning and gapping spark plugs, and replacing batteries. Record and sign it under 43.9.

items.q: You find an item inoperative and the aircraft has no minimum equipment list. What does 91.213 require?
items.a: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d) (Part 91, Subpart C, Inoperative instruments and equipment), the item may be left inoperative only if it is not part of the VFR-day type certification requirements in the equipment list or kinds of operations list, not required by an airworthiness directive, not required by 91.205 for the kind of flight, and not required by any other rule. If it clears all four, it must be removed or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE, and a pilot or mechanic must determine the aircraft is safe to fly without it.

items.q: What if the inoperative item is required and you still need to move the airplane?
items.a: You apply for a special flight permit, often called a ferry permit, under 14 CFR 21.197 (Part 21, Subpart H, Special flight permits). It is issued by the FSDO or a designee for an aircraft that does not currently meet airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight, for purposes such as flying to a base where repairs will be made, delivering or exporting it, or evacuating it from danger. The permit carries conditions and limitations, such as day VFR only and no passengers.

items.q: What are the problems with the manufacturer's performance charts?
items.a: They were flown by a factory test pilot in a brand new airplane with a fresh engine, a clean, correctly rigged airframe, a level, dry, hard-surfaced runway, exact speeds and correct leaning, and some numbers were computed rather than actually flown. Nothing accounts for a worn engine, a dirty airframe or an average pilot. They are the best case, not a promise, so add a margin: a common standard is 50 percent on takeoff and landing distances.

items.q: How do you compute density altitude, and what changes it?
items.a: Set 29.92 to read pressure altitude, then correct for temperature: density altitude is roughly pressure altitude plus 120 feet for every degree Celsius that the outside air is above standard, where standard is 15 degrees at sea level falling 2 degrees per 1,000 feet. It is changed by field elevation, altimeter setting or ambient pressure, temperature, and humidity, with water vapor making air less dense because a water molecule is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it displaces.

items.q: How does a high density altitude affect the wing?
items.a: The wing needs a certain mass of air per second to make the lift that equals weight. In thin air it must move faster through it, so it flies at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed. That means a longer acceleration to lift-off and a higher groundspeed at rotation and at touchdown, so both takeoff and landing rolls stretch. The indicated stall speed does not change, but everything happens further down the runway and with less margin.

items.q: How does a high density altitude affect the engine and the propeller?
items.a: A normally aspirated engine makes power by burning a mass of air, so with fewer molecules per cubic foot it produces less power, roughly 3 percent less per 1,000 feet of density altitude, and it must be leaned to keep the mixture right. The propeller is a rotating aerofoil and suffers the same loss the wing does: at the same rpm it bites less air and produces less thrust. Wing, engine and propeller penalties all stack, which is why hot-and-high accidents are so common.

items.q: What are the effects of loading toward the forward CG limit?
items.a: More stable, less efficient. A forward CG needs more tail download to balance, so the wing must lift more than the airplane weighs: the stall speed rises, cruise speed falls for the same power, and the takeoff run lengthens. The airplane is very stable in pitch, resists stalling and recovers easily, but the elevator may run out of authority in the landing flare, giving a flat or nose-first arrival. Loaded ahead of the forward limit, you may not be able to round out at all.

items.q: How does runway surface affect takeoff performance?
items.a: Anything other than dry pavement adds rolling resistance and lengthens the ground roll. Short dry grass typically adds roughly 10 to 15 percent; long or wet grass considerably more; soft ground, sand, mud, slush or snow can easily double it or prevent takeoff entirely. An upslope adds distance, a downslope reduces it. Loose gravel also risks propeller damage. Use the POH correction if one is published, and if none is, apply a generous margin of your own.

items.q: How does runway surface affect landing performance?
items.a: Braking is what stops you, and braking depends on friction. Wet pavement, grass, and any loose or contaminated surface all reduce braking effectiveness and lengthen the landing roll; wet grass is particularly poor. Standing water or slush brings the risk of hydroplaning, where the tire rides on a film of water and steering and braking are lost until it slows. A downslope lengthens the landing roll and an upslope shortens it, the opposite of takeoff.

items.q: What is Va and how do you find it at a weight below gross?
items.a: Va is design maneuvering speed: the speed at which the wing stalls at exactly the limit load factor, so full abrupt deflection of one control in one direction cannot break the airplane. Below gross weight it goes down, in proportion to the square root of the weight ratio: multiply the POH value at gross by the square root of actual weight over maximum gross weight. At 80 percent of gross, that is the square root of 0.8, about 89 percent of the published speed.

items.q: What does normally aspirated mean?
items.a: The engine draws its induction air at ambient atmospheric pressure, with no turbocharger or supercharger to compress it. Manifold pressure can therefore never exceed the outside air pressure, and in practice is slightly less because of induction losses. Power falls with density altitude at roughly 3 percent per 1,000 feet, which sets a relatively low service ceiling and makes leaning and density altitude planning central to operating one.

items.q: What does direct drive mean?
items.a: The propeller is bolted straight to the crankshaft, with no reduction gearbox, so propeller rpm always equals engine rpm. It is simple, light and reliable, with nothing to fail between engine and propeller. The cost is that the engine is limited to whatever rpm keeps the propeller tips comfortably below the speed of sound, because supersonic tips produce noise, vibration and a sharp loss of efficiency, so power has to come from displacement rather than revolutions.

items.q: What happens if you climb to altitude without adjusting the mixture?
items.a: The mixture becomes progressively too rich. The metering system delivers roughly the same fuel to a steadily smaller mass of air, so the fuel-to-air ratio climbs. The result is a loss of power, rough running, wasted fuel, and lead and carbon fouling of the spark plugs, which shows up later as a rough magneto check. Lean in accordance with the POH, typically above about 3,000 feet density altitude or at cruise power settings below 75 percent.

items.q: What is detonation?
items.a: Detonation is the fuel-air charge in the cylinder exploding all at once instead of burning progressively away from the spark, after normal ignition has occurred. The pressure spike and shock wave hammer the piston and the cylinder head. It is caused by fuel of too low a grade, a mixture too lean at high power, high cylinder head temperatures, or a prolonged full-power climb at low airspeed. You will rarely hear it in flight; you will see high CHT, power loss and roughness.

items.q: What is pre-ignition, how does it differ from detonation, and what do you do about either?
items.a: Pre-ignition is the charge being lit before the spark plug fires, by an incandescent hot spot such as a glowing carbon deposit, a cracked plug insulator or an overheated valve, so the burn opposes the rising piston. Detonation happens after ignition, pre-ignition before it, and detonation often creates the hot spots that then cause pre-ignition. Either can destroy a cylinder in minutes. The response for both is the same: enrich the mixture, reduce power, open cowl flaps, lower the nose for cooling airflow, and land.

items.q: How does a magneto get its power?
items.a: It makes its own. A magneto is a self-contained, engine-driven generator: a rotating permanent magnet induces current in a primary coil, the breaker points then open and the collapsing magnetic field induces a very high voltage in the secondary winding, which the distributor sends to the correct spark plug; the condenser stops the points arcing. It needs nothing from the battery or the alternator, which is why the engine keeps running after a total electrical failure, and why a propeller must always be treated as live.

items.q: What is the benefit of two spark plugs in each cylinder?
items.a: Redundancy and better combustion. Two independent ignition systems mean the failure of one magneto, one lead or one plug does not stop the engine. Two flame fronts starting from opposite sides of the combustion chamber also meet in the middle, so the charge burns faster and more completely, giving roughly 10 percent more power, better fuel economy and smoother running. That is exactly why switching to a single magneto produces a small, expected rpm drop.

items.q: During the magneto check you get an unusually large rpm drop. What is happening and what do you do?
items.a: Compare it with the POH figures, commonly a maximum drop of about 125 to 175 rpm and a maximum difference between magnetos of about 50. An excessive drop with roughness is most often a fouled spark plug from lead deposits after prolonged rich ground running. The fix is to lean the mixture and run the engine at higher power, around 2,000 rpm per the POH, for 15 to 30 seconds to burn the deposits off, then re-check. If it does not clear, taxi back; a failed lead, plug or magneto timing is a maintenance item.

items.q: What if there is no rpm drop at all when you select one magneto?
items.a: Suspect a broken or disconnected P-lead, the wire through which the ignition switch grounds the magneto. If the magneto cannot be grounded it is hot: it will keep firing with the switch off, and the engine can start if anybody moves the propeller. Confirm it with the brief grounding check at idle called for in the POH, shut down with the mixture, treat the propeller as live, and have maintenance correct it before the next flight.

items.q: What grade of fuel does the airplane use, and how do you confirm it?
items.a: Use the grade on the filler placard and in the POH, never a lower grade, because low-octane fuel invites detonation. In common use, 100LL is blue, grade 100 is green, the old grade 80 was red, and unleaded replacements such as UL94 or G100UL are approved by supplemental type certificate for specific aircraft. Jet A is clear or straw and smells of kerosene; if a sample looks or smells wrong, or is cloudy, assume misfueling and do not fly.

items.q: If you found water in a fuel sample, where would it sit in the jar and why?
items.a: At the bottom, below the fuel. Water weighs about 8.35 pounds per gallon against roughly 6 for avgas, so it is denser and sinks, showing as a clear globule or a distinct line with the dyed fuel above it. That is why the sumps and drains sit at the lowest points of the system. It arrives mostly by condensation in partly empty tanks, so top off after the last flight; keep draining and re-sampling until every sample is clean, clear and the right color.

items.q: What is the difference between de-icing and anti-icing, and what does a typical training airplane have?
items.a: Anti-ice prevents ice from forming and must be on before you enter the conditions: pitot heat, heated stall warning vane, heated fuel vents, windshield heat or alcohol, propeller alcohol or electric boots. De-ice removes ice that has already formed: inflatable pneumatic boots, cycling propeller boots. Most training singles have only pitot heat, an alternate static source and carburettor heat or alternate air, and are placarded against flight into known icing. Check the POH or AFM for the airplane flown.

items.q: When would you turn on pitot heat?
items.a: Before you need it, not after the airspeed starts misbehaving: any time you are entering or expect visible moisture with the temperature near or below freezing, before entering cloud or instrument conditions, in precipitation, at night in cloud, and any time icing is possible. Many POHs simply say to use it in instrument conditions or in visible moisture below about 10 degrees Celsius. Check it during preflight, remember it draws a heavy current, and do not touch the tube afterwards.

items.q: The three stages of a stall. Go.
items.a: Approaching the stall, the full stall, and the recovery. Approaching: angle of attack nearing critical, horn and buffet, mushy controls, high sink rate, wing still flying. Full: critical angle of attack exceeded, airflow separated, lift falling away and the nose dropping. Recovery: reduce angle of attack first, level the wings, add power, return to the flight path without a secondary stall. This is the question the last candidate missed.

items.q: You hit a runway light. Do you have to report it, and where does the rule live?
items.a: The rule is 49 CFR Part 830, an NTSB rule, not a Federal Aviation Regulation. Test it: nobody was killed or seriously injured, and damage to gear, wheels, tires, flaps or wingtips is expressly excluded from substantial damage, so on those facts it is an incident and no report is required. It becomes reportable if the airplane takes substantial damage, or if damage to the light and its cabling exceeds $25,000 under 830.5.

items.q: Which items in 830.5 will never apply to your Warrior?
items.a: The ones written for transport aircraft: in-flight failure of electrical or hydraulic systems, and sustained loss of thrust from two or more engines, which apply only to large multiengine aircraft of more than 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight; an evacuation using an emergency egress system; ACAS resolution advisories on an IFR flight plan; helicopter rotor blade damage; and the air carrier wrong-runway and runway incursion items.

items.q: Is a flap position light required? Show me the whole chain of reasoning.
items.a: There is no MEL, so I start at 14 CFR 91.205 for day VFR and run the list: it requires a landing gear position indicator on a retractable and says nothing about flaps. Then the kinds of operation equipment list in Section 2, which does not list one; then the airplane's equipment list; then any airworthiness directive or STC supplement. Nothing requires it, so it is not required equipment, and if it were fitted and inoperative I would work 91.213(d).

items.q: A non-pilot customer hires you to fly his airplane, then rents one when his is grounded. Talk me through both halves.
items.a: First half: he supplies the airplane and keeps operational control, I supply pilot services only, so it is Part 91 and my commercial certificate covers it. Second half turns on the same question. If he rents in his own name and still decides the flight, nothing changes. If I rent the airplane and then carry him for compensation, I am supplying aircraft and crew for hire and that needs a Part 119 certificate. If it is unclear, I decline or call the FSDO.

items.q: What documents must the pilot have to fly? Be careful with this one.
items.a: Pilot certificate, an appropriate medical certificate or BasicMed documentation, and government-issued photo identification, per 14 CFR 61.3. The Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit is an FCC document required only for international operations and does not belong on this list. Say it that way and you have turned the standard trap into a point in your favor; volunteer the permit only when the question turns to flying outside the country.

items.q: Your handbook has no kinds of operation equipment list. Now what?
items.a: Then the airplane is one of the many certificated before the GAMA format made the list standard, and I say so rather than inventing one. Required equipment then comes from 14 CFR 91.205 and whatever other operating rule applies to the flight, the airplane's own equipment list, the type certificate data sheet, and any airworthiness directive or STC supplement. For an inoperative item, 91.213(d) is the path, with a placard and a hazard determination.

items.q: Simulated engine fire. Memory items and then what?
items.a: Fuel selector OFF, throttle closed, mixture idle cut-off, electric fuel pump checked OFF, heater OFF, defroster OFF, then the power-off landing procedure. Descend fast, up to but not exceeding VNE, 160 KIAS, because an airframe fire is measured in minutes. Declare with mayday on the frequency or 121.5, squawk 7700, give souls and fuel, brief the passengers once established, and check the ELT after landing.

items.q: The CG is inside the envelope but close to the forward limit. What do you do about it?
items.a: Move weight aft or add it aft, and show the arithmetic. The baggage compartment arm is 142.8 inches, far behind the rear seats at 118.1 and the aft limit at 93.0, so it is the strongest lever: at 2,000 pounds, 17 pounds of baggage moves the CG half an inch aft. Then recheck gross weight against 2,325 pounds, the 200-pound baggage placard, the aft limit, and the landing case, because burning fuel here moves the CG forward.

items.q: Time, fuel and distance to climb. How do you get the number?
items.a: By subtraction, not by one lookup. Enter the chart at the departure field's pressure altitude and temperature, read time, fuel and distance; enter again at cruise altitude and temperature; subtract the first set from the second. Add the start, taxi and run-up allowance, and convert the chart's still air distance into ground distance using the climb groundspeed. Higher temperature and higher altitude increase all three numbers.

items.q: What are the two types of stress and how do they show up in a pilot?
items.a: Acute and chronic. Acute is the short-term response to a present demand, such as a warning light or a runway change, and it narrows attention and causes fixation; chronic is the continuing, unresolved load of money, a job or a family problem, and it shows up as fatigue, poor decisions and indifference to risk. Chronic stress consumes the reserve you need for the acute events of a flight, so the two stack. Both are the S in IMSAFE.
